Learned counsel has then drawn our attention to the proceedings of Thirteenth Meeting of the Board of Governors held on 12.3.2004, wherein, reference has been made to the recommendations of the Sub-committee and that the amendment was approved by deciding to amend regulation 17(a). He has also drawn our attention to the letter of the Director Colleges dated 6.8.2001 and the deliberation thereon by the Board of Governors. According to the learned counsel, however, amendment was not made retrospectively and was applicable from 12.3.2004.  9. On the basis of the aforementioned submissions, learned counsel has argued that no regulation which may have force of law has been enacted by the University on 31.7.2001 when the applicants were to be promoted to the Vth semester. The recommendations were made by the Sub-committee of Principals dated 15.7.2001 on the basis of delegated power given by the Academic Council on 6.4.2001, it cannot be concluded that an enforceable regulation came into force as the proposed amendment was only at a draft stage. The Academic Council has approved it on 22.4.2003 in its Eleventh Meeting and the Board of Governors could approve it only on 12.5.2004. On the basis of the aforementioned submission, learned counsel has argued that order dated 23.5.2002 passed by the Division Bench purportedly relying on rules as amended on 30.5.2000 in para 1 of the order is liable to be reviewed as it is an error apparent on the face of the record. He has placed reliance of Order 47, Rule 1 and Section 114 of the Code and argued that this Court on the discovery of new and important evidence which after the exercise of due diligence was not within the knowledge of the applicant-petitioners at that time, when the order was passed, could always review its order especially when students' career is at stake. Learned counsel has also referred to the omnibus principle of ensuring advancement of justice especially in deciding the petitions filed under Article 226 of the Constitution. In support of this submission learned counsel has placed reliance on a judgment of the Supreme Court in case of S. Nagaraj v. State of Karnataka, 1994(1) SCT 99 (SC) : 1993(5) SLR 1.  10. Mr. Atul Nehra, learned counsel for the non-applicant respondent No. 1 has argued that applicants are not entitled to grant of any relief as they have not approached this Court with clean hands. According to learned counsel, the petitioners were fully aware about the existence of the amended regulations, because they were permitted to be registered for IIIrd and IVth semesters even though they had failed to earn 24 credits in their Ist year, which was required as per the earlier regulations applicable to them. It has further claimed that once they are aware of item No. 7.36 of the Seventh Meeting of Academic Council, it cannot be claimed that they were oblivious of item No. 7.36 of the same Meeting, because the proceedings of Seventh Academic Council Meeting were circulated to all the concerned colleges on 25.8.2000. Learned counsel has further elaborated the question of concealment by referring to order Annexure P-3 dated 30.11.2000 by arguing that the aforementioned letter had been withdrawn as it was applicable to some other courses. In any case, it was later on clarified on 27.3.2001 (R-1/1) that this letter was applicable to BBA/BCA students who were to appear in Vth semester in December, 2000. Learned counsel has claimed that Academic Council approved the proposed amendment in Sixth Meeting held on 6.4.2001. By referring to Section 10(5) & (8) that the Vice Chancellor is the conscious keeper (conscience keeper ?) of the University and is entitled to exercise general control over its affairs, in accordance with the regulations learned counsel has maintained that when there is an emergency then immediate action was required to be taken, and that the Vice Chancellor is fully clothed with powers by sub-section (8) of Section 10 to pass any order. Learned counsel has pointed out that merely because the recommendations made by the Sub-committee were ratified subsequently on 6.4.2001/ 23.9.2002 by the Academic Council or the recommendations of the Academic Council were approved by the Board of Governors on 12.3.2004 would not make any significant difference because such a ratification would have the effect of relating back as has been held by the Supreme Court in the case of Punjab University v. V.N. Tripathi and another, 2001(4) SCT 333 (SC) : JT 2001(7) SC 96. He has placed reliance on another judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Marathwada University v. Sesh Rao Balwant Rao Chauhan, JT 1989(2) SC 276. Learned counsel has argued that review of an order is an extraordinary remedy and can only be permitted in case of error apparent on the face of record and not by going into the pleothra of evidence which require reappreciation. According to the learned counsel in the present case for review of the order dated 23.5.2002 a large number of papers by summoning the Registrar of the University are required to be gone into which in fact is not the real scope of the review. In support of his submission learned counsel has placed reliance on a judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aribam Piskak Sharma, AIR 1979 SC 1047 and Smt. Meera Bhanja v. Smt. Nirmala Kumari Choudhary, 1995(2) R.R.R. 440 : AIR 1995 SC 455 and argued that once the finding has been recorded by this Court in its order dated 23.5.2002 dismissing the writ petition i.e. rules did not permit promotion of the applicants to Vth Semester on account of the fact that they had remained unable to clear the Ist semester examination, no review is entertainable and the application is liable to be dismissed. Learned counsel has maintained that the scope of review cannot be expanded because the impugned order can only be challenged by way of Special Leave Petition before the Supreme Court.  11. Having heard the learned counsel on various dates at a great length, we have reached the conclusion that the instant application deserves to be allowed and order dated 23.5.2002 passed by the Division Bench is liable to be reviewed. There is an error apparent on the face of record which has crept in while passing order dated 23.5.2002 inasmuch as it was presumed and accepted that the rules/regulations governing the course and applicable to academic year 1999-2000 were amended on 30.5.2000. It is evident from various documents placed on record collectively as Annexure R-1/4 that there was no amendment effected in the rules on 30.5.2000. A persual of the minutes of the Seventh Meeting of the Academic Council would show that the meeting was held on 30.5.2000 and vide item No. 7.3(b), the rules was sought to be changed by introducing Ist semester to Vth semester and 2nd semester to 6th semester for the students of 1999-2000 batch. However, the views of the Sub-committee as to whether the amended rule was applicable to 1998 batch were solicited. Item No. 7.3(b)/Item No. 3(b) read as under :-  "7.3(b)/Item No. 3(b) : - Change in 24 & 25 Credit Rules. It was decided that 24 & 25 credit rule will be changed with immediate effect for 1999 batch and onwards. Thus a student must clear Ist semester before he/she can be registered for 5th semester, and must clear 2nd semester before registering for 6th semester and so on. However, for 1998 batch, the Sub- committee formed under agenda item No. 2 will discuss the issue and submit a recommendation as to whether the same decision be applied to 1998 batch also or not. In this regard all the colleges were requested to send a status report on the expelled students from 1998 batch to the University." The Sub-committee which made these recommendations was comprised of :-  "(a) Sh. N.S. Rattan, IAS, Vice Chancellor, PTU. (b) Dr. Naresh Kumar Gupta, Advisor (Academic & Planning). (c) Dr. Ashwani Kumar, Principal, AIE&T, Faridkot - respondent No. 2. (d) Dr. G.S. Walia, Mata Gujri Institute of Management, Fatehgarh Sahib. (e) Dr. D.S. Kumar, Principal, SUS CET Mohali, (f) Dr. Gurdeep Singh." The aforementioned item clearly shows that the Academic Council had desired to enforce the rules for 1999-2000 batch immediately, whereas no approval of the Board of Governors in terms of Section 14(8) read with Section 18 of the University Act was taken. However, a perusal of item No. 8.3 from the proceedings of the Eighth Meeting of the Board of Governors held on 14.2.20002 shows that decision of the Seventh Meeting of the Academic Council held on 30.5.2000 was approved by the Board on that date. Item No. 8.3 approving the decisions taken by the Academic Council in its Seventh Meeting reads as under :-  "Item No. 8.3 : To consider & approve the proceedings of the 7th meeting of the Academic Council held on May 30, 2000. The Board approved the decisions taken at 7th meeting of the Academic Council held on May 30, 2000. The Board, however, desired that the decisions of the Academic Council involving the financial implications may be placed before the Finance Committee at its next meeting." It is, thus, evident that the Board of Governors approved the amendment on 14.2.2004.  13. The law making process of the University is regulated by various provisions of the University Act. A persual of Section 18 makes it evident that first set of regulations of the University were to be published by the State Government by notifying the same in the Official Gazette. The Board of Governors has been empowered to make new or additional regulations or it may amend or repeal the regulations. The Board of Governors has also been given the power to disallow or remit the regulations under Section 19 of the University Act. The regulation may provide for all or any of the matters including the admission of students to the University and their enrolment as such. Sections 18 and 19(h) are reproduced hereunder for facility of reference :-  "18. Making amendment, repeal and operations of Regulations. - (1) The first Regulations of the University shall be made by the State Government and notified in the official Gazette. (2) The Board of Governors may, from time to time make new or additional Regulations or may amend or repeal the Regulations : Provided that the Board of Governors shall not propose the draft of amendment of the regulations affecting the status, powers or constitution of any existing authority of the University until such authority has been given an opportunity of expressing an opinion upon the proposal and any opinion so expressed shall be in writing and shall be considered by the Board of Governors. (3) Every new Regulations or addition to the Regulations or any amendment or repeal of a Regulation shall require the approval of the Board of Governors who may approve, disallow or remit it for further consideration. ............. 19. Regulations. - (a) to (g) xx xx xx (h) the admission of students of the University and their enrolment as such." 14. It is further pertinent to mention that under Section 14(8) of the University Act, it is proved (provided ?) that the Board of Governors is the supreme authority of the University which enjoys the powers and duties to frame and approve the rules of the University. Section 14(8)(d) of the University Act reads as under :-  "14. Board of Governors - (1) to (7) xx xx xx xx xx xx xx (8) (a) to (c) xx xx xx (d) to frame and approve rules and regulations of the University." 15. A further perusal of the provisions of Section 15 would show that Academic Council has been constituted to be the academic body of the University and is ordained to act subject to the provisions of the University Act and Regulations. It is entitled to advise the Board of Governors on all academic matters. Section 15(1) of the Act reads as under :-  "15. Academic Council. - (1) The Academic Council shall be Academic Body of the University and shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and Regulations, have control and general regulation and be responsible for the maintenance of standards of instruction, education and examination within the University and shall exercise such other powers and perform such other duties as may be conferred or imposed upon it by the Regulations. It shall have the right to advise the Board of Governors on all academic matters." It is, thus, evident that the amendment suggested on 30.5.2000 by the Academic Council in its meeting was not complete in its effect and in the absence of any approval by the Board of Governors, it would be deemed to be a still born regulation which was at embryo stage. Such an amendment cannot be considered to be enforceable nor it would have any force of law. Therefore, no reliance on the aforementioned amendment could be placed.  16. However, learned counsel for the University has insisted that credit system of 24/25 credit continues to exist. On the contrary, the applicant- petitioners have claimed that the regulation providing for credit system was amended and the credit system was abandoned. Regulation 16 as mentioned of the Regulations for B. Tech. and B. Arch. courses reads as under :-  "16. (a) A student will not be allowed to register for the third semester and shall be required to repeat first year if (i) he/she fails to earn a minimum of 24 credits out of the total credits offered in the approved scheme of courses for the first year. However, while repeating first year he/she will not be allowed to repeat courses in which the marks earned are more then 40 per cent in the earlier attempt. (b) If a student after repeating first year under 16(a) fails to earn a minimum of 45 credits till the end of second year, he/she shall be required to leave the institute/college and his/her enrolment shall stand cancelled. (c) A total of 6 years from the date of admission, shall be given to a candidate to pass all the courses and to fulfil all the requirements for the completion of degree of Bachelor of Technology and 7 years for the course of Bachelor of Arch. Provided further that maximum period for qualifying for the award of degree will be seven years and eight years for engineering and architecture students respectively, for those who are required to repeat their first year under clause 16(a)." However, the aforementioned regulation was amended by the Academic Council in its Seventh Meeting as per item No. 70.6 for the academic year 1998-99 and the same reads as under :-  "7.36/Item No. A-2.24 : Credits cases for Academic Year 1998-99. The Academic Council approved the discontinuation of the 24/25 credit rules but on the recommendations of the Sub-committee in this regard decided that no new conditions will be imposed on 1998 batch students." The aforementioned regulation as amended has not been applied to the candidates of 1998-99. In other words, the system of 24/25 credit rules provided in the unamended regulation was done away with. The aforementioned regulation as amended has not been subject-matter of challenge before us and the averments made by the applicant-petitioners in paragraphs 3 and 4 of the writ petition asserting that the carry forward system has been followed for 1998 batch and the subsequent batches except 1999-2000 batch. The assertions made by the applicant-petitioners have been accepted by the University in its reply.  17. It is further pertinent to make a reference to the affidavit filed by Ganganmeet Bains on 25.8.2004 (C.M. Nos. 15236-37 of 2004). A perusal of the affidavit would reveal that carry forward rule was not applied to Shri Manav Ahluwalia, a student from GTB Institute of Engineering and Technology, Malout, Ramandeep Singh, Inderjit Singh and Harmeet Singh Kochhar. Similarly, four instances of the students of Shaheed Udham Singh College of Engg. & Technology, Tangori (Mohali) have been quoted i.e. Manish Birdi, Ramandeep Singh, Amit Garcha and Puneet Bains. The facts narrated in the aforementioned affidavit have not been controverted. It is, thus, evident that 24 credit rule was dispensed with for the students of B.Tech. course of 1998-99 batch. The aforementioned rule continued to apply to the batch of 1999-2000 i.e. the applicant-petitioners.  18. In view of the above, it is clear that Ist to Vth or IInd to VIth semester rule or 24/45 credit rule were not applicable. Therefore, it is abundantly clear that the argument raised by learned counsel for the University is erroneous and cannot be accepted.  19. Another argument raised by Mr. Atul Nehra, learned counsel for the University is based on the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Marathwada University (supra). The view taken by the Supreme Court in the aforementioned judgment is that Vice Chancellor in an emergent situation could always take a decision and implement the same because the Vice Chancellor is a conscious keeper (conscience keeper ?) of the University. However, in the instant case, there is no emergency either pleaded or revealed necessitating the application of Ist to Vth and IInd to VIth semester rule to the batch of applicant-petitioners for the year 1999. There is no decision of the Vice Chancellor taking the view that there was an emergency and the decision was required to be implemented even in the absence of approval by the Board of Governors as required by Section 14(8)(d) of the University Act. The proceedings of various meetings of the Board of Governors also do not refer to any such decision of the Vice Chancellor, Therefore, to apply the amended regulation retrospectively would not be justifiable on that ground. Thus, the argument is without any merit and we have no hesitation to reject the same.  For the reasons stated above, the review application and the writ petition are allowed. All the interim orders are made absolute. The applicant-petitioners shall be entitled to all the consequential benefits viz. issuancee of certificate/degree etc. wherever applicable. The University is directed to declare the result of the applicant-petitioners.  Petition allowed.
summary: The Examination Rules of B.Tech. as amended on May 30th, 2000, in conjunction with the Punjab Technical University Act of 1996, specifically Sections 14(8), 18(3) and 19, are applicable to students of the AIET from the 1999-2000 academic year. However, any decision made by the Academic Council without Board of Governors approval or notification under the aforementioned Act or any decision made by the Vice Chancellor, unless deemed an emergency that warranted immediate implementation, is not enforceable. Furthermore, on February 14th, 2004, the Board of Governors approved the amendment without retroactive effect. The Academic Council's decision to mandate that students earn a minimum of 24 credits from the first-year scheme of courses cannot be applied to the 1999-2000 batch. [Paras 12 to 19]

text: A.L. Bahri and N.K. Kapoor, JJ. - In spite of notice of motion having been issued and two adjournments sought on behalf of the State, no written statement has been filed. Otherwise, on going through the writ petition and the documents accompanying thereto, we are of the view that the present case is fully covered by several decisions of this Court, already made. The question involved in the present case is with respect to grant of selection grade to the employees (petitioners-teachers), taking into consideration the total strength of the cadre, permanent as well as temporary. This question was decided by Division Bench of this Court in Letters Patents Appeal No. 135 of 1986 (State of Punjab v. Hira Lal and others), decided on January 15, 1990. Special Leave Petition filed against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court. Thereafter the Division Bench again grated similar relief in Civil Writ Petition No. 16880 of 1991 (Bhan Chand v. State of Punjab and others) decided on April 2, 1992, copy of judgment Annexure P-4. The District Education Officer Sangrur, vide his letter dated November 27, 1992, (Annexure P-6), declined to grant relief to one of the teachers, namely Dharamvir, on the ground that there were no instructions to grant selection grade to the non-petitioners indicating that only such persons who had filed writ petitions were to be granted selection grade as per decision made.  2. After hearing counsel for the parties, we are of the view that such like petitions should be treated as "Public Interest Litigation" and when directions have been given, which are general in nature i.e.to treat the cadre strength clubbed together of permanent and temporary for the purposes of consideration for grant of selection grades, they were to be implemented in general for all the employees in the State. It was highly arbitrary on the part of the District Education Officer, Sangrur, to say that such like relief could not be granted to other employees, who did not approach this Court. The State should not have compelled its employees to indulge in litigation, unnecessarily.  For the reasons recorded above, this petition is allowed with directions to the respondents to consider the case of the petitioners for grant of selection grade clubbing the cadre of temporary and permanent posts. The petitioners would be paid arrears of pay for the period of three years and two months prior to the filing of the writ petition. They would also get costs, which are quantified at Rs. 1,000/-. Let these directions be complied within a period of three months.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 226 - Selection grade - Claim of selection grade identifying the posts of clubbing the regular and temporary posts - Previous decisions in different petitions must be applied to all - Consider petition as public litigation - It is arbitrary to grant relief only to those who filed writ petitions - Respondents ordered to grant selection grade to all, with arrears of 38 months in the cadre of both temporary and permanent posts. [Para 2]

text: M.H.S. Ansari, J. - The petitioner has in the instant writ application questioned the panel prepared by the Selection Committee constituted for the purpose of recruitment of an Assistant Teacher in Science Group in Kaliaganj Milanmayee Girls High School whereby the petitioner was placed in the second position.  2. The grievance of the petitioner is that the private respondent No. 5 (Smt. Paramita Adhikary) has been illegally awarded marks for B.Ed. Qualification despite the fact that the Employment Exchange while sponsoring her name had not specified the said qualification of B.Ed.  3. The qualifications possessed by the petitioner are Madhyamik Parikshya conducted by the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education, petitioner obtained first division securing 66.22% marks. In Higher Secondary Examination conducted by West Bengal Council of Higher Secondary Education in second division securing 54.2%. Bachelor of Science (B.Sc.) in Botany (Hons.) from University of North Bengal. Master of Science in Botany from the University of Kalyani in First Class obtaining 67.5% marks and B.Ed. Examination from the University of North Bengal in First Class securing 69.5% marks.  4. Private respondent No. 5 in the affidavit-in-opposition stated that her qualifications are Secondary Examination from West Bengal of Secondary Education in First Division, Higher Secondary Examination in Second Division in Science Stream from the West Bengal; Council of Higher Education. Bachelor of Science (Hons.) in Second Class in Botany from the University of North Bengal; Master of Science (M.Sc.) in Botany in First Class from the University of Kalyani having secured more than 68% of marks. B.Ed. examination in 1993 placed in First Division having secured more than 70% of marks.  5. It is not in dispute that the names of the petitioner as also the private respondent No. 5 were sponsored by the Employment Exchange for the post in question.  6. It is the case of the private respondent that the petitioner as also private respondent No. 5 appeared for the B.Ed. Examination from the same University, results whereof were published in the first week of January, 1994. This is sought to be demonstrated from the mark sheets submitted with the writ application and the affidavit-in-opposition.  7. Private respondent No. 5 applied for registration of the B.Ed. Qualification to the National Employment Exchange through the Local Employment Exchange. The District Employment Exchange Officer by his Memo dated 10th March, 1994 intimated the same to the Employment Officer P.E. Section (Annexure `P' to the affidavit-in-opposition).  The interview was held on 24th April, 1994.  8. The panel prepared by the Selection Committee was duly approved by the Managing Committee and forwarded to the District Inspector of Schools concerned whereupon a query was raised relating to awarding of marks of B.Ed. Examination to private respondent No. 5 and in reply thereto, the Secretary of the Managing Committee informed the District Inspector of Schools that by a subsequent corrigendum dated 24th March, 1994, District Employment Officer intimated the Secretary of the Managing Committee that the private respondent has duly registered her name of B.Ed. Qualification and as such, marks have been awarded for B.Ed. Examination to the said private respondent No. 5.  9. From the facts as above, it will be apparent that both the petitioner as also the private respondent No. 5 fulfilled the eligibility criteria prescribed for the post in question. As a matter of fact both the candidates have similar qualifications.  10. The only controversy in the instant writ application is thus with regard to awarding of marks for B.Ed. to the private respondent No. 5. If the same are excluded from consideration, then the petitioner would be entitled to be placed at Sr. No. 1 of the panel.  11. It is the contention of Mr. Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharjee, learned Sr. Advocate for the petitioner that in accordance with the Recruitment Rules, no credit can be given for the B.Ed. Qualification said to have been possessed by the private respondent No. 5, inasmuch as, the said qualification had not been stated by the employment exchange while sponsoring the names of eligible candidates. Reliance has been placed upon Rule 6A of the Recruitment Rules to buttress the said contention.  12. On the other hand, Mr. R.L. Maitra, learned counsel appearing for the respondent No. 5 submitted that the marks for B.Ed. Qualification cannot be denied to respondent No. 5 on any valid or tenable grounds. The petitioner as also the respondent No. 5 passed the B.Ed. Examination from the same University in the same year. Referring to Annexure `C' to application being CAN 5595 of 1994 (at page 28) and Annexure `B' (at page 30) of the writ application, it is demonstrated that both the candidates i.e. petitioner as also the respondent No. 5 appeared and passed the B.Ed. Examination from the North Bengal University held in 1993. The mark sheets established the said position.  13. The further submission of Mr. R.L. Maitra is that the private respondent had applied on 19th January, 1994 after the results of the B.Ed. Examination were published to the National Employment Exchange through the Local Employment Exchange for incorporating the B.Ed. Qualification. By Annexure `P' dated 10th March, 1994 the District Employment officer intimated the same to the Employment Officer (P & E), 11, Camac Street, Calcutta. Thereafter, by a memo dated 24th March, 1994, the Employment Officer-in-charge, District Employment Exchange, Raiganj informed the Secretary of the Managing Committee that the respondent No. 5 had registered her name for B.Ed. Qualification in the P & E. Cell and request was made for taking necessary action.  14. Mr. Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharjee, learned Sr. Advocate for the petitioner, however, relied upon the pleadings in the affidavit-in-opposition to submit that the respondent No. 5 applied for registration on 10th March, 1994 which is after the date of the names having been sponsored by the employment exchange.  15. A factual dispute is thus sought to be raised with respect to the date when the application was made by private respondent No. 5 for incorporating with the employment exchange, the acquisition of the qualification of B.Ed. by private respondent No. 5.  16. The undisputed fact, however, is that the private respondent No. 5 obtained the B.Ed. qualification at the same time as the petitioner and that action was taken for incorporating the said qualification with the employment exchange. 19th January, 1994 is said to be the date when the application was made by the respondent No. 5 as per the oral submission made by the learned counsel Mr. Maitra whereas in the affidavit-in-opposition the date of such request was made for incorporation is stated to be 10th March, 1994. The further fact is that by the memo dated 20.3.94 (Annexure `P' to the affidavit-in-opposition), the District Employment Officer intimated the Employment Officer (P & E) with respect to the said B.Ed. qualification obtained by respondent No. 5 and for incorporation thereof in the employment exchange. The employment exchange intimated the school authorities by a letter dated 24.3.1994. When the candidates were called upon to appear along with all original mark-sheets of all examinations, xerox copies thereof as also with other testimonials. Based thereon, the Selection Committee prepared panel wherein the respondent No. 5 was placed at serial No. 1 and the petitioner at serial No. 2.  17. In the affidavit-in-reply certain additional facts have been stated namely that the District Inspector of Schools (SE) on 3.8.1994 informed the Director of School Education that he is not in a position to approve the panel as the respondent No. 5 has been awarded marks for B.Ed. although the same was not mentioned when the names were sponsored by the employment exchange. The Deputy Director of School Education is said to have taken the view that the respondent No. 5 has "no eligibility of having marks awarded on B.Ed. as the training qualification has not been mentioned by the employment exchange."  18. The only question, therefore, for consideration is whether the respondent No. 5 is not entitled to the awarding of marks for the B.Ed. Qualification possessed by her.  19. This aspect of the matter has been considered by the Division Bench of this Court in Pintu Achariya v. State of West Bengal & Ors., reported in 1997(2) C.L.J. 428. In that case, similar question arose for consideration viz., whether the B.Ed. Qualification of the writ petitioner in that case could have been taken into consideration by the Selection Committee. In paragraph 16 facts have been noted of that case which are to the effect that the employment exchange sponsored the name of the writ petitioner in that case having merely a B.Sc. (Hons.) qualification. The qualification of B.Ed. although could have been recorded in the local employment exchange was not so recorded nor the said qualification could have been sent as employment exchange admittedly sponsored the names of the candidates much prior to the writ petitioner's acquisition of the said qualification.  20. In that factual matrix, the Division Bench held that in terms of 1993 Recruitment Rules which govern the recruitment process only the qualification recommended by the employment exchange can be taken into consideration.  21. Another Division Bench, in a later judgment in Sankar Das v. Arup Kumar, 1991(1) C.L.J. 11, construed the provision of Rule 6A of 1993 Rules and the synopsis of instruction on employment exchange procedure issued in 1998 by the Government of West Bengal (Directorate of Employemnt) which lay down detailed procedure for ensuring that candidates obtaining additional qualifications but originally registered in the local employment exchanges and they can informed about their additional qualification to the employment exchange concerned who shall after verifying the relevant documents send information to P. & E. Office for registration. The said communication has been extracted in the said judgment. The Division Bench in paragraph `9' of the said judgment held as under :  "Undoubtedly Rule 6A (supra) of the Recruitment Rules issued on 20th May, 1993 does lay down that no credit shall be given to a candidate in respect of the qualification which has either not been mentioned by the D.I.S. in the prior permission communication or by the Employment Exchange in the sponsoring communication. We are also quite clear that Rule 6A is required to be followed. However, when this Rule refers to the expression "mentioned by the Employment Exchange", such "mentioning" relates to an act validly and properly done by the Employment Exchange. If the Employment Exchange is seized of an information with regard to a candidate being possessed of a particular qualification and yet does not mention the same in the sponsoring communication, this cannot be called a valid or proper "mentioning" by the Employment Exchange and merely because by such improper or invalid "mentioning" the qualification of the candidate has been omitted, he cannot be deprived of the credit in respect thereto. Similarly, therefore, if the candidate has done all that was required of him to be done and, for no fault of his, the Employment Exchange concerned because of some Systems Failure, or otherwise does not mention the qualification, this cannot be construed to be of any disadvantage of the candidate concerned and the candidate cannot be deprived of the credit in respect of such qualification, if he is otherwise possessed of the same as on, or before the cut-off date and had taken all due steps to inform the Employment Exchange concerned regarding his having obtained such qualifications." Then Division Bench also considered the rights guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution and in relation to Rule 6A of the Recruitment Rules, the Division Bench in paragraph `10' of the said report held as under :  "Article 14 of the Constitution guarantees equality of opportunity. No one can be denied the equality of opportunity. If therefore the appellant and respondent No. 1 are similarly situated, it was not permissible to the authorities to treat the appellant differently and to deprive him of the advantage which had accrued to him, along with respondent No. 1, in the matter of getting credit of B.Ed. qualification. It appears to us clearly that the authority by practicing hostile discrimination against the appellant have accorded undue benefits and illegitimate favour of respondent No. 1 and the merit obtained by the appellant, by such unconstitutional act of the respondents has been converted into demerit. The D.I.S. committed a patent illegality by ordering the recasting of the panel. It appears that by placing on illogical and absurd interpretation upon Rule 6A and by improper application of this Rule to the facts of the present case, D.I.S. in utter disregard to established norms and principles illegally deprived the appellant of the benefit which had stood accrued in his favour on account of his having acquired the qualification of B.Ed. We can even go to the extent of saying that even independent of Rule 6A, on the reasoning and logic of common law and common sense, if a person has acquired a qualification before the cut-off date and if such qualification is to be counted for the purposes of either determining the eligibility or giving credit to the candidate, and the selection panel is convinced of the authenticity of the information regarding the qualification, the candidate concerned cannot be deprived of the benefits flowing therefrom. No rule can take away such benefit from the candidate. Rule 6A also undoubtedly does not attempt to take away any such benefit; only it has to be properly applied and its proper application has to be understood in its true perspective. So much for the merits of the controversy." 22. The controversy in the instant case, in my view, is squarely covered by the Division Bench in Shri Sankar Das' case, cited supra. Admittedly, the petitioner and the respondent No. 5 herein had obtained B.Ed. qualification from the same University and at the same examination. While the B.Ed. qualification in respect of petitioner was mentioned while sponsoring the names of candidates, the aforesaid qualification of B.Ed. in so far as respondent No. 5 is concerned, the same was intimated on 24.3.1994 to the institution though registered with the employment exchange by 10.3.94 and it must be assumed that application for incorporation thereof would have been made earlier thereto. The said qualification was obtained much prior to the names having been sponsored by the employment exchange. It is not a case where the B.Ed. qualification was obtained by the petitioner after "any cut off date". The delay with regard to the incorporation of the B.Ed. qualification in so far as respondent No. 5 is concerned can be attributed to the employment exchange. Even otherwise as held by the Division Bench in Sankar Das's case, supra, if a person has acquired the qualification before the cut off date, the same is liable to be taken into account. Candidate, it was categorically held, cannot be deprived of the benefit.  23. Mr. B.R. Bhattacharjee, however, sought to rely upon the Supreme Court judgment in Ashok Kr. Sharma & Anr. v. Chandra Sekhar & Ors., 1997(2) SCT 123 (SC) : reported in 1997(4) SCC 18, wherein, it was held that the eligibility of the candidates shall have to be judged with reference to the last date for filing the application. It was further held therein that a person who acquires the prescribed qualification subsequent to such prescribed date cannot be considered at all.  24. In my view, the aforesaid decision is of no avail to the writ petitioner and on the contrary is of some benefit to the respondent No. 5, inasmuch as, she is entitled to have the qualification of B.Ed. considered as the same was acquired by her prior to the last date of applications in the instant case, the same being the date when the employment exchange sponsored the names of candidates. At the cost of repetition, it must be stated that the respondent No. 5 acquired the qualification of B.Ed. much prior to the names having been sponsored by the employment exchange and at the same time as the writ petitioner. In terms of rule 6(b) of the Recruitment Rules all relevant qualifications are to be taken into consideration by the Selection Committee.  25. In the circumstances, it must be held that the Selection Committee/Managing Committee have not committed any illegality in taking into consideration the B.Ed. Qualification of respondent No. 5. The view of the DIS (SE) and that of the Deputy Director in that behalf it must be held is erroneous and suffers from error apparent on the face of record.  26. In the result, the instant writ application is disposed of with a direction upon the Director of School Education to call for the records from the Office of the DIS (SE) Uttar Dinajpur and to pass appropriate orders in accordance with the law with regard to the approval of the panel in the light of the observations made hereinbefore and communicate his decision with regard to the panel submitted for approval by the school authorities within a period of 6 weeks from date of communication of a copy of this order uninfluenced in any manner with the opinion of the DIS (SE) or the Deputy Director referred to hereinbefore. It is clarified that it shall be open to the Director of School Education to call for the information from the office of the employment exchange to ascertain whether the application for incorporation of the B.Ed. degree by Smt. Paramita Adhikary, respondent No. 5, was made on any date prior to 10.3.94 and if so the date when the application was made and particularly whether the same had been made prior to the names having been sponsored by the employment exchange to set at rest any factual dispute in the matter.  There shall, however, be no order as to costs.  Let urgent Xerox certified copy of this judgment and order be furnished to the appearing parties expeditiously, if applied for.  Orders accordingly.
summary: Constitution of India, Article 226 and 227 - Appointment for post of Assistant Teacher - Panel prepared by Selection Committee - The selected respondent was chosen based on their B.Ed. marks, with the petitioner in second place - The petitioner argues that the awarded marks were obtained illegally because the qualification of B.Ed. was not specified on the sponsoring of names by the Employment Exchange - However, both the respondent and petitioner obtained their B.Ed. qualification at the same time - The Panel was duly approved by the Managing Committee and forwarded to the District Inspector of Schools, who raised a query on the B.Ed. marks - Clarification was accepted, and the Writ was disposed of by directing the Director of School Education to call for records and pass appropriate orders within 6 weeks. [Paras 6, 8 and 24 to 26]

text: A.N. Varma, J. - Through the instant writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India the petitioner has assailed the validity of the order dated 13-6-2000 passed by the Senior Superintendent of Police, Lucknow, whereby his services have been terminated in purported exercise of powers conferred under Section 3 of the U.P. Temporary Government Servants (Termination of Service) Rules, 1975 (to be hereinafter referred to as the Rules).  2. The petitioner after having qualified for the written test, physical test and medical test, was declared successful for being appointed on the post of Constable in the Police Department. Accordingly pursuant to his letter of appointment which has been filed as Annexure No. SCA-1 along with the Supplementary Affidavit, he joined the Department on 15-5-1995 at Police Lines, Kanpur. Upon being so appointed the petitioner was required to undergo Junior Training Course (J.T.C.) of one month. After completion of the said training he was further required to undergo nine months' training of Recruitment Training Course, which Course he joined on 15-6-1995 at Lucknow. While undergoing the aforesaid training the petitioner on 12-4-1996 proceeded on casual leave for three days and went to his native place at Bahraich where he fell ill. On 18-4-96 he is said to have intimated the Superintendent of Police about his illness on telephone. According to the petitioner he all along remained indisposed and after having recovered from his illness on 27-7-1996 he submitted his joining before the authority concerned but was not allowed to join. Thereafter he made several representations before the appropriate authorities, copies of which have been annexed along with the writ petition, as Annexures No. 10 to 14 but to no avail. Finally vide impugned order dated 13-6-2000, a copy of which has been annexed along with the writ petition as Annexure No. 1, the services of the petitioner were terminated in exercise of powers conferred under Rule 3 of the Rules.  3. Learned counsel for the petitioner Shri U.N. Misra vehemently argued that though the order of termination is simpliciter but the same is punitive in nature inasmuch as the motive behind passing of the said order is his absence from duty which in fact, was beyond his control. It was also argued, that he intimated the authorities about his illness and also sent leave applications along with the medical certificate but the same were not considered and his services were dispensed with by a simple order of termination. According to him since the order impugned has been passed on the ground of alleged misconduct of the petitioner, for remaining absent from duty an opportunity of hearing was required to be given to him and without such an opportunity having been afforded the impugned order is manifestly unjust, illegal and against the provisions of the U.P. Police Officers of the Subordinate Rank (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1991 (to be hereinafter referred to as 1991 Rules).  4. In opposition the learned standing counsel Shri Harshvardhan, argued that the petitioner was only a temporary employee and was undergoing training. He had not even completed nine months Recruitment Training Course, therefore, he had no right to hold the post. His services have been terminated by giving him one month's notice. He further submitted that the order impugned is an order of termination simpliciter which has been passed in exercise of powers conferred under the Rules, as such, it does not suffer from any illegality and infirmity. According to him since the order impugned has been passed in exercise of powers conferred under the Rules, therefore, the same is not liable to be interfered with and the writ petition deserves to be dismissed. Learned Standing Counsel also drew the attention of this Court towards the Guidelines known as 'Aarakshi Nagrik Police Avam P.A.C. Ka Pathkaram Tatha Samanya Nirdesh' (to be hereinafter referred to as the Guidelines), paragraph 16(Da) of which contemplates that a trainee who is absent for more than 30 days for any reason during the course of training will be debarred from appearing in the final examination. It further provides that the said recruit trainee will be given an opportunity to appear in the Supplementary Examination after taking three months more training. In case any recruit trainee is found absent for more than 45 days the Head of the Training Institute will refer the case of such trainee to the Appointing Authority for terminating his services.  5. A detailed counter-affidavit has been filed on behalf of opposite parties along with which an extract of the said Guideline has been filed as Annexure No. C.A.1. In paragraph No. 5 of the said counter affidavit it has been averred that the petitioner on 24-10-1995 proceeded on leave for 15 days during the course of his training but did not return in time and he was unauthorizedly absent for four months seven days nine hours and forty minutes. Again on 12-4-1996 he went on casual leave to his home District and was again absent from training. According to the opposite parties he was unauthorizedly absent for one year eleven months nine hours and forty minutes which is a serious misconduct and unbecoming of a Police official. Similar averments have been made in paragraphs No. 6 and 8 of the counter-affidavit. In para 13 it has been stated that an enquiry in respect of unauthorized absence of the petitioner was made by the Assistant Superintendent of Police, Lucknow and on the basis of the said report the petitioner was discharged from service. According to the learned Standing Counsel the order of termination does not suffer from any illegality. As per his argument the power of termination flows out from the provisions of the aforesaid Guidelines and the same has rightly been exercised as the petitioner was absent from duty for more than 45 days in which eventuality his case could be recommended to the concerned authority for termination of his services. It was further submitted that since in an enquiry conducted by the Assistant Superintendent of Police, Lucknow, it was found that the petitioner was unauthorizedly absent, therefore, no further enquiry was required to be gone into and thus the order impugned is perfectly justified and is within the four corners of the powers conferred under the said Guidelines. Thus, according to him the impugned order does not deserve to be interfered with.  6. The learned counsel for the petitioner in reply thereto submitted that in the enquiry which is said to have been conducted, the petitioner was not given any opportunity nor was he heard in the matter. His argument further was that the said enquiry is not an enquiry which is contemplated and is required to be gone into under the Rules. He further submitted that the motive behind the order of terminating the services of the petitioner was his unauthorized absence from duty which impelled the employer to take such drastic action of termination of service by an order simpliciter. He strenuously argued that the act of the petitioner of being unauthorisedly absent from duty was the motive behind the passing of the impugned order of termination. According to him in such a situation he was required to be given an opportunity, for want of which the order impugned cannot be sustained. He further submitted that even if he over-stayed his leave, the services could not be terminated unless the petitioner was afforded an opportunity of showing cause. This admittedly having not been done, the order terminating his services was not warranted.  7. In case reported in Chandra Prakash Shahi v. State of U.P., 2000(2) SCT 946 (SC) : (2000)5 SCC 152 : (2000 All LJ 1445), the Hon'ble Supreme Court laid down certain principles to determine with regard to order of termination being simpliciter or punitive. In this connection it also propounded the concept of motive and foundation which may lead to the passing of the order of termination simpliciter. In paragraphs 28 and 29 of the said judgment the Apex Court observed as follows :  "28. The important principles which are deducible on the concept of "motive" and "foundation", concerning a probationer, are that a probationer has no right to hold the post and his services can be terminated at any time during or at the end of the period of probation on account of general unsuitability for the post in question. If for the determination of suitability of the probationer for the post in question or for his further retention in service or for confirmation, an inquiry is held and it is on the basis of that inquiry that a decision is taken to terminate his service, the order will not be punitive in nature. But, if there are allegations of misconduct and an inquiry is held to find out the truth of that misconduct and an order terminating the service is passed of the basis of that inquiry, the order would be punitive in nature as the inquiry was held not for assessing the general suitability of the employee for the post in question, but to find out the truth of allegations of misconduct against that employee. In this situation, the order would be founded on misconduct and it will not be a mere matter of "motive". 29. "Motive" is the moving power which impels action for a definite result, or to put it differently, "motive" is that which incites or stimulates a person to do an act. An order terminating the services of an employee is an act done by the employer. What is that factor which impelled the employer to take this action ? If it was the factor of general unsuitability of the employee for the post held by him, the action would be upheld in law. If, however, there were allegations of serious misconduct against the employee and a preliminary inquiry is held behind his back to ascertain the truth of those allegations and a termination order is passed, thereafter, the order, having regard to other circumstances, would be founded on the allegations of misconduct which were found to be true in the preliminary inquiry." 8. In Jai Shanker v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1966 SC 492, the services of an employee were terminated on the ground of overstaying leave. In the said case the relevant provisions under which action was taken i.e., Regulation 13 was as follows :  "13. An individual who absents himself without permission or who remains absent without permission for one month or longer after the end of his leave should be considered to have sacrificed his appointment and may only be reinstated with the sanction of the competent authority." 9. In the said case, it was contended by the State that the Regulation operated automatically and no question of removal from service could arise because Jai Shanker must be considered to have sacrificed his appointment. The Apex Court held as follows :-  "It is true that the Government may visit the punishment of discharge or removal from service on a person who has absented himself by over-staying his leave, but we do not think that Government can order a person to be discharged from service without at least telling him that they propose to remove him and giving him an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be removed. If this is done the incumbent will be entitled to move against the punishment for, if his plea succeeds, he will not be removed and no question of reinstatement will arise. It may be convenient to describe him as seeking reinstatement but this is not tantamount to saying that because the person will only be reinstated by an appropriate authority, that the removal is automatic and outside the protection of Article 311. A removal is removal and if it is punishment for overstaying one's leave an opportunity must be given to the person against whom such an order is proposed, no matter how the Regulation describes it. To give no opportunity is to go against Article 311 and this is what has happened here. (7) In our judgment, Jai Shanker was entitled to an opportunity to show cause against the proposed removal from service on his overstaying his leave and as no such opportunity was given to him, his removal from service was illegal." 10. In Deokinandan Prasad v. State of Bihar, AIR 1971 SC 1409, on August 5, 1966 the Director of Public Instruction passed an order that the petitioner "having not been on his duties for more than five years since March 11, 1960, has ceased to be in Government employment since March 12, 1965 under Rule 76 of the Bihar Service Code". The petitioner made representation against the said order but to no avail. Rule 76 of the Bihar Service Code reads as follows :  "Unless the State Government, in view of the special circumstances of the case shall otherwise determine, a Government servant after five years of continuous absence from duty; elsewhere than on foreign service in India, whether with or without leave, ceases to be in Government employment." 11. The Hon'ble Supreme Court after considering the matter at length held in paragraphs 23 and 25 of the judgment as follows :  "23. A contention has been taken by the petitioner that the order dated August 5, 1966 is an order removing him from service and it has been passed in violation of Article 311 of the Constitution. According to the respondents there is no violation of Article 311. On the other hand, there is an automatic termination of the petitioner's employment under Rule 76 of the Service Code. It may not be necessary to investigate this aspect further because on facts we have found that Rule 76 of the Service Code has no application. Even if it is a question of automatic termination of service for being continuously absent for over a period of five years. Article 311 applies to such cases as is laid down by this Court in Jai Shanker v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1966 SC 492 (supra)." "25. In the case before us even according to the respondents a continuous absence from duty for over five years, apart from resulting in the forfeiture of the office also amounts to misconduct under Rule 46 of the Pension Rules disentitling the said officer to receive pension. It is admitted by the respondents that no opportunity was given to the petitioner to show cause against the order proposed. Hence there is a clear violation of Article 311. Therefore, it follows even on this ground the order has to be quashed." 12. State of Assam v. Akshaya Kumar Deb, AIR 1976 SC 37, is a case wherein the services of a permanent Government servant were terminated under Fundamental Rule 18 of Assam Fundamental and Subsidiary Rules on account of his continuous absence from duty for more than five years and no opportunity was given to him to show cause. The Apex Court in paragraph 13 held as follows :  "13. From a reading of F.R. 18, it is discernible that it regards continuous absence of an employee, whether with or without leave, for a period of five years or more, as conduct which must normally entail "cessation" or termination of his service. Although not in so many words, but by necessary intendment, the Rule regards such conduct of the employee, as a fault or blameworthy behaviour which renders him unfit to be continued in service. In this contest, the "cessation" of service pursuant to this Rule would, in substance and effect, stand on the same footing as 'his removal' from service within the contemplation of Article 311(2) of the Constitution, particularly when it is against the will of the employee who is willing to serve, or who had never lost the animus to rejoin duty on the expiry of his leave. Another reason for equating 'cessation' of service under this Rule with 'removal' within the meaning of Article 311(2), is that it proceeds on a ground personal to the employee involving an imputation which may conceivably be explained by him in the circumstances of a particular case. Cases are not unknown where the absence of a Government servant, even for prolonged periods, has been due to circumstances beyond his control. The case of the Japanese soldier who remained cut off and stranded in the jungles of a remote Pacific island for three decades after the termination of World War II, is a recent instance of his kind." 13. Thus what is discernible from the aforesaid decisions and the principle laid down by the Apex Court therein that though the Rule may prescribe automatic termination for continuous absence for long years the order passed to that effect without any opportunity to the person concerned is violative of Article 311(2) of the Constitution of India.  14. In the case at hand also the Guidelines may be to the effect that if a person is absent for a period specified therein, his case can be recommended for terminating his services, still an order of termination thereto cannot be resorted to unless the employee is afforded an opportunity to defend his case. Since no opportunity was afforded to the petitioner to show cause and his services were done away with by a simple order of termination, the action of the opposite parties is illegal and manifestly unjust which cannot be allowed to stand.  15. In view of the above, the writ petition succeeds and is allowed. The order dated 13-6-2000 passed by the Senior Superintendent of Police, opposite party No. 5, as contained in Annexure No. 1 to the writ petition, is hereby quashed. Petitioner shall be reinstated in service and shall be allowed to complete his training which was required to be undergone by him but could not be completed on account of the fact that he absented himself consequent upon which his services were terminated.  16. Since the petitioner had not completed the requisite training, therefore, he would not be entitled for the salary and other benefits for the period he was out of job.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 311, 16 and 309 - U.P. Temporary Government Servants (Termination of Services) Rules (1975), Rule 3 - Termination simpliciter - Termination on ground of unauthorised absence without prior opportunity to show cause - The order of termination for the police constable undergoing training course by simple dismissal is deemed illegal. [Para 14]

text: Harjit Singh Bedi, J. (Oral) - The petitioner was enrolled in the Indian Army on 26.5.1969 and while undergoing training as a recruit suffered a Fracture of the Middle Phalange and was invalided out of military service. In consequence thereof, he was also granted a disability pension w.e.f. 7.10.1969 to 11.9.1971. He was, thereafter, called before a Re-Survey Medical Board first in the year 1971 and again in 1978 but the disability pension was not granted to him. The petitioner was once again brought before the Re-Survey Medical Board in the year 1992 but his claim was yet again rejected. His appeal before the Central Government was, however, allowed on the ground that the CCDA(P) had reduced his disability to less than 20% and that this action was uncalled for. The petitioner's claim to the service element, however, continued to be rejected, which led the petitioner to filing Civil Writ Petition No. 12530 of 1995. This Court disposed of the Civil Writ Petition by observing that the petitioner was entitled to the service element for a short term only and this amount was ultimately released. The petitioner was thereafter brought before the Re-Survey Medical Board in the year 1997 for determining the extent of his disability and this was assessed at 20%. The disability pension was, however, stopped from 14.10.1997 on the ground that his claim had been rejected by the CCDA(P), Allahabad vide its letter dated 12.2.1998, Annexure P-6, on the ground that the Medical Advisor (Pensions) had opined that the petitioner's disability had been reduced to 11% to 14% i.e. less than 20% for a period of five years upto 24.7.2002. An appeal was also filed by the petitioner against this order but the same remains undecided so far. The petitioner moved various representations for the release of his disability pension and ultimately, vide Annexure P-10 dated 3.9.1998, he was informed that the matter was under consideration with the Army Headquarter and in any case as the petitioner's claim to disability element of the pension had been rejected, the service element could also not be given to him.  2. Mr. B.S. Sehgal, the learned counsel for the petitioner, has argued only one point before me. He has urged that in the light of the Supreme Court decision in Ex. Sapper Mohinder Singh v. Union of India, Civil Appeal No. 164 of 1993 decided on 14.1.1993, the CCDA(P), Allahabad, could not sit in the judgment over the opinion of the Medical Board and to re-determine afresh the extent of disability of a claimant. He has also pointed out that the judgment had been followed in a number of cases including a Division Bench judgment of this Court in Ujagar Singh v. Union of India and others 1997(4) RSJ, 587. In paragraph 3 of this judgment, it has been observed as under :-  "From the above narrated facts and the stand taken by the parties before us, the controversy that falls for determination by us is a very narrow compass viz whether the Chief Controller of Defence Accounts (Pension) has any jurisdiction to sit over the opinion of the experts (Medical Board) while dealing with the case of grant of disability pension, in regard to the percentage of the disability pension, or not. In the present case, is no where stated that the petitioner was subjected to any higher medical board before the Chief Controller of Defence Accounts (Pension) decided to decline the disability pension to the petitioner. We are unable to see as to how the accounts branch dealing with the pension can sit over the judgment of the experts in the medical line and comment upon the extent of disability without making any reference to a detailed or higher medical board which can be constituted under the relevant instructions and rules by the Directory General of Army Medical Core." 3. The above observations fully apply to the facts of the present case. This petition is accordingly allowed, the order, Annexure P-6 in toto as also the order Annexure P-10 in so far it denies the petitioner's claim to the service element, are quashed and a direction is issued to the respondents to pay the disability pension (Keeping in view that his disability has been assessed at 20%) within a period of four months from the date a certified copy of the order is supplied to the respondents. It is clarified that the petitioner's claim as of now would be for a period of five years i.e. upto 24.7.2002 and after that date the petitioner would have to undergo a re-survey of his medical disability.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Article 226 - Disability pension - A petitioner who was training as a recruit fractured the Middle Phalange and was invalidated out of military service. CCDA(P) decreased his disability to less than 20%, and his claim for pension was denied because he was not sent to a higher medical board before the Chief Controller of Defence Accounts (Pension). It was held that the accounts branch responsible for the pension cannot override judgments made by medical experts without referring the matter to a higher medical board. As a result, disability pension was granted for the petitioner. [Paras 2 & 3]

text: Gitesh Ranjan Bhattacharjee, J. - The writ petitioner joined police service in Calcutta Police in 1956. In his Service Book opened at that time his date of birth had been recorded as 29th November, 1934. The contention of the petitioner is that, as a matter of fact, his date of birth was wrongly recorded by the dealing clerk in his Service Book and his actual date of birth is 15h August, 1937. It is also the contention of the petitioner that although at the time of entry in the service he told his correct date of birth to the dealing clerk, the latter made a mistake in recording the same in his Service Book and the petitioner was not aware of the same. It is also the case of the petitioner that subsequently when he came to know that his date of birth was wrongly recorded in the Service Book, he submitted a representation dated 30.9.1989 to the Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, which is Annexure `C' to the writ petition. Along with the said representation he also submitted two xerox copies of his school leaving certificates. One of those certificates was granted by the Headmaster of Sundarganj A. Majid H.E. School district Rangpur of the erstwhile East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). That certificate is dated 20.4.48 and in that certificate it is stated inter alia that on 20.4.48 the age of the petitioner, who was reading in class VI at that time, was 10 years 5 months 5 days according to the admission register. According to that certificate, his date of birth is 15th August, 1937. Subsequently the petitioner read in Maharaja Nripendra Narayan High School of Cooch Bihar and he read there upto class VIII. He subsequently obtained a certificate from the Head-master of the said school (Annexure `B' to the writ petition) wherein it is certified by the Headmaster on the basis of the admission register maintained in the school that the date of birth of the petitioner as recorded in the admission register was 15.8.37. The xerox copies of both those certificates were enclosed with the representation dated 30.9.1989 addressed to the Commissioner of Police for correction of his date of birth in his Service Book. It was also mentioned in that representation that Shri Tapash Chandra Ghosh, the elder brother of the petitioner, was a Government servant working in a gazetted post and he was to retire on attaining the age of superannuation on 20.3.1994. This fact was mentioned in the said representation only to show that he being the younger brother, cannot reach the age of superannuation before his elder brother. In this writ petition the petitioner has also enclosed a xerox copy of his said elder brother's School Final Examination Certificate (Annexure `D' to the writ petition) where the date of birth of his elder brother has been recorded as 23rd October, 1936. Be that as it may, the petitioner was not given any hearing by the departmental authority about his representation for correction of his age nor was he informed specifically about the fate of his representation. A copy of D.O.No. 3403 dated 13.9.90 was only forwarded, to the petitioner for information. In the said D.O. it was recorded by the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Branch, Calcutta, that the date of birth as recorded in the Service Book of the petitioner, who was working as Sub-Inspector in the Special Branch, Calcutta Police, was accepted under Rule 9(1) of W.B.S.R./Part 1. Nothing is indicated therein as to whether his representation in the matter and the documents enclosed therewith regarding his age were at all taken into consideration and if so, why the same could not be accepted or acted upon by the authorities concerned.  2. The facts and the supporting documents are so plain and simple that there is seemingly no reason, far less any good reason, as to why the petitioner's date of birth as supported by the documents should not have been accepted by the authorities concerned.  3. It is the case of the respondents that the petitioner made declaration of his age under Rule 9 of W.B.S.R. Part 1 in the prescribed form at the time of his entry in service. This again is plainly not correct because W.B.S.R. Part 1 of which Rule 9 has been referred to, I find, came into force in October 1971, whereas the petitioner joined his service as far back as in 1956 when the present W.B.S.R. was not in existence and consequently, the form of declaration as appended to Rule 9 was also not there. As a matter of fact, the Service Book of the petitioner also as now produced before me, shows that there is no declaration of age of the petitioner in the form which is appended under Rule 9 of the present W.B.S.R. Part 1. The date of birth as recorded in the Service Book plainly appears to have been recorded in a different ink by a different hand compared to the signature of the petitioner thereby lending support to the petitioner's contention that he only signed the form but the particulars were entered by the dealing clerk and the dealing clerk made a mistake in recording the date of his birth. At any rate, nothing convincing is forthcoming from the side of the respondents to sustain and support the recorded date of birth as appearing in the Service Book, whereas from the petitioner's side very convincing materials have been produced which I have already discussed. In this connection Mr. Chatterjee appearing for the petitioner has attracted my attention to a Division Bench decision of this Court in Nihar Ranjan Bhowmick v. State of West Bengal, 1991 (1) CLJ 93 wherein it has been held that mere self-serving declaration of a recruit, in particular, in public employment, can never be the proof of age of the declarant and that ordinarily the oral statement can hardly be useful to determine the correct age of a person. Mr. Chatterjee has also referred to a Supreme Court decision in the case of State of Orissa v. Dr. Binapani Dei, AIR 1967 SC 1269. That was also a case in connection with Age dispute. There it was held that even if an order is administrative in character, yet an administrative order which involves civil consequences, must be made consistently with the rules of natural justice after informing the person concerned of the case of the State, the evidence in support thereof and after giving an opportunity to the person concerned of being heard and meeting or explaining the evidence. In the present case no hearing was given to the petitioner by the concerned authorities even when he made a representation supported by documentary evidence for correction of his age in the Service Book. What is worse is that the authorities concerned even did not inform the petitioner that his representation was ever or at all considered, not to speak of assigning any reason as to why his representation and the documents produced in support thereof could not be accepted.  4. In the circumstances, the whole action of the respondents in totally ignoring the petitioner's representation and/or the documents produced therewith for correction of his age in the service record, is wholly arbitrary and the same cannot be sustained as it entails civil consequence of a drastic nature. Relying upon the age recorded in the Service Book, steps have been taken by the respondents to superannuate the petitioner on and from 30th November, 1992 which, however, cannot be the case if the wrong recording of his date of birth in the Service Book is corrected by inserting his correct date of birth which, from the undisputed materials placed on record, appears to be 15th August, 1937.  5. The writ petition is accordingly allowed. The action and steps taken by the respondents for superannuating the petitioner on and from 30th November, 1992 are hereby quashed. The respondents are directed to amend the entry regarding the petitioner's age in the Service Book by deleting the existing entry and entering instead `15th August, 1937' as the date of his birth on the basis of the school leaving certificates mentioned above. It is needless to mention that the petitioner's superannuation will follow the date of birth now directed to be entered in his Service Book which is 15th August, 1937. The respondents will act accordingly.  Let xerox copy of this judgment be given to the learned Advocates for both sides on the usual terms.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution, of India, Article 226 - Date of birth - Correction of date of birth - The service book of the petitioner incorrectly records a wrong date of birth - Despite the fact that there is no declaration made by the petitioner, it is reasonable to change the date of birth as supported by documents provided - The authorities must change the date of birth of the petitioner based on the school leaving certificate and adjust the age of superannuation accordingly. [Paras 2 to 5]

text: N.K. Agrawal, J. - This is a petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution against the order of the Labour Court, Jalandhar, whereby the workman's application under Section 33-C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (for short, 'the Act') has been allowed.  2. The petitioner is engaged in the business of constructing buildings as a contractor. Respondent No. 2 Lal Ji filed an application before the Labour Court under Section 33-C(2) claiming himself to be employed with the petitioner and demanding a sum of Rs. 35,000/- as arrears of wages for the period from 1981 to February, 1983 with interest @ 18% per annum. The petitioner in his reply denied any relationship of employer and employee between himself and the respondent. The petitioner disputed the claim on merits as well. The Labour Court, after recording the evidence of the parties, allowed the workman's claim and also ordered that in case of non- payment of the arrears within four months, the amount shall be paid with interest @ 12 per cent.  3. Learned counsel for the petitioner has argued that the Labour Court proceeded to determine the rights and obligations of the parties without jurisdiction. The Labour Court had a very limited jurisdiction in the matter. It could only execute an award already given by a competent Court. The petitioner had raised a serious dispute by denying relationship of master and servant. The Labour Court and no jurisdiction to go into that dispute. It could only be seen in a reference made under Section 10(1)(c) of the Act. Moreover, the workman had put forward his claim with abnormal delay. He demanded wages from 1981 to February, 1983 and filed the claim in December, 1991. Even an ordinary civil suit was barred by limitation by that time. It is further argued that though Section 33-C(2) did not provide for any period of limitation, the claim should be filed within a reasonable period. Further, the workman's claim was wholly vague and lacked specific particulars. The workman did not state in his claim petition as to in what capacity he had worked with the petitioner and what were his monthly wages. He did not clarify if he had left the job or his services were terminated. He even did not explain in his petition as to how he had computed and worked out the amount of Rs. 35,000/-.  4. Learned counsel for the respondent-workman has, on the other hand, argued that the workman was engaged on a salary of Rs. 4,000/- per month. He used to look after the construction work. The employer did not produce any record to show the payment of wages to the workman. The Labour Court has not allowed payment of interest as claimed. It is only the future interest @ 12 per cent which has been allowed.  5. A question once arose in Municipal Committee, Mansa v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Bathinda and another, 1997(1) A.I.J. 138 : 1996(4) SCT 720 (P&H), whether the workman had been posted as Clerk or he performed the duties of Clerk. It was held that such a dispute could not be adjudicated under Section 33-C(2) of the Act. It was further held that although no limitation had been provided for filing a claim under Section 33-C(2), it would not entitle a workman to raise a claim which is unreasonably belated without a plausible explanation.  6. The Supreme Court had also an occasion to examine a matter on the ground of laches in Nanoo Ram v. Mahesh Chandra and another, 1990 Supp. S.C.C. 752. That was a case where the workman had filed an application under Section 33- C(2) for certain benefits consequent upon his reinstatement in service. He filed a second application claiming allowances and other benefits. It was held that his second application was rightly rejected on the ground of laches.  7. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Ganesh Razak and another, 1995 Lab I.C. 330 : 1995(1) SCT 408 (SC), it has been again held by the Supreme Court that where the very basis of the claim or entitlement of the workman to a certain benefit is disputed there being no earlier adjudication or recognition thereof by the employer, the dispute relating to entitlement is not incidental to the benefit claimed and is, therefore, clearly outside the scope of a proceeding under Section 33-C(2) of the Act.  8. Learned counsel for the respondent-workman has, on the other hand, placed reliance on a decision of the Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench) in Ramkishan Ramnath Bidis Manufacturing, Kamptee v. Labour Court, Nagpur, 1963 I.L.L.J. 417. It has been held that Section 33-C(2) comes into play when the benefits have to be computed and calculated and there is a dispute as to the calculation or computation.  9. The learned counsel has further referred to a decision of the Supreme Court in The Central Bank of India Ltd. v. P.S. Rajagopalan etc., AIR 1964 S.C. 743. It has been held that in determining the scope of Section 33-C care must be taken not to exclude cases which ultimately fall within its purview. It must, however, also be borne in mind that the cases which fall within Section 10(1) of the Act cannot be brought within the scope of Section 33-C.  10. On a consideration of the controversy, it is found that the workman filed a vague application claiming wages from the year 1981 to February, 1983. He did not specify the month in the year 1981 from which the salary was due to him. The amount of monthly salary was also not specified in the claim petition. He stated in his petition as under :-  "That I was employed with the abovesaid employer and working as (A) the said employer did pay my earned wages for the period of 1981 to February, 1983 which becomes Rs. 35,000/-.  It is, therefore, prayed that the court be pleased to determine the amount due to the petitioner with 18% interest which becomes to Rs. 35,000/- + Rs. 55,650/- interest  35000.00  55650.00  ---------  G. Total = 90650.00  ---------  Sd/- Applicant."  11. The workman did not produce any evidence to show that he had worked with the petitioner. He did not explain the delay also. The question of relationship as master and servant has been raised. The Labour Court had no jurisdiction to adjudicate thereon. The workman did not specify as to what post he held and the work he performed. The order of the Labour Court is, thus, found to be wholly unsustainable in law.  12. The writ petition is, therefore, allowed. Order of the Labour Court dated October 20, 1997 is quashed. No costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India Article 226 and Industrial Disputes Act 1947 Section 33-C(2) discuss the jurisdiction of the Labour Court. The workman in this case filed a vague application for wages from 1981 to 1983 without specifying the month in 1981 in which he was due payment. The application was filed in December 1991, and no evidence was produced to prove his working relationship with the petitioner.
