The petitioner would have been entitled to take the re-appear examination in both the subjects instead of one, but for the intimation given to him in November, 1997 when the University on 23.12.1998 again informed the petitioner that two chances of re-appear had already gone by, which could not be availed of by the petitioner for no fault of his own.  9. We are of the considered view that no fault is attributable to the petitioner and from the above narrated facts it is clear that the petitioner could not take the examination 7th semeseter when he has admittedly attended the entire course of the 7th semester. Consequently, we allow this writ petition and direct the respondents to permit the petitioner to take the examination of the 7th semester which are to commence from April, 1999 and also permit the petitioner to take the chance of re-appear of his remaining papers of the 3rd semester in accordance with the intimation given by the University dated 23.12.1998 along with these examinations in accordance with law. The writ petition is allowed to the above extent. However, the parties are left to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16 and 226 - Maharishi Dayanand University Ordinance, Clause 6, Rule 11 - Examination - Re-appear - Petitioner was supposed to take reappear in two papers of 3rd semester examination of B.E. degree course. However, after clearing one of the reappear subjects, he was informed that he only had to reappear in one subject. Acting on this communication, he only took reappear in one paper. Later, he was informed again that he had to take reappear in the 7th semester as he had not cleared the 3rd semester. The University ordinance cannot permit the University to benefit from its own mistake and deprive the petitioner of one chance of reappear. The respondents have been directed to allow the petitioner to take the examination of the 7th semester. [Paras 7 to 9]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. (Oral) - The petitioner was appointed as a teacher vide order dated December 21, 2001. A copy of this order is at Annexure P-8 with the writ petition. In pursuance of this offer of appointment the petitioner joined service on December 24, 2001. On July 15, 2002 the petitioner's services were "terminated with immediate effect during the probation period as she did not fulfil the requisite qualifications as published in the advertisement" for the post of JBT teachers. A copy of the order has been produced as Annexure P-10 with the writ petition. Aggrieved by this order, the petitioner has approached this Court through the present writ petition. It is alleged that the petitioner is qualified for the post of J.B.T. Teacher.  2. Dr. Sachdeva, learned counsel for the petitioner, submits that she possesses the qualification of BA with three years Diploma in Physical Education. This Diploma, according to the learned counsel, is equivalent to the degree of Bachelor of Education. He further submits that this equivalence is recognised by the statutory rules. Thus, the counsel contends that the respondents have erred in holding that the petitioner did not fulfil the qualification for appointment to the post of Junior Basic Trained teacher.  3. The short question that arises for consideration is that - Does the petitioner fulfil the qualifications for appointment to the post of a J.B.T. teacher ?  4. Admittedly, the posts of J.B.T. Teacher had been advertised. The qualifications of the posts were duly mentioned. It was laid down that the candidates must have qualified "Elementary Teacher Training Course of two years from the Punjab State." Even others, who had passed the J.B.T. course or BA. B.Ed. were also to be considered. The qualification of Diploma in Physical Education was not mentioned in the advertisement. It is thus clear that persons with Diploma in Physical Education were not qualified to apply.  5. Dr. Sachdeva submits that this qualification is recognised under the statutory rules. Thus, the petitioners were eligible to be considered for appointment, as J.B.T. Teachers. Is it so ?  6. The recruitment to the post of Primary School Teachers is governed by the provision of Punjab State Education Class III (Primary School Cadre) Service Rules, 1997. Rule 6 lays down the method of recruitment and qualifications. It has been, inter-alia, provided that the post shall be filled up in accordance with the manner laid down in appendix B. Clause 2 specifically provides that "no person shall be appointed to a post in the service, unless he possesses the qualifications and experience as specified against that post in appendix B." The relevant entry in appendix B is as under :-  "4. Junior BasicTrained Teacher/Elementary Trained Teacher 100% Direct Appointment (i) Matric/10-+2 (ii) Training/ Elementary Teachers Training two years course of Punjab State or from any other State or Union Territory declared equivalent and recognised by the Punjab Government."  7. A perusal of the above provision would show that the posts have to be filled up by direct appointment. Persons who possess the qualification of Matric or 10+2 with Elementary Teachers Training course of two years are eligible. The rule does not recognise a Diploma in Physical Education as a qualification for appointment to the posts of J.B.T. teachers.  8. Dr. Sachdeva refers to an entry in Appendix-B of the Punjab State Education Class II (school Cadre) Service Rules, 1978, as amended in 1995, and contends that the qualification of diploma in Physical Education has been treated as equivalent to B.T. or B.Ed.  The relevant entry is as follows :-  "(g) Social Studies Master/Mistress B.A. with subject Combination as approved by Government from time to time with B.T. or B.Ed. OR Senior Basic Trained (including service of D.P.Ed. and B.P.Ed. as Master/Mistress with at least three years actual teaching experience)." 9. A perusal of the above provision shows that the qualifications relate to the posts of Social Studies Masters and not to those of J.B.T. teachers. The two posts belong to different service and are governed by separate set of Rules. We cannot read the provision to mean that a person trained in Physical Education is qualified to teach Hindi, English and Arithmetic to tiny toddlers.  10. The rule making authority is best equipped to know the needs of a particular job and to prescribe the qualifications therefore. The Courts are normally reluctant to enter academic thickets. The Courts do not have the expertise. Thus, the Courts normally avoid a microscopic examination of the qualifications or the equivalence thereof. In the present case, on a perusal of the rules, it is clear that the recruitment to the post of teachers in Primary Schools is governed by a separate set of statutory rules enacted by the Government. These rules do not recognise the qualification of Diploma in Physical Education which the petitioner possesses. Even in the advertisement this was not prescribed as one of the qualifications. Thus, the petitioner who had applied in response to the advertisement did not actually fulfil the qualifications for the post. Resultantly, we can find no fault with the order passed by the authorities.  No other point has been raised.  In view of the above, we find no merit in this writ petition. It is consequently dismissed in limine.  Petition dismissed.
summary:
A. Punjab State Education Class III (Primary School Cadre) Services Rules 1997, Rules 6 - Appointment to the post of J.B.T. teacher - To be eligible to apply for the post, candidates must possess the minimum qualifications of Elementary Teacher Training Course or J.B.T. Course or B.A. B.Ed. - Diploma in Physical Education is not a recognized qualification for the post and was not advertised as such - Non-fulfillment of required qualifications can lead to termination of service. [Paras 4 & 6]

B. Punjab State Education Class III (Primary School Cadre) Services Rules, 1997, Rule 6 - Qualifications for the post of J.B.T. teacher - The minimum qualifications advertised were Elementary Teacher Training Course or J.B.T. Course or B.A. B.Ed. - Diploma in Physical Education is not mentioned as a qualification in the advertisement or in the rules - This qualification is relevant only to the post of Social Studies Masters and not the J.B.T. teacher post - The two posts belong to different services and are governed by separate rules - A person with a physical education background may not be qualified to teach subjects such as Hindi, English, and Arithmetic to young children. [Para 9]

C. Punjab State Education Class III (Primary School Cadre) Services Rules 1997, Rule 6 - Qualifications for post of J.B.T. - The rule-making authority is best equipped to determine the qualifications necessary for a particular job - Courts do not have the expertise to prescribe qualifications for a post. [Para 10]

text: N.K. Sodhi, J. - This order will dispose of two civil writ petitions No. 11137 and 13180 of 2001 in which common questions of law and fact arise. Since arguments were addressed in civil writ petition No. 11137 of 2001, the facts are being taken from this case.  2. Petitioners herein are students of Shaheed Udham Singh College of Engineering & Technology, Tangori (Mohali) in the District of Roopnagar (for short the college). They were admitted in the year 2000 to the first year of the 4-years B.Tech. Courses in different disciplines on the basis of their merit in the Common Entrance Test - 2000 (CET - 2000) conducted by the Punjab Technical University, Jalandhar (hereinafter referred to as the University). On the basis of this test the University made admissions to various Degree level Engineering and Architecture courses as are being run in institutions and Universities located in the State of Punjab for the academic session 20000-2001 including the college. The admissions for this year were completed by August 2000 and the academic session commenced with effect from August 9, 2000. Students who were admitted to different courses in different institutions were required to deposit fee in their respective institutions by August 11, 2000. The schedule regarding change of branch was fixed in the Brochure issued by the University and branches could be changed by the Head of the Institution on 16/17-8.2000. Second counselling for filling up the resultant vacancies concluded on 23.8.2000 whereafter the admissions in each institution became final. 85 per cent of the total seats in all the institutions in the State of Punjab were reserved for the internal candidates from within the State and 15 per cent were open to candidates on All India basis. Petitioners No. 1, 3 and 4 were admitted against the 15 per cent seats whereas petitioners No. 2 and 5 were admitted against the 85 per cent seats. The college is approved by All India Council for Technical Education, New Delhi (AICTE), Government of Punjab and is affiliated to the University. The approval granted to the college by AICTE is in the following disciplines with an annual intake as noted against each :  i) Computer Science & Engineering 60 ii) Electronics & Communication Engineering 60 iii) Electrical Engineering 60 iv) Mechanical Engineering 60 Total intake capacity :  240 Additional 10 per cent seats of the sanctioned intake strength in each course are also filled up in the second year of B.Tech. programmes on the basis of the Lateral Entry Engineering Test (LEET) conducted by the University for diploma holders.  3. The question of approval for introduction of additional/increase in intake capacity in Degree course in Information Technology related areas in the college was under consideration of AICITE. By letter dated 13.11.2000 addressed to the Secretary, Technical Education & Industrial Training, Government of Punjab, Chandigarh, AICTE accorded approval to the college for starting the additional course in Information Technology and also increased the intake capacity of the already running courses as under :  Course(s)  Existing approved intake New approved/revised intake Duration (years) Computer Science & Engineering Degree 60 90 4 Electronics & Communication Engineering Degree 60 90 4 Electrical Engineering Degree 60 60 4 Mechanical Engineering Degree 60 60 4 Information Technology Degree 0 60 4 Total :  240 360 4. The increase in intake/additional courses was approved only for the year 2000-2001 and further extension was to be granted after due consideration. Approval for the increase intake capacity and for starting the additional course in Information Technology was received from AICTE for the year 2001- 2002 as well by letter dated 14.6.2001. Since the approval for the increase in intake capacity was received in November, 2000 long after the course of studies had commenced for the academic year 2000-2001, the University did not think it proper to fill up the additional seats because that would have resulted in large scale dislocation of the students and would have disturbed their studies. Moreover, students could not have been admitted against the additional seats as late as in November, 2000 as they would not have been able to complete the course of their studies for the first semester. The University, however, decided to offer additional seats to the students of 2000 batch in the third semester on the basis of their merit in the first semester examination. A notice was published in the daily Tribune on 14.7.2001 informing the students that the University shall carry out up-gradation of branches of the students admitted through CET-2000 based on the result of the first semester examination held in December 2000. It may be mentioned that first semester examination was held in December, 2000 and the result of that examination had been declared. Students had also appeared in their second semester examination but result of that examination was still awaited. The notice further stated that students interested in the up-gradation of their branches and change of institutions could appear in the joint counselling to be conducted by the University on its campus on 19.7.2001 at 9 A.M. 134 students were up-graded on this date. Some of the students who had appeared in the first semester examination but could not clear the same had applied for re-evaluation of their result. Such students were also given a chance to apply for up-gradation provided they were declared pass as a result of re- evaluation. The counselling was held for them on 8.8.2001 and a notice in this regard was published in the leading local newspapers including The Tribune, Punjab Kesari and Ajeet. In this counselling 23 students were up- graded. Petitioners No. 1, 4 and 5 had to re-appear in some of the papers in the first semester examination and they had applied for re-evaluation of their result. They did not clear the re-appear papers even after re-evaluation. Petitioners No. 2 and 3 were also to re-appear in some of the papers in the first semester. They did not apply for re-evaluation of their result. Since none of the petitioners had cleared the first semester examination even after getting their result re-evaluated, they were not considered eligible for up- gradation in the counselling held on 19.7.2001 and again on 8.8.2001. It was then that they filed the present petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the action of the University in offering the additional seats in the college to all the students of different institutions in the State of Punjab. Their plea is that the additional seats should have been offered only to the students of the college like the petitioners who had been admitted to the course in the year 2000.  5. In response to the notice of motion, the University has filed its reply. It was later allowed to file an amended written statement. The factual position as stated above has not been disputed though the plea of the petitioners that additional seats should have been offered only to the students of the college has been controverted on the ground that it would not have been fair to the students of different institutions who had been given admission in different institutions on the basis of CET-2000.  6. It was strenuously urged by Shri G.K. Chatrath, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners that the additional seats had been sanctioned by AICTE in the college and it was but proper that those seats should have been offered only to the students of the college like the petitioners to up-grade them in different branches of the Engineering courses. He contended that the action of the University in this regard was contrary to para 5 in Part-B of the Admission Brochure issued by the University for admission to first year of Bachelor of Engineering/Technology courses in the year 2000. He stated that additional seats had been sanctioned in the Punjab Engineering College and also in Chemical Engineering department of the Punjab University as well and those were offered only to the students who had been admitted in those institutions. Learned counsel appearing fro the University, on the other hand, placed reliance on clause (v) of the General Conditions contained in the notification dated 4.3.2000 whereby the University had been appointed as the authority competent to conduct the CET-2000 to contend that since the approval for the additional seats had been received long after the admissions for the academic session 2000-2001 were over, admission against the additional seats could not be made for that session and the University had perforce to offer seats to the candidates in the third semester to up-grade themselves.  7. We have heard counsel for the parties and find no ground to interfere in the exercise of our jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. There is no gain saying the fact that approval from the AICTE for the additional seats was received for the first time in November, 2000 when admissions for the academic session had come to an end and the course of studies had already begun. Not only this, first semester was about to come to a close and the examinations for that semester were held, in December, 2000. This being the position, the University could not admit the students against additional seats in the first year for the academic session 2000-2001 because in that event students so admitted would not have completed their course of studies. This apart, since the seats were being offered to the students of other institutions as well, it would have resulted in dislocation of studies of the students of other institutions. In these circumstances, the University in its wisdom thought it proper to throw open the additional seats to the already admitted students in all the institutions on the basis of their merit in the first semester examination. Admissions were to be made in the third semester and by that time the result of the first semester had been declared. This was a policy decision taken by the University presumably because it thought that had the approval for the additional seats been received before counselling was over in August, 2000 these seats then would have been available to the candidates of all the institutions who were seeking admission for the academic session 2000-2001. The petitioners contend that additional seats should have been thrown open only to the students like the petitioners who were admitted in the college for the academic year 2000-2001. This could be an another way of dealing with the additional seats. As already observed, the University decided to thrown open the additional seats to the students of all the institutions. There does not seem to be any arbitrariness in this decision as the decision taken by the University applies equally to all students of different institutions who were similarly placed and were given admission on the basis of their merit position in CET-2000. There were two different ways of dealing with the additional seats which became available after the admission to the first year of the course had closed and the University choose one of them which we have already held is not arbitrary. It is well settled that in a situation when two courses are open to the University and it chooses one which is not arbitrary, this court does not interfere in the exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. Even if one were to agree with the petitioners that the seats should have been confined to the students admitted in the college, it is not for us to substitute our own opinion for that of the experts who are governing the University and its affiliated institutions. We do not agree with the learned senior counsel for the petitioners that para 5 in Part-B of the Brochure stood violated in the present case. Before we observe any more, it would be relevant to notice that para which is reproduced hereunder for facility of reference:  "5. Allotment of Institution and Branch : The allotment of the institution and the branch of study will be made at the time of the counselling on the basis of candidate's merit position in CET-2000, availability of seats, the choice and the eligibility of the candidate. Candidate should be fully prepared to select the institution and branch from amongst those available at the time of his/her counselling. No subsequent change of institution shall be permitted under any circumstances. In case of vacancies occurring within an institution a candidate already admitted to that institution may exercise his/her option in writing for change of branch, which will be considered by the Institution strictly in accordance with CET- 2000 merit and in accordance with the instructions to be issued by Punjab Technical University as per the schedule given in this brochure."  A bare reading of this paragraph makes it clear that it applies to admissions originally made before counselling was over in August, 2000 and does not cover the filling up of additional seats which became available after the admissions were over. It is true that allotment of the institution and the branch of study is offered to the candidate at the time of counselling on the basis of his merit position in CET-2000 and admittedly, this was done when admissions were made in July/August, 2000. It was on the basis of their merit position in CET-2000 that the petitioners were offered admission in the college in different branches of the Engineering course. It is further clear from the aforesaid paragraph that once a student has selected an institution and the branch from amongst those available at the time of counselling, no subsequent change of institution is permitted. However, in the case of vacancies occurring within the institution a candidates is given right to exercise his option in writing for change of branch which would be considered as per his merit position in CET-2000. This paragraph refers to vacancies and not to additional seats. If a seat were to become vacant i.e. a student admitted was to leave the institution for any reason whatsoever that seat would be filled up in accordance with this paragraph but additional seats which became available after the admissions are over cannot in the very nature of things be governed by paragraph 5. Again vacancies as referred to in this paragraph would mean a vacancy occurring from amongst the original seats for which admissions were originally made. We have, therefore, no hesitation in holding that this paragraph does not apply to the additional seats.  8. It is common case of the parties that the petitioners did not clear the first semester examination by 8.8.2001 when second counselling was held to up-grade the students admitted in different institutions in the State. They were, thus, ineligible for being considered for up-gradation. No fault can, thus, be found with the action of the University in this regard.  In the result, the writ petitions fail and the same stand dismissed leaving the parties to bear their own costs.  Petitions dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Article 226 - Scope and discretion of Court - Admissions - Additional seats - University policy of filling up mid-session additional seats is a matter of University policy - The Court cannot substitute its own choice of other mode. [Para]

text: R.P. Sethi and R.L. Anand, JJ. - This is an L.P.A. filed by the Central Bank of India through its Chief Manager, Zonal Office, Chandigarh (hereinafter called 'the Bank') and it has been directed against the judgment dated 9th March, 1994 passed in C.W.P. No. 57 of 1981 vide which the learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition and the order of dismissal of respondent No. 1 from service dated 20th March, 1980 passed by the punishing authority and the order dated 16th December, 1980 passed by the appellate authority were quashed. It was, however, ordered by the learned Single Judge that the disciplinary authority will be at liberty to take such action against the employee as is warranted under the Regulations and in the light of the observations made in the judgment. The disciplinary authority will take into consideration while imposing the punishment that respondent No. 1 had suffered the agony for all these years commencing from January 7, 1976.  2. The brief facts of the case are that Shri Balwant Rai Nayyar, respondent No. 1, was an employee of the Central Bank of India. He was posted as Sub Accountant in the Nizam Road Branch at Ludhiana in the year 1972-73. A criminal case was registered against him under Sections 408/420, 468/467, Indian Penal Code, in Police Station Division No. 1, Ludhiana, on the basis of a complaint filed by one Nahar Singh, who had a Saving Bank Account in the said branch. On the above charges, respondent No. 1 was tried by the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Ludhiana, and was convicted for the offence under Section 420, I.P.C., vide judgment dated 19th January, 1980. However, the Chief Judicial Magistrate did not sentence respondent No. 1. Rather he released him on probation under Section 4(1)(c) of the Probation of Offenders Act on his entering upon a bond in the sum of Rs. 7,000/- with one surety of the like amount so as to appear and receive sentence when called upon during the period of one year from the date of the order and respondent No. 1 was also directed to maintain peace and be of good behaviour. On the basis of the order of the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, respondent No. 1 was dismissed from service by the disciplinary authority vide order dated 20th March, 1980. Respondent No. 1 filed an appeal against the order of his dismissal and the appeal was also dismissed by the appellate authority, i.e., respondent No. 3 vide order dated 16th December, 1980 and it was observed by the appellate authority as follows :-  "The aforesaid appeal is being disposed of by the undersigned as a duly competent Appellate Authority under the Central Bank of India Employees (Discipline & Appeal) Regulations, 1976. In the said appeal, Shri Nayyar had requested that a personal hearing should be given. The undersigned acceded to this request and accordingly a hearing was given to him on 27.11.1980 at Chandigarh when he was permitted to appear along with any other Officer employee as his representative. Shri Nayyar, however, chose to appear personally and also chose to make only written submissions. I have gone through the papers on record and very carefully considered all the submissions made by Shri Nayyar, those contained in his appeal as well as in the written submissions made by him on 27.11.1980. After duly examining the same, I have to observe that :-  The judgment indicates that merely because the member is given the benefit under the Probation of Offenders Act, he is not necessarily required to be reinstated. It should be noted that in arriving at a decision in this case, I have taken into account the entire conduct of the delinquent employee, the gravity of the misconduct committed by him, namely, the charge of cheating has been duly established against him and the impact which his misconduct is likely to have on the administration. I, therefore, come to the conclusion that considering all the relevant aspects, the punishment of dismissal is appropriate within the competence of the Disciplinary Authority and I, therefore, confirm that Shri B.R. Nayyar should be dismissed." Respondent No. 1 challenged the orders of dismissal passed by the punishing authority as well as by the appellate Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 57 of 1981 and it was allowed by the learned Single Judge vide the impugned judgment dated 9th March, 1994 and it was inter alia held by the learned Single Judge as follows :  ".... A proviso has been added to Regulation 11 saying that the Disciplinary Authority will give an opportunity to the delinquent officer employee to make representation against the proposed penalty under Regulation 4. The proviso contains a salutary provision consistent with the principles of natural justice. Since the Disciplinary Authority has wide option of imposing any of the penalties mentioned in Regulation 4, it is obligatory for it to give an opportunity of hearing against the proposed punishment to the delinquent officer employee. Admittedly, in the instant case, no opportunity was afforded by the Disciplinary Authority to the petitioner before inflicting the penalty of dismissal from service. He was given an opportunity of hearing when he filed an appeal against the order of dismissal from service. This opportunity of hearing by the Appellate Authority is not a substitute for an opportunity of hearing by the Disciplinary Authority before imposing the penalty of dismissal from service. The order of dismissal from service cannot be sustained as it was passed in violation of the principles of natural justice and in violation of the first proviso to Regulation 11 of the Regulations." The appellant-Bank is not satisfied by the judgment of the learned Single Judge and has challenged it in the present appeal, mainly on the plea that the learned Single Judge has relied upon the proviso to Regulation 11 of the Punishment and Disciplinary Rules, which was introduced for the first time in the year 1988 and at the time of the passing of the impugned orders dated 20th March, 1980 and 16th December, 1980 this proviso was not in force. The Bank also took the stand in the L.P.A. that the Punishing as well as Appellate Authorities were justified in passing the order of dismissal as per Regulation 10, which was in force at the time of the awarding of the punishment and the learned Single Judge erred in holding that the Disciplinary Authority was under duty to issue a show cause notice to respondent No. 1 before passing the impugned order dated 20th March, 1980. It is also the stand of the Bank that irrespective of the fact that respondent No. 1 has been released on probation by the Chief Judicial Magistrate and that the appeal of the employee has also been dismissed by the Additional Session Judge, Ludhiana, the provisions of Section 12 of the Probation of Offenders' Act do not save the services of the employee and the Bank was justified in passing the orders of dismissal.  3. The stand of the bank was resisted by the employee in the civil writ petition primarily on the ground that the principles of natural justice have been violated by the Disciplinary Authority when he passed the impugned order dated 20th March, 1980. No doubt the Appellate Authority gave the opportunity to respondent No. 1 before passing the order dated 16th December, 1980, but this has not been done by the Punishing Authority, as a result of that a prejudice has been caused to respondent No. 1. The second stand of the employee is that on account of the probation given to him by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, his services could not be terminated on account of the provisions of Section 12 of the Probation of Offenders' Act. With above rival contentions of the parties, now the point for determination before us is whether the principles of natural justice were required to be complied with by the Bank before passing the impugned order dated 20th March, 1980 and whether respondent No. 1 can take the benefit of Section 12 of the Probation of Offenders' Act in order to save his services.  4. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and with their assistance have gone through the record of the case. Annexure P5 of the writ petition is the order dated 20th March, 1980 passed by Shri S. Subramanyam, Assistant General Manager (Disciplinary Authority), which runs as follows :-  "Shri B.R. Nayyar, Sub Accountant (under suspension) of Nizam Road, Ludhiana Branch, is hereby informed that as he has been convicted vide the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Ludhiana, order dated 19.1.1980 under Section 420 IPC in case State v. Balwant Rai, FIR No. 475/73 PS Division No. 1, Ludhiana, he is hereby dismissed from services of the Bank with immediate effect in pursuance of the provisions of Section 10 of the Banking Companies Regulations Act, 1949 as also under Regulation No. 11 of the Central Bank of India Officer Employees (Discipline & Appeal) Regulations, 1976." A perusal of the above would show that at no point of time respondent No. 1 was ever called upon by the punishing authority to show cause why the major penalty, like dismissal, be not passed against him. The perusal of the above would also show that the punishing authority was exercising its power under the provisions of Section 10 of the Banking Companies Regulations Act, 1949, as also under Regulation No. 11 of the Central Bank of India Officer Employees (Discipline & Appeal) Regulations, 1976. These regulations were having the statutory force. The relevant extract of Section 10 of the Banking Companies Regulations Act, 1949, is quoted as follows :-  "10(1) No banking company :-  (a) x x x (b) shall employ or continue the employment of any person; (1) who is or at any time has been, adjudicated insolvent, or has suspended payment or has been compounded with his creditors, or who is, or has been convicted by a criminal court of an offence involving moral turpitude." A proviso was added to Regulation No. 11 of the Central Bank of India Officer Employees (Discipline & Appeal) Regulations, 1976, in its unamended form in the year 1983, and the same is reproduced as follows :-  "Provided that the officer employee may be given an opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed to be imposed before any order is made." At the first instance we may mention that since the proviso had been added much subsequent to the impugned orders dated 20th March, 1980 and 16th December, 1980, it could not be given effect to nor the Disciplinary Authority was obliged to adhere to the provisions of the proviso as commented upon by the learned Single Judge in his judgment.  5. Now the point for determinations is whether the provisions of natural justice should be made available to the respondent in the present case or not. In this regard, we have to see the gravity of allegations against the Bank employee. As we have stated above, the respondent was convicted for an offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, though charged for other offences, such as 408, 468 and 471, Indian Penal Code. The offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code involves the allegations of moral turpitude. Respondent No. 1 was serving a Banking-institution, which is supposed to carry on business on trust, as these types of institutions are the custodians of the public money. Once an employee is involved in an offence of moral turpitude, in order to meet such exigency, Regulations 10-A, quoted above, has been incorporated. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the employee submitted that the principles of natural justice have been put at knot by the Punishing Authority and that very solemnity of the principles of natural justice has been flouted and as such, the judgment of learned Single Judge should be upheld.  6. On the contrary, learned counsel for the appellant drew our attention to the proviso added to Article 311 of the Indian Constitution and submitted that the Legislature has introduced this proviso keeping in view the public policy and therefore, the principles of natural justice would not come into play at the level of the Punishing Authority once the Punishing Authority has taken notice of the fact that by virtue of Article 10, the employee is not entitled to be heard at the time of awarding the sentence. Even otherwise, the punishment imposed by the Punishing Authority is not disproportionate with the charge proved. We are in agreement with the submission raised by learned counsel for the appellant. In Union of India and another v. Tulsiram Patel, 1995(2) Services Law Reporter 576, while dealing with the scope of natural justice in such like cases, as in the instant case, the Hon'ble Supreme Court was pleased to hold that a government servant convicted of an offence of moral turpitude is not entitled to any opportunity of being heard, before taking any decision by the Punishing Authority and the objective consideration before passing the punishment was not necessary. The only requirement on the part of the Punishing Authority is whether the conduct of the employee, which has led to his conviction, was such as warrants imposition of penalty and if so, what that penalty should be. In order to reach this conclusion all the facts and circumstances of the case and various factors, as set out in Challappan case, should be taken into consideration.  7. The guidelines of the said case were taken into consideration while passing the order dated March 20, 1980. The Punishing Authority took into consideration that the bank-employee was convicted for an offence punishable under Section 420, Indian Penal Code, and this order has been passed in conformity with Regulation 10, to which there is no challenge from the side of the respondent.  8. The next point, which now remains in the present appeal for our determination, is whether any benefit could be given to the respondent- employee for the fact that he was released on probation by the Chief Judicial Magistrate while imposing the sentence of punishment. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the benefit of probation granted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate does not remove the stigma of conviction and Section 12 of the Probation of Offenders' Act does not come to the rescue of respondent No. 1. Irrespective of the fact that respondent No. 1 was released on probation, the management was competent to proceed for those conducts of respondent No. 1 which led to his conviction and the orders passed by the Punishing Authority as well as by the Appellate Authority were perfectly justified and legal. For the sake of convenience we would like to reproduce the provisions of Section 12 of the Probation of Offenders' Act, which are as follows :-  "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, a person found guilty of an offence and dealt with under provisions of section 3 or section 4 shall not suffer disqualifications, if any, attaching to a conviction of an offence under any law. Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to a person who, after his release under Section 4, is subsequently sentenced for the original offence." On the contrary it was submitted by the learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 1 that once a person has been released on probation, such person does not suffer from any disqualification attaching to his conviction of an offence under any law and that the Banking Authorities were not justified in proceeding against respondent No. 1 under the disciplinary rules. We have given deep thought to this matter also and are of the view that release of the offender on probation does not obliterate the stigma of conviction on such person. An employee is not entitled to reinstatement in service automatically by getting the benefit of probation of good conduct. In this regard we are fortified by a judgment of the Supreme Court reported as Union of India and others v. Bakshi Ram, AIR 1990 SC 987, where it was held as under :-  "In criminal trial the conviction is one thing and sentence is another. The departmental punishment for misconduct is yet a third one. This Court while invoking the provisions of Section 3 or 4 of the Act does not deal with the conviction; it only deals with the sentence which the offender has to undergo. Instead of sentencing the offender, the Court releases him on probation of good conduct. The conviction, however, remains untouched and the stigma of conviction is not obliterated. In the departmental proceedings the delinquent could be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which had led to his conviction on a criminal charge; Section 12 of the Act does not preclude the department from taking action for misconduct leading to the offence or to his conviction thereon as per law. The Section was not intended to exonerate the person from Departmental punishment. Case law discussed." Conviction in a criminal charge and release of the accused on probation does not exonerate such offender from the stigma leading to his conviction. No part of Section 12 of the Probation of Offender's Act is intended to exonerate a Government servant of his liability to departmental punishment for misconduct. The provisions of Section 12 do not afford immunity against the disciplinary proceedings for the original misconduct. What formed basis of the punishment was the misconduct and not the conviction. Also it is not necessary that the offence of which the employee was convicted must involve a moral turpitude. Counsel for respondent No.1 placed reliance on Om Prakash v. The Director Postal Services (Posts and Telegraphs Department) Punjab Circle, Ambala, AIR 1973 Punjab and Haryana 1, a Full Bench decision of this Court. Incidentally this decision was also considered in the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court quoted above, but their Lordships were pleased to hold :-  "..... Apparently, such a view has no support by the terms of Section 12 and the order of the High Court cannot, therefore, be sustained." Thus we are not in agreement with the learned counsel appearing for respondent No. 1 that by virtue of the probation granted to his client by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, the departmental action was not justified in proceeding against him.  In the light of the above discussions, we have been left with no other option but to accept this appeal, setting aside the judgment dated 9th March, 1994, passed by learned Single judge in Civil Writ Petition No. 57 of 1981.  Consequently this appeal is allowed. The judgment of learned Single Judge is set aside, as a result of which Civil Writ Petition No. 57 is also hereby dismissed. No order as to costs.
summary: A. Constitution of India, Article 311 - Banking Companies Regulations Act, 1949, Section 10(1) - Moral turpitude - Conviction in moral turpitude - Dismissal from service - A bank employee convicted of cheating in the course of employment is guilty of moral turpitude, and therefore, not entitled to be heard by virtue of the proviso (b) (1) to Section 10 of Banking Companies Regulations Act, which was introduced keeping in view the public policy - Principles of natural justice would not come into play at the level of punishing authority - A Govt. servant convicted of an offence of moral turpitude is not entitled to any opportunity of being heard before passing the punishment order [Para 6]  B. Constitution of India, Article 311 - Probation of Offenders' Act, Section 12 - Conviction - Release on probation - Release on probation does not erase the conviction - An employee is not automatically entitled to reinstatement in service by getting the benefit of probation - Section 12 of the Act does not exonerate a Govt. Servant of his liability to departmental punishment for misconduct and does not afford immunity against the disciplinary proceedings for the misconduct - The offence need not involve moral turpitude.  [Paras 8]

text: T.H.B. Chalapathi, J. - Invoking the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the petitioner is seeking issuance of a writ of certiorari to quash the order dated 30th November, 1992 terminating the services of the husband of the petitioner and also to issue a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to release the consequential benefits.  2. The husband of the petitioner joined Haryana Roadways in March, 1968. While working as a Driver in the Haryana Roadways, he met with an accident on 23.6.1988 and sustained injuries on the head and both bones of his right leg were fractured. He was admitted in the Hospital and remained under treatment till 14.2.1989. The husband of the petitioner joined the duty on 1.5.1989, but due to his injury to the right leg, he could not perform his duties efficiently. Thereafter he remained on leave from 25.2.1991 to 25.2.1992. Though the petitioner's husband requested the authorities to give him light work, the authorities of the respondent-department insisted that he should perform his duty as a Driver. The petitioner's husband made a representation to the authorities to permit him to take voluntary retirement on 1.10.1992, but his request was rejected. Thereafter the department instituted a departmental enquiry under Rule 7 of the Punishment and Appeal Rules. The enquiry proceeded ex parte and on the basis of the enquiry report, the husband of the petitioner was issued a show cause notice why his services should not be terminated. Thereafter the impugned order dated 30.11.1992 was passed by the authorities terminating the services of the petitioner's husband. The husband of the petitioner preferred an appeal to the 2nd respondent which was also dismissed on 11.10.1995. Subsequently, the petitioner's husband submitted another appeal to the Government. Meanwhile the husband of the petitioner died on 29.5.1996. After the death of the petitioner's husband, she approached the authorities to release the pension of her husband since her husband put in service of 24 years. Challenging the order of termination and seeking direction to release pension to the husband of the petitioner, the petitioner filed this writ petition.  3. In the written statement, it is admitted that the petitioner's husband met with an accident and sustained injuries. But according to the respondents, the husband of the petitioner was declared medically fit for duty and, therefore, he was asked to perform his duty as a Driver, but the petitioner's husband pleaded lame excuses to perform his duty for which he was recruited. In spite of notice, the petitioner's husband was not present and, therefore, the enquiry was proceeded ex parte and on the basis of the report of the Enquiry Officer the services of the petitioner's husband were terminated and there are no grounds warranting interference with the same.  4. The fact remains that the petitioner's husband while working as a Driver in Haryana Roadways was involved in an accident resulting in injury to his head and fracture of both the bones of his right leg. The report of the Medical authorities also shows that there was a shortening of the leg. After the discharge from the Hospital and availing of leave and taking rest, the petitioner's husband resumed the duty, but the petitioner's husband was asked to drive the vehicle. The petitioner's husband pleaded with the authorities that he was not fit to drive the vehicle in view of the fracture to his leg in the accident and therefore, he be assigned some light work, but the authorities insisted that he should perform the duties of a Driver for which he was recruited. Even in the written statement, the stand of the respondents is that the husband of the petitioner was avoiding to do the duties for which he was recruited. There cannot be any dispute that a person who suffered injury to his leg should not be allowed to drive a passenger vehicle since his driving capacity was not the same as used to be prior to his suffering the injury to his right leg. It can be seen from the record produced that the husband of the petitioner had been making representations time and again to give him light work due to his incapacity to drive the heavy vehicle owing to weakness in his right leg. He had also pointed out that it involved risk to the precious life of the passengers. It is also on record that the petitioner's husband sought the voluntary retirement on 1.10.1992, but instead of acceding to his request for voluntary retirement, the Department has chosen to proceed against him departmentally and ultimately terminated his services by the impugned order. The appeal filed by the petitioner's husband was also rejected on 11.10.1995. The petitioner's husband died on 29.5.1996. That necessitated the petitioner to approach this court seeking the relief of quashing the order of termination of her husband and to release the pension and family pension.  5. In these circumstances of the case, I am of the opinion that the order of termination cannot be sustained. It is not a case where the driver was guilty of any misconduct. He genuinely made a request to the authorities that he was not able to drive the heavy vehicle at the risk of the life of the passengers since he suffered a fracture to his right leg. When the petitioner's husband was not able to perform the duty, he sought voluntary retirement. In all fairness the Department should have acceded to his request for voluntary retirement.  6. During the course of arguments, the learned Additional Advocate General, Mr. P.K. Mutneja sought for time to get instructions from the Department in view of the facts and peculiar circumstances of this case and fairly stated that the case of the petitioner's husband should have been considered on sympathetic grounds since the petitioner's husband suffered injuries while on duty. Accordingly, the hearing of the case was adjourned. On the next date of hearing, the learned Advocate General produced a letter from the Transport Commissioner, Haryana, to Advocate General, Haryana, bearing No. 1315/A- 2/DA/98 dated 22.2.1998, wherein it has been stated as follows :-  "Keeping in view the observation of the Hon'ble Punjab and Haryana High Court, Chandigarh about the quantum of punishment the case of the petitioner has been considered sympathetically and this office has no reservation, if the punishment of termination of services of the deceased husband of the petitioner is substituted to that of administering the warning and of accepting the voluntary retirement of the deceased husband of the petitioner from the date his services were terminated by treating the period of absence from duty of the deceased as leave of the kind due." In view of the stand taken by the Transport Commissioner, Haryana, and in the circumstances of the case, I feel that it is just and proper in the interests of justice to set aside the order of termination and substitute the same with a warning and to accept the voluntary retirement of the husband of the petitioner from the date when his services were terminated by treating the period of absence from duty as leave of the kind due. In case the petitioner's husband was not having leave to his credit for the entire period of absence, the same may be treated as extraordinary leave and on that basis the pensionary benefits of the petitioner's husband should be calculated and the petitioner be paid all the arrears of pension within two months from the date of receipt of this order and also grant the Family Pension to the petitioner in accordance with the rules.  The writ petition is, accordingly, disposed of. No order as to costs.  Petition allowed..
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 21 and 311 - Termination - Absence from duty - The petitioner's husband, a driver in Haryana Roadways, was injured in an accident and unable to perform his duty as a driver due to his fractured leg. Despite his requests for alternative light duty being turned down and his subsequent absence from work, his voluntary retirement request was declined and his services were terminated. The court found the authority's actions unjustified and substituted the termination order with acceptance of voluntary retirement, directing the release of retiral benefits and pension with arrears and grant of family pension to the petitioner. [Paras 4 to 6]

text: B.L. Hansaria, J. - Kerala State Electricity Board, hereinafter the `Board', had one common establishment prior to 1964. A need having been fell to have a separate and distinct establishment, named as secretariat establishment, the same came to be formed with effect from 1.4.1964, vide order of the Board dated 31.3.1964. With a view to ensure smooth functioning of the Secretariat Service so formed, the Board, in exercise of power conferred by section 79(c)(k) of the Electricity (Supply) Act, made certain regulations which, inter alia, laid done the principle of inter-se seniority in its clause VII reading as below:  "VII. The inter se seniority of all categories of persons so appointed initially to the Secretariat will be determined and finalised with reference to the relative general seniority they held in the parent department and their services in the parent department will count for all purposes in the Secretariat Service also." 2. It was, however, felt that the separate service was not conducive to the smooth and efficient discharge of the administrative functions of the Board; and so, by order dated 14.1.1981 the separate and independent status of the Secretariat Service was brought to an end by making regulations called the Kerala State Electricity Board (Integration of Board Secretariat Establishment and General Establishment) Regulations, 1981. In these regulations the principle of seniority was laid down as below in clause 5(c):  "5(c). Subject to clause (f), relative seniority of persons drawn from the Secretarial Establishment and General Establishment including Accounts Wing and holding equated posts shall be determined on the basis of their length of service in the cadre/category concerned at the time of integration." 3. This principle was a mended to read as below by order of 7.11.1985: "(a) xxx xxx xxx (b) The relative seniority of persons drawn from the secretariat establishment and the general establishment including the Accounts Wing shall be determined based on their ranking in the advice list of the Kerala Public Service Commission or the Board, as the case may be, at the time of initial recruitment by the Kerala Public Service Commission or the Board to the respective establishments under the Board subject to the application of rules regarding obligatory departmental tests." This virtually required length of service to be taken note of for determining inter-se seniority.  4. The High Court of Kerala was approached mainly by officers of the erstwhile Secretariat Service challenging the revised principle of seniority as laid down in 1985. The High Court, by the impugned judgment, held that the principle was hit by Article 14 as unequals were treated as equals and has, therefore, quashed the same. These appeals are by the Board and by some persons of the General Establishment.  5. Shri Poti, learned senior counsel appearing for the Board, has urged that the High Court was not justified in setting aside the principle of 1985, as such a principle had indeed been found valid by this Court in Om Parkash Sharma v. Union of India, 1985 (Supp.) SCC 218 which was wrongly distinguished by the High Court. Shri Iyer, learned senior counsel appearing for the private respondents has, however, urged that Om Parkash's case was different on facts and High Court was right in not following the same to sustain the principle of inter se seniority as spelt out in 1985.  6. In our opinion, the decision in Om Parkash's case has to be applied in the instant appeals as well, because there the accelerated promotion which some of the respondents got in the cadre of Head Clerks because the trifurcation was not required to be given weight after the different services/departments were amalgamated again. Here too, the principle of inter-se seniority in the order of 1985 has basically sought to do so the same by requiring the inter se seniority to be determined on the basis of the length of service in the cadre/category at the time of integration, and not by taking note of promotions earned in the Secretariat Service.  7. We have another reason to sustain the aforesaid principle and the same is that we are not quite satisfied if, while forming the Secretariat Service, the selection of the optees was really on the basis of merit, ability and suitability as was required to be. We have said so because the Chairman of the Board, who had played a pivotal role in the selection, had stated before the arbitrator, whose award was pressed into service by Shri Iyer and to which we shall advert later, thus : "No tests were conducted for these appointments nor interviews. The selection for this wing was made by me taking into consideration their fidelity, the confidence that I can have on them. Only persons known to me were selected." In view of this, the award of the arbitrator dated 14.3.1967 holding that there was no mala fide or victimisation while making actual selection is not much significant.  8. Shri Iyer's main concern was that the aforesaid principle of inter- se seniority, if sustained, would result in reversion of the persons who had got accelerated promotion in the Secretariat Service. This was illustrated by the learned counsel by drawing our attention to equation of posts as finding place at page 66 of the Paper Book of C.A. No. 3974/90 wherein the post of Assistant Secretary of the Secretariat Establishment has been shown as equal to Assistant Accounts Officer - the next post below whom in the General Establishment being of Senior Superintendent. Learned counsel contended that the aforesaid principle would require reversion of the Assistant Secretary of the Secretariat Service to Senior Superintendent of the General Establishment, as the latter may be senior to the former if the ranking at the time of the initial recruitment alone was to be taken into consideration. According to us, however, this is not the correct reading of the principle inasmuch as that only speaks about fixation of relative seniority, and does not visualise by reduction in rank or reversion. It may be that the following of 1985 principle would make the Assistant Secretary of the illustration junior to the Senior Superintendent, but that would not require the Assistant Secretary to be demoted to the post of Senior Superintendent.  9. In the aforesaid view of the matter, we set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court, subject to the clarification/observation made above. In the fact and circumstances of the case, we leave the parties to bear their own costs.  Appeal allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Kerala State Electricity Board (Integration of Board Secretariat Establishment and General Establishment) Regulations, Regulation 5(c) - Seniority - Integration of cadres in one common establishment - After integration, inter se seniority should be determined based on the length of service in the cadre. Promotions earned in Secretariat Service should not be the basis for seniority. Although the post of Assistant Secretary may be treated as junior to the Senior Superintendent of the General Establishment, the Rule does not allow for demotion of Asstt. Secretary to the post of Senior Superintendent. [Paras 6 and 8]

text: S.P. Kurdukar, C.J. - Admitted. Pleadings of the parties are complete. By consent the writ petition is placed on board and called out for hearing.  2. It is needless to set out in details the averments made in the petition. Suffice it to state that the petitioner was appointed as temporary engineer in Class II service and was promoted as Executive Engineer in Class I on 13.7.1971. Some time in the year 1986 a charge-sheet was served upon the petitioner relating to misconduct of the year 1982-83. During pending enquiry the petitioner came to be promoted as Superintending Engineer on 18.2.1987. The enquiry was completed by the Enquiry Officer and he submitted his report in August 1992 exonerating the petitioner. However, the formal order of dropping the charges against the petitioner came to be passed on 11.10.1993. On 21.7.1993 six Superintending Engineers came to be promoted to the rank of Chief Engineers. It is alleged by the petitioner that out of these six promoted Superintending Engineers, five persons were junior to him.  3. After having been exonerated from charges in August 1992, the petitioner on 28.7.1993 made a representation to the Chief Minister requesting him to consider his claim for promotion. On 13.10.1993 the petitioner again made another representation to the Minister concerned to consider his claim for promotion to the rank of Chief Engineer. Pending decision on these two representations, it is common premises that on 8.2.1994 a fresh charge-sheet was served upon the petitioner in respect of alleged mis-conduct of the year 1989. This mis-conduct relates to an award given by the petitioner in the year 1989. It is common premise that against the said award, FAO is pending in this Hon'ble High Court.  4. The petitioner on 10.10.1994 submitted his reply to the charge-sheet. An Enquiry Officer has been appointed and enquiry is likely to be commenced very soon.  5. Mr. Khehar, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner informed us that the petitioner is to retire on 31.5.1995.  6. The principal contention which needs to be considered in this writ petition is as to whether the State Government can ignore the claim of the petitioner for consideration of promotion to the rank of Chief Engineer after he has been exonerated on 11.10.1993 when five persons junior to him were considered and promoted on 21.7.1993 as Chief Engineers. As of that date i.e. 21.7.1993 there were neither any allegations of mis-conduct nor any charge- sheet was served or any enquiry was pending. Learned counsel for the petitioner urged that the petitioner was not considered for the post of Chief Engineer when persons junior to him were promoted on 21.7.1993, because at that time departmental enquiry was pending in respect of alleged mis-conduct of the year 1982. Mr. Khehar urged that the respondent is bound to consider the case of the petitioner for the promotional post of Chief Engineer on the date when the charges against him were dropped and if he was found suitable, he ought to be promoted to the post of Chief Engineer w.e.f. 21.7.1993 when persons junior to him (the petitioner) were promoted.  7. Mr. Arun Sekhri, Under Secretary to Government of Punjab, Irrigation & Power Department, Punjab, filed the written statement on behalf of the respondent and he admits that six Superintending Engineers were promoted on 21.7.1993 and the petitioner was ignored because departmental proceedings were/are pending against him. The only reason given by the respondent in the written statement is that since fresh enquiry is pending against the petitioner, he could not be considered for the promotional post of Chief Engineer.  8. Rule 9 of the Punjab Service of Engineers Class-I P.W.D. (Irrigation Branch) Rules 1964, is the relevant rule for the purpose of promotion in the present case. The petitioner has set out the said Rule at page 7 of the writ petition, the correctness thereof is not disputed before us.  9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and in view of the facts narrated hereinbefore, in our opinion, it was obligatory for the respondent- State of Punjab to consider the claim of the petitioner for the post of Chief Engineer when he was exonerated on 11.10.1993. The petitioner having been found `not guilty of any mis-conduct', it was necessary for the respondent to consider the petitioner's claim for the post of Chief Engineer in accordance with Rules and Regulations, particularly, Rule 9 which is set out at page 7 of the writ petition. The petitioner's claim for promotion to the post of Chief Engineer having not been considered by the respondent until second charge- sheet was served upon him on 8.2.1994, it would not be open to the respondent to take shelter of second charge-sheet dated 8.2.1994 to deny the claim of the petitioner for the post of Chief Engineer, which claim was due to him by virtue of his having been exonerated by the disciplinary authority vide order dated 11.10.1993. It is on these admitted facts, we are of the opinion that the claim of the petitioner ought to have been considered for the post of Chief Engineer some time in October 1993. Obviously he should have been considered for the post of Chief Engineer from the date his juniors were promoted as Chief Engineers.  10. We accordingly direct the respondent to constitute a Departmental Promotion Committee (D.P.C.) and submit the papers of the petitioner for consideration to the said Committee for considering his claim to the post of Chief Engineer. The Departmental Promotion Committee to complete the entire exercise preferably on or before 31.5.1995 and at any rate before 31.7.1995. If the petitioner is found suitable by the Departmental Promotion Committee in term of Rule 9, the respondent will pass appropriate order giving benefits of this promotional post of Chief Engineer from the date when his juniors were promoted i.e. 21.7.1993. This is, however, subject to the decision of the Departmental Promotion Committee.  This Writ Petition to stand disposed of in the above terms.  A copy of the order be given dasti.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Punjab Service of Engineers Class-I P.W.D. (Irrigation Branch) Rules, 1964, Rule 9 - Promotion - Departmental enquiry - Promotion to the post of Chief Engineer - The petitioner was passed over for promotion on the basis of ongoing departmental proceedings against him, but was later exonerated. After a second charge-sheet was issued, the petitioner should have been considered for promotion immediately upon exoneration and the respondents cannot argue the second charge-sheet as sufficient reason for overlooking the petitioner's promotion. The court has directed the competent authority to immediately consider the petitioner for promotion to the post of Chief Engineer. [Paras 9 and 10]

text: K. Ramaswamy, J. - The report of the Registry indicates that the service is complete. However, the respondents are not appearing either in person or through counsel.  2. Leave granted.  3. The question limited to the notice is: whether the respondent would be entitled to payment of salary under the Grant-in-Aid Scheme from the date of initial appointment till he improved his qualification or from the date of his acquiring the qualification ? The admitted position is that respondent No. 1 came to be appointed as a lecturer in 1978. The Government issued clarification on January 5, 1987 that unqualified lecturers having minimum second class, i.e.. 48% or above and below 54% of marks in P.G. examination and appointed on or after 1.8.1977 in recognised non-Government Colleges would be eligible to receive grant-in-aid. The Resolution dated September 13, 1983 issued by the Government prescribes the qualifications for recruitment of Lecturers of affiliated Colleges which indicates that "candidate not holding an M.Phil. degree should possess a high second class Master's degree, i.e., 54% marks and a second class Honours/Pass in the B.A./B.Com./B.Sc. examination." Respondent No. I secured 53.9% marks, which is almost equivalent of 54% marks, on July 10, 1987. Therefore the question arises: whether the second respondent is entitled to receive grant-in-aid for payment of salary to the first respondent from the date of his acquiring qualification or from the date of initial appointment ? Admittedly, since the first respondent on the date of his appointment was not possessing the requisite qualification and acquired the same only on July 10, 1987 he will be eligible to the benefit of the grant-in-aid w.e.f. August 1, 1987 and onwards.  4. The appeal is accordingly allowed and the order of the High Court passed on April 23, 1996 in OJC No. 3548/96. to that extent stands modified. No costs.  Appeal allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Salary - Qualification - Lecturers in college who improve their qualifications during service are entitled to receive salary under grant-in-aid from the date of improvement. [Para 3]

text: G.R. Majithia, J. - This regular second appeal is directed against the judgment and decree of the first appellate Court dated September 16, 1988, affirming on appeal those of the trial Judge dated June 4, 1987, dismissing the suit of the plaintiff-appellant for declaration that the order dated May 5, 1982, imposing the penalty of withholding of annual increment with cumulative effect was illegal.  2. The appellant is employed as a Conductor in the Punjab Roadways. General Manager, Punjab Roadways, Ferozepore, vide order bearing No. 979/TC, dated May 5, 1982, imposed the penalty of withholding three annual increments with cumulative effect. The appellant challenged the order in Civil suit bearing No. 54-a instituted on January 31, 1986. The trial court found that a regular departmental enquiry was conducted and the disciplinary authority accepted the enquiry report and imposed the punishment after following the procedure prescribed. On the question of limitation, the trial Court found that the suit was filed beyond limitation and, on ultimate analysis, it dismissed the suit. The judgment and decree of the trial Judge were challenged in the first appeal. The first appellate Court found that the order inflicting the penalty of stoppage of three increments was not a speaking order and as such was held to be illegal. On the question of limitation, the first appellate Court affirmed the finding of the trial Judge and held that the suit was filed beyond limitation. The order imposing the punishment was made on May 5, 1982 and the suit was filed on January 31, 1986. Thus, obviously it was barred by time having been filed after three years.  3. When the regular second appeal came up for motion hearing, the learned Single Judge expressed doubt about the Correctness of the judgment reported as State of Punjab v. Malkiat Chand, 1988(4) S.L.R. 243 and admitted the case to Division Bench and it is how this regular second appeal has been placed before us for disposal.  4. It is no more open to dispute that the suit of the nature as filed by the plaintiff-appellant will be governed by the residuary Articles 113 of Limitation Act, 1963. It was authoritatively laid down by the apex Court in State of Punjab and others v. Gurdev Singh, Ashok Kumar, A.I.R. 1991 S.C. 2219 : 1991(3) SCT 93 (SC), that a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal in ultra vires and will be governed by residuary Articles 113 of the Limitation Act. The question posed was answered thus :-  "It will be clear from these principles, the party aggrieved by the invalidity of the order has to approach the Court for relief of declaration that the order against him is inoperative and not binding upon him. He must approach the Court within the prescribed period of limitation. If the statutory time limit expires, the Court cannot give the declaration sought for."  After so observing, the apex Court approving the view of the Allahabad High Court and the Oudh Chief Court observed thus :-  "The Allahabad High Court in Jagdish Prasad Mathur v. United Provinces Government, AIR 1956 All. 114, has taken the view that a suit for declaration by a dismissed employee on the ground that his dismissal is void is governed by Articles 120 of the Limitation Act. A similar view has been taken by Oudh Chief Court in Abdul Vakil v. Secretary of State, AIR 1943 Oudh 368. That in our opinion is the correct view taken. A suit for declaration that an order of dismissal or termination from service passed against the plaintiff is wrongful, illegal or ultra vires is governed by Article 113 of the Limitation Act. The decision to the contrary taken by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in these and other cases (State of Punjab v. Ajit Singh, (1988) 1 Serv. LR 96 (Punj & Har) and (ii) State of Punjab v. Ram Singh, (1986) 3 Se v. L.R. 379 (Punj & Har) is not correct and stands overruled."  In the light of this authoritative pronouncement of the apex Court, it has to be held that the suit filed by the plaintiff-appellant is beyond limitation and has to be dismissed as such.  For the reason stated above, the regular second appeal fail and is dismissed, but there will be no order as to costs.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: According to Article 113 of the Limitation Act, any suit for declaration against an order of punishment imposed on an employee will be governed by the residuary Article 3 of the Limitation Act. However, if the suit is filed after three years, no declaration can be granted. [Paras 3 and 4]

text: S.B. Sinha, J. - Leave granted.  2. Inter se seniority amongst the teachers of Kumaon University is in question in this appeal which arises out of a judgment and order dated 21.3.2006 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of Uttaranchal at Nainital in Writ Petition No. 71 of 2004).  Before adverting to the aforementioned question, we may notice the factual matrix involved in the matter.  3. First Respondent was appointed on an ad hoc basis as a Lecturer in Government P.G. College, Almora by the State of Utter Pradesh through Vice- Chancellor, Kumaon University on or about 22.9.1975. The said College was declared as the Campus College of the University. All Lecturers including the first respondent were continued and treated on deputation with the University; the cut off date wherefor was fixed 16.8.1977. The State of Utter Pradesh framed U.P. Regularization Rules, 1979, the relevant provisions whereof reads as under :  4. (i) Any person who (i) was directly appointed on ad hoc basis before 1.1.1977 and is continuing in service. (ii) Possessed requisite qualification prescribed for regular appointment at the time of such ad hoc appointment, and (iii) Has completed or, as the case may be, after he has completed three years continuous service. Shall be considered for regular appointment in permanent or temporary vacancy as may be available on regular appointment is made in such vacancy in accordance with the relevant service rules or orders." 4. Pursuant to and in furtherance of the said Rules, services of 355 ad hoc Lecturers were regularized. However, the cases of nine Lecturers including the first respondent, who had been working on deputation, were left out. It is contended that one Savita (Mohan) Dhondiyal who had also been appointed as an ad hoc Lecturer on 17.4.1975 and, thus, being junior to the first respondent was regularized.  5. Representations were made by the respondents and others. The Directorate of Higher Education, Uttar Pradesh asked the Vice-Chancellor of the University to forward the list of the said Lecturers pursuant whereto, services of nine Lecturers including the respondent were regularized by an order dated 11.7.1980, stating :  "The appointing authority in exercise of powers conferred by Rule 5 of the Regularisation of Ad hoc Employees on the posts within the jurisdiction of the U.P. Public Service Commission Rules, 1979 issued by the Department of Personnel vide its Notification No. 19/8/75[1] dated 14th May, 1979, and in view of the recommendations made by the Selection Committee constituted for regularization of the ad hoc lecturers working in various Government Colleges under the Directorate of Education prior to 1st January, 1977 in the pay scale of 700-1600, hereby regularizes appointments of the lecturers with effect from the date of issuance of this order and they are being given temporarily regular appointments on the posts of Lecturers w.e.f. 11th July, 1980. However, the seniority of these lecturers shall be according to their Serial number given in the enclosed Annexure and they will be junior to those lecturers who have been regularized and appointed prior to the date of regular appointment of these lecturers." 6. Aggrieved by the said order, they made a representation.  7. By an order dated 9.6.1988, the services of the respondent were appointed with effect from 1.7.1983, it was stated :  "Following officers of the Government Colleges working as Lecturers in Botany Science in the pay scale of 2200-4000 are hereby appointed on probation period of two years on the same dates with effect from the dates mentioned against their names and their earlier services would be counted towards this probation period and they are hereby regularized on the said post and in the same pay scale. However, their seniority would be determined later on. Sr. No. Name and designation of Officer who has BEEN regularised Date of regularized Details of vacancies 1-20 XX XX XX 21. Shri Madan Mohan Joshi Lecturer in Botany Science 1.7.1983 8. The State of Uttarakhand then known as State of Uttaranchal has been curved out from the State of Uttar Pradesh. In the seniority list, the first respondent was placed at serial number 137 whereas Mrs. Savita (Mohan) Dhondyal was placed at serial No. 102. Objections were filed to the said seniority list wherefor recommendations were made by the Directorate of Higher Education in the following terms :  "Dr. Joshi was appointed on ad hoc basis and pursuant to his appointment he joined Almora College on 22nd September, 1975. Later on his services were approved by the Director of Education (Higher Education), Uttar Pradesh, Allahabad on 27th March, 1976 with effect from the date of his joining the post. His name in the seniority list would have been mentioned at Sr.No. 102 after the name of Smt. Deveshwari Bisht on the basis of his order of first appointment. But it would have been possible if his name would have been considered in the order of regularization dated 22nd May, 1980. It appears that his name was not included in the said order dated 22nd May, 1980 although Shri Joshi was fully eligible for being considered in the said order dated 22nd May, 1980 according to the Regularisation Rules of 1979. Therefore, if the Government so wishes, his order of regularization dated 11th July, 1980 should be amended to the above effect." 9. A writ petition was filed by the first respondent before the High Court of Uttaranchal at Nainital which by reason of the impugned judgment has been allowed.  10. Mr. Gopal Subramanium, learned Additional Solicitor General appearing on behalf of the State, would submit that the High Court committed a serious error insofar as it failed to take into consideration that the State Uttaranchal, having framed the Uttaranchal Higher Education (Group A) Service Rules, was bound by the provisions thereof and in that view of the matter, the High Court committed a serious error insofar as it failed to take into consideration the effect of the statutory rules governing the field in their proper perspectives.  11. Mr. Garg, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent, on the other hand, would contend that as the instant case is governed by the Rules which were applicable prior to coming into force of 2003 Rules, the High Court has not committed any illegality or the impugned judgment is unassailable.  12. It was contended that in the writ petition it was not necessary for the first respondent even to implead the said Savita (Mohan) Dhondyal and others as party respondents, as no relief had been claimed against them.
