(iii) A person who has passed the test in any of the first five chances and is appointed by promotion to the post of Assistant against the existing vacancy, he will be assigned the seniority in the cadre of Assistants in accordance with his seniority in the appointment from which he has been promoted to the post of Assistant. (iv) If a person does not qualify the test in any of the first five chances but qualifies the test in any of the chances from 6th to 10th and is appointed by promotion to the post of Assistant he will not be entitled to assignment of seniority in the cadre of Assistants in accordance with his seniority in the appointment from which he had been appointed by promotion to the post of Assistant and he will be assigned seniority in the cadre of Assistant from the date he was appointed by promotion as such." 7. During the course of hearing of these writ petitions, it was brought to our notice that the petitioners were not promoted as Assistants although they has passed the qualifying test prior to the private respondents and the vacancies of Assistants were available. The factual assertion has not been controverted by the State. The instructions issued by the State Government which are inconsistent with the rule of law laid down above are declared invalid.  8. Before we part with this judgment, in fairness to Mr. K.K. Jagia, counsel for the petitioners, Mr. Jagia's challenge to the proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 be dealt with. Proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 reads thus :-  "Provided that if such a person fails to qualify the test within the aforesaid first five chances, he shall, on his promotion to the post of Assistant, be assigned seniority in the cadre of Assistants from the day he is promoted as such." According to Mr. Jagia, this proviso is arbitrary. He says that if a person can qualify the test in any number of chances, the proviso nullifies those provisions and makes the same ineffective. The submission is devoid of any merit. The proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 10 relates to safeguarding the seniority, while Rule 8 provides for number of chances which can be availed by eligible persons for passing the test. The object of the proviso is that if a person qualifies the test in any of the first five chances, he maintains his seniority in the appointment from which he has been promoted to the post of Assistant. If he does not qualify the test in the first five chances, he will be assigned seniority in the cadre of Assistants from the day he is promoted as such. A person may make himself eligible for appointment by promotion to the post of Assistant by passing the test in any number of chances. But, if he wants to retain his original seniority in the appointment from which he has been promoted to the post of Assistant, he has to qualify the test in first five chances, failing which he will be assigned the seniority in the cadre of Assistants from the day he is promoted as such. We do not find any arbitrariness in the proviso to sub-rule (2) of Rule 10. In fact, this proviso has been inserted for achieving the purpose for which the Rules have been enacted and to create a competitive set-up out of which more brilliant people may come up to man the Service.  For the reasons stated above, the writ petitions are disposed of. The official respondents are directed to give effect to this judgment within six months.  Order disposed of.
summary: The Rules must be interpreted together so that they can be enforced harmoniously, giving effect to each rule's words, indicating the framers' intent. After promotion from the feeder cadre, seniority in the Assistant cadre is linked with the passing of the Assistant Grade Examination, as per the Punjab State Assistant Grade Examination Rules, 1984. If an individual passes the test in any of the first five attempts, they keep their seniority in the feeder cadre, and those who pass in attempts six through ten obtain seniority from their appointment as an Assistant. If a person passes the test in the first five chances and is appointed to an available Assistant position, they will join the cadre with their seniority from their feeder cadre appointment. If a person passes the test after their first five chances, they will get seniority on their appointment as an Assistant. Those who pass the test in the first five attempts and are appointed as an Assistant get their seniority from their feeder cadre appointment. The person appointed by promotion when no posts are available is appointed based on seniority from those who passed the test, regardless of the number of chances they took.

text: Basudeva Panigrahi, J. - This writ petition has been filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India against respondents, particularly respondent Nos. 3 and 4 by making a prayer therein to issue confirmation letter in favour of the petitioner for the post of Assistant Teacher (Physical Training) in terms of the service condition as laid down in the Code of Regulation for Anglo Indian and other listed schools 1993 and to disburse the full salary in her favour as per the condition of services of staff. The petitioner has stated inter alia that she was appointed as an Assistant Teacher (P.T.) in Saint Joseph Convent School, Chandannagore, against a regular vacancy since 3rd April, 1996. The respondent No. 3 has been receiving dearness allowance from the Government of West Bengal and also performing a public duty. Pursuant to a regular vacancy of an assistant teacher (physical training) in the Saint Joseph Convent School, the petitioner had, thus, applied and was successful in interview followed by a letter of appointment on and from 3rd April, 1996. As per the regulation No. 21 sub-regulation (a) thereof, ordinarily a teacher appointed against a permanent vacancy should be confirmed within one year from the date of appointment but the probation period may be extended by a further period of one year. If no such extension has been made, the said teacher shall be deemed to be confirmed in that appointment. The petitioner was since appointed on 3rd April, 1996 against a regular vacancy, her probation expired on or from about 2nd April, 1997. No notice for a further probation period of one year was served upon her within 2nd April, 1997. Therefore, it is according to the petitioner to presume that she was deemed to have been regularly appointed after expiry of the probation period. The management allowed the petitioner a sum of Rs. 2,500/- consolidated pay per month. Initially she was given a consolidated salary of Rs. 2,000/- per month which was subsequently enhanced to Rs. 3,500/-. Therefore, she made a representation before the management to allow her the usual salary as other teaching staff were receiving. The respondent No. 4 seems to have sent a reply on 1st March, 1999 that her case would be considered after the respondent No. 4 would be free from the burden of process of examination of the students. Even thereafter the petitioner did not receive any positive reply, therefore, her apprehension was gradually hardened into true that she had been discriminated compared to other teaching staff. She also received similar reply on 17th March, 1999. Thus in the aforementioned situation she was forced to file the present case. The school authority, namely the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 have filed an application for vacating the interim stay which was subsequently treated as affidavit in opposition. They strongly disputed and denied that the petitioner was appointed as a permanent staff in a permanent vacancy and was kept on probation. The respondents have, further, claimed that the petitioner having come to the court with unclean hands by making untrue and misleading statement deliberately in order to get the ex parte order as would be evident from the facts and documents in affidavit in opposition such interim order should be vacated.  2. The need for a temporary appointment of an assistant teacher in physical training arose during the pendency of litigation by two permanent physical training teachers Mrs. Kavita Neogi and Mrs. Kajali Bhattachariya against whom the disciplinary proceedings were initiated and they were placed under suspension by the School authority in 1993. Those two teachers had further challenged the order of suspension in the Civil Court of Chandannagore and obtained an order of injunction. As a result, they have continued to enjoy the benefits without work. Challenging the aforesaid order passed by the court below, the respondents had filed a civil revision in C.O. No. 1909 of 1998. In the aforesaid circumstances when there was no physical training assistant teacher in the school, therefore, the management deemed it proper to manage the Classes, issued an order of appointment on 3rd April, 1996 to the petitioner for a period from 1st April, 1996 till the end of the session, i.e. the last day of March, 1997 on a consolidated salary.  3. The respondents have further stated that on expiry of the term of appointment the petitioner was appointed again on a purely temporary basis on 1st April, 1997 till the end of March, 1998. The second letter of appointment will indicate the terms and conditions of appointment and the petitioner has agreed to such terms by putting her signature. Those facts have been suppressed by the petitioner and she has unreasonably held back the appointment letter deliberately.  4. By a letter dated 6th August, 1998 the petitioner was informed that her agreement with the managing committee as an assistant teacher for physical training is renewed for the present academic year 1998-99. Had these appointment letters been brought to the notice of the court while the petitioner moved the interim injunction, possibly, the court could have declined to grant any interim relief. Since the petitioner seeks equitable relief she should not have behaved in the manner as she did in this case. Therefore, her application should be dismissed on that ground alone.  5. Mr. Banerjee, the learned Advocate appearing for the writ petitions had vehemently argued that the petitioner was appointed against a permanent vacancy and she has been continuing till today, no condition was mentioned in her appointment letter that the petitioner shall serve in a leave vacancy. She is working in an approved sanction post. Before issuing the order of appointment to the petitioner the managing committee scrupulously and meticulously followed the recruitment procedure. But when she claimed usual salary in par with the other teaching staff, possibly, the managing committee did not appreciate the claim of the petitioner, therefore, they unlawfully, whimsically and illegally wanted to get rid of the petitioner.  6. Mr. Sarkar, the learned Advocate appearing for the Managing Committee has, however, argued with strong intensity of conviction that the petitioner having suppressed the material facts in the writ petition by not stating that she was appointed in a temporary vacancy, her writ petition on that ground alone should be dismissed. She has not come to the court with clean hands while withholding the letter of appointment which would disclose that her appointment was only for one year. The second appointment was also on the same term. The third appointment revealed that the petitioner would serve for a temporary period. Therefore, the petitioner does not have any lien of service and accordingly the writ petition should be dismissed. The expression probation has not been mentioned in the appointment letter. Regulation 21A of the regulation has laid down the procedure for appointment in the case of a temporary vacancy. Regulation 21C had laid down the procedure in respect of permanent vacancy and there may be a situation for keeping a staff appointed against a permanent vacancy under probation. Regulation 21E will hold the field in case of a permanent vacancy. The Clauses in the appointment letter would, however, reveal that the petitioner was appointed on temporary basis by mentioning the period therein. Therefore, in the aforesaid situation the petitioner has to be treated to have been employed for a temporary period.  7. While examining the rival contentions advanced by both parties, it is necessary to go in depth about Clause 21 of Code of Regulation Anglo Indian and other listed Schools 1993. Both parties have admitted that the said Regulation is applicable to this case.  8. Regulation 21 is quoted hereunder :-  "Appointment of all categories of staff shall be made as per rules framed by the founder. Every employee, whether a teaching or a non-teaching staff, shall be engaged by a letter of appointment which shall state clearly the type of employment offered - Permanent, temporary or against a leave vacancy. The letter of appointment shall describe the nature of the duties, salary and emoluments, term for which the employment is offered, the period of probation, if any, requirement of training and manner of termination of the appointment. In the case of an appointment against a permanent vacancy, the terms and conditions of appointment, salary, initial salary and retiring benefits shall be stated clearly in writing and shall be signed by both the parties and returned to the school. A copy of the same shall be given to the teacher for future reference. Ordinarily, a teacher appointed against a permanent vacancy will be placed on probation, a letter terminating the service or extending the period of probation, as the case may be, shall be served to him/her, one month before the end of the probationary period filling which, the teacher will be deemed to be confirmed in that appointment." 9. The petitioner has, however, not enclosed any letter of appointment issued by the managing committee. The respondent 4 and 5 have placed the xerox copy of the appointment letter dated 3.4.96. In the appointment letter it has been clearly stated that the petitioner was appointed on a purely temporary basis for a period from 1.4.96 to end of March, 1997 at Rs. 2,000/- per month. It has been further laid down that during the period of appointment the managing committee of the school will be entitled to terminate the service even before the expiry of the period for which the petitioner was appointed without assigning any reason whatsoever upon one month notice in writing. In the appointment letter the petitioner as well as the Headmistress of School had signed. Similarly, she was appointed temporarily from 1st April, 1997 till 1st March, 1998 at Rs. 2,460/- upon same terms and conditions including the termination of service. The managing committee further issued a notice that the petitioner's service was no longer required after 31st March, 1999. The managing committee does not wish to re-appoint her.  10. From the Regulation it is crystal clear that the letter of appointment shall precisely describe the nature of duties, the salary and emoluments, terms on which the employment is offered. From the xerox copy of the letter of appointment, it has been disclosed that it was for temporary period for one year and after expiry of one year a fresh letter of appointment was given for a further period of one year. The appointment letter, however, is silent as regards the period of probation. In case of appointment against a permanent vacancy the appointment order should further disclose salary, all allowances, initial salary and the retirement benefits. In such case it should be signed by both parties. Therefore, those terms are conspicuously absent in the appointment letter. The respondent Nos. 3 and 4, however, have advanced a contention that since there are two cases pending in respect of assistant teacher in physical training there was pressing exigency for appointing a temporary teacher to obviate the said impasse.  11. Mr. Banerjee has relied upon a decision reported in 1997 (II) page 613 in the case of Don Bosko School and another v. Luton Thakur and others and has contended that the managing committee cannot claim an unlimited right to run the institution in accordance with their own whims. "The administration does not, however, include maladiminstration". Such privilege is not a unfettered right but is subject to the principle of equality in the eye of law natural justice, impartiality and human rights. On a careful reading of the facts of that case I found Luton Thakur was appointed as a permanent teacher after expiry of probation but thereafter his services were terminated without following any disciplinary proceedings. Therefore, there was such occasion for the court to heavily comment upon the managing committee. But in this case I found from the terms of appointment that the writ petitions was favoured with an order of appointment for a specific term and after its expiry she was further given a fresh appointment. The terms of the appointment also clearly envisaged that it could be terminated even during the continuance of term with one month salary. Therefore, in my considered view after expiry of the term, the petitioner cannot claim any legal right against the management to confirm her in the said post.  12. The petitioner having been appointed against a suspended or vacancy for a temporary period not even on probation, therefore, she cannot claim right to be appointed permanently. Thus I do not find any merit in the writ petition. Accordingly the same is dismissed but in the circumstances without costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: The petitioner for the post of Assistant Teacher (Physical Training) in terms of service conditions claims confirmation, however, the appointment letter only specified a temporary period of one year and then a further period of one year. The absence of salary, allowances, initial salary, and retirement benefits in the appointment letter leads to the conclusion that deemed confirmation cannot be inferred, and the petitioner has no right to be appointed permanently, having been appointed against a temporary vacancy. The Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16, and 226, along with the Code of Regulations for Anglo Indian and Other Listed Schools, 1993, Clause 21 are all pertinent documents in this case. [Paras 10, 11, and 12]

text: S.S. Subramani, J. - Third respondent is a School Assistant Grade II in the petitioner-School. Vacancy arose in the School for the post of School Assistant (Science). Third respondent has been working as a Secondary Grade Teacher. He is a Graduate and has passed B.Ed. Even though the third respondent had the requisite qualification fixed, the School did not think of appointing him to that post in view of the fact that the third respondent was not vigilant in the performance as teacher. He achieved only poor results. It is also said that the petitioner did not think of promoting the third respondent to the newly created post and the fourth respondent was preferred, who is also qualified to hold the same post. He is also a graduate in Science and also holds a degree in Education. Fourth respondent has also previous experience in a post analogous to the post of School Assistant and has handled higher classes with credit in other schools. On the basis of the credentials of the fourth respondent and also taking into consideration the previous experience, petitioner appointed the fourth respondent as School Assistant by direct recruitment.  2. The same was challenged by third respondent by filing a petition before the Grievance Committee of Arch Diocese of Pondicherry and Cuddalore on 15.1.1993. Petitioner placed all documents before the Grievance Committee. The Grievance Committee did not think of interfering in the appointment of fourth respondent. Thereafter, third respondent filed an Appeal before second respondent under Rule 7(iii) of the Government Aided Private School Teachers (Discipline, Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1959, praying for setting aside the appointment of fourth respondent as School Assistant and for directing the Management to consider the third respondent for promotion to the post of School Assistant. Second respondent allowed the Appeal of third respondent and directed the petitioner to appoint him as School Assistant. The same is challenged in this writ petition by petitioner-School, wherein it has prayed for issuance of a writ of certiorari or any other appropriate writ, order or direction in the nature of a writ calling for the records relating to the proceedings of 2nd respondent in No. 44956/GIAD/U-1/Edn./93-94 dated 30.6.1994, quash the same and pass such further or other orders as this Court may deem fit and proper.  3. In the various grounds raised in the writ petition, it is said that the School is a minority institution and the question as to who should be appointed to a post is really a matter governing the establishment and management of the School under Art. 30 of the Constitution of India. It is further said that the Appeal filed by third respondent itself was not maintainable, and second respondent has also no jurisdiction to pass the impugned Order. It is further said that the third respondent cannot claim the post as of right. Usually only the Management selects a candidate, and it is only in rare cases the seat is filled by promotion. Even in the case of promotion, third respondent can only have his name considered, but cannot insist that he should be appointed. Being a minority institution, when two persons are qualified to hold a post, petitioner must be given a choice of appointing the suitable person. It is also said that as between third respondent and fourth respondent, a comparative assessment has been made, and third respondent was found not suitable to hold the post and, therefore, the selection of fourth respondent is correct.  4. Counter-affidavit has been filed by third respondent, disputing the claim put forward by petitioner. According to him, he has got better experience than fourth respondent, and during his entire career, not even a single memo has been issued to him stating that he is inefficient. It is also said that he has got more experience than the fourth respondent. Third respondent has qualified himself as a B.Ed. Teacher even in the year 1988, whereas fourth respondent qualified himself only in the year 1990. The contention that second respondent has no jurisdiction to entertain the Appeal is also disputed. A further contention is taken that whenever a vacancy of School Assistant Grade II arises, mostly the same is filled up by the senior-most teacher who is already working in the School. According to him, order of second respondent is not liable to be interfered with, and the same is based on materials. The Authority has taken into consideration only the qualification and experience of third respondent. Interest of justice also requires that the Order of second respondent should be confirmed. He prayed for dismissal of the writ petition.  5. Heard learned counsel for all the parties.  6. One of the arguments that was raised by learned counsel for petitioner- School is that the second respondent has no jurisdiction to pass the impugned Order. After the fourth respondent was appointed, third respondent represented to the Grievance Committee. Since it did not take any decision, appeal was filed under Rule 7(iii) of the Government Aided Private School Teachers (Discipline, Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1959. The Appeal was presented before the Appellate Tribunal (Education Department), Pondicherry.  7. Learned Counsel for petitioner brought to my notice Rule 6 in Annexure I of Government Aided Private School Teachers (Discipline, Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1959, pertaining to the constitution of an Appellate Tribunal. That Rule says that all appeals against orders of the Punishing Authority will be heard by an Appellate Tribunal consisting of the Director of Education (Chairman) and two non-official members, namely (i) a Manager of an aided school (representing the Managers' Association) and (ii) a Principal/Headmaster of an Aided School (representing teachers), both to be nominated by the Chief Commissioner. For this purpose, the Managers' Association as well as the Recognised Teachers' Association of Aided Schools shall be asked to submit a panel of five names each out of whom the Chief Commissioner will nominate members of the Appellate Tribunal. The Manager and the Principal/Headmaster of a School to which the dispute relates shall not function as Members of the Appellate Tribunal when that case is heard. Rule 7 of that Annexure-I reads thus :-  "7. Appeal : (i) No appeal shall lie against any order or punishment specified in Clause (i) of Rule I. (ii) A teacher may make an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal in respect of penalties referred to in the Clauses (ii) to (vii) of Rule I. (iii) A teacher may also appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against an order of the Management which denies or varies to his disadvantage his pay, allowances and other conditions of service. (iv) No appeal shall lie against the decision of the Appellate Tribunal." 8. Annexure I deals with Government Aided Private School Teachers (Discipline, Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1959. On going by the relevant portions of Rules 6 and 7, and taking into consideration the purpose of the Rules, I do not think that an Appeal lies against an Order refusing to promote a person. Nobody has got a right of promotion, unless such right is given by the Service/Rules, taking into consideration the seniority. The only right a candidate has is, consideration for promotion. If that be so, under clause (iii) of Rule 7 (extracted above), it cannot be said that the Management has denied or varied the pay or allowances or conditions of service, to the disadvantage of the third respondent. I do not think that a right to promotion is a condition of service. At the most, it may amount only to a legitimate expectation. Again, the variation or denial to the disadvantage of third respondent must also be in the nature of punishment which alone enables the delinquent to file an appeal. Denial of promotion cannot be considered as a violation of conditions of service. If that be so, I do not think that an appeal lies to the Second Respondent.  9. Another formidable argument was also advanced by learned Counsel for petitioner regarding the jurisdiction of second respondent to act as Appellate Authority. As per Rule 6 of the Rules referred to above, the Appellate Tribunal consists of Director of Education and two non-official members, one appointed by the Management of the Aided School and another by the Teachers Association. It is these Members who constitute the Tribunal. It is this Tribunal that has to decide regarding the maintainability of the Appeal. Second respondent cannot act as Tribunal. In this case, neither the representative of the Management nor representative of the Teachers' Association has heard the case. Second respondent, in his capacity as Director of Education alone, has decided the matter. He is not acting as Chairman of the Tribunal.  10. When the Rules enjoin that the Tribunal consisting of Chairman and Members should hear the Appeal and decide the same, it follows that the Appeal has to be heard and decided only by the Tribunal, and not by a Member of the Tribunal. A Member by himself cannot be considered as a Tribunal. In that view, even the very hearing of the Appeal by second respondent was without jurisdiction.  11. Coming to the merits of the case also, I do not think that the third respondent has an arguable case before Court.  12. It is admitted by both sides that the petitioner-School is a minority Institution. It has got a fundamental right under Art. 30 of the Constitution to establish and maintain educational institutions of its choice. Right to manage includes the right to appoint a teacher to a particular post, of its choice. In this case, there is no Rule which prescribes that appointment to the vacancy must be only by promotion. In fact, even the third respondent only says in para 6 of his counter, `whenever a vacancy arose for the post of School Assistant Grade II, mostly the same was filled up by promoting the senior-most teacher'. So he is not relying on any rule, on the basis of which he makes the claim. Petitioner has a definite case that appointment to such post is only by selection, taking into consideration the better qualification and experience of a teacher. It is the definite case of the Management that all along the practice of the Management was to appoint only persons by direct recruitment. When the third respondent himself has no case that his claim is not based on any particular Rule, and going by his own affidavit, it is clear that the admission could be made by direct recruitment, there is no scope for claiming that right which the third respondent has, is that his name must also be considered for that post, if found eligible.  13. Being a minority institution, it is for the Management to decide as to who should be appointed to that post. In a recent decision of the Supreme Court reported in1998(6) SCC 674 (N. Ammad v. Manager, Emjay High School) : 1998(4) SCT 313 (SC) the question that came for consideration was, whether the senior-most teacher is to be appointed as Headmaster in a minority school. While considering the same, in para 15 of the judgment, their Lordships have held thus:-  "A Constitution Bench of seven Judges of this Court in Kerala Education Bill, 1957, Re (AIR 1958 SC 956) has examined the constitutional validity of the Bill which was the precursor to the Act when the President of India had sought the advice of the Supreme Court under Article 143 of the Constitution. One of the propositions laid down by the said Constitution Bench in the said decision is this : the right guaranteed under Article 30(1) is a right that is absolute and any law or executive direction which infringes the substance of that right is void to the extent of infringement. But the absolute character of the right will not preclude making of regulations in the true interests of efficiency or instruction, discipline, health, sanitation, morality, public order and the like, as such regulations are not restrictions on the substance of the right guaranteed by the Constitution." In paragraph 21, Their Lordships followed the opinion expressed by the Honourable Supreme Court in regard to the Kerala Education Bill, referred under Art. 143 of the Constitution of India (reported in AIR 1958 SC 956 In re : Kerala Education Bill), wherein Justice H.R. Khanna has adopted a still broader view that even selection of teachers is of great importance in the right to manage a school. In para 21, Their Lordships have quoted the very words of the learned Judge. That portion reads thus :-  "The selection and appointment of teachers for an educational institution is one of the essential ingredients of the right to manage an educational institution and the minorities can plainly be not denied such right of selection and appointment without infringing Art. 30(1)." Regarding the appointing of Headmaster, Their Lordships of the Honourable Supreme Court have said thus :- (vide para 26)  ".......The Management of a minority school is free to find out a qualified person either from the staff of the same school or from outside to fill up the vacancy. We may point out, in this context that the Division Bench in Henry Gomez Case, ILR 1994(1) Ker 808 has quoted with approval the following observations of another earlier Division Bench decision of the same High Court in Manager Corporate E. Agency v. State of Kerala, 1990(2) Ker LT 240:- The right to appoint the Headmaster of a school or the Principal of a college, is one of prime importance in the administration of the institution. The right of the minority to administer an educational institution of its choice requires the presence of a person in whom they can repose confidence, who will carry out their directions, and to whom they can look forward to maintain the traditions, discipline and the efficiency of the teaching....." "According to me, the principle regarding the appointment of Headmaster equally applies to the appointment of teacher also when the same is not filled up by seniority. In the case of selection and direct recruitment, third respondent will have only a right to be considered, and he cannot have a claim as of right, and insist that he should be promoted to that post. When two qualified persons are available before the Management, it is for the management to decide as to who should be considered. In this case, the Management has a definite case against the third respondent that even though he has got experience and also educational qualification, his performance is not good. In all such cases, it cannot be said that it is not a case of adverse remark against third respondent. It is only a consideration of inter se suitability between respondents 3 and 4. Except the fact that the third respondent is not selected, he is not in any way affected in his service as a teacher. The Honourable Supreme Court has held in the case referred to supra, that the right of the minority to administer an education institution of its choice requires the presence of a person in whom they can repose confidence, who can maintain tradition, discipline and efficiency of teaching. If the Management could find these qualifications in the fourth respondent, that cannot be considered as adverse remarks against third respondent.  14. Second respondent rejected the plea of petitioner on the ground that third respondent has not been communicated about this advese remark, and so far he has not been served with any memo, and he has a blemishless service. I do not think that the second respondent has approached the question in the proper perspective.  15. In the result, the impugned Order is quashed. The writ petition is allowed. No costs. Connected W.M.P. is closed.  Petition allowed.
summary:
A. The Petitioner-School appointed fourth respondent as School Assistant based on previous experience instead of the third respondent, leading to an appeal against denial of promotion. However, denial of promotion cannot be considered a violation of service condition, and hence cannot be appealed against unless there is a variation in pay, allowances or other service conditions that disadvantages the employee. [Para 8]
B. Non-consideration of third respondent for promotion in a minority institution where there is no rule enabling appointment only by promotion is not a violation of service condition. The management can appoint a person of their own choice where two people of similar experience and qualifications are available. Fourth respondent is duly qualified and experienced. [Para 12]
C. Under Rule 6 of Govt. Aided Private School Teachers (Discipline, Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1959, the Appellate Tribunal must consist of the Director of Education (D.O.E.) and two non-official members. Therefore, appeals heard only by the D.O.E. is without jurisdiction as the D.O.E. alone cannot act as the Tribunal. [Paras 9 & 10]

text: Kuldip Singh, J. - The petitioners and respondents 4 to 16 are District and Sessions Judges in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The petitioners are direct recruits whereas the respondents were promoted from the subordinate judiciary. The respondents were initially appointed on temporary basis in the year 1978/1979 but they were made substantive in the year 1983. The petitioners who were appointed substantively in the year 1981 claim seniority over the respondents by way of this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.  2. The recruitment to the Andhra Pradesh Higher Judicial Service (the Service) is governed by the Rules called "The Andhra Pradesh State Higher Judicial Service Special Rules" (the Special Rules). Rules 1, 2, 4 and 6 of the Special Rules which are relevant are as under:  "Rule 1. Constitution:- The Service shall consist of the following categories: Category-I :- District and Sessions Judges 1st Grade.  Category-II :- District and Sessions Judges, Second Grade including Chairman, Andhra Pradesh Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal Chief Judge, City Civil Court, Additional Chief Judge, City Civil Court, Chief Judge, Court of Small Causes, Chief City Magistrate, Chairman, Tribunal for Disciplinary Proceedings, Presiding Officers, Labour Courts and Addl. District and Sessions Judges. Rule 2. Appointment :- (a) Appointment to Category-I shall be made by promotion from Category-II and appointment to Category-II shall be made: (i) by transfer from among: (a) Sub-Judges in the Andhra State Judicial Service; or in the Hyderabad State Judicial Service; and (ii) by direct recruitment from the Bar: Provided that 33<$E1/3>% of the total number of permanent posts shall be filled or reserved to be filled by direct recruitment. Explanation :- In the determination of 33<$E1/3>% of the total number of permanent posts, fractions exceeding one-half shall be counted as one and other fractions shall be disregarded. (b) All promotions shall be made on grounds of merit and ability, seniority being considered only when merit and ability are approximately equal. Rule 4. Probation :- Every person appointed to Category-II otherwise than by transfer shall from, the date on which he joins duty be on probation for a total period of one year on duty. Rule 6. Seniority :- The seniority of a person appointed to Category I or Category 2 shall be determined with reference to the date from which he was continuously on duty in that category." 3. We may briefly notice the scheme of the Special Rules. Rule 1 constitutes the Service. Category-I consists of District and Sessions Judges Ist grade and Category-II consists of District and Sessions Judges Second grade. Rule 1 does not say that Service shall consist of only permanent posts. All the posts designated as District and Sessions Judges Second grade under Category-II are part of the service under Rule 1. In other words, as and when a post of District and Sessions Judge Second Grade is created permanent or temporary it becomes part of the Service under Rule 1 of the Special Rules. Rule 2 provides the method of appointment. Appointment to Category-I is from Category-II Appointment to Category-II is from two sources. By transfer from amongst the Subordinate Judges and by direct recruitment from the Bar. Proviso to Rule 2 states that 33<$E1/3>% of the total number of permanent posts shall be filled or reserved to be filled by direct recruitment. All the posts of District and Sessions Judges Second Grade are part of the Service but quota for the direct recruits is provided only in the permanent posts. Rule 6 of the Rules provides for the fixation of seniority. Under Rule 6 of the seniority of persons appointed to Category-I or Category-II posts is fixed on the basis of continuous length of service in their respective posts.  4. On the plain reading of the Special Rules the salient features of the Service can be culled out as under:  1. Rule 1 provides for the constitution of the Service. All the posts of District and Sessions Judges Second grade created from time to time are part of the Service. The natural corollary is that the Service consists of permanent as well as temporary posts.  2. The recruitment to Category-II of the service is by transfer from amongst the Subordinate Judges and also by direct recruits from the Bar.  3. 33<$E1/3>% of the total number of permanent posts in Category-II of the Service are to be filled by way of direct recruitment.  4. The seniority under Rule 6 is to be determined with reference to the date from which a person is continuously on duty. Whether the person is continuously on duty against a temporary post or permanent post is of no consequence. A person is entitled to the fixation of his seniority on the basis of continuous length of service rendered either against permanent post or temporary post.  5. The three petitioners were appointed as District and Sessions Judges Second grade by direct recruitment on October 12, 1981. Petitioners 1 and 2 joined service on October 23, 1981 and petitioner 3 on October 30, 1981. Respondents 4 to 16 were appointed District and Sessions Judges Second Grade by transfer from amongst the Subordinate Judges during the years 1978/79. It is not disputed that permanent vacancies in their quota became available in the year 1983. We, therefore, proceed on the basis that the petitioners were appointed substantive members of the Service earlier to respondents 4 to 16.  6. We may at this stage notice Rule 10(a)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules (the State Rules). The State Rules are general rules which are applicable to all the services in the State of Andhra Pradesh. Needless to say that to the extent the Special Rules are applicable to the  service the State Rules are excluded. Rule 10(a)(i) of the State Rules is as under:  "10. Temporary appointments. (a)(i) Where it is necessary in the public interest to fill emergently a vacancy in the post borne on the cadre of a service, class or category and if the filling of such vacancy in accordance with the rules is likely to result in undue delay, the appointing authority may appoint a person temporarily otherwise than in accordance with the said rules." 7. Mr. P.P. Rao, learned counsel for the petitioners has raised the following contentions for our consideration:  1. That the Service consists of only permanent posts under the Special Rules. There is no provision under the Special Rules for adding temporary posts to the cadre. The appointment of respondents to the posts of District and Sessions Judges Second Grade on temporary basis can at best be treated under rule 10(a)(i) of the State Rules.  2. The temporary service rendered by respondents 4 to 16 - being outside the cadre - cannot be counted towards seniority.  3. Proviso to Rule 2 and Rule 6 of the Special Rules have to be read together and doing so the permanent vacancies having been made available for respondents 4 to 16 in the year 1983 their service prior to that date cannot be counted towards seniority.  8. Before dealing with Mr. Rao's contentions, we may notice two preliminary contentions raised by Mr. K. Madava Reddy, learned counsel for the respondents.  9. Mr. Madava Reddy has invited our attention to the judgment of a Division Bench of Andhra Pradesh High Court in T.H.B. Chalapathi v. High Court of Andhra P., Writ Petition Nos. 1968/82, 5283 and 12282/85 decided on December 28, 1985. Those writ petitions were filed before the Andhra Pradesh High Court by the direct recruits to Category-II of the Service claiming seniority over the persons who were appointed to category-II on temporary basis earlier to them. Similar questions were raised as are being raised by Mr. P.P. Rao before us. By a well-reasoned judgment the High Court rejected all the contentions of the direct recruits and dismissed the writ petitions. It is not disputed that Special Leave Petition No. 1035 of 1986 against the said judgment was dismissed by this Court on January 30,1988. Mr. Madava Reddy plausibly contends that all the contentions which are being raised by the petitioners in this Court, having been rejected by the High Court and special leave petition against the judgment of the High Court having been dismissed by this Court the same cannot be agitated once over again.  10. Mr. Madava Reddy then contended that the petitioners were appointed in the year 1981 and since then till the year 1988 twelve seniority lists have been published showing the petitioners below respondents 4 to 16. At no point of time they challenged the seniority lists in the Court. Even when the writ petitions filed by Chalapathi and others were pending they did not intervene before the High Court. The petitioners, according to Mr. Madava Reddy, are guilty of gross delay and laches and as such are not entitled to get relief by way of this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.  11. We see considerable force in both the contentions raised by Mr. Madava Reddy. We are, however, of the view that it would be in the larger interest of the Service to dispose of this petition on merits.  12. We see no force in the contention of Mr. Rao that the Service consists of only permanent posts under the Special Rules. We have already interpreted Rule 1 to mean that the Service under the Special Rules consists of all the posts - permanent and temporary - which have been designated as District and Sessions Judges Second grade. Even otherwise in the absence of any prohibition under the Special Rules the State Government can always create temporary posts as additions to the cadre. Rule 10(a)(i) of the State Rules has no application to the Service which is governed by the Special Rules. Rule 10(a)(i) provides for emergency appointments made on stop gap basis to meet a temporary exigency. Apart from that the temporary appointments under the said Rules are made without following the procedure prescribed under the Rules governing the relevant service. The appointments of respondents 4 to 16, on the other hand, were made under Rule 2 of the Special Rules by the State Government in consultation with the High Court. We are of the view that the Special Rules provide a complete scheme for the appointment and seniority of the members of the Service. Rule 10(a)(i) of the State Rules has no application to the Service constituted under the Special Rules. We, therefore, reject the contention raised by Mr. Rao.  13. Having taken the view that the Service under the Special Rules consists of permanent as well as temporary posts the second contention of Mr. Rao looses its ground. Temporary posts of District and Sessions Judges Second Grade being part of the Service the seniority has to be counted on the basis of length of service including the service against a temporary post.  14. The third contention of Mr. Rao is mentioned to be rejected in view of Rule 6 of the Special Rules. Rule 6 of the Special Rules is in no way dependent on proviso to Rule 2 of the Special Rules. Both are to be operative independently. In the scheme of the rules the seniority rule is not dependent on the quota Rule. Quota has been provided for the direct recruits only against permanent posts. The seniority rule permits the counting of total period of service from the date a person is on duty against a post in the category. Even though the petitioners were appointed substantively to the service earlier to respondents 4 to 16 but in view of Rule 6 they cannot be declared senior on the basis of continuous length of service - against temporary as well as permanent posts - respondents 4 to 16 have been rightly given seniority above the petitioners.  15. We, therefore, find no force in any of the contentions raised by Mr. Rao.  16. The writ petition is consequently dismissed. No costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: Article 16 of the Indian Constitution - The Andhra Pradesh State Higher Judicial Service Rules, Rules 1 and 6 - Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules, Rule 10(a) (i) - Seniority - Quota Rule - Special Rules for appointment and seniority of District and Sessions Judges Second Grade - Seniority determined on the basis of length of service including temporary posts - Rule 6 of Special Rules operates independently and is not dependent on the proviso to Rule 2 - Seniority is not dependent on quota rule - Quota only applies to direct recruits against permanent posts. [Paras 12 and 14]

text: Amarjeet Chaudhary J. (Oral) - The petitioner, who is an Agriculture Inspector in the Agriculture Department, Punjab, has filed the present writ petition under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India praying for issuance of a direction to the respondents to quash the order dated 8.12.1988, Anenxure P-2, whereby the petitioner has been ignored for promotion to PAS Class II (Administrative Wing) and the respondents be further directed to treat the petitioner promoted w.e.f. the date i.e. 8.12.1988, the persons junior to him were promoted.  2. In brief, the case of the petitioner is that he was selected as Agriculture Inspector in the Punjab Agriculture Department through the Subordinate Service Selection Board and joined as such on 1.6.1965. The State of Punjab notified Punjab Agriculture Services (Class-II) Rules, 1974, hereinafter referred to as the 'Rules' for making promotion to the post of Agriculture Officer (Class II) post. Rule 8 of the Rules provides for method of recruitment to the Service. As per clause (1)(b) of the said Rule, 66-2/3 per cent of the posts are to be filled in by promotion from amongst the members of the subordinate services. As per provisions contained in this Rule, a member of the subordinate services having a minimum experience of five years is eligible to be considered for promotion to the post of Agriculture Officer on the basis of seniority-cum-merit. Rule 9 of the Rules prescribes, qualifications for appointment to the post of Agriculture Officer. The respondents circulated a seniority list, as it stood on 1.5.1979, in which the petitioner's name figured at Sr. No. 270.  3. The petitioner claims that though he fulfilled all the requisite qualifications prescribed under the Rules, but he was not considered for promotion. Faced with the situation, he filed writ petition No. 7921 of 1988 on this Court claiming his right of consideration for promotion. The respondent-State filed the written statement to the said Writ Petition and in para No. 18 thereof, it was stated that the name of the petitioner was under consideration for promotion to P.A.S. Class-II. It was further stated therein that he would be considered alongwith the other Agriculture Inspectors on the basis of their service record. The said writ petition was disposed of having become infructuous vide order dated 16.11.1988 in view of the stand taken by the respondent in the above said written statement. The petitioner was not promoted despite the fact he had also a good service record.  4. The Director, Agriculture Department, Punjab, Chandigarh respondent No. 2 had issued order dated 10.6.1988, Annexure P-1 whereby recovery of Rs. 50,191.96 was ordered to be effected from the petitioner. He challenged the same by way of filing another writ petition No. 6317 of 1988 in this Court and the recovery of the said amount was ordered to be stayed.  5. The learned Counsel for the petitioner contended that the respondent- department vide order dated 8.12.1988, a copy of which is Annexure P-2 to the writ petition, promoted as many as nine Agriculture Inspectors to the post of P.A.S Class-II Officers, but the petitioner was ignored despite the fact that he had a good service record. However, in the impugned order of promotion, there was a clear mention that one post of PAS Class-II had been kept vacant for the petitioner, and he was to be considered for promotion after the settlement of the amount which was due from him to the Government. Feeling aggrieved against the impugned order Annexure P-2 ignoring the petitioner for promotion, he filed the present writ petition.  6. On the other hand, the stand taken by the respondent in the written statement is that the case of the petitioner was considered for promotion in terms of the written statement filed in the earlier writ petition No. 7921 of 1988, but he was not found suitable for the same. A sum of Rs. 50101.96 is also to be recovered from him on account of seed depot money. It was further stated therein that one post of PAS Class-II was kept vacant for the petitioner while issuing the impugned order of promotion, Annexure P-2. It has also been stated in para No. 12 of the written statement that the petitioner will be again considered after he settled the amount due from him to the Government. It is also averred in the written statement that no Govt. servant can claim promotion as a matter of right. The promotions are made after taking into consideration the entire service record as well as the work and conduct of the employee. Two increments of the petitioner were stopped by way of punishment after holding enquiry for claiming false T.A. Since the petitioner was not possessing neat and clean service record, he was rightly ignored for promotion.  7. I have considered the submissions made at the Bar by the learned Counsel for the petitioner.  8. In para 18(ii) of the written statement it has been clearly averred by the respondents that the order of recovery Annexure P-1 had to be withdrawn as certain formalities viz. opportunity of being heard to the petitioner or holding of enquiry and fixing the responsibility, were not observed before passing the same, the action against the petitioner is being taken after following the procedure as laid down in the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970. Under these circumstances, it cannot be concluded whether any action under the Rules has been taken against the petitioner or not till date.  9. In view of the categorical stand taken by the respondents in para No. 18(ii) of the written statement and in case no order adversely affecting the petitioner has been passed by the respondent-department till date as per procedure laid down in the Service Rules, a direction is issued to the respondents to consider the case of the petitioner for promotion to the post of P.A.S. Class-II within one month from the receipt of a copy of this judgment.  10. The writ petition stands disposed of in the terms indicated above. No order as to costs.  Ordered accordingly.
summary: Punjab Agriculture Services (Class II) Rules, 1974, Rule 8 - Constitution of India, Articles 226 and 227 - Probation - Consideration - The order of recovery passed against the petitioner has been withdrawn as necessary formalities were not observed for passing orders for recovery - Due to the same order of recovery, the petitioner was not considered for promotion - However, it is important to note that there was no adverse order against the petitioner - Therefore, the court has issued directions to consider the petitioner's case for promotion. [Paras 8 and 9]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. - The petitioner is aggrieved. by the action of the respondents in not promoting him to the rank of Subedar with effect from October 1, 1989 and his consequential retirement from service with effect from October 1, 1990. His statutory complaint having been rejected, the petitioner has approached this Court through the present writ petition.  2. A few facts May be noticed. The petitioner was born on April 4, 1947. He was enrolled in the Indian Army (Medical Corps) on September 18, 1964. He was promoted to the rank of Nursing Assistant with effect from July 1, 1976 and to that of Havildar on August 21, 1982. The petitioner was promoted to the rank of Naib Subedar on July 1, 1988. He was retired from the army on completion of 26 years of service on October 1, 1990. The petitioner claims that he was never conveyed and adverse report.  3. On October 10, 1986, the petitioner was posted to N.C.C. 5 Punjab (G) B. Moga as Nursing Assistant on instructional duties. It is averred that the normal tenure of service in the N.C.C. is only two years, but the petitioner remained posted in the N.C.C. from October 10, 1986 to April 24, 1989. He earned his confidential reports for the years 1986, 1987 and 1988 as High /Above Average and was recommended for promotion. He was promoted to the rank of Naib Subedar but was denied promotion to the rank of Subedar which was due to him on October 1, 1989. This was done on the ground that he did not earn his annual confidential report in the regiment. On a representation, he was informed vide Annexure P-1 that he was not eligible for promotion to the rank of Subedar as he did not fulfil "A.C.R. grading criteria" (Def. of Regimental A.C.R. in the present rank). He was, however, informed that his case would be reviewed on receipt of A.C.R. for the year 1989. Vide letter dated March 10, 1990 the petitioner was informed that "he was considered for promotion to the rank of subedar against the vacancy of April 1, 1990. He is not eligible for the reasons as he does not fulfil A.C.R. grading criteria. Hence, he has been superseded for promotion by his qualified and eligible juniors." The petitioner submitted a statutory complaint vide Annexure P-4, which was followed by a reminder, a copy of which has been appended as Annexure P-5. On October 1, 1990, the petitioner was retired. On completion of tenure of 26 years which have been prescribed for the post of Naib Subedar. If he had been promoted as Subedar with effect from October 1, 1989 he would have been entitled to continue till he completed the pensionable service of 28 years. This would have also resulted in other benefits like Honarary rank and higher rate of pension. The petitioner served a notice on the respondents. Vide letter dated December 12, 1990 the counsel for the petitioner was informed that the statutory complaint submitted by the petitioner had been rejected by the Chief of the Army Staff. A copy of this letter has been placed as Annexure P-7. Aggrieved by the action of supersession and the consequential retirement on completion of 26 years of service, the petitioner has approached this Court through the present writ petition.  4. Written statement has been filed on behalf of the respondents. Their case is summarised in paragraph 3 of the written statement. This reads as under :-  "3. In reply to para 3 of the writ petition, it is submitted that the petitioner was posted to 5 Punjab (G) Bn. NCC, Moga on 10 Oct. 86 as Nursing Assistant on instructional duties. He was promoted to Nb/Sub on 01 July 88. The correct details or gradings earned by the petitioner in the ACRs for the years 1984 to 1989 are as under : Year Grading Recommendation on awarded for promotion Rank in which initiated Unit by which initiated 1989 'Average' 'R' Nb/Sub 151 BN (Regt) 1988 ' High Average' 'R' Nb/Sub 5 Punjab (G) Bd. NCC(EBE) 1987 'Above Average' 'R' Hav 5 Punjab (G) Bd. NCC(EBE) 1985 ' High Average' 'R' Hav 433 Fd Amb(Regt) 1986 'Above Average' 'R' Hav 433 Fd Amb (Regt) 1984 'Above Average' 'R' Hav 433 Fd Amb (Regt) 5. It is submitted that in terms of Army HQ letter No. 09930/AG/PS 2(c) dated 18 Dec. 85 for promotion to the rank of Subedar a Naib Subedar should have at least three ' High Average' reports during the last 5 years and one ' High Average' out of three must be on regimental duty. The petitioner was earlier considered for promotion to the rank of Subedar (Nursing Assistant) against the vacancy of 01 Oct. 89 and was superseded due to non-availability of Regimental ACR of requisite grading in the present rank. Intimation regarding his supersession was sent to his unit vide this office letter No. 356006 J(N Asst) dated 05 Sep. 89. The petitioner was posted to 151 Base Hospital vide this office letter No 341007 JPT/NUR (CN-3615) dated 25 Nov. 88 for earning a regimental ACR in the present rank. However, he moved to his new unit only on 25th April 89. On receipt of regimental ACR for the year 1989 he was considered for promotion to Subedar (N Asst) against the vacancy of 01 April 90 and was superseded due to ACR grading criteria since he was graded 'Average' in the ACR 1989 (Regimental ACR) against the requirement of ' High Average' grading. Intimation regarding his supersession was sent to his unit vide this office letter No. 356005 J(N Asst) dated 10 March 90. It is added that had the petitioner earned at least ' High Average' grading in the ACR for the year 1989, his seniority for promotion would have been protected under the provisions of Army HO letter, No. 94930/Ag/Ps-2(c) dated 18 Aug. 88. A copy of the army HQ letter dated 18.12.85 is annexed as Annexure R 1."  The instructions to which reference has been made above, were issued by the authorities on February 27, 1986. Clause 3(c) which has been relied upon by the respondents provides as under :  (c) For promotion to the rank of Ris/Sub.  (i) Three out of the last five reports rendered on an individual should be ' High Average' out of which at least one should be on regimental duty or as an instructor in an army school or institution in the Rank of Nb. Ris/Nb Sub. (ii) No report should be lower than 'Average' in the last three years (iii) Should have been recommended for promotion in the last three reports. Even these instructions appear to have been issued on the basis of the letter dated December 18, 1985. The respondents have produced only an extract from the letter. A complete copy thereof has been produced by the learned counsel for the petitioner. It is placed on record as Mark 'A'. Note (4) provides as under :  "(4) Reports earned by JCOs/NCOs while serving with Army HQ/Other formation HQs/Establishment/NCC units Indian Missions aboard etc. will not be treated as regimental reports. However, in order to safeguard the promotion prospects of such personnel on ERE the following measures may be adopted :  (i) JCOs/NCOs who are expected to get promotion to the higher ranks during the period of their tenure on ERE should not be detailed on ERE. (ii) Only junior JCOs/NCOs whose tenure on ERE will not interfere with their promotion prospects should be posted on ERE. (iii) Only those JCOs/NCOs who have already earned one regimental/instructional reports in the rank held as per the criteria should be posted on ERE and be reverted to regimental/instructional duty in time to remain eligible for promotion. (iv) The tenure of Clerks (GD) on ERE with Army HQ may be allowed upto 4 years provided the promotion prospects of the JCOs/NCOs concerned do not suffer adversely owing to their not having earned at least one regimental/instructional report in the rank held." 6. A perusal of the pleading for the parties shows that the petitioner was initially due for promotion on October 1, 1989. According to the criteria laid down by the respondents, his last five annual confidential reports had to be taken into consideration. The summary of reports as given in the written statement shows that two reports i.e. for the years 1986 and 1988 were ' High Average' and the three reports viz., for the years 1984, 1985 and 1987 were 'Above Average'. According to the instructions produced on behalf of the respondents, a person with three ' High Average' reports out of five was eligible. The petitioner fulfilled this criteria. In fact, in his case, two reports were ' High Average' and 3 were 'Above Average'. According to Major Aggarwal, who appeared on behalf of the respondents, an 'Above Average' report is better than an ' High Average' report. Consequently, the petitioner was fully qualified. The only hurdle in his way was that one of the reports did not relate to regimental duty as an instructor in any army school or institution. This was not on account of any fault on the part of the petitioner. The employer and in this case the Army authorities had posted the petitioner on extra regimental assignment. The petitioner could not earn a report on regimental duty unless he was posted thereto. In accordance with the instructions on which the respondents are relying and an extract from which has been appended as Annexure R-1, only such JCOs/NCOs "who have already earned one regimental/instructional reports in the rank held as per the criteria should be posted on ERE and be reverted to regimental/instructional duty in time to remain eligible for promotion." (Refer to Note 4(iii) of Mark 'A').  The petitioner should have been posted on extra regimental assignment only after he had earned one regimental/instructional report. This was not done. Having posted him to the NCC, the respondents cannot be permitted to take advantage of their own wrong and deny the petitioner his legitimate due. If such a course of action is permitted it would be open to the authorities to post all the senior persons to extra regimental assignments, and deny them the promotion while their Juniors who are not so posted shall remain eligible for promotion. Such a course of action would completely defeat the guarantee of equality of opportunity as enshrined in Article 16 of the Constitution of India.  7. In the present case, the respondents themselves had posted the petitioner to NCC in the year 1984 and remained as such till April 25, 1989. The instructions violated by the authorities, the mandate contained in Note 4 of the instructions was not followed, still the stipulation contained in paragraph 3 of the instructions is sought to be enforced against the petitioner. This is wholly unfair and arbitrary. I am accordingly of the view that the order superseding the petitioner for the vacancy which became available on April 1, 1989 was wholly unfair. It resulted in violation of the guarantee of equality of opportunity enshrined in Article 16 of the Constitution of India.  8. I accordingly allow this writ petition. The impugned order viz. Annexure P-1 and the order dismissing the petitioner's statutory complaint are accordingly quashed. The respondents are directed to consider the petitioner's claim for promotion to the rank of Subedar with effect from October 1, 1989 without insisting on his having one report on regimental duty. If he is found suitable for promotion, necessary orders shall be passed by the respondents within three months of the date of the receipt of a copy of this order. He will then be entitled to have his tenure of 28 years service as provided for a person in the rank of Subedar. The petitioner shall also be entitled to his costs which are assessed at Rs. 2000/-.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Article 16 specifies the conditions of promotion. In this case, the petitioner was considered fully qualified for promotion to the post of Subedar but was denied the promotion as the confidential report was not received from the Regiment. The petitioner cannot be held responsible for the fault of the authorities, and the respondents cannot use their own error to deny the petitioner's legitimate right. Such an action is violative of Article 16. [Paras 6 and 7]

text: T.H.B. Chalapathi, J. - This writ petition is filed to quash the award of the Labour Court, Chandigarh, dated September 4, 1992.  2. The petitioner is a Co-operative Society known as the Haryana State Federation of Consumers' Co-operative Wholesale Stores Limited (hereinafter referred to as the Society) registered under the Co-operative Societies Act. Its employees formed an association called as the Haryana Confed Employees' Welfare Union, Chandigarh (hereinafter referred to as the Union for brevity). On February 9, 1988, the Union served a charter of demands on the Society. By an order dated October 23, 1988, the matter was referred to the Labour Court, Chandigarh, for adjudication. By the impugned award dated September 4, 1992, the Labour Court allowed the demands Nos. 2, 3, and 6 and rejected the other demands of the Union. The demands Nos. 2, 3 and 6 which have been allowed by the Labour Court are in respect of the following matters :-  1. To give regular pay scale to Salesmen/helpers on doctrine of equal work-equal pay. 2. Implementation of Fourth Pay Commission report with effect from January 1, 1986. 3. Revision of pay scales of Accountants. 3. The Society filed this writ petition challenging the award of the Labour Court. In this writ petition, the learned counsel for the petitioner-society confined his arguments in respect of equal pay to salesmen working in rural outlets of the Society and in regard to the date from which the revised scales of pay should be implemented.  4. For a proper appreciation of the controversy involved, it is necessary to narrate certain facts.  5. The Society was established in the year 1966 to ensure proper public distribution system of the essential consumer commodities in the urban areas of the State of Haryana. The petitioner-society was created as an apex society having Central Co-operative Consumers Stores in the urban areas as its members. In the year 1979, the State of Haryana launched a massive production-cum-distribution of Essential Commodities Scheme with the objective to provide the essential commodities at reasonable rates to the consumers living in far off places in the States including in the rural areas. The task of implementing the Scheme was entrusted to the petitioner-society. Consequently, the petitioner-society decided to open retail outlets in the rural areas of the State having population of 2000 and above in order to implement the Scheme effectively. Prior to the implementation of the Scheme of the Government, the petitioner-society was having common cadre of salesmen working in the urban areas and they were appointed on regular pay scales and were governed by the Staff Service Rules of the petitioner-society.  6. In order to implement the Scheme of the Government of Haryana in the rural areas of the State, the petitioner-society created certain posts of salesmen/helpers with a fixed pay to work in the outlets of the petitioner- society in the rural areas. The salesmen/helpers were also allowed to have sales incentives so as to enable them to promote the sales of certain items in the rural areas. The Board of Directors passed resolutions on April 22, 1980, and on January 15, 1981, creating the posts of the salesmen to work in the rural areas. In pursuance of the said resolutions, certain salesmen have been appointed in outlets of the petitioner-society in the rural areas of the State of Haryana and they are being paid the fixed salary with the incentives. The demand of the Union is that the salesmen working in the rural areas should also be paid the salary on regular pay scales at par with the Salesmen working in the outlets of the petitioner-society in urban areas.  7. The real controversy therefore centres round the question whether the salesmen working in the rural areas are entitled to the same scales of pay which their counterparts in the urban areas are getting.  8. The learned counsel for the petitioner-society relied upon the letter of appointment of the salesmen in the rural areas dated June 10, 1981, (Annexure P-2).  The relevant portion reads as follows :-  "You are appointed to the post of Salesman on a consolidated salary of Rs. 300/- per month with the following sales incentives :- 1.A) For Salesman posted in the villages having population upto 5000 and also sale incentive will be as under :- i) Monthly sale upto Rs. 8000/- = no incentive ii) Monthly sale exceeding Rs. 12,000/- and upto Rs. 20,000/- = 2% of the sale exceeding Rs. 12,000/- iii) Monthly sale exceeding Rs. 20,000/- = 3% of the sale exceeding Rs. 20,000/- B) For salesman posted in village exceeding population 5000 will be as under :- i) Monthly sale upto Rs. 10,000/- = no incentive  ii) Monthly sale exceeding Rs. 10,000/- and upto Rs. 15,000/- 1% of the sale exceeding Rs. 10,000/-  iii) Monthly sale exceeding Rs. 15,000/- and upto Rs. 25,000/- = 2% of the sale exceeding Rs.15,000/- iv) Monthly sale exceeding Rs. 25,000/- = 3% of the sale exceeding Rs. 25,000/- The sale incentive will be calculated on monthly basis and will be paid to at the end of the quarter. Sale of levy sugar and other rationed commodities will not be included at the time of calculating the incentive to be given to the Salesman. The work of the Salesman will be considered and the salesmen are now getting fixed wages of Rs. 1046.70 per month with effect from July 1, 1992.  9. The learned counsel for the petitioner-society contended that the salesmen working in rural outlets form a separate class and they are given Sales incentives whereas the salesmen working in urban areas have to attend more work and they have to cater large number of customers when compared to the salesmen working in the rural areas and they have not been paid or granted any sales incentives and, therefore, that there cannot be any comparison among the salesmen working in the rural areas and the salesmen working in the urban areas. They are not equals and, therefore, the salesmen in the rural areas have been put on consolidated salary with sales incentives.  10. On the other hand, it is contended by the learned counsel for the respondents-salesmen that the functions, duties and responsibilities of both the salesmen working in rural areas and urban areas are similar and identical and they cannot be discriminated. The Salesmen working in the rural areas have not been paid any incentive till now and, therefore, salesmen working in rural areas are entitled to equal pay for equal work.  11. Admittedly, the posts have been created by resolutions of the Board of Directors of the Petitioner-society passed on April 22, 1980, and January 15, 1981. At the meeting held on April 22, 1980, the item on the agenda was to consider scheme of public distribution and its implementation. The resolution is to the effect that office proposal/suggestions regarding implementation of Scheme was considered and approved. The matter was further considered by the Board of Directors at its meeting held on January 15, 1981, and the relevant portion of the resolution reads as follows :-  "Further resolved to create the following additional posts and proposed for successful implementation of the scheme- 1. Managers 32 (their pattern given in Annexure 'A') 2. Assistant Managers 32  3. Storekeepers 224 (160 for local points and 64 for the Hqs of Sub Division Office) 4. Salesmen 1600 to be opened by Confed. This number includes 400 posts of Salesmen created under item No. 6.  5. Helpers 800 The posts will carry usual pay scales. The post of helper will be on a fixed salary of Rs. 250/- per month keeping in view the Minimum Wages Act. These posts should be filled keeping in view the actual requirement." 12. Thus, it is clear that according to the resolution dated January 15, 1981, the posts created therein will carry usual pay scales as applicable to regular employees working in the urban areas.  13. The letter of appointment was issued on June 10, 1981, that is subsequent to the resolution. When the Board decided to extend the usual scales of pay to the newly created posts for successful implementation of the scheme, there is no question of giving them the consolidated salary. The intention of the Board is very clear that they want to treat the salesmen working in the rural areas at par with their counterparts working in the urban areas.  14. Further, from the record produced before me, the Salesmen working in the rural areas have been transferred to urban areas and vice-versa. The office orders dated November 11, 1987, (Annexure D), dated November 20, 1992, (Annexure B) dated September 24, 1992, (Annexure C), dated February 16, 1993, (Annexure A), dated October 4, 1994, (Annexure F) and dated January 12, 1996, (Annexure E) are some of the instances to show where the posts of salesmen working in the rural areas and in urban areas are inter-transferable. The functions and duties of the salesmen working in different outlets are practically the same. They have to promote the sales. With regard to payment of incentives, the respondents vehemently denied that they have been paid any incentive. They also filed an affidavit to this effect. In the counter affidavit filed by the Managing Director it was stated that some of the Salesmen working in the rural outlets at Faridabad, Panchkula, and Bhiwani districts had been paid some incentives during the years 1980-81 and 1981-82. But there is nothing on record to show that any incentive was ever paid to the salesmen after 1982. There is nothing on record to show that even during 1980-82 the salesmen working in the rural outlets of the other districts have been paid any incentive. It is, thus, clear that no incentive has been ever paid to any salesmen working in the rural areas after 1980-82. Therefore, the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner-society that the salesmen working in the rural areas are paid incentives which have been denied to the salesmen working in the outlet in the urban areas.  15. The principle of equal pay for equal work is now well recognised and is no longer res integra. In a recent judgment of this court in Girdhari Lal and others v. State of Haryana, 1996(2) SCT 132 (P&H) : 1996(1) SLR 152 several authorities of the Supreme Court have been considered as it was held as follows :-  "The principle of 'equal pay for equal work' was further enunciated and approved by the Supreme Court in Savita v. U.O.I., AIR 1985 SC 1124, Dhirendra Chamoli v. State of U.P., 1986(1) SCC 637, Surinder Singh v. Engineer-in-Chief AIR 1986 SC 594 Bhagwan Dass v. State of Haryana, AIR 1987 SC 2049 Jaipal v. State of Haryana, AIR 1988 SC 150 V. Markendeya v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1989 SC 1308, State of U.P. v. J.P. Chaurasia,AIR 1989 SC 19 and host of other authorities." After referring to its various earlier judgments, the Supreme Court in Grih Kalyan Kendra Workers Union v. Union of India, 1991(2) SCT 95 (SC) : AIR 1991 SC 1173 : (1991(1) SLR 618 (SC) held :- ".....Equal pay for equal work is not expressly declared by the Constitution as a fundamental right but in view of the Directive Principles of State policy as contained in Article 39(d) of the Constitution 'equal pay for equal work' has assumed the status of fundamental right in service jurisprudence having regard to the constitutional mandate of equality in Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution equal pay for equal work and providing security for service by the regularising casual employment within a reasonable period has been accepted by this court as a constitutional goal to our socialist pattern. It has ceased to be a judge made law as it is the part of the constitutional philosophy which ensures a welfare socialistic pattern of a State providing equal opportunity to all and equal pay for equal work for similarly placed employees of the State. This Court has zealously enforced the fundamental right of equal pay for equal work in effectuating the constitutional goal of equality and social justice in a number of decisions." In this case, the Supreme Court further held that the principle of equal pay for equal work was applicable in its full vigour even in establishments which were not a regular department of the State but were instrumentality of the State. The Court further held that while considering the principle of equal pay for equal work it was not necessary to find out the similarities by mathematical formula. Reasonable similarity in the nature of work, performance of duties, qualifications and quality of work was sufficient." 16. On a consideration of the nature of work, duties and functions of the salesmen working in the outlets of the petitioner-society in the rural areas and the outlets in the urban areas and also in view of the decision of the Board of Directors dated January 15, 1981, and in view of the fact that both the posts are inter-transferable, I am of the opinion that the salesmen working in the rural areas are also entitled to the regular pay scales and conditions of service at par with their counterparts working in the outlets situated in the urban areas.  17. The next question that falls for my consideration is in regard to the date from which the pay scales have to be applied. The Labour Court directed to apply the pay scales with effect from June 1, 1986, on the basis (sic) State Government Employees have been given the revised scales of pay with effect from that date in pursuance of the recommendations of the Fourth Pay Commission. But it cannot be said that the employees of the petitioner-society are to be treated at par with the Government employees.
