Appeal from the Courts of original jurisdiction to the High Court in its appellate jurisdiction. - And we do further ordain that an appeal shall lie to the said High Court of Judicature at Madras, Bombay, Fort William in Bengal from the judgment (not being a judgment passed in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction in respect of a decree or order made in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction by a Court subject to the superintendence of the said High Court and not being an order made in the exercise of revisional jurisdiction, and not being a sentence or order passed or made in exercise of the power of superintendence under the provisions of Section 107 of the Government of India Act, or in the exercise of criminal jurisdiction) of one Judge of the said High Court or one Judge of any Division Court, pursuant to Section 108 of the Government of India Act, and that notwithstanding anything hereinbefore provided, an appeal shall lie to the said High Court from a judgment of one Judge of the said High Court or one Judge of any Division Court, pursuant to Section 108 of the Government of India Act, on or after the first day of February 1929 in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction in respect of a decree or order made in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction by a Court subject to the superintendence of the said High Court where the Judge who passed the judgment declares that the case is a fit one for appeal; but that the right of appeal from other judgments of Judges of the said High Court or of such Division Court shall be to Us, Our heirs or successors in Our or Their Privy Council, as hereinafter provided." 8. A close reading of the provision, quoted above, shows that it has three limbs : the first limb specifies the type of judgments of one judge of the High Court which is appealable in that High Court and the categories of judgments/orders which are excluded from its ambit; the second limb provides that notwithstanding anything provided in the first limb, an appeal shall lie to that High Court from judgment of one judge of the High Court or one judge of any Division Court, pursuant to Section 108 of the Government of India Act (now Article 225 of the Constitution of India), on or after February 1, 1929, passed in exercise of appellate jurisdiction in respect of a decree or order made in exercise of appellate jurisdiction by a Court subject to the superintendence of the said High Court where the judge who passed the judgment declares that the case is a fit one for appeal; and the third limb says that the right of appeal from other judgments of judges of the said High Court or such Division Court shall be to "us, our heirs or successors in our or their Privy Council, as hereinafter provided".  Here, we are concerned with the type of judgments mentioned in the first limb.  9. The above analysis of Clause 15 of the Letters Patent will equally apply to Clause 10 of the Letters Patent of Patna. It follows that an appeal shall lie to larger Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Patna from a judgment of one judge of the said High Court or one judge of any Division Court pursuant to Article 225 of the Constitution of India. The following categories of judgment are excluded from the appealable judgments under the first limb of Clause 10 of the Letters Patent :  (i) a judgment passed in exercise of appellate jurisdiction in respect of a decree or order made in exercise of appellate jurisdiction by a Court subject to superintendence of the said High Court; in other words no letters patent appeal lies to the High Court from a judgment of one judge of the High Court passed in second appeal; (ii) an order made by one judge of the High Court in exercise of revisional jurisdiction; and (iii) a sentence or order passed or made in exercise of power under the provisions of Section 107 of Government of India Act, 1915 (now Article 227 of the Constitution of India) or in exercise of criminal jurisdiction. 10. From the above discussion, it is clear that from all judgments except those falling under the excluded categories, an appeal lies to the same High Court.  11. The next question which needs to be considered is, what does the expression `judgment' mean ? That expression is not defined in Letters Patent. It is now well-settled that definition of `judgment' in Section 2(9) of Code of Civil Procedure, has no application to Letters Patent. That expression was interpreted by different High Courts of India for purposes of Letters Patent. In Asrumati Debi v. Kumar Rupendra Deb Rajkot 1953 SCR 1159, a four-Judge Bench of this Court considered the pronouncements of the High Court of Calcutta in Justices of the Peace for Calcutta v. Oriental Gas Co., 8 Beng. L.R. 433, the High Court of Rangoon in Dayabhai v. Murugappa Chettiar, ILR 13 Rang. 457, the High Court of Madras in Tuljaram v. Alagappa, ILR 35 Mad. 1, the High Court at Bombay in Sonebai v. Ahmedbhai, 9 Bombay H.C.R. 398 as also the High Court at Nagpur, the High Court at Allahabad and Lahore High Court and observed as follows :  "In view of this wide divergence of judicial opinion, it may be necessary for this Court at some time or other to examine carefully the principles upon which the different views mentioned above purport to be based and attempt to determine with as much definiteness as possible the true meaning and scope of the word `judgment' as it occurs in clause 15 of the Letters Patent of the Calcutta High Court and in the corresponding clauses of the Letters Patent of the other High Courts." 12. Such an exercise was undertaken by a three-Judge Bench of this Court in Shah Babulal Khimji v. Jayaben D. Kania and another, 1981(4) SCC 8. Fazal Ali, J. speaking for himself and Varadarajan, J. after analysing the views of different High Courts, referred to above, observed as follows :  The intention, therefore, of the givers of the Letters Patent was that the word `judgment' should receive a much wider and more liberal interpretation than the word `judgment' used in the Code of Civil Procedure. At the same time, it cannot be said that any order passed by a Trial Judge would amount to a judgment; otherwise there will be no end to the number of orders which would be appealable under the Letters Patent. It seems to us that the word `judgment' has undoubtedly a concept of finality in a broader and not a narrower sense." It was pointed out that `judgment' could be of three kinds :  (1) A final judgment. - in this category falls a judgment by which suit or action brought by the plaintiff is dismissed or decreed in part or full; (2) A preliminary judgment. - this category is sub-divided into two classes : (a) where the Trial Judge by an order dismisses the suit, without going into the merits of the suit, only on a preliminary objection raised by the defendant/respondent on the ground of maintainability; (b) where maintainability of the suit is objected on the ground of bar of jurisdiction, e.g., res judicata, a manifest defect in the suit, absence of notice under Section 80 and the like; and (3) Intermediary or interlocutory judgment. - in this category fall orders referred to in clauses (a) to (w) of order 43 Rule 1 and also such other orders which possess the characteristic and trappings of finality and may adversely affect a valuable right of the party or decide an important aspect of the trial in an ancillary proceeding. Elucidating the third category, it is observed :  "Every interlocutory order cannot be regarded as a judgment but only those orders would be judgments which decide matters of moment or affect vital and valuable rights of the parties and which work serious injustice to the party concerned." 13. In the instant case, we are concerned with the last mentioned category. From the above discussion, it follows that to determine the question whether an interlocutory order passed by one judge of a High Court falls within the meaning of `judgment' for purposes of Letters Patent the test is : whether the order is a final determination affecting vital and valuable rights and obligations of the parties concerned. This has to be ascertained on the facts of each case.  14. Adverting to the facts of this case, Section 17-B of the I.D. Act confers valuable rights on the workmen and correspondingly imposes an onerous obligation on the employer. The order in question passed by the learned Single Judge determines the entitlement of the workmen to receive benefits and imposes an obligation on the appellant to pay such benefits provided in the said section. That order cannot but be `judgment' within the meaning of Clause 10 of Letters Patent, Patna. The High Court is obviously in error in holding that the said order is not judgment within the meaning of Clause 10 of the Letters Patent of Patna.  15. For the above reasons, we hold that the order of the learned Single Judge passed on application under Section 17-B of the I.D. Act on April 26, 1999 is judgment within the meaning of Clause 10 of the Letters Patent of Patna and is, therefore, appealable. The order of the High Court is accordingly set aside, the Letters Patent Appeal is restored to the file of the High Court and the case is remanded to the High Court for deciding the LPA on merits in accordingly with law.  16. The appeal is accordingly allowed. In the circumstances of the case, the parties are directed to bear their own costs.  Appeal allowed.
summary: The Constitution of India, Article 225 and the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 17-B, are referenced in relation to Letters Patent Appeal. The issue at hand is whether an LPA against an order made by a Single Judge under Section 17-B of the ID Act is maintainable under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent of Patna before a Division Bench of the High Court. The decision was that the Single Judge's order made under Section 17-B of the ID Act constitutes a "judgment" as per Clause 10 of the Letters Patent of Patna, and therefore, it is appealable. As a result, the case was remanded to the High Court to decide the LPA on its merits in accordance with the law. [Para 15]

text: M.N. Rao, J. - The petitioner who was the Branch Manager of the State Bank of Hyderabad was dismissed from service as a disciplinary measure by an order Dt. 16.11.1987 passed by the second respondent-Managing Director State Bank of Hyderabad, Gunfoundary, Hyderabad, which was confirmed by the appellate authority, the first respondent by an order dated 30.11.88. This writ petition was filed for a certiorari calling for the records of the order of dismissal as confirmed by the appellate authority and to quash the same.  2. The alleged acts of misconduct attributed to the petitioner occurred in 1985 when he was working as Manager of the Shabad Branch. Four staff members of the Shabad Branch gave a written representation to the Regional Manager, State of Bank of Hyderabad making certain allegations against the petitioner; they pertain to the fictitious overdraft relating to a customer by name. T. Papi Reddy, misuse of the motor-cycle bearing Regn. No. AAX 8925 belonging to the Bank and incurring of false expenditure to the tune of Rs. 1100/- by the petitioner on the ground of having hired a jeep purportedly for official purposes. A preliminary investigation was conducted by one K. Raghunatha Rao, Zonal Officer (examined as MW 10 before the Enquiry Officer) of Hyderabad Office and based upon his report dated 11.5.85 the petitioner was kept under suspension by an order dated 17.5.85. A charge-sheet dated 21.8.85 containing the three following charges was served on the petitioner and he was asked to submit a written statement.  "During your incumbency as Branch Manager of Shabad Branch from 9.2.85 to 20.5.85 : (1) You failed to ensure and protect the interest of the Bank and discharged your duties with utmost devotion and integrity, honesty and diligence and acted in a manner unbecoming of a Bank's official as : (i) you granted an overdraft to one Shri T. Papi Reddy, even though it was known to you that it was not for his use; (ii) You passed for payment on 1.5.1985 a cheque No. 116479 for Rs. 8,000/- in the above account even though the cheque was forged. (iii) You received the payment of the cheque above referred yourself discharging it. (2) You accepted on 30.4.1985 a late receipt for Rs. 8,205/- from Shri Gaddam Krishna Murthy, a constituent of the Bank, in a highly irregular manner and acted in a manner detrimental to the interest of the Bank. (3) You utilised the Bank's motor-cycle and the jeep hired, for your personal purposes and at the cost of the Bank and thus failed to discharge your duties with utmost devotion, integrity and honesty. Your above acts are in violation of Regulation 50(4) of the State Bank of Hyderabad (Officers') Service Regulations. Sd/-  Disciplinary authority/General Manager  (Operations)" Dt. 21st Aug., 85.  In his explanation the petitioner asserted that he was victim of a conspiracy hatched by certain staff members who were disposed inimically towards him. On 30.4.84 an overdraft facility was given to Papi Reddy, one of the customers of the bank after his financial soundness was ascertained. The customer Papi Reddy was not given a cheque book. Therefore, one loose cheque bearing No. 116473 was given to him. The customer signed the cheque and presented the same for encashment. At that time there were no issuable notes in the Bank (the branch being very small) and the customer continued to wait at the bank hoping that some other customers might credit amounts sufficient for the bank to pay him the cash of Rs. 8,000/-. After the office hours also Papi Reddy continued to wait at the bank and at that time one customer by name G. Krishna Murthy had sent cash of Rs. 8,205/- for crediting to his account and from that amount Rs. 8,000/- was paid to Papi Reddy and a debit voucher was obtained from him with a clear understanding that he would present another cheque the next day morning. Papi Reddy did not come to the bank the next day as he was attending a marriage function and, therefore, a message was sent to Papi Reddy to present the cheque so that the amount could be adjusted. The Head Cashier, Kulkarni (examined as M.W.2) refused to honour the cheque on the ground that Papi Reddy was not physically present and, therefore, the petitioner acknowledg the cheque on the reverse and asked Kulkarni to post the amount against late receipt. The other allegations relating to misuse of office motor-cycle and false expenditure in relation to hiring of jeep were also denied by him.  3. As the explanation was found to be not satisfactory, the management appointed one B. Someswara Rao as the Enquiry Authority by an order dated 20th December, 1985 to conduct enquiry against the petitioner in respect of the three charges. On behalf of the management 10 witnesses were examined and 46 exhibits were marked. On behalf of the charged petitioner only one witness was examined and three documents were marked as exhibits. Among the witnesses examined was one S.K. Jain, (M.W.9), Government examiner of questioned documents. His opinion was marked as Ex.M.E.28 before the Enquiry Officer. His testimony was to the effect that the specimen signature of Papi Reddy did not tally with the signature found on the reverse of the cheque bearing No. 116479 dated 1.5.85 and that the writing on the leave application of the petitioner (treated as specimen handwriting of the petitioner) and the writings on the body of the cheque bearing No. 116473 are by one and the same person. In other words, his testimony is to the effect that the signature of Papi Reddy on the cheque presented in the name of the Papi Reddy was a forged one. As regards charge No. 3 the Enquiry Officer held that :  "there was misuse of Bank's motor-cycle by Sri Jayachandra Rao (the petitioner for his personal visits. However, it is difficult to estimate to what extent the vehicle was misused." As regards the hire charges in relation to the jeep the finding of the Enquiry Officer was that :  "......the jeep hired for the purpose of inspection of assets charged to the Bank was not used mainly for the said purpose but mostly misused by Sri Jayachandra Rao at Bank's cost." The disciplinary authority, the General Manager (Operations) felt that appropriate punishment for the charges held proved was dismissal from service and as the said punishment was a major penalty which could be imposed only by the appointing authority in terms of Regulation 68(3)(iii) of State Bank of Hyderabad (Officers') Service Regulations, he forwarded the entire record to the appointing authority with a recommendation to impose the penalty of dismissal. Pursuant to that the appointing authority passed an order dated 16.11.87 imposing the punishment of dismissal. The petitioner preferred statutory appeal to the appellate authority, the Executive Committee of the State Bank of Hyderabad and without waiting for the decision of the appellate authority he filed the present writ petition. During the pendency of the writ petition, the appellate authority passed the order dated 30.11.88 in No. DPC/1757 dismissing the appeal. Thereafter W.P.M.P. No. 12171 of 89 was filed by the petitioner to quash the said appellate Order.  4. Shri Ananth Babu, learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the petitioner was appointed by the Board of Directors as officer of the State Bank of Hyderabad and, therefore, the second respondent, the Managing Director, had no jurisdiction to pass the order of dismissal. The dismissal order is liable to be set aside on the ground of want of jurisdiction, he contends.  5. He also contends that the order of dismissal must be struck down on the ground that it was passed in violation of principles of natural justice. The investigation report submitted by M.W. 10. Sri K. Raghunatha Rao was not made available although a specific request was made by the petitioner. The Enquiry Officer declined the request on the ground that the said investigation report was not supplied to him as in terms of Regulation 68(2)(xii) the authority having custody of the document is permitted to claim privilege.  6. The most important witness to unfold the primary charge of forgery was T. Papi Reddy, but he was not examined. The petitioner could not examine him because the said Papi Reddy gave a letter to the petitioner clearly stating that because of the pressure exerted by the staff members of the Bank he had given the complaint against the petitioner and when the petitioner requested him to appear as witness on his behalf he declined stating that there was no need to figure as witness in view of the letter given by him to the petitioner.  7. The enquiry involved legal complexities and the material brought on record was voluminous. The presentation Officer who represented the management before the Enquiry Officer was specially trained to conduct prosecutions. He underwent special training in this regard. The petitioner was represented by another Officer to conduct defence on his behalf. A handwriting expert testified on behalf of the management in respect of the allegation of forgery. When the petitioner had requested for permission to engage a counsel, the same was declined. Within half an hour after the chief examination of the expert witness was over, the defence was asked to proceed with cross-examination. This attitude on the part of the Enquiry Officer had disabled the petitioner from effectively representing his case. The reasonable opportunity which he is entitled to establish his innocence is a basic principle of natural justice; in the absence of an advocate to defend him his defence was seriously crippled and, therefore, natural justice was breached. The report of the Enquiry Officer was supplied to the petitioner along with the order of dismissal. The appointing authority before making up of his mind to impose the punishment of dismissal ought to have furnished a copy of the Enquiry Officer's report to the petitioner so as to enable him to make a representation with reference to the findings recorded by the Enquiry Officer. Supply of the report of the Enquiry Officer to enable the petitioner to prefer appeal would not cure the illegality. When the petitioner wanted time to produce defence witnesses the same was not granted, although the management had taken several months to produce their witnesses. Failure to afford reasonable opportunity to the petitioner to produce his witnesses had resulted in breach of principles of natural justice.  8. The enquiry was vitiated because of the bias on the part of the Enquiry Officer : he not only rejected the just and legitimate request made by the petitioner, but he also did not record the evidence of the witnesses faithfully. He used to prompt the witnesses while recording the evidence.  9. In opposition to these submissions, Shri Srinivasa Murthy, learned counsel for the Bank maintains that the order of dismissal was passed after fully complying with all the legal formalities. By the date of imposition of punishment of dismissal, under the Regulations, the competent authority to make appointments to the post held by the petitioner was the Managing Director and, therefore, the order of dismissal is not afflicted with legal infirmity of want of jurisdiction. The petitioner is not entitled to a copy of the investigation report since the Enquiry Officer did not take that into consideration in assessing the guilt of the petitioner in respect of the charges levelled against him. The petitioner was permitted to be represented by an officer of the Bank. On behalf of the management also another officer was kept engaged as presentation officer. As no advocate or legally trained person represented the management before the Enquiry Officer the petitioner was not entitled to be represented by a counsel. Sub-Clause (vii) of clause (2) of Regulation 68 of the S.B.H. (Officers') Service Regulations does not permit a charged officer to engage a legal practitioner in disciplinary proceedings. The Regulations also do not entitle the petitioner to have a copy of the Enquiry Officer's report before the punishment was imposed. No second show-cause notice is contemplated under the Regulations and the competent authority is obliged to take a decision based on the evidence already recorded. To enable the petitioner to effectively pursue his remedy of statutory appeal he was furnished with a copy of the Enquiry Officer's report and, therefore, it could not be said that natural justice was breached. Non-examination of Papi Reddy was inevitable. He went back on the written complaint submitted by him to the bank authorities about the acts of misconduct committed by the petitioner and shortly thereafter gave a letter to the petitioner denying the allegations levelled by him against the petitioner. No useful purpose would be served by examining such a person. No one prevented the petitioner from examining Papi Reddy on his behalf. The Enquiry Officer acted fairly and impartially. There is no basis for the allegation that he was biased against the petitioner.  10. The first point to be considered is whether the order of dismissal passed by the second respondent-Managing Directors was vitiated due to want of jurisdiction. It is true that the appointing authority when the petitioner was recruited as an Officer in 1979 was the Board of Directors as per the rules then in existence-Staff Assistant Service Rules. The State Bank of Hyderabad (Officer's) Service Regulations, 1979 (hereinafter called as the Regulations) came into force with effect from 1.10.79 except to the extent Chapter 10 relating to disciplinary proceedings which was brought into force with effect from 1.4.80. After the Regulations came into force, the State Bank of Hyderabad Assistants Service Rules ceased to have operation. Regulation 67 specifies major and minor penalties. 'Disciplinary authority' as defined in clause (p) of Regulation 3 means the authority specified by the Executive Committee from time to time. Regulation 68 says that the disciplinary authority or any higher authority may impose the penalties mentioned in Regulation 67. The proviso to Regulation 68 is to the effect that where the disciplinary authority is lower in rank than the appointing authority in respect of the category of officers to which the officer belongs, no order imposing any of the major penalties shall be made except by the appointing authority or any authority higher than it on the recommendations of the disciplinary authority. By Circular No. OPD/4 the Executive Committee had specified the General Manager as the disciplinary authority in respect of Officers in MMGS-II, the post which the petitioner was holding at the relevant time. A Division Bench of this Court in W.P. No. 7398 of 1988 considered an identical question and held that clause (p) of Regulation 3 does not empower the Executive Committee to delegate its power to another person and, therefore, the major penalty imposed by the General Manager who was lower in rank than the Executive Committee was liable to be quashed. A similar question arose before the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal Nos. 3392-3394 of 1990 in respect of certain orders passed by the General Manager, State Bank of India. Interpreting Regulation 55 of the State Bank of India General Regulations, 1955 which is similar to Regulation 68, the Supreme Court held in the above civil appeals :  "...The only right conferred under the said provision is that the officers or employees of the State Bank cannot be dismissed by an authority lower than the appointing authority. With the risk of repetition it may be stated that on the date when the order of dismissal has been passed, Chief General Manager had already become the appointing authority and as such the order of dismissal has not been passed by an authority lower than the appointing authority. Apart from the view taken by us as mentioned above the Regulation 55 has been amended by a resolution of the Central Board dated August 25, 1988 with retrospective effect. It has now been made clear in the explanation that for the purpose of clause (b) the term appointing authority shall mean and include the authority who has been designated as such in respect of such class or grade of officers or employees to which the officer or employee concerned, as the case may be, belongs at the time when such order is passed or any proceeding leading to such order or termination is initiated. This provision now concludes the controversy if any and clearly provides that the appointing authority shall mean and include the authority who has been designated as such at the time when such order is passed."  The Supreme Court also held that if on the date of the order of dismissal the authority who passed that order happened to be the appointing authority, although the charged officer was appointed by a different authority, the dismissal order would not suffer from any legal infirmity on that score. As admittedly by the date of the order of dismissal the second respondent/Managing Director, was the appointing authority in respect of the post held by the petitioner, the order of dismissal, cannot be faulted on the ground of want of jurisdiction.  11. The petitioner, it is not in dispute, made a request for production of the investigation report submitted by K. Raghunath Rao (M.W.10 before the Enquiry Officer). That request was rejected by the Enquiry Officer observing :  "The documents over which the Bank has claimed privilege is the "Investigation report" as different from material documents like statement of witnesses etc. The said investigation report is not provided to the Enquiry Authority along with the appointment letter and the charge-sheet. In terms of Regulation 68(2)(xii) the authority having custody of the document is permitted to claim privilege. The investigation report is the document of the Bank and in my view the Bank can exercise the option available to it, in respect of this particular document". Sub-clause (xii) of clause (2) of Regulation 68 reads : On receipt of the requisition under clause (xi), the authority having custody or possession of the requisitioned documents shall arrange to produce the same before the Inquiring Authority on the date, place and time specified in the requisition : Provided that the authority having custody or possession of the requisitioned documents may claim privilege if the production of such documents will be against the public interest or the interest of the Bank. In that event, it shall inform the Inquiring Authority accordingly." No record has been produced before me to show on what ground privilege was claimed by the Bank. The Enquiry Officer has not asked the Bank to produce the investigation report. Privilege can be claimed under the proviso to sub-clause (xii) of Regulation 68(2) only if the production of a document will be against the public interest of the Bank. It is not shown how the public interest or the interest or the interest of the Bank would suffer adversely if the investigation report was produced at the time of the enquiry. The investigation report is dated 11.5.85. The officer who investigated and submitted the report is one Shri K. Raghunatha Rao who was examined as M.W.10 before the Enquiry Officer. This report was the basis for placing the petitioner under suspension. In his evidence as M.W.10 he stated the details of the investigation conducted by him. He asserted that he went to Shabad on 9.5.85 to conduct investigation. He stated that when he was conducting investigation, the Head Cashier and other staff members stated to him about the petitioner remitting money and arranging payment of the amount collected by him from his brother-in-law. To a question put by the presentation officer whether the staff members told him orally or had given anything in writing, he replied :  "The staff members have given in writing some of the above events and some were told orally which was forwarded to Head Officer." Thereafter he identified the document M.E.15- the written complaint dated 6.5.85 submitted by the members of the staff to the Regional Manager. He also testified before the Enquiry Officer what certain persons stated before him. One of his answers was to the effect that :  "Shri P. Jayachandra Rao (the petitioner) also told him (Papi Reddy) that the amount will be utilised by his brother-in-law for purchased of a vehicle. Shri Papi Reddy also stated that he is not responsible for the over-draft granted in his name by Shri P. Jayachandra Rao for which he signed the documents." From his evidence as M.W.10, it would appear that Shri K. Raghunath Rao had recorded the statements of some persons in the course of his investigation report which was placed before me does not contain any statements recorded by Shri Raghunath Rao. When an officer conducts a preliminary investigation and submits a report and later on figures as a witness in the enquiry and testifies as to the details of the investigation conducted by him, it is necessary that the report submitted by him should be produced to enable the delinquent to cross-examine the officer to test the veracity of his oral evidence with reference to the contents in the investigation report. It would have been a different thing if the Officer had not testified in his evidence as to the details of the investigation conducted by him and what his report incorporated, but when he chose to depose as to the details of the investigation conducted by him, it was incumbent upon him to produce the investigation report. The situation is akin to the evidence of an investigation officer in criminal trials. Whatever statement an investigation officer records must be produced before the court to enable the accused to cross-examine as to the veracity of the evidence, regarding what has been recorded. Sri Srinivasa Murthy, learned counsel for the Bank says that the Investigation Officer has not recorded statements of any witnesses but as already observed by me supra, the trend of the evidence given by Sri Raghunatha Rao, M.W.10 before the Enquiry Officer shows that he had recorded the statements of some persons. It is difficult to conclude definitely as to whether or not M.W.10 had recorded the statements of any persons during the preliminary investigation. The Supreme Court in Krishna Chandra v. Union of India, AIR 1974 SC 1594 at 159 para 16, adverting to the question whether a charged officer was entitled to a copy of the investigation officer's report observed :  "It is obvious that the appellant was not entitled to a copy of the report made by Mr. Srivastava or any other officer unless the enquiry officer relied on these reports. It is very necessary for an authority which orders an enquiry to be satisfied that there are prima facie grounds for holding a disciplinary enquiry and, therefore, before he makes up his mind he will either himself investigate or direct his subordinates to investigate in the matter and it is only after he receives the result of these investigations that he can decide as to whether disciplinary action is called for or not. Therefore, these documents of the nature of inter-departmental communications between officers preliminary to the holding of enquiry have really no importance unless the Enquiry Officer wants to rely on them for his conclusion. In that case it would only be right that copies of the same should be given to the delinquent." 12. In the present case the contents of the investigation report formed part of the testimony of the investigation officer M.W.10. In the assessment of the guilt of the petitioner the evidence of M.W.10 assumes great relevance. It, therefore, follows that the contents of the investigation report as spoken to by M.W.10, the investigation officer, also formed one of the basis for the Enquiry Officer to assess the guilt of the petitioner. In the circumstances, it cannot be said that no prejudice was caused to the petitioner by reason of failure to furnish a copy of the investigation officer's report and this, I think, amounts to violation of principles of natural justice.  13. From 11.3.86 to 4.2.87 on different dates the prosecution witnesses were examined. A detailed statement in this regard as mentioned in the reply affidavit is as follows :-  Witness No. Date on which examined Time allowed for prosecution between one witness and the other for examination. M.W.I 11.3.86 to 18.6.1986 Time allowed for prosecution for presenting M.W.I was 3 months and 7 days i.e. from 12.3.86 to 17.6.1986. M.W.II, III, IV, V 17.6.1986 to 29.7.1986 Adjourned for 3 months from 16.3.1986 to 16.6.86. M.W.VI 29.7.1986 Time allowed for production of MW VI by prosecution was one month nine days, i.e. from 21.6.86 to 28.7.86. M.W.VIII 29.7.1986 to 2.8.1986, 25.9.1986 to 20.9.1986 and 20.11.1986 to 21.11.86. Time allowed for prosecution one month twenty days from 27.9.86 to 19.11.86. M.W.IX 5.2.1986 Time allowed for presenting expert witness by the prosecution was fifteen days from 22.11.1986 to 4.12.1986. M.W.X 6.12.1986 to 2.2.87 to 4.2.1987. Time allowed for prosecution to produce MW-X was one month 25 days i.e., from 7.12.1986 to 1.2.87. The first witness for defence was examined on 7.2.87 and the enquiry was adjourned to 10.2.87. The charged officer could not produce his witness and, therefore, his representative asked for some more time. That request was rejected very unjustly by the Enquiry Officer. The following is the enquiry proceedings held on 10.2.87 :  "ENQUIRY PROCEEDINGS DT. 10.2.87 at HYDERABAD. PRESENT : S/Sri B. Someswara Rao-Inquiring Authority (I.A.) K. Syama Sundara Prasad-Presenting Officer. P. Jayachandra Rao-Charged official. P. Subba Rao-Defence representative. IA : The defence to produce the next witness. D.R. : As the witnesses are not available, I request to allow some more time. I.A. : As the enquiry proceedings are adjourned on two occasions earlier at the request of the defence and also at the request of the charged official and the defence representative the venue of the enquiry is shifted to Hyderabad to enable them to present their witness, further postponement of the case is not allowed. The request of the D.R. for further time is allowed. I.A. : Please let me know whether Sri P. Jayachandra Rao is being examined as defence witness. D.R. : No. I.A. : Please let me know whether any other witnesses are being produced in defence. D.R. : Though we prepare to produce some more witnesses, as the time was not allowed and the proposed witnesses are at present not available, the request was to allow for some time. I.A. : The charged official has been provided with sufficient time and opportunity to produce the witnesses in defence. As already explained no further time could be allowed." The action of the Enquiry Officer in refusing the legitimate request of the petitioner for some more time to produce his witnesses had undoubtedly disabled the petitioner from adducing evidence in support of his plea of innocence which, I must hold, is violative of principles of natural justice. Had some reasonable time been granted to the petitioner he would have brought witnesses in support of his plea of innocence in respect of the charges. 14. Dealing with a similar situation in which an Enquiry Officer declined the request of the charged officer for time to produce witnesses, the Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. C.S. Sharma, AIR 1968 SC 158 at 161 paras 8 and 9, held :  "This commission in our judgment was sufficient to vitiate the whole proceeding because no enquiry of this type in which there are charges of a criminal nature, can be said to be properly conducted when the defence of the officer is either frustrated or ruled out ...... It is possible that if a date had been fixed, he would not only have led evidence with regard to the car, but would have brought witnesses to clear himself of other charges, but no such opportunity was clearly afforded to him." The above observations apply on all fours to the case on hand.  15. When the hand-writing expert M.W.9, S.K. Jain was produced as a witness before the Enquiry Officer, the defence representative requested for permission to engage a counsel to cross-examine the expert stating that :  ".......only an advocate who by virtue of his experience in handling the expert witnesses can do justice. A hand-writing expert or for that matter any other technical expert cannot be considered an expert in cross-examination. In view of this I request the I.A. (Inquiry Authority) to permit us to engage a lawyer/advocate whose charges also may be paid by the Bank as per eligibility." This request was rejected by the Enquiry Officer observing :  "In terms of Regulation 68(2)(vii) engaging a legal practitioner by the officer is prohibited and to my knowledge there is no amendment to the said Regulation." After the chief examination of the report was over half an hour time was given to the defence representative to cross-examine the expert. The defence representative requested one week's time to prepare for the cross-examination. That request was rejected by the Enquiry Officer stating :  "The request of the D.R. is overruled. The defence representative is advised to take up cross-examination of MW IX." The attitude exhibited by the Enquiry Officer was anything but fair. The defence representative was an Officer of the Bank and he was not an expert. The hand-writing expert M.W.9 was a veteran with thirty years of experience to his credit. He was Government Examiner of questioned documents. It is impossible for a lay person to cross-examine a hand-writing expert. Only a trained lawyer with experience in cross-examination can effectively cross-examine the expert M.W.9. Further, the presenting officer was an experienced person who according to the petition :  ".......had been specially trained to conduct disciplinary enquiries. He attended several training programmes and conducted several enquiries as prosecution officer. He has also functioned as Inquiring Authority in several cases and was fully familiar with the relevant law and rules. He can reasonably be described as a trained prosecutor." This assertion appears to be true. A lay officer untrained in the technicalities of adducing evidence and cross-examining the witnesses cannot discharge his functions effectively when pitted against a trained prosecutor. A similar question fell for consideration before the Supreme Court in C.L. Subramaniam v. Collector of Customs, Cochin, AIR 1972 SC 2178 at 2180 para 13. His Lordship Hegde, J. speaking for the court held :  "The grievance of the appellant was that he was pitted against a trained prosecutor and not that Sivaraman was a legal practitioner. The Disciplinary Authority did not consider that grievance. It brushed aside the request of the appellant on the ground that Sivaraman was not a legal practitioner, a consideration which was not relied on by the appellant. The grounds urged by the appellant in support of his request for permission to engage a legal practitioner were by no means irrelevant. The fact that the case against the appellant was being handled by a trained prosecutor was a good ground for allowing the appellant to engage a legal practitioner to defend him lest the scales should be weighed against him. The Disciplinary Authority completely ignored that circumstance." I am unable to accept the contention of Shri Srinivasa Murthy that as no advocate was appointed to prosecute the case on behalf of the Bank the petitioner was not subjected to any disability by not having a legal practitioner to defend him. The decision of the Supreme Court in Board of Trustees Port of Bombay v. Dilipkumar, AIR 1983 SC 109 relied upon by the Shri Srinivasa Murthy deals with a situation where the prosecution was represented by a legal practitioner but permission to engage a counsel was denied to the charged officer. The Supreme Court rule that in such a situation the charged officer also must be permitted to have the services of a legal practitioner. In the case on hand, although the presenting officer was not a legal practitioner, he appears to be a trained prosecutor and in the circumstances of the case refusal to permit the petitioner to have the services of a legal practitioner had seriously prejudiced his case and, therefore, the enquiry was vitiated due to violation of principles of natural justice.  16. The report of the Enquiry Officer, it is not in dispute, was supplied to the petitioner only along with the order of dismissal. The Regulations do not provide for a second show cause notice. Even in respect of Government employees holding civil posts to whom the prosecution of Article 311 is available, it was held by the Supreme Court, in Kailash Chander v. State of U.P., AIR 1988 SC 1338 at 1340 para 5, that failure to supply a copy of the enquiry officer's report would not afflict the order of punishment with any illegality. Speaking for the Court His Lordship L.M. Sharma, J. ruled :  "The question of service of copy of the report arose on account of right of a second show cause notice to the Government servant before the 42nd amendment and since present disciplinary proceeding was held later, the petitioner cannot legitimately demand a second opportunity. That being the position, non-service of a copy of the report is immaterial." The contention of Shri Anantha Babu in this regard, therefore, must fail.  17. Shri Srinivasa Murthy contends that even if Charge No. 1 goes, on the ground of refusal of permission to the petitioner to engage an advocate before the Enquiry Officer, the findings in respect of the other two charges stand and, therefore, this court should not interfere with the punishment. In support of this he placed reliance upon a decision of the Supreme Court in Pyare Lal Sharma v. Managing Director, J&K Industries Ltd., AIR 1989 SC 1854 at 1860 para 20. His Lordship Kuldip Singh, J. speaking for the Court held :  "Once it is established to the satisfaction of the authority that an employee remains on unauthorised absence from duty, the only action which can be taken is the termination of his services. Similar is the case when an employee takes part in active politics. The finding in the termination order regarding taking part in active politics cannot be sustained because no notice in this respect was given to Sharma but the order of termination can be supported on the ground of remaining unauthorised absence from duty. This Court in State of Orissa v. Vidyabhushan Mohapatra (1963) Supp. 1 SCR 648 : AIR 1963 SC 779 and Railway Board v. Niranjan Singh (1969) 3 SCR 548 : AIR 1969 SC 966 has held that if the order can be supported on one ground for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed it is not for the courts to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority punishing the public servant. Thus there is no force in this argument." The above ruling has no application to the case on hand. Violation of principles of natural justice permeate the entire gamut of all the charges. The failure to supply a copy of the investigation report and the failure to give reasonable time to the petitioner to produce defence witnesses cannot be said to be confined to any particular charge. The bias of the Enquiry Officer is clearly established. While recording the evidence he had conducted himself in such a way as to cause reasonable apprehension in the mind of the petitioner that the enquiry would not be fair. The following extracts from the Enquiry Proceedings indicate the bias of the Enquiry Officer.  "I.A. : I have noticed that the witness MW-I is deposing what he knew. Further, there is no allergy for hearsay evidence in departmental enquiries; provided it has reasonable nexus and credibility. However, whether the deposition of MW-I is hearsay or otherwise will be examined by me." (He never examined this point later)  D.R. : I pray the I.A. not to prompt the witness and request him to note down whatever the witness deposed. If any clarification need to be sought, may please be recorded.  I.A. : The opinion of the D.R. that I am prompting the witness is not correct. I am ensuring in my words to the witness. What he meant is recorded in the proceedings. It is very much open for the witness to correct any thing which is different from what he meant to say. M.W. I may continue his deposition."  18. The last contention urged by Sri Srinivasa Murthy is that the appellate order into which the order of dismissal passed by the second respondent was merged, has not been questioned and, therefore, even if the dismissal order passed by the second respondent is quashed, the appellate order will survive. I cannot agree (See S.S. Rathore v. State of M.P., AIR 1990 SC 10). It is true that the original order gets merged with the appellate order. When the writ petition was filed the petitioner had entertained a legitimate hope that by virtue of the judgment of this Court in W.P. No. 7398 of 1988 he would succeed on the ground of want of jurisdiction on the part of the second respondent to pass the order of dismissal. After the writ petition was filed he preferred the appeal and during the pendency of the writ petition the appellate authority has passed the order confirming the order of dismissal. He filed W.P.M.P. No. 12171 of 1989 to call for the records pertaining to the appellate order and quash the same. Since that M.P. is allowed, I do not find any legitimate ground to sustain the present objection. The legal infirmity attached to the original order of dismissal passed by the second respondent viz., breach of principles of natural justice, afflict the appellate order in equal measure.  19. For the above reasons, the writ petition is allowed. The order passed by the appellate authority dated 30.11.88 in No. DPC.1757 confirming the order of the second respondent dated 16.11.87 is set aside. This will not preclude the respondents from conducting a fresh enquiry against the petitioner in accordance with law. But if they choose to do so they shall appoint an officer other than Sri B. Someswara Rao an enquiring authority. There shall be no order as to costs.  Petition allowed.
summary:
A. State Bank of Hyderabad (Officers) Service Regulations, 1979, Regulation 68(2)(xii) - Appointing Authority - Jurisdiction - On the date the dismissal order was passed, the Appointing authority passing the order was legal. Even if the appointment was made by a different authority, the order still stands legal. [Para 10]

B. State Bank of Hyderabad (Officers) Service Regulations, 1979, Regulation 68(2)(xii) - Rule of Natural Justice-Bias-Departmental enquiry - Disadvantages of not supplying the CO with the copy of Preliminary Enquiry Report-not fair to conduct of a prosecution Witness in the Enquiry - It is in principles of natural justice that the CO at issue must have been affected as the report of Pre-Investigation formed part of the Statement and will be prejudiced. [Para 12]

C. Failure to supply a copy of Investigation Report - Principles of natural justice violated - Failure to give reasonable time to produce defence witness - Bias of E.O. - Enquiry unfair - Refusal to legitimate request of petitioner - Violation of principles of natural justice. [Paras 13 and 17]

D. State Bank of Hyderabad (Officers) Service Regulations, 1979, Regulation 68(2)(xii) - Legal Assistant - Presenting officer with training in conducting enquiries as Prosecution officer - Expert witness with long experience, Handwriting Expert - Layman cannot cross-examine such expert and experienced witnesses effectively - By denying legal assistance, C.O. subjected to disability Cause of the petitioner seriously prejudiced - Violation of natural justice - Inquiry vitiated [Para 15]

E. Doctrine of merger - The original order gets merged with the appellate order - However, original order suffers from legal infirmity and breach of principles of natural justice - Appellate order shall equally be bad and has to be set aside. [Paras 18 and 19]

text: R.M. Sahai, J. - Railway employees working in Loco Running Staff, of different zones numbering approximately 800, were dismissed under Rule 14(2) of Railway Service (Discipline and Appeal) Rules for their participation in Loco Running Staff Association strike in January 1981. In each of these cases the disciplinary authority held that it was not reasonably practicable to hold any inquiry. Since then most of the employees have been pursuing their remedy by way of appeals, revisions, writ petitions and claim petitions. They have also been making effort politically to get themselves reinstated. The legal battle has been long one. Some of it is noticed in the order passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal (referred as 'CAT'), Hyderabad. Other orders impugned are passed by CAT, Jodhpur and CAT, Chandigarh. Appeal Numbers 4681-82 of 1992 and 4651-4680 of 1992 raise out of the order passed by the CAT, Hyderabad. Earlier the employees challenged their dismissal by way of writ petitions in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. Some of these petitions were allowed as the appellate authority had passed non-speaking orders. Others were dismissed. Against the orders dismissing the writ petitions the employees filed a review petition which was allowed in view of decision of this Court in Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel, 1985(3) SCC 398 and a direction was given to the appellate authority to decide the appeals afresh in light of observations made by this Court in Satyavir Singh v. Union of India & others, 1985(4) SCC 252 and Ram Chander v. Union of India s, 1986(3) SCC 103. The appellate authority once again maintained the order of dismissal it has been set aside by the CAT both for failure to apply mind and absence of any material justifying dismissal. Following direction were issued :  "In the result, we set aside the orders of the appellate authorities/reviewing authorities rejecting the appeals/review petition of the applicants and the orders of the disciplinary authorities dismissing the applicants from service. In O.A. Nos. 24/86, 369/86, 232/87, 402/88, 403/88, 694/88, 808/88, 809/88, 810/88, 811/88, 812/88, 865/88, 868/88, 869/88, 870/88, 871/88, 883/88, 44/89, 46/89, 92/89, 93/89, 103/89, 231/89, 298/89, 299/89 and 300/89, we direct the appellate authority to conduct an enquiry either himself or through an enquiring authority appointed by it in accordance with the Railway Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1968. If an enquiry is not possible at all, the applicants will be entitled to be reinstated with all consequential benefits. In O.A. Nos. 233/87, 329/87, 767/87, 43/89 and 45/89 it is represented that the applicants have since retired. The question of holding an enquiry in their cases does not, therefore, arise. The orders of the disciplinary authority/appellate authority in these cases are set aside as has been done by the Gauhati Bench in O.A. No. 408/86 (Golul Ch. Barua v. Union of India.). The applicants there will be entitled to receive the salary for the period from the date of dismissal to the date of their attaining the age of superannuation and thereafter to pension as if they had retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation."  2. Special Leave Petitions have been filed against the order of CAT, Jodhpur. The employees working in Loco Running Sheds of Jodhpur had challenged their order of dismissal by way of appeals. As the appeals were not decided within reasonable time they filed writ petitions in the Rajasthan High Court which were transferred to this Court on an application made by the Union of India. All these petitions were disposed of along with the decision in Tulsiram Patel. In view of the observation made in that decision the employees whose appeal had been rejected during pendency of the writ petition filed revision before the revising authority which was dismissed. Against the order dismissing their revision they filed the claim petition which was decided in July 1992 and following directions were issued :  "In view of the above discussion, we allow the applications partly, quash the orders passed by the Revisional Authority and direct that a fresh order may be passed in the Revision Petition of the applicants after taking into account observations contained in this order. Since applicants are out of job for over 11 years, the revisional authority shall pass the fresh orders on the Revision Petitions within 4 months of receipt of the copy of this order. The respondents are directed to allow the applicants to retain their quarters until 2 months after the fresh orders are passed in their Revision Petition, or until the normal period for which they are entitled under rules to retail the quarters after superannuation in case of those who have attained the age of superannuation, subject to payment of all arrears of rent at the rate applicable before their dismissal from service within 4 months of this order. Where the revisional authority holds or orders an enquiry under D.A.R., the applicants will be allowed to retain the quarters till final decision in the enquiry proceedings subject to the above conditions. Parties to bear their own costs."  So far the appeals arising out of order passed by CAT, Chandigarh are concerned the employees working in that area also challenged the orders of disciplinary and appellate authority by way of writ petitions which were transferred to this Court. After the decision of the case in Tulsiram Patel the employees filed Revision Petition and sought a direction that the concerned authorities be directed to decide the same. The CAT Chandigarh held that the ratio of Tulsiram Patel was of no assistance as the appeal had been rejected earlier and nothing was pending.  3. So far the political endeavour is considered it is narrated in an affidavit that in March 1990 the then Railway Minister made a statement on the floor of the House assuring that the cases of the dismissed employees would be reviewed and a decision would be taken for their reinstatement. It is further stated that in pursuance of the said statement of the Minister an order was passed on 20th June 1990 by the Board for review of cases and on 8th September 1991, 37 employees of South Central Railway were recommended for reinstatement. Later on the Chairman of the Railway Board submitted a note to the Railway Minister that instead of reinstating the employees they may be paid one time compensation. The affidavit states, that it was not agreed to by the Minister and a decision was taken by him to reinstate all the employees which was approved by the Cabinet. However since the decision was taken one day prior to the fall of the Ministry it was rescinded by the President. The affidavit states that the Railway Minister of the interim Government again made a statement in 1991 on the floor of the House that all the dismissed employees shall be reinstated. The succeeding Government, however, did not pass any order of reinstatement. But the learned counsel for respondents have produced a copy of the Government's decision made in 1993 to re-employ all such employees who had not approached the Court.  4. When the Special Leave Petition was filed by the Union of India against the order of CAT, Hyderabad, a statement was made on 14th November 1991 that the Government was seriously considering the question of withdrawing the proceedings against all the persons who took part in the strike in 1981. The statement was supported by an affidavit filed in January 1992, by Senior Personnel Officer. In March 1992 another affidavit was filed by another Chief Personnel Officer stating categorically that the Government of India had decided not to reinstate these employees in service. In yet another affidavit filed in July 1992 it was stated that the matter was receiving attention of Ministries concerned and a recommendation was being made for grant of monetary benefit to the employees. The statement was supported by an affidavit and it was stated that although the punishment of dismissal was not being withdrawn the Government as a matter of sympathetic consideration had decided to examine the feasibility of granting to the employees ex-gratia payment. In October 1992 the Deputy Director, Eastern Railway Board filed an affidavit stating that the railway employees who had been dismissed due to participation in the trade union agitation will be paid ex-gratia as one time payment on certain terms and conditions. In November 1992 when the petitions were taken up for hearing it was stated that the attempt to settle the dispute, amicable, has failed.  5. More than a decade has gone since these employees were dismissed for participating in strike called by the Union recognised by the Railways. But end had not reached. Barring appellate and revisional authority whose discretion too was attempted to be curtailed by issuing circular no Court or Tribunal has found the orders to be well founded on merits. True the jurisdiction exercised by the High Court under Article 226 of the tribunal is not as wide as it is in appeal or revision but once the Court is satisfied of injustice or arbitrariness then the restriction, self imposed or statutory, stands removed and no rule or technicality on exercise of power, can stand in way of rendering justice. We are not impressed by the vehement submission of the learned Additional Solicitor General that the CAT, Hyderabad, exceeded its jurisdiction in recording the finding that there was no material in support of the finding that it was not reasonably practicable to hold an enquiry. The jurisdiction to exercise the power under Rule 14(2) was dependent on existence of this primary fact. If there was no material on which any reasonable person could have come to the conclusion as is envisaged in the rule then the action was vitiated due to erroneous assumption of jurisdictional fact therefore the tribunal was well within its jurisdiction to set aside the orders on this ground. An illegal order passed by the disciplinary authority does not assume the character of legality only because it has been affirmed in appeal or revision unless the higher authority is found to have applied its mind to the basic infirmities in the order. Mere reiteration or repetition instead of adding strength to the order renders it weaker and more vulnerable as even the higher authority constituted under the Act or the Rules for proper appraisal shall be deemed to have failed in discharge of its statutory obligation.  6. Reliance was placed on the Cabinet decision taken in November 1990 and it was urged that the succeeding Government should have honoured it and directed reinstatement of all employees and payment of back wages. We do not think that we are called upon to decide it as the decision was rescinded by the President. Suffice it to say that in Parliamentary system of Government the democracy grows and matures by healthy conventions and traditions. Should an outgoing Government take a policy decision one day before quitting the office or should the succeeding Government honour it, cannot be regulated by Courts.  7. However, what is apparent is that the order of dismissal against the employees has not been sustained in the Courts. Although Jodhpur Bench has not examined the matter on merits and the CAT Chandigarh has dismissed the claim petitions on bare technicality, yet there can be no doubt that the Government whether in 1990 or in 1991 or in 1992 has been considering the matter, and efforts had been made to grant relief to these employees. What should be done then which may do justice to both the parties? Overall picture is that there are five types of employees, one, whose claim petition before tribunal has been allowed and they have been directed to be reinstated; second, whose claims petition had been allowed to a limited extent, namely, the appellant and revising authority had been directed to re-examine their cases; third, those who have retired during pendency of the claim petitions; fourth, where the claim petitions have been dismissed because the appeals filed had already been dismissed; and fifth; those who did not approach the Court and the Government have taken a decision to re-employ them. We are not concerned with last category. But the rationale behind this decision of the Government is to atone the injustice done to these employees. It has not been found by any tribunal that the orders passed against the respondents was in any manner justified. In other words, the exercise of power was arbitrary. If this be so as is apparent then there can be no justification for denying the benefit to employees. Technical arguments apart once this court is satisfied that the participants in the strike were unjustly treated the Court is not only competent but has an obligation to act in a manner which may be just and fair. Keeping this in light we issue following directions :  (i) Employees who were dismissed under Rule 14(2) for having participated in the Loco Staff Strike of 1981 shall be restored to their respective post within a period of three months from today.  (ii) (a) Since more than three years have elapsed from the date the orders were found to be bad on merits by one of the tribunal it is just and fair to direct the appellant to pay the employees compensation equivalent to three years salary inclusive of dearness allowance calculated on the scale of pay prevalent in the year the judgment was delivered, that is, in 1990.  (b) This benefit shall be available even to those employees who have retired from service. In those cases where the employees are dead the compensation shall be paid to their dependents. The compensation shall be calculated on the scale prevalent three years immediately before the date of retirement or death.  (iii) Although the employees shall not be entitled to any promotional benefit but they shall be given notional continuity from the date of termination till the date of restoration for purposes of calculation of pensionary benefits. This benefit shall be available to retired employees as well as to those who are dead by calculating the period till date of retirement or death.  8. All the appeals and petitions are disposed of accordingly. Since the employees are being directed to be paid compensation there shall be no order as to costs.  Order accordingly.
summary:
A. Railway employees were terminated for participating in a strike by the Loco Running Staff Association without an enquiry, and as long as the Court is convinced that the strikers were treated unfairly, the Court has both the power and the responsibility to act in a just and fair manner as a result. [Paras 5 and 7]
B. Courts cannot regulate whether an outgoing government's policy decisions should be honored by the succeeding government, as that is something that should be left to the healthy conventions and traditions that grow and mature in a parliamentary system of government. [Para 6]

text: M. Jagannadha Rao, C.J. - This is a Letters Patent appeal against the Judgment of the learned Single Judge in CWP 3555/91 dated 3.12.94. The writ petitioner is the appellant. The 1st respondent is Engineer (India) Ltd. represented by its Chairman and Managing Director while the 2nd respondent is its Director (Technical).  2. The appellant was recruited as a typist by the 1st respondent organisation on 29.12.1965 and got her promotions at the relevant time and was working as the Private Secretary to the Deputy General Manager (Engineering). Her case was that on 19.5.1989, when she visited the office of Mr. M.M. Lal, Dy. General Manager (Admn.) for some work, the said officer touched her and pushed her (But the officer's case is that she shouted at him when asked why she had come to the Administration department and she left and came later on 4.30 PM with union members and for the first time raised a plea that at 2.30 PM or so, the officer had pushed her). On 19.5.1989 she filed a complaint against the said officer. The Secretary of the Union also complained on 19.5.1989 against Mr. Lal while forwarding the appellant's complaint. On 21.5.89, the said Mr. M.M. Lal filed a complaint against the appellant and also against some officers of the Union. The charge against the appellant as disclosed from the charge sheet given to her before inquiry was (as extracted in the judgment under appeal) that:  (i) on 19.5.89, at 2.40 PM, the appellant was going from the seat of Smt. Adrash Kapahi (Jr. Asstt. Gr. 1) in the Administration department and Mr. Lal noticed her (she belogs to Eng. Deptt) in his deptt. (i.e. Administration) and asked her the purpose of her visit to the Administration Department. Instead of giving a reply, appellant challenged the authority of Mr. Lal to put her that question. Mr. Lal told her he wanted to know the purpose of her visit to his department. He proceeded to the seat of Mr. R.B. Kapoor, Manager (Admn). and then appellant followed, shouted at Mr. Lal and misbehaved using derogatory and indecent language, hurledy insults and disrupted office work. (ii) At 4.30 pm, she went to the office of Mr. Lal and joined Mr. R.C. Naithani, Rakesh Rohtagi, S.P. Khware and K.P. Singh who were already there, making baseless accusations against Mr. Lal and demanding unqualified apology from him for his alleged misbehaviour. Appellant persisting with unruly behaviour, insulted and threatened Mr. Lal and disrupted normal working of the office till 5.10 pm. The appellant accompanied by the employees went to Mr. Lal's residence and insulted him in the presence of his family members. (iii) At 5.15 pm. appellant and other employees stopped Mr. Lal's car when he was leaving the office along with Mr. R.C. Chowdhary, General Manager (Engg) and used offending language, tried to get into the car. The car was detained for 1 hour. 3. A preliminary inquiry was made recording statement of witnesses. On 2.6.89, appellant was suspended by order of the 2nd respondent and on 12.6.89, charge sheet was served mentioning also names of certain other employees involved in the incident. On 7.7.89, appellant was informed that an inquiry will be held. Inquiry was held and ultimately, the Inquiry Officer found against the appellant and sent a report of findings etc. on 17.12.90. The appellant sent reply to the report on 22.2.91. An order of dismissal was passed on 29.4.91.  4. Appeal dated 29.5.91 to the Chairman of the company was dismissed on 30.7.91. Writ petition was filed on 30.10.91 and was dismissed by the learned Single Judge holding:  (1) that the preliminary objection raised by the respondent that the appellant was a workman and ought to have availed the remedy under the Industrial Disputes Act, was correct. It is not her case that she was having any managerial or administrative duties. She was only a 'private secretary'. She was a 'workman'. Appellant had not stated in her rejoinder that she has any such duties which exclude her from the definition of 'workman'. Learned Single Judge followed Hariba v. KSRTC, 1983(11) LLN 76 (Karn) as approved in Sreeramulu v. KSRTC, 1982(2) LLN 864, VISL Contract Workers Assn. (R) & another v. Vishwaswaraya Iron and Steel Ltd., 1990(2) Current L.R. 700. (2) Petitioner's reliance on Article 14 as regards discrimination and victimization cannot be accepted as there is no proof adduced in that behalf. (3) Petitioner has not even examined herself in the inquiry before the Inquiry Officer. She did not lead any evidence. She specifically refused to cross-examine witnesses and said she will not examine herself. Her participation was confined to her mere presence and raising a few objections. No genuine attempt was made to dislodge the evidence adduced by the company. 5. In the grounds of appeal, the appellant contended in the grounds of appeal that (i) documents sought for were not furnished to the appellant on the ground that they were not relied upon by the Inquiry Officer nor were the basis for framing charges, (ii) Appellant was denied assistance of legal practitioner, (iii) Co-delinquents who were charge-sheeted in connection with the incidents dated 19.5.89 were let off and no action was taken against them. Some of them (Mr. K.L. Rekhi) was let off with a warning. This offended Article 14 of the Constitution of India, (iv) Appellant was victimised for lodging a complaint against Mr. M.M. Lal. As regards the preliminary objection, it is stated that once the writ petition was admitted in the presence of the respondent's counsel on 31.3.92, the said objection cannot be permitted at a later stage. It is contended that when violation of principle of natural justice was pleaded, there was no need to avail the alternative remedy or go to the Industrial Court, that denial of copies of the complaint which is the foundation of the case, vitiated the entire proceedings, copies of charge-sheets served on co-delinquents were not given, that the action was mala fide and was a counter-blast, that copies of the statements of witnesses who deposed in the preliminary inquiry were not given and that learned Single Judge erred in holding appellant was a workman.  6. The points for consideration in this appeal are:  (1) Whether the learned Single Judge was wrong in holding that the appellant was a 'workman' and should have pursued alternative remedy under the Industrial Disputes Act ? (2) Whether there was violation of principles of natural justice in that certain relevant documents were not supplied or legal assistance was not given and there was consequent gross prejudice and hence petitioner was justified in invoking the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India ? (3) Whether because of the co-delinquents were not visited with same punishment but were either let off or given only a warning, that amounted to discrimination under Article 147 ? (4) Whether the action was mala fide ? POINTS 1 & 2  7. These two points are somewhat interconnected. If the petitioner's case under point 2 that there was gross violation of natural justice and consequential prejudice caused to the appellant is to be accepted, it can perhaps be said that petitioner need not have proceeded under the Industrial Disputes Act.  8. First, we shall deal with the question whether appellant was a `workman'. Now, so far as the pleading of the respondent that the appellant was a `workman' as pointed by the learned Single Judge, the apellant did not allege either in her rejoinder that she had any managerial or administrative functions which will take her out of the category of 'workman'. There was no such plea in the rejoinder nor in the grounds of appeal. Except to say that she was not a workman as found by the learned Single Judge, it was not stated even in the grounds of appeal that she had any managerial or administrative functions. Hence, there is no real attack to the finding of the learned single Judge that appellant was not a `workman'. The learned Single Judge was right that she should have proceeded under the Industrial Disputes Act. It is true that the writ petition was admitted in the presence of respondent's counsel but there is no material to say that any such objection raised by the respondent was rejected at that stage. In the order admitting the writ petition, there is no reference to rejection of any objection of the respondent at the stage of admission. Objection to the maintainability of the petition can still be canvassed at the stage of final disposal especially when appeal or petition is being dispoed of expeditiously.  9. We shall now examine if there was any violation of principles of natural justice and if so, whether there was proof of any prejudice to the case of the appellant during the inquiry and whether she could have straight-away approached this Court. As already stated, the appellant did not examine herself in the inquiry in regard to the allegations against her and contented herself by being preseat and raisimg a few objections.  (i) Non-supply of copy of complaint by Mr. Lal  10. As we shall presently show, this plea was never raised in the inquiry. The charge sheet against the appellant is charge sheet No. 5011 dated 12.6.89 and was served on her long before inquiry. From the record of the Inquiry Officer which we have called for, we find that the charge sheet dated 12.6.89 was given to the appellant and she admitted the same when questioned by the Inquiry Office on 5.9.1989. It is in the light of this fact that if assuming that a copy of the complaint of Mr. M.M. Lal was not given to the appellant, we have to decide whether any principle of natural justice was violated or prejudice caused.  11. It is argued that it was only in this Court that the copy of the complaint, was produced but the copy of it was not given to her during the inquiry. Now it is not contended that there is any variation between the facts stated in the complaint and those stated in the charge sheet. Further, it is not contended that any facts stated in the complaint and not stated in the charge sheet have been relied upon by the Enquiry Officer or the disciplinary authority.  12. In fact, in the departmental appeal date 29.5.91 the only grievance of the appellant is  "I requested for two things (1) the help of a defence assistant; and (2) the copies of the statements recorded during the preliminary inquiry, in order to conduct effective cross-examination of the witnesses and prepare a cogent and forceful defence." In the departmental appeal, no ground was raised that she had asked for a copy of the complaint given by Mr. Lal on the basis of which the charge sheet could have been prepared or that its absence prejudiced the case of the appellant.  The law relating to violation of principles of natural justice and the need to prove 'prejudice' has now been clearly laid down by the Supreme Court in a recent judgment in State Bank of India v. S.K. Sharma, 1996(3) SCC 364. A proof of prejudice is, in disciplinary inquiries, an essential requirement and as there is no plea either before the Inquiry Officer or before the Appellate Authority that she had asked for a copy of the complaint or it contained more prejudicial allegations than those contained in the charge sheet nor there is any plea of consequential prejudice, hence the non-supply of the complaint did not, in our view, vitiate the inquiry.  13. Therefore the ruling in Jog Raj Singh v. The Delhi Administration, Delhi and others, 1970 SLR (Delhi) 400 is of no help to the apellant.  (2) Non-supply of statements of witnesses examined in the preliminary inquiry.  14. It is not the cse of the appellant that the Inquiry Officer or the Disciplinary Authority has relied upon any statement of witnesses recorded in the preliminary inquiry. The Inquiry Officer's report dated 17.12.90 runs into 29 pages of very detailed discussion of the evidence of witnesses adduced in the case. It says that the inquiry was conducted at 22 sittings. As stated below the finding is that the appellant shouted at Mr. Lal at 2.30-2.40 PM, left and came back at 4.40 PM with union leaders and for the first time contended that at 2.40 PM she was pushed by Mr. Lal. At p. 18 the report says:  "Mrs. Gupta did not produce any witness nor cross-examined the PO's witnesses. In her defence against the charge sheet issued and witnesses produced in suport of the charges, Mrs. Gupta refused to cross-examine the witnesses produced, did not examine herself nor produced any witnesses in her support or any statement of eye witnesses nor made any attempt to disprove or challenge their statement. As regards her allegation that Mr. Lal touched her body or manhandled or pushed her into a corner, the Inquiry Officer found it to be totally false. Actually the allegation of Mrs. Gupta was that this happened when Mr. Lal questioned her why she had come to the Administrative department. The Inquiry Officer stated:  "Mrs. Adarsh Kapahi has mentioned that Mrs. Pushpa Gupta, a friend and acquaintance of 10 years standing, had come to her on that day on personal work, Mr. Kapahi & Mr. M.M. Singh without hesitation has given evidence that at no time Mr. Lal even touched Mrs. Gupta's person nor was he near enough to do so, leave aside his manhandling and pushing her to a corner. No witnesses have come forward, nor statement of witnesses have been produced to support Mrs. Gupta's serious complaint even though it was in open hall during busy working hours. Mr. Kapoor, Mr. Ghuliani and Capt. Yadav have stated that when Mrs. Gupta followed Mr. Lal into Mr. Kapur's room also, she never mentioned anything about Mr. Lal having touched or manhandled her near the fourth floor entrance." It is found that this allengation by Mrs. Gupta was made when she came back at 4.30 PM along with office-bearers of the staff association. The evidence as summarised by the Inquiry Officer is as follows: "Mr. M.M. Singh, Mr. Kapur, Capt. Yadav have stated that this allegation they heard first in Mr. Lal's cabin around 4.30 PM when Mrs. Gupta came along with some of EILEA office- bearers."  As regards the events at 2.40 PM  "Mrs. Kapahi, Mr. Manmohan Singh have, while describing the incident and interaction between the two at 2.40 PM near the travel section stated that Mr. Lal neither shouted, nor was he made nor used derogatory language but was trying to clam and pacify Mrs. Gupta while Mrs. Gupta raised her voice and was questioning the authority of Mr. Lal and used offensive language and words which is not expected to be used while interacting with another senior employee and that too without serious provocation."
