In our view, the view of the State Government is not at all perverse.  22. The Tribunal has held that the disparity in the promotional chances of the officers is not a relevant consideration in declaring equivalence. Even assuming that it is not a relevant consideration, we find that the decision of the Government is not based on that consideration alone. Even if that consideration is ignored, the Expert Committee had given other valid and sufficient reasons for dispensing with the equation and the State Government accepted them. In other words, the decision of the State Government was based on and supported by other relevant and valid considerations. Hence the Government order was not liable to be quashed by the Tribunal,  23. Having considered all the facts and circumstances of this case, we are of the view that the impugned Government Order dated 25-9-2000 is not vitiated by any mala fides. Nothing was pleaded and established in the Original Applications to prove any mala fides.  24. It is also relevant that based on the representations submitted by the officers, the Government in G.O. (MS). No. 133/96/GAD dated 24-4-1996 had cancelled with retrospective effect G.O. (MS) 651/79/GAD dated 15-12-1979 declaring the post of Deputy Superintendent of Police and above in the Telecommunication Unit as equal in status and responsibility to that of the Deputy Superintendent of Police in the Principal Police Service. In the same Government Order dated 24-4-1996, Government did not cancel the equation of officers of MSP and AP Battalion and Armed Reserve with the officers of the General Executive Branch only because the equation was made many years ago and it had not caused any serious difficulties till then. At the same time, the Government also proposed to take special steps to ensure that the officers were not found wanting in any respect in the discharge of their duties when assigned to senior positions in the IPS. Indirectly, the Government admitted that those officers were found wanting in the discharge of their duties when assigned to senior positions in the IPS. Now the Expert Committee has found that even the equation of Armed Police Battalions and Armed Reserve with Principal Police Service should be dispensed with and the Government has accepted the recommendation of the Expert Committee.  25. In the above circumstances, the Original Petitions are allowed and the impugned order of the Tribunal is set aside. Consequently, the O.As. filed before the Tribunal will stand dismissed. No costs.  Petitions allowed
summary: A. Indian Police Service (Appointment by Promotion) Regulations, 1954, Regulation 2(1)(j) - Appointment by promotion from State Police Service - The government withdrew its order stating that Armed Police and Armed Reserve were equivalent to Principal Police Service of State for promotion to IPS - If the government had the power to make this declaration, it also has the power to revoke it with valid reasons provided by an expert committee - The revocation order was upheld as it was not arbitrary or based on irrelevant factors. [Paras 12, 13, 16, 17, 21, 23] B. Constitution of India, Article 226 - Judicial review of administrative decisions - Principles for reviewing administrative decisions were established. [Para 14]

text: S.S. Saron, J. - The petitioner joined the respondent-department in the year 1976 and is working as Safai Karmachari/Sweeper with respondent No. 3 Municipal Council Jagadhri. During the course of service case FIR No. 313 dated 11.3.1997 under Section 34 of the Police Act was registered against him at Police Station City Jagadhri. He was acquitted in the said case by the learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jagadhri, vide judgment dated 22.8.2000 (Annexure P1). The grievance of the petitioner is that despite his acquittal, he is being proceeded against by way of a departmental enquiry and has been charge-sheeted in pursuance of the impugned charge-sheet dated 14.3.2001 (Annexure P4). This is termed as illegal, unlawful, erroneous and against Article 14 of the Constitution of India. Besides, the petitioner claims that he is not being paid his full salary and the balance amount of suspension period is also not paid. He also claims that his basic salary is Rs. 4600/- which has not been paid since 11.3.1990. The department is to pay him more than Rs. 1,30,000/- as balance salary. He further claims that he is being paid 50% of his salary.  2. Notice was issued to the respondents. Written statement has been filed by the Executive Officer, Municipal Council, Jagadhri. It is pleaded that the writ petition is not maintainable as the petitioner has not exhausted the alternative remedy available to him under the provisions of Haryana Municipal Safai Mazdoor Service Rules, 1976 (hereinafter to be referred as the `1976 Rules') and the Haryana Municipal Act, 1973. It is contended that as per Rule 27 of the 1976 Rules, the petitioner has a remedy before the Deputy Commissioner which has not been availed of. It is further averred that the charge-sheet has been framed against the petitioner which is to be enquired into by the respondent-department keeping in view his service record. The petitioner is stated to be a drug addict and his service record is very bad and blemished. It has been stated that the petitioner came to the office of the Municipal Committee, Jagadhri, in a drunken condition on 7.11.1997 at 9.00 A.M. He abused and misbehaved with the officials and officers of the Municipal Committee. The matter was reported to the police and the petitioner was ordered to be placed under suspension vide order dated 24.11.1997. It is further stated that on 8.1.1998 the petitioner presented an application before the Executive Officer of respondent No. 3 Municipal Council in which he admitted the above facts. He pleaded that he admits his guilt. Further he gave an undertaking and promised that in future he would not do so. The said application and undertaking are appended as Annexure R-3/1 with the written statement. It is in this view of the matter that taking a lenient view, the petitioner was reinstated on 3.3.1998. He was warned not to commit such like acts in future otherwise strict disciplinary action would be taken against him.  3. Despite this, the petitioner again on 10.3.1998 at 4.45 PM i.e. just after one week of his reinstatement, took liquor and under the influence of liquor in drunken condition came to the office of respondent No. 3 and started abusing and misbehaving with the officers/officials. He obstructed the working of the council. The matter was reported to the police for taking action against him. The police registered a case under Section 34 of the Police Act. It has further been averred that the petitioner was placed under suspension vide order dated 12.3.1998. Besides, it is stated that the petitioner did not join his duties on 22.8.2000 i.e. on the date he was acquitted. In this view of the matter, the petitioner is entitled to the balance amount of suspension allowance after completion of the enquiry, if found innocent. It is also denied that the basic salary of the petitioner comes to Rs. 4600/- or that the petitioner is not being paid his salary since 11.3.1990. It has been specifically denied that Rs. 1,30,000/- are due to the petitioner from respondent No. 3. The petitioner is being paid his salary as per rules and no salary of the petitioner has been withheld.  4. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties.  5. Primarily, the case of the petitioner is that in respect of the occurrence which took place on 10.3.1998, a case under Section 34 of the Police Act was registered and he was acquitted of the same by the learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jagadhri vide judgment dated 22.8.2000 (Annexure P1). In these circumstances, it is claimed that he cannot be tried in respect of the same allegation by way of departmental enquiry.  6. The learned Additional Advocate General, Haryana, and learned counsel for respondent No. 3, however, contend that the standard of proof in a departmental enquiry and a criminal trial is entirely different and, therefore, there is no bar to the initiation of departmental enquiry with respect to the same allegation. Counsel for respondent No. 4 further contends nothing is due from the Municipal Council towards the petitioner.  7. We may first consider the preliminary objection of respondent which is that the petitioner has a right of appeal in accordance with Rule 27 of the 1976 Rules. Therefore, he is liable to be non-suited and relegated to the alternative remedy provided under the said Rules. Rules 27 of the 1976 Rules reads as under :-  "Right of appeal :- The members of the Service upon whom any penalty has been imposed by the authority specified on column 3 of Appendix III shall be entitled to make an appeal to the authority specified in column 4 of the Appendix against the authority in column 3 thereof. 8. Service has been defined in Rule 2(of the 1976 Rules as follows :-  "Service" means the Municipal Safai Mazdoor Service of a Committee. 9. A perusal of the above rules show that a member of service i.e. Municipal Safai Mazdoor Service of Committee upon whom any penalty has been imposed by the authority specified in column 3 of the Appendix II is entitled to make an appeal to the authority specified in column 4 of the Appendix against the authority in column 3 thereof. The right of appeal is, therefore, maintainable only in the event of the penalty being imposed. In the present case no penalty has been imposed and only a charge-sheet has been issued. The penalties have been specified in column 2 of Appendix III of the 1976 Rules which are removal, dismissal, suspension, stoppage of increment and other punishments. The petitioner is only assailing his charge-sheet and is claiming for grant of full salary. In these circumstances the petition is not liable to be dismissed on the sole ground of alternative remedy being available. The preliminary objection as raised by the respondents is without any substance and is accordingly rejected.  10. The charge-sheet dated 14.3.2001 Annexure P4 has been served upon the petitioner on the allegation that on 10.3.1998 at 4.45 PM he came in the office of the Municipal Council in an inebriated state and started abusing the employees and the officer and made Halla-gulla (revelry) and obstructed working of the office. Even after consolation by Chief Sanitary Inspector, he did not stop. Thus, in short, the allegations are that the petitioner under the influence of liquor started abusing the employees and officer. It is not in dispute that the petitioner was tried for the said offence and was acquitted vide order dated 22.8.2000 Annexure P1 passed by the learned Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jagadhri. The said order shows that prosecution in order to substantiate its case examined PW-1 ASI Ajit Kumar and PW-2 Dr. D.P. Singh Medical Officer. Thereafter the prosecution despite availing numerous opportunities including last opportunity, failed to produce its entire evidence. The cse had become old and finding no justification, the learned trial Magistrate closed the prosecution evidence. The statement of the petitioner was recorded under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and he denied the allegations. The learned Magistrate found that the prosecution version was not substantiated by independent corroboration. The evidence in ASI Ajit Kumar was held to be that of mere hearsay evidence. Besides, Dr. D.P. Singh PW-2 had stated that he conducted medico-legal examination of the petitioner and in his opinion the patient had consumed alcohol and to that effect his detailed report was Ex. PC. The learned trial Magistrate observed that the perusal of the report reveals that the patient had denied to give urine and blood samples whereas no such specific denial was mentioned in the report Ex. PC. Therefore, it was in these circumstances that the trial Magistrate came to the conclusion that it cannot be conclusively proved that the petitioner had consumed alcohol. Accordingly, the petitioner was acquitted.  11. In the case in hand, the charge-sheet dated 14.3.2001 (Annexure P4) gives the list of witnesses against the petitioner. Two witnesses, namely, Chief Sanitary Inspector Nachhatar Singh and Antu Ram Saini Assistant Municipal Council, Jagadhri have been cited as witnesses. Therefore, the witnesses who saw the occurrence or otherwise are in the knowledge of it are to be examined. Besides, it may be noted that the standard of proof in a criminal case and in a departmental proceedings is entirely different. In a criminal case the prosecution is liable to establish and prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. Thus, the standard of proof of prosecution to prove the guilt beyond any reasonable doubt belongs to criminal jurisprudence. However, in a departmental proceedings, the liability can be made out on preponderance of probabilities. A disciplinary enquiry which is contemplated against the petitioner is not be placed on the pedestal of a criminal trial. The standard of proof that is required is preponderance of probabilities and not the proof beyond reasonable doubt. Besides, technical rules of evidence are not applicable in a departmental enquiry. In other words preponderance of probabilities and conclusions drawn as a reasonable man would draw from the evidence on record is sufficient for the purpose of departmental enquiry. Therefore, we are of the view that the charge-sheet served upon the petitioner is not be quashed or dropped merely on the ground that the petitioner has been acquitted in the criminal case. Respondent No. 3 Municipal Council is entitled to conduct the enquiry and establish the charge against the petitioner. At the same time, the petitioner is also entitled to participate in the enquiry, defend himself and prove his innocence.  12. The other relief by the petitioner is with regard to payment of full salary. It has been pleaded by him that he has not been getting full salary and the balance amount of subsistence allowance for the suspension period is not being paid as he has been acquitted. He also stated that his basic salary comes to Rs. 4600/- and that he has not been paid his salary since 11.3.1990. In this manner, the department is to pay him Rs. 1,30,000/- as balance salary.  13. The allegations in this regard have been denied. It is stated in the written statement that the petitioner is entitled to the balance amount of suspension allowance after completion of enquiry if he is found innocent. Besides, it has been specifically denied that the balance salary of the petitioner comes to Rs. 4600/-. It also denied that he is not being paid his salary since 11.3.1990 and that an amount of Rs. 1,30,000/- is due to him from the Municipal Council. In view of the disputed questions of facts, we are of the view that this Court is not to go into these matters. It would be in the fitness of things that the petitioner makes a representation to the respondents with regard to his claims and the respondents thereafter pass a speaking order on the said representation with regard to his dues as may be claimed. If such a representation is made, the respondents would consider the same and dispose it of within four months of its receipt.  14. Consequently, the writ petition is disposed of and is dismissed insofar as the prayer of the petitioner for quashing the charge sheet dated 14.3.2001 Annexure P4 is concerned and with regard to other relief of payment of subsistence allowance and full salary, the petitioner may make a representation and if such a representation is made, the respondents would dispose of the same by passing a speaking order within a period of four months for the date of its receipt. No costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: A. Municipal Safai Mazdoor Service Rules, 1976, Rule 2(F) and 27 - Constitution of India, Article 226 - Departmental appeal against charge sheet issued by the Committee - Although alternative remedy is available, petition cannot be dismissed solely on that ground. [Para 9] B. Constitution of India, Article 226/227 - Departmental proceedings - Discipline can continue despite acquittal in a criminal case involving similar facts - Disciplinary enquiries are not compared to criminal trials, and are not bound by technical rules of evidence - Charge sheet can't be dropped based on acquittal in a criminal case. [Para 11] C. Constitution of India, Article 226 - Disputed questions of facts - The court is not authorized to address such matters. [Para 13]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. (Oral) - The petitioners in these two cases are aggrieved by the order dated July 8, 1994 by which respondent No. 2 was promoted as a Senior Manager. They pray that this order be quashed and a writ of mandamus be issued to the first respondent to consider their claim for promotion to the post of Area Manager/Senior Manager. A few facts may be noticed.  2. The petitioners and respondent No. 2 were working as Managers in the Respondent-Bank. Admittedly, the petitioners were at Sr. Nos. 11 and 12 in the seniority list while respondent No. 2 was at No. 13. In the year 1986, the bank took a decision to create 8 posts of Area/Senior Managers. It decided that all the posts shall be filledup by promotion on the basis of seniority-cum-merit. The criteria for promotion was also laid down. It was provided that the promotion shall be ordered on the basis of the performance, length of service, educational qualifications and interview. On January 1, 1987, the Bank interviewed 24 candidates including the two petitioners and the second respondent. All the three were rejected. The second respondent filed Civil Writ Petition No. 6004 of 1989. This writ petition came up for hearing alongwith a bunch of other petitions including Civil Writ Petition No. 3459 of 1988. The learned Judge while following the view taken by the Karnataka, Kerala and Calcutta High Courts, held that the criterion adopted by the Respondent-Bank in making selection was not valid. According to the learned Judge, the fitness of each candidate had to be individually considered and the inter se merit had not to be compared. This was so on account of the fact that the promotion had to be made on the basis of seniority-cum-merit and not merit-cum-seniority. As a result, all the writ petitions including Civil Writ Petition No. 6004 of 1989 filed by respondent No. 2 were allowed. The Bank was directed to consider the claims of the petitioners "with effect from the date their juniors were promoted". In pursuance to this direction, respondent No. 1 passed the order dated July 8, 1994 by which respondent No. 2 was promoted. This was, however, subject to the final decision in the Letters Patent Appeal that had been filed by the Bank.  3. The sole grievance made by the petitioners is that the action of the Bank in ignoring them for promotion is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.  4. A written statement has been filed only by respondent No. 1. It has been inter alia averred that the petitioner has concealed material facts inasmuch as he has not disclosed the orders of punishment/warning etc. that had been duly conveyed to him. It has also been pleaded that the writ petition deserves to be dismissed on the ground of delay and laches. According to the respondent, the petitioner cannot claim promotion with effect from the year 1987 by filing a petition in the year 1994. The respondent maintains that on these grounds alone, the writ petition deserves to be dismissed. On merits of the controversy, detailed facts to justify the criterion adopted by the Bank have been given. However, it has not been suggested even remotely that the petitioner's claim was considered before the respondent passed the order dated July 8, 1994. In view of the pleas raised in the written statement, the respondent prays that the writ petition be dismissed with costs.  5. In Civil Writ Petition No. 11166 of 1994, a detailed replication had been filed. It has been inter alia averred that the petitioner has not concealed any material facts. As for the objection of delay, it has been pointed out that respondent No. 2 having been promoted vide order dated July 8, 1994, and other junior persons having been promoted even thereafter, the petitioner's claim could not be defeated on the ground of delay. The petitioner also avers that he had a right to be considered for promotion before any one junior to him could be promoted.  6. Learned counsel for the parties have been heard.  7. The solitary contention raised on behalf of the petitioners is that the action of the respondents in not considering the claim of the petitioners at the time of the promotion of respondent No. 2 is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Consequently, the order dated July 8, 1994 is illegal and deserves to be quashed. This claim has been controverted by the learned counsel for the respondent, on the ground that the petition suffers from delay and laches.  8. The two questions arise for consideration are :  (i) Is the action of the respondents violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution ? (ii) Is the petition liable to be dismissed on the ground of delay alone ? Reg :(i)  9. Mr. S.S. Nijjar, learned counsel for the Respondent-Bank has very fairly conceded that the claim of the petitioners was not considered when the Bank promoted respondent No. 2 vide order dated July 8, 1994. He, however, submits that the Bank was only considering that claim of respondent No. 2 in pursuance to the directions issued by this Court. It was not required to consider the claim of any one else.  10. Article 14 guarantees equality of opportunity. Article 16 entitles all citizens to an equality of opportunity in the matter of employment under the State. These provisions contain a mandate to the State and its instrumentalities. It is the duty of the State to ensure that each citizen is treated equally in the matter of appointment to various posts. It is undoubtedly correct that respondent No. 2 had approached this Court with a grievance that the Bank had wrongly ignored him for promotion by adopting a criteria which was not legally tenable. This claim was sustained. The criterion adopted by the Bank was held to be illegal. A direction for consideration of the petitioner's claim was issued to the Bank. However, it did not mean that while considering the claim of the second respondent in pursuance to the directions of this Court, the claims of other eligible persons who were senior to the said respondent had not to be considered. The consideration had to be in accordance with law. Every person senior to the second respondent had a right to be considered. It was never said by this Court that the claims of the seniors shall not be considered. Equally, it was the duty of the Bank to ensure that there was no denial of equality of opportunity. The mandate of Articles 14 and 16 being clear, it could not be deviated from on the pretext that the Bank was merely carrying out the directions of this Court.  11. Learned counsel for the respondent-Bank having admitted that the claim of the petitioners was not considered in spite of the fact that they were senior to the second respondent and were otherwise eligible, it has to be held that there was violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.  12. The first question is, consequently, answered in the affirmative and it is held that order dated July 8, 1994 is violative of the provisions of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.  Reg : (ii)  13. It is the admitted position that one Mr. R.B. Kanodia, who was placed at No. 17 in the seniority list, was promoted as an Area Manager in the year 1987. The second respondent had challenged his promotion by filing an appeal before the Board of Directors. This appeal having been rejected in December 1988, he had approached this Court through CWP No. 6004 of 1989. It was in pursuance to the directions of this Court that the Bank had passed the order dated July 8, 1994 and ordered the promotion of the second respondent with effect from the year 1987. On these facts, learned counsel for the respondents contend that the petition is highly belated and deserves to be dismissed.  14. On behalf of the petitioners, it is submitted that the cause of action had accrued only on July 8, 1994 when a person junior to them was promoted. Furthermore, it has been pointed but that even earlier, representations had been filed by the petitioners in the year 1988 against the promotion of a junior person. No decision on that representations had been conveyed.  15. Whatever be the position regarding the promotion of Mr. Kanodia, the grievance as made out in the present petition is only against the order dated July 8, 1994 by which respondent No. 2 had been promoted. Admittedly, the first petition against this order had been filed on July 25, 1994. This was within less than a month. Even the second petition had been filed on August 17, 1994. Even if it is assumed, as alleged by the respondent-Bank, that the petitioners had not filed any representation in the year 1988, it cannot be said that there is any delay whatsoever in so far as the present petitions are concerned. The sole grievance made by the petitioners in these two cases is against the order dated July 8, 1994. The writ petitions have been filed without any avoidable delay. The cause of action so far as the present petitions are concerned, had accrued only on July 8, 1994. Whenever a junior person is promoted without the consideration of the claim of a senior, a fresh cause of action arises. Merely because the petitioners had not challenged the order of promotion of Mr. Kanodia, cannot mean that they are estopped from challenging even the subsequent orders by which their juniors may be promoted.  16. Learned counsel for the respondent have referred to the decisions of the Full Bench of this Court in Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashok Sehgal, AIR 1990 P&H 117 and of the Supreme Court in P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of Tamil Nadu, 1976(1) SLR 53.  17. In Sadasivaswamy's case, their Lordships were pleased to hold that an order of promotion should be challenged within a period of six months. The petitioners have complied with the rule as enunciated in this case. They have approached this Court within less than two months of the passing of the order. Consequently, the learned counsel can derive no advantage from these decisions.  18. Accordingly, the second question is answered in the negative and it is held that petitions are not liable to be dismissed on the ground of delay.  19. In view of the above, both the petitions are allowed. The respondents are directed to consider the claims of the petitioners for promotion to the posts of Senior Manager/Area Manager w.e.f. the date respondent No. 2 was promoted. The petitioners shall be entitled to the consequential reliefs that may ensue from their promotion. In the circumstances of these cases, there will be no order as to costs.  As a result, Civil Misc. Application filed by respondent No. 2 for vacation of the interim stay order which had been passed on September 22, 1995 has become infructuous and is accordingly, disposed of.  Order accordingly.
summary: A. The Constitution of India's Articles 14 and 16 address Promotion and Seniority, with court-issued directions dictating that the case of the private respondent for promotion must be considered alongside all eligible candidates in accordance with seniority-cum-merit. The Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution are violated when eligible candidates are not considered together. [Paras 10 to 13]  B. Under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, Delay and Laches must be taken into account when considering promotion and a Person who is ignored while considering his juniors for promotion may file a writ petition for every promotion of a junior that violates seniority rule. Refusal to dismiss a Writ Petition due to delay or laches is possible if it follows the promotion of the last person and is filed immediately. [Paras 15 and 17]

text: Hemant Gupta, J. - This order shall dispose of CWP Nos. 9651; 9664 and 10276 all of 2002, filed by the Chandigarh Administration as well as the selected candidates, the appointment of whom was set aside by the Central Administrative Tribunal, Chandigarh Bench, Chandigarh (for short `the Tribunal') on 6.3.2002 on an application filed by Ravinder Singh, respondent No. 1 (hereinafter referred to as the applicant).  2. The brief facts, which led to the passing of the order by the Tribunal are that on 24.9.1999, the Chandigarh Administration accorded sanction to the engagement of 39 apprentices in the Engineering Department during the year 1999-2000 as per the provisions of the Apprentices Act, 1961 (for short `the Act'). Out of the said 39 posts, 2 posts were meant for apprentices in Mechanical Engineering and three in Civil Engineering in the Public Health Wing of Chandigarh Administration. A requisition was sent by the Chandigarh Administration to the Regional Employment Exchange, Chandigarh for recommending the names of the eligible candidates, who could be appointed as apprentices. The Employment Exchange recommended the names of the candidates for apprentices. On the basis of the recommendations of the Employment Exchange, a duly constituted Committee selected such apprentices for training. The said apprentices completed their successful training in December, 2000 as well. The applicant filed an Original Application before the Tribunal pleading that he belongs to the Scheduled Castes category and possesses a degree of B.E. (Civil) from the Punjab Engineering College and that he got apprenticeship training as well but has not been appointed.  3. The grievance of the applicant is that three posts of Junior Engineer were neither advertised nor any requisition was sought from the Employment Exchange and the apprentices, who had completed training in December, 2000 were considered and appointed vide letter dated 30.1.2001. It is further alleged that father of Ishwar Saini, a selected candidate, is serving as a Senior Assistant, whereas father of Gurvinder Singh is working as Junior Engineer in the Public Health Wing. Similarly, father of Amit Gupta, is also working in the Department. It was, thus, alleged that the candidates have been appointed in a clandestine manner without advertising the vacancies and without giving opportunity to the candidates, who were trained apprentices for a higher post.  4. The learned Tribunal found that the appointment to the post of Junior Engineer is governed by the Chandigarh Engineering Department (Group-C), Sectional Officers of (Construction, Public Health and Electrical Wing) (Chandigarh Amendment) Rules, 1988, and the educational qualification is diploma in Civil Engineering. The Tribunal found that even if two posts of apprentices for mechanical diploma holders were sanctioned in the Public Health Wing, it will not amount to creation of regular post of Sectional Officer/Junior Engineer. It was further found that it could not be shown on record number of any regular posts of Sectional Officers/Junior Engineers Mechanical in the Public Health Wing of the Engineering Department, U.T., Chandigarh. Thus, the Tribunal found that the appointment is in violation of the recruitment Rules. Considering the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in U.P. Road Transport Corporation v. U.P. Parivahan Nigam Shishukhs Bereozgar Sangh & Ors., 1995(2) SCT 367 : AIR 1995 Supreme Court 1115, the Court found that neither the said judgment nor the instructions do away with the requirement of competition/selection process with the other candidates as required under the law. The Tribunal relied upon its judgment in Jaswinder Singh v. Union of India etc., OA No. 570-CH-1993 decided on 23.5.2001, wherein it was held that the candidates who were selected and given training as Apprentices did not mean that there was a guarantee or even a promise for an employment before sending them for training. The Tribunal did not record any definite finding in respect of the relations of the selected candidates working with the administration, but still inferred that one cannot rule out the possibility of undue favour extended to the selected candidates, who have been appointed without advertising the posts.  5. While challenging the aforesaid order passed by the Tribunal, reliance was placed upon the letter of Govt. of India, Ministry of Labour and Rehabilitation dated 23.3.1983, wherein 50% posts against the direct recruitment were recommended to be filled up by absorption of apprentices. After the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in U.P. Road Transport Corporation's case (supra), another circular was issued on 15.3.1996 by the Govt. of India, incorporating the decision of the Supreme Court in the said circular. It was pointed out that seven posts of Junior Engineers fell vacant in the Public Health Circle. Four of such vacancies were filled up by direct recruitment and the remaining three vacancies were considered to be filled up from amongst the trained apprentices. It is also pointed out that the applicant applied for open advertisement post, but could not succeed. The petitioner relied upon Rule Annexure P.9 to contend that the post of Junior Engineer exists in all streams i.e. Mechanical, Engineering and Civil Wing of the Public Health. The qualification of Diploma in Civil Engineering is mentioned in the qualification for direct recruitment. The Rules have to be read harmoniously and the mistake in not mentioning any qualification for the other streams cannot have any effect for nullifying the other streams in the Department. The qualification for the streams of Junior Engineer (Public Health), Junior Engineer (Mechanical), Junior Engineer (Electrical) and Junior Engineer (Horticulture) have been specified by Chandigarh Engineering Department (Group C) Junior Engineers (Construction, Public Health, Electrical, Mechanical and Horticulture Wing) (Chandigarh Amendment) Rules, 2004. Such Rules have been published in supersession of the earlier notification dated 31.5.1982. Therefore, the mistake of not specifying the qualification for the purposes of direct recruitment to the post of Junior Engineer stands corrected. The apprentices, have been absorbed relying upon the earlier orders of the Tribunal, directing the consideration of trained apprentices for absorption as well as the orders of absorbing apprentices on other posts.  6. The question of right of absorption of the apprentices in the establishment where they have undergone the training, has been examined in detail in Civil Writ Petition No. 12204 of 2007 (Darshan Singh and others v. Bhakra Beas Management Board and another). Vide separate order announced today, it has been held that though it is not obligatory for the employer to employ the apprentices, but it is permissible for the employer to appoint apprentices in preference to the candidates, in response to public advertisement. That was a case where the Bhakra Beas Management Board, has assigned five marks to the candidates, having undergone apprenticeship training under the Board, who applied in response to the public advertisement and by subjecting them to trade test and interview.  7. The fact that the names of the apprentices, who have been absorbed were recommended by the Employment Exchange is not disputed in the written statement filed before this Court. In the present case, the appointment has been given to the apprentices without any public advertisement. Once the candidates were taken as apprentices in terms of the recommendations of the Employment Exchange, the argument that the post was filled up by public advertisement loses its significance. The recommendation of the employment exchange is a valid source of employment. Once, the candidates have been recommended for apprenticeship by the Employment Exchange, the argument that there was no public notice before making appointment, is not tenable.  8. The only question, which is required to be examined is whether the Administration was required to give some preference to the apprentices or absorb such apprentices without considering the other eligible candidates for appointment to the said post.  9. In U.P. Road Transport Corporation's case (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court considered the effect of Section 22 of the Act and held that it is not obligatory for the employer to offer employment merely on the basis what has been stated in Section 22 of the Act. It was further held that what is required to be seen is that the nation gets the benefit of time, money and energy spent on the trainees, which would be so when they were employed in preference to non-trained direct recruits. This would also meet the legitimate expectations of the trainees. After holding so, the Court culled out the circumstances, which are required to be taken into consideration in respect of the employment of the trainees. It was held to the following effect :-  "(1) Other things being equal, a trained apprentice should be given preference over direct recruits. (2) For this, a trainee would not be required to get his name sponsored by any employment exchange. The decision of this Court in Union of India v. Hargopal, AIR 1987 SC 1227, would permit this.  (3) If age bar would come in the way of the trainee, the same would be relaxed in accordance with what is stated in this regard, if any, in this concerned service rule. If the service rule be silent on this aspect, relaxation to the extent of the period for which the apprentice had undergone training would be given.  (4) The concerned training institute would maintain a list of the persons trained year wise. The persons trained earlier would be treated as senior to the persons trained later. In between the trained apprentices, preference shall be given to those who are senior." 10. In the present case, the apprentices were recommended by the Employment Exchange and have been absorbed against the available vacancies. The Administration has spent time, money and energy on the training of the apprentices, who were recommended by the Employment Exchange. Therefore, such candidates were required to be given preferential treatment for appointment and by giving such preferential treatment, they have been absorbed. The reasoning given by the Tribunal that the posts of apprentices were created vide the circular issued by the Administration and not the post of Junior Engineer (Mechanical) in the Public Health Wing, is misconceived. There is no post of apprentice. The apprentices are taken for training and are paid stipend. Rule 10 of the Rules, provides that the posts are that of Junior Engineer alone. The circular granting permission to engage 39 apprentices permits the Administration to take 39 apprentices in different streams including that in Mechanical and Public Health. The reasoning given by the Tribunal in respect of the posts of apprentices is absolutely untenable.  11. Reliance upon Mitrangshu Roy Chowdhary & others v. Union of India and others, 1999(2) SCT 676 (SC) : 1999(2) SLR 772, by the learned Tribunal in its earlier judgment in Jaswinder Singh's case (supra), which has formed basis of the order passed by the Tribunal, is misconceived. That was the case where the applicants were sponsored by the Employment Exchange for recruitment as apprentices. They completed their training and were given appointment but subsequently, the appointments were cancelled and they were given group-D posts. The Hon'ble Supreme Court found that under Rule 159 of the Rules of Recruitment and Training, candidates against 25% of the posts are to be selected from the apprentices, who have completed the course, but such apprentices cannot claim appointment as a matter of right.  12. We find that though it is not obligatory for the employer to provide a regular job to the trainees, but it is equally incumbent on the employer to give preference to a trained apprentice(s) over direct recruits. The age of the apprentice can be relaxed and the training institute is required to maintain a list of the persons trained year-wise and the persons trained earlier have to be treated as senior to the persons trained later. It has also come on record that the apprentices have undergone their successful training and for such training they were paid stipend in terms of Rule 11 of the Apprenticeship Rules, 1992. The Administration has thus, spent time, money and energy on the trainees to train them in the trades prevalent in the Administration. Therefore, such training cannot be permitted to go waste. If the preference is not given to such apprentices, it will not be utilization of the man power trained by the Administration. If the employer chooses to employ the apprentices by giving preference to the apprentices, who have undergone training from the employer, the same satisfies the requirement of Constitutional scheme of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India.  Once, the Administration has decided to absorb the apprentices, the said absorption would be in terms of the order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in U.P. Road Transport Corporation's case (supra).  For the reasons recorded as also the reasons recorded in CWP No. 12204 of 2007 (Darshan Singh and others v. Bhakra Beas Management Board and another), we are of the opinion that the order passed by the learned Tribunal is not sustainable. Consequently, the present writ petitions are allowed and the order passed by the learned Tribunal is set aside. As a consequence thereof, the OA filed by the applicant is dismissed.  Appeal dismissed.
summary:
A. Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Apprentices Act, 1961, Section 22 - Apprentices - Right of apprentices to preferential appointment - Employers are not obligated to provide regular jobs to apprentices-trainees, however, they are required to give preference to trained apprentices over direct recruits when filling job openings - Trained apprentices are also to be given age relaxation for the duration of their apprenticeship if needed - The training institute must keep a record of trained apprentices to ensure they are given preference based on seniority - Adhering to this process satisfies the requirements of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [Paras 9, 10 and 12]
B. Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Apprentices Act, 1961, Section 22 - Apprentices - Posts for apprentices - Apprenticeships do not constitute a post, and instead are for training purposes where apprentices receive a stipend according to the rules. [Para 10]

text: Swatanter Kumar, J. - Challenge in this petition under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India is to the award dated 12.4.2002 vide which petition of the workman under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act was allowed and the respondent-Society therein was directed to pay a sum of Rs. 24035/- to the workman. The claim was allowed with 6% interest per annum from the date of filing of the application till the payment. According to the petitioner the said award is liable to be set aside as it is based upon misappreciation of evidence and is contrary to the record. It is stated that in the written statement filed on behalf of the petitioner herein, the workman had embezzled certain amounts and a case under Sections 409/420 IPC was registered against the workman, resultant to which services of the petitioner were terminated. The matter which regard to embezzlement was also referred to the arbitrator and the workman had taken time to deposit the money before the arbitrator. On these premises it is submitted that the workman was entitled to the salary for the period 2.9.1982 to 20.7.1984.  2. As already noticed, the Learned Labour Court after considering the contentions raised held as under :-  "Development (Developing ?) his submission further, representative of applicant has submitted that Baljit Singh Secretary of respondent society while appearing as RW/1 has admitted during cross-examination that he known that a criminal case was registered against the workman and he stands acquitted therein. He also has admitted that workman has not been paid the amount which has been claimed. He has also admitted that workman was getting Rs. 1070/- per month as wages. Coming to objections raised regarding maintainability of the claim application, representative of workman has submitted that provisions of Limitation Act are not applicable to an application filed under Section 33C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Principle of the res-judicata as well is not attracted to the facts of the present case since no copy of the order has been placed on record by the management in support of its case. Claim under Section 33C(2) is maintainable in the instant case as per averments made in the application. Findings accordingly on both these issues may be recorded in favour of applicant and against the respondent. In support of his contention he has referred to AIR 1968 S.C. 218, Chief Mining Engineer M/s East India Coal Co. Ltd; Bararee Colliery Dhanbad v. Rameshwar and others." 3. The learned Labour Court further held that legal remedy is available to the management to which it could take recourse for recovery of the amount if any payable. As it appears from the record before us that the alleged award of the arbitrator or the admission of the workman to pay the amount was never placed before the Labour Court nor have been placed before us. The onus to prove such issue even if of some consequence was upon the management and the management has failed to discharge such onus. Once the services of the workman were terminated without following the prescribed procedure without any notice, the said illegally cannot be cured merely on the ground that there was an allegation of embezzlement against the workman, particularly when the management had taken the stand that services of the workman have not been terminated, but he is not entitled to salary because of the allegations of the management.  In the circumstances afore-stated we see no reason to interfere in the impugned award. The petition is dismissed in limine.  Petition dismissed.
summary: According to Section 33(C) 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the termination of a workman cannot be denied on the grounds of embezzlement and cannot be remedied if the proper procedure is not followed. The labour court has sided with the workman and the award was deemed appropriate. [Para 3]

text: G.S. Singhvi, J. (Oral) - This petition has been filed for issuance of a writ directing the respondents to consider the petitioner for appointment as J.B.T. Teacher against one of the posts reserved for Ex-Servicemen (General).  2. It appears from the record that the petitioner as well as respondent No. 4 (who is a dependent of ex-Serviceman) applied for recruitment as J.B.T. Teacher in pursuance of advertisement No. 4/96 issued by the Subordinate Services Selection Board, Haryana (renamed as Haryana Staff Selection Commission). They claimed consideration against the posts reserved for Ex- Servicemen (General). Petitioner's contention is that respondent Nos. 2 and 3 have manipulated the selection of respondent No. 4, ignoring his preferential right to be appointed against the post reserved for Ex-Servicemen in view of the instructions issued by the Government of Haryana vide circular letter dated 21st May, 1979.  3. In the written statement filed today, the Board has questioned the locus standi of petitioner to be considered for appointment as J.B.T. Teacher on the ground that he does not possess the essential qualifications. In support of this assertion, respondent No. 3 has relied on following decisions of this Court :-  (i) C.W.P. No. 8882 of 1997 (Azad Singh v. State of Haryana ), decided on 8.7.1997. (ii) C.W.P. No. 8871 of 1997 (Chander Pal Sharma v. State of Haryana ) decided on 24.7.1997. 4. We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and have perused the orders passed in Azad Singh's case (supra) and Chander Pal Sharma's case (supra) and in our opinion, the petitioner, who has passed the Unit Education Instructor's Course, cannot be treated for recruitment as J.B.T. Teacher because the qualification possessed by him is not equivalent to J.B.T.  For the detailed reasons recorded in the order passed in Azad Singh's case (supra), which shall be treated as part of this order, the writ petition is dismissed.  Petition dismissed.
summary: According to Articles 16 and 226 of the Constitution of India, an ex-serviceman petitioner requested appointment as a J.B.T. Teacher for one of the posts reserved for Ex-servicemen (General). However, since the petitioner only passed the Unit Education Instructor's Course and it is not considered equivalent to J.B.T., the petitioner was found ineligible for the position. [Para 4]

text: Dr. Mukundakam Sharma, J. - An order of punishment dated 23rd January, 1988, passed by the respondent No. 1 bank against the petitioner, whereby the petitioner was dismissed from service pursuant to a departmental proceeding held against him, is under challenge in this petition.  2. A departmental proceeding was instituted against the petitioner by the respondents by communicating the charge-sheet dated 18th June, 1986. The said charge-sheet contains certain charges on account of alleged irregularities/malpractices allegedly committed by the petitioner while working as Branch Manager, Azadpur and Jahangir Puri branches of the State Bank of India in Delhi. The charges that were drawn up against the petitioner related to indiscriminate grant of overdrafts, cash credit limits and other malpractices in violation of the laid down instructions of the bank. The aforesaid inquiry into the charges was conducted by the respondent bank in terms of Rule 50(2)(1) of the State Bank of India (Supervising Staff) Service Rules. Upon conclusion of the inquiry, the inquiry officer submitted his report. The inquiry officer held that the charges drawn against the petitioner are partly proved. The Chief General Manager, New Delhi who was the Disciplinary Authority of the petitioner accepted the findings rendered by the inquiry officer and opined that the penalty of dismissal from service should be imposed on the petitioner. The Deputy Managing Director, who was the Appointing Authority, before whom the aforesaid records were placed agreed with the findings and passed the order imposing on the petitioner the penalty of dismissal from bank's service. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order the petitioner filed an appeal. In the said appeal the petitioner submitted that the Deputy Managing Director is incompetent to pass the order of dismissal as he had no power to do so. Another issue that was raised by the petitioner before the Appellate Authority was that the Deputy Managing Director invoked the provisions of paragraph 19(3) of the SBI (Determination of Terms and Conditions of Service) Order, 1979 for the purpose of continuation of disciplinary proceeding against the petitioner after he ceased to be in service in February, 1988. It was submitted that any order under the said provision has to be passed by an authority not below the rank of Managing Director. It was also submitted that the disciplinary proceeding against the petitioner should be treated as closed after he ceased to be in service in February, 1988.  3. The Appellate Authority considered all the aforesaid pleas which were raised in the appeal. With regard to the first issue that was raised about competency of Deputy Managing Director, who passed the order of dismissal, the Appellate Authority held that in terms of the service rules, the major penalty order in this case was passed by the Deputy Managing Director who was the Appointing Authority for officers in middle management grade scale-III and, therefore, he was empowered to impose a penalty on the petitioner. With regard to the second contention, it was held that the Deputy Managing Director had invoked the provisions of paragraph 19(3) of the State Bank of India (Determination of Terms and Conditions of Service) Order, 1979 on 20th January, 1988 for the purpose of continuing the disciplinary proceeding after the petitioner ceased to be in bank's service with effect from 1st February, 1988. It was also held that the aforesaid approval was given in January, 1988 when the post of Managing Director of the Bank was vacant and in the absence of the Managing Director, the Deputy Managing Director was the Competent Authority to invoke the provisions of paragraph 19(3) of the State Bank of India (DTCS) Order and in terms of the instructions in force. Both the aforesaid contentions were, accordingly rejected. On the other contentions of the petitioner that the Disciplinary Authority as also the Appointing Authority acted on the advice of the Central Vigilance Commission in imposing the penalty of dismissal on the petitioner without independent application of mind, the Appellate Authority held that the Disciplinary Authority has furnished cogent and relevant reasons in support of his recommendation for imposing the penalty of dismissal of the petitioner and that the Appointing Authority upon independent application of mind to all the facts and evidence on record accepted the findings/views of the Disciplinary Authority and passed the order of dismissal. It was also held that the penalty of dismissal inflicted on the petitioner was called for and was necessary in view of the fact that the petitioner committed serious irregularities in sanctioning advances and overdrafts in violation of the laid down instructions resulting in substantial financial loss to the bank and, therefore, the penalty imposed is commensurate with the offence. The Managing Director who was the Appellate Authority in terms of the aforesaid SBI (DTCS) Order, rejected the appeal and a review filed by the petitioner was also dismissed by the reviewing authority. Consequently, the present petition is filed challenging the aforesaid orders.  4. Counsel appearing for the petitioner confined himself to the order of punishment imposed upon the petitioner. He submitted that in the facts and circumstances, the penalty of dismissal from service imposed on the petitioner in the present case is too harsh. In support of the said contention Counsel for the petitioner drew our attention to the comments of the Disciplinary Authority/Chief General Manager repeatedly recommending to the vigilance head of the bank that the imposition of extreme penalty of dismissal on petitioner was not justified. Specific reliance was placed on letter dated 22nd January, 1988 wherein it was stated that the Disciplinary Authority had advised change in the penalty as deterrent punishment of dismissal in the case would not only be too harsh but also may prove out to be counter-productive and may lead to a situation of frustration for others as well in an industry like banking which is mainly dealing with finance. It was submitted that there are repeated recommendations of the aforesaid nature by the Disciplinary Authority which, however, was not accepted due to the advice given by the Central Vigilance Commission and, therefore, the order passed by the Appointing Authority is influenced by extraneous factors and was passed at the behest of a third party and not based on and passed on proper appreciation of the evidence on record.  5. The aforesaid contention of the Counsel appearing for the petitioner was, however, refuted by the Counsel appearing for the respondents who has drawn our attention to the reasoning recorded by the Disciplinary Authority. Reference was also made to the fact that under the Rules, opinion of the Central Vigilance Commission was required to be sought for. It was submitted that same was also considered along with the other records by the Competent Authority and on consideration of all the factors the impugned order was passed. At one stage it was submitted by the Counsel appearing for the petitioner that in fact no loss is caused to the bank which is apparent and established from the communication dated 2nd January, 1988. The said submission is, however, refuted by the respondents by filing an affidavit on 5th September, 2005 wherein it is stated that an estimated amount of loss of Rs. 5.11 lacs as on July, 2005 was suffered by the bank. Details of the estimated amount of loss is also placed on record through Annexure A. Therefore, in the light of the aforesaid submissions of the Counsel appearing for the parties we may proceed to dispose of this writ petition.  6. Rule 20B of the Service Rules of the petitioner, which is relevant for the purpose of deciding this matter, provides as follows :  "In case disciplinary proceedings under these rules have been initiated against an employee before he ceases to be in the Bank's service by the operation of, or by virtue of any of these rules, the disciplinary proceedings may, at the discretion of the Managing Director, be continued and concluded by the authority by which the proceedings were initiated in the manner provided for in these rules as if the employee continues to be in service, so, however, that he shall be deemed to be in service only for the purpose of the continuance and conclusion of such proceedings." 7. A bare reading of the said provision would establish that a disciplinary proceeding can be continued at the discretion of the Managing Director and concluded by the authority by whom the proceedings were initiated even after the employee reaches the age of superannuation, provided the aforesaid disciplinary proceeding was initiated against the employee before he ceases to be in the bank's service. But such continuation in service shall be deemed only for the purpose of continuation and conclusion of the said departmental proceeding. Therefore, although the petitioner reached the age of superannuation yet an effective order was passed by the respondents continuing the departmental proceeding and an order to the effect that he shall continue to be in service for the purpose of continuation and conclusion of the said proceeding was passed. As the said order was passed by the respondent bank in terms of the powers vested for continuation and conclusion of the departmental proceeding by the Competent Authority, the same is legal, valid and justified. The main contention that was made before us by the Counsel appearing for the petitioner is that in view of the earlier recommendation made by the disciplinary Authority for taking a lenient view in the matter the subsequent change in the stand by the Disciplinary Authority was uncalled for and unjustified. It is true that at different stages of the proceeding the Disciplinary Authority made such recommendations that extreme penalty may not be imposed upon the petitioner but at the same time the said authority has also held at the time of making such recommendation that there is no denial of the fact that the irregularities committed by the petitioner are of serious nature. Taking an overall view of the matter, the Disciplinary Authority thereafter prepared a note giving his comments to the Deputy Managing Director who is the Appointing Authority of the petitioner. In that note containing his recommendations he held the petitioner guilty of the charges as mentioned therein, both in respect of the alleged irregularities in the accounts of Azadpur Branch as also in respect of Jahangirpuri Branch. The Chief General Manager considered the evidence and spelt out the irregularities committed in respect of the accounts in the aforesaid branches and thereafter it was observed that the petitioner paid scant attention to the bank's laid down instructions and had thrown all the norms of banking to winds with a view to accommodating various borrowers thus jeopardising the bank's interest. The Disciplinary Authority also held that having regard to the gravity of the charges. proved against the petitioner and upon consideration of all the aspects of the case, the petitioner be dismissed from bank's service. The Central Vigilance Commission has also given their advice almost to the similar effect to the Deputy Managing Director, who was the Appointing Authority of the petitioner. In his order he has stated that he has gone through the records of the proceeding and that on independent examination of the documents and evidence adduced during the inquiry proceeding he was of the opinion that the reasoning and findings of the Disciplinary Authority have to be concurred to the extent that the majority of the charges levelled against the petitioner have been successfully established. He also held that considering the serious nature of the offences and the consequential risk of financial loss to which the bank has been exposed, the petitioner be dismissed from service of the bank. The affidavit filed by the respondents also clearly establishes that even as of now the bank has not been able to recover the loss suffered by it due to the aforesaid irregularities committed by the petitioner. This Court cannot reappreciate the evidence on record in order to come to a different conclusion that what is arrived at by the Disciplinary Authority, Appointing Authority as also by the Appellate Authority and the Reviewing Authority. When the charges drawn against the petitioner are held and found to be partly proved and since it was also found that the offences which are proved are of serious nature and that there has been financial loss to the bank, the action of the respondents in dismissing the petitioner from service cannot be said to be too harsh and not commensurate with the offences alleged. The reviewing authority which has passed the order dated 27th September, 2001 recorded the following finding :  "The proven allegations, to mention a few, speak that the petitioner had opened current accounts in favour of various persons, granted clean overdraft facilities to them on the date of the opening of such accounts without verifying their antecedents and without studying the conduct of their accounts in gross violation of RBI/Bank instructions. Those loans had become doubtful of recovery. He issued term deposit receipts/special term deposit receipts by debit to the accounts of the depositors although funds were not available in these accounts. He accumulated (accommodated ?) various account holders by granting them overdraft beyond the available drawing powers and in some cases even in excess of the face value of the securities..... There was no plausible reason as to why he flouted the rule and regulations of the bank with a view to enable third parties to derive benefits detrimental to and at the cost of Bank's interest." 8. In the case of Disciplinary Authority v. Nikunja, 1996(2) SCT 760 : (1996)9 SCC 69, it was held as under :  "In the case of a Bank for that matter in the case of any other organization every officer/employee is supposed to act within the limits of his authority. If each officer/employee is allowed to act beyond his authority, the discipline of the organization/bank will disappear; the functioning of the Bank chaotic and unmanageable. Each officer of the Bank cannot be allowed to carve out his own little empire wherein he dispenses favours, and largesse...... The very action of acting beyond authority ... is by itself a misconduct ... acting beyond one's authority is by itself a breach of Regulation 31. It constitutes misconduct within the meaning of Regulation 24. No further proof of loss is really necessary."  9. In Union Bank of India v. Vishwa Mohan, 1998(2) SCT 382 : IV (1998) SLT 267 : AIR 1998 SC 2311, the Supreme Court has held as follows :  "It needs to be emphasised that in the banking business absolute devotion, diligence, integrity and non est (honesty ?) needs to be preserved by every bank employee and in particular the bank officer. If this is not observed the confidence of the public/depositor would be impaired." 10. It is held thus by the Supreme Court in a recent decision in Regional Manager v. Hotilal, 2003(1) SCT 941 : 2003 II AD (S.C.) 483 : 11(2003) SLT I 12 : AIR 2003 SC 1462 :  "If the charged employee holds a position of trust where honesty and integrity are inbuilt requirements of functioning, it would not be proper to deal with matter leniently. Misconduct in such cases has to be dealt with iron hands. Where the person deals with public money or is engaged in financial transactions acts in a fiduciary capacity, the highest degree of integrity and trustworthiness is a must and unexceptionable." 11. We may also appropriately refer to the decision of the Supreme Court in Damoh Panna v. Munna Lal, 2005(1) SCT 477 : I (2005) SLT 146 : (2005)1 LLJ 730, wherein it was held thus :  "The common thread running through in all these decision is that the Court should not interfere with the administrator's decision unless it was illogical or suffers from procedural impropriety or was shocking to the conscience of the Court, in the sense that it was in defiance of logic or moral standards." 12. In B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India, 1996(1) SCT 617 : AIR 1996 SC 484, the Supreme Court opined as under :  "They are invested with the discretion to impose appropriate punishment keeping in view the magnitude or gravity of the misconduct. The High Court/Tribunal while exercising the power of judicial review cannot normally substitute its own conclusion on penalty and impose some other penalty. If the punishment imposed by the Disciplinary Authority or the Appellate Authority shocks the conscience of the High Court/Tribunal. It would appropriately mould a relief." 13. In that view of the matter, we find no reason to interfere with the conscious and considered decision taken by the respondents as also by the appellate and reviewing authorities. The petition is misconceived and is dismissed accordingly. Rule is discharged.  Petition dismissed.
summary:
A. State Bank of India (Supervisory Staff) Service Rules, Rule 20 - Departmental proceedings - Dismissal - The Disciplinary Authority imposed a penalty on the charge of indiscriminate grant of overdrafts, cash credit limits, and malpractices, despite claiming to have acted on the advice of the Central Vigilance Commission. The rules state that an opinion from the Commission must be sought. As a result, under the given facts and circumstances, the order of dismissal cannot be considered excessively harsh. [Paras 13, 7]

B. State of Bank of India (Supervisory Staff) Service Rules, Rules 19, 20 - Disciplinary proceedings - Continuation after superannuation - The rules specify that disciplinary proceedings can be concluded by the authority that initiated them at the discretion of the Managing Director, even after the employee reaches the age of superannuation, as long as the proceeding was initiated before the employee ceased to be in service. Therefore, the continuation of proceedings after superannuation was legal and justified. [Para 7]

text: A.P. Shah, C,J. - As these writ petitions involve common question of law and facts, they are being disposed of by this common judgment and order.  2. In August, 2005, the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission (in short 'the Commission') invited applications in respect of appointments to the post of 'Veterinary Assistant Surgeon (Direct Recruitment) in the Tamil Nadu Animal Husbandry Services for the year 2005-06. The total number of vacancies specified in the notification was 250. Clause 6 of the Notification prescribed the following qualifications:  "6. Qualification : Candidate should possess the following or its equivalent qualification on the date of the Notification viz. 05-08-2005 : (i) B.V. Sc. Degree of any University or Institution recognised by the University Grants Commission for the purpose of its grant; and (ii) Must be a Registered Practitioner within the meaning of Tamil Nadu Registration of Veterinary Practitioners Act, 1957 (Tamil Nadu Act XXI of 1957) ... ... ..." Clause 12 of the Notification enumerated the list of enclosures to be sent along with the application. It was further informed that the selection will be made in two successive stages, viz. written examination and oral test in the shape of an interview. The total marks obtained by the candidates in the written examination and oral test will be taken together for making the final selection subject to the rule of reservation. The last date for submission of the filled up application was fixed as 9th September, 2005 and the date of written examination was fixed as 20th November, 2005.  3. With reference to the above notification, 1390 candidates had applied to the Commission for this direct recruitment. Out of 1390 applications, a total number of 942 candidates were found eligible to take up the examination for the recruitment and the applications of 448 candidates were found liable for rejection for one or other reasons and therefore rejected.  4. The present petitioners, who are 154 in number, either apprehending rejection of their applications or whose applications have been rejected, have filed these petitions seeking a direction to the Commission to process their applications for the written examination and oral test for selection of the post of Veterinary Assistant Surgeon (Direct Recruitment) in the Tamil Nadu Animal Husbandry Services for the year 2005-06.  5. By interim orders passed by this Court, the petitioners were permitted to write the examination held on 22nd November, 2005 subject to the outcome of the writ petitions.  6. The petitioners in their writ petitions have contended that rejection of their applications on technical reasons such as "OMR Application not signed", "Declaration Column not signed", "Non Production of Veterinary Council Registration Certificate" is arbitrary, unreasonable and in violation of the principles of natural justice.  7. It is seen from the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the Commission that 448 applications were rejected for the reasons viz. 'OMR Application not signed', 'Declaration Column not signed', 'Photo Identity not signed' Registration Certificate of Veterinary Council not produced', 'No evidence of date of birth' etc. In so far as the present petitions are concerned, as per the information furnished by the Commission, 68 applications were rejected on the grounds of not signing the OMR Application and/or not signing the Declaration Column or not signing Photo Identity, and the rest of 86 applications were rejected on the ground of non-production of Veterinary Council Registration Certificate.  8. We will first take up W.P. No. 37309 of 2005 batch of writ petitions. In this batch of writ petitions, in all 68 applications were rejected on the grounds of 'OMR Applications not signed' and/or 'Declaration Column not signed', and/or Photo Identity not signed. We hasten to add that in some of these cases, the applications were also rejected on the ground of 'Non Production of Registration Certificate of Veterinary Council'.  9. Mr. H.S. Mohamed Rafi, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, submitted that though all the columns in the application were duly filled in by the petitioners, the reason for not affixing their signatures under 'OMR Application' and/or 'Declaration Column', etc. was due to ambiguous formatting of the application form. The failure to sign in the OMR Application and/or the Declaration Column would not in any way affect the validity of the applications since the applicants had signed the application at all other places. The omission to sign the 'OMR Application' and/or the 'Declaration Column', etc. was only a bona fide mistake and, in any event, such omission is only an irregularity which can be rectified at any stage of the recruitment. The rejection of the applications on this ground is too technical, arbitrary, unjust and unreasonable.  10. On the other hand, Mr. R. Suresh Kumar, learned counsel appearing for the Commission, submitted that paragraph 17 of the Commission's 'Instructions, etc. to Candidates', which was supplied along with the application form, makes it clear that the applications which are not signed will be considered defective and will be summarily rejected. He submitted that pages 13 and 14 of the 'Information Brochure' supplied along with the application form gives all the details as to how the application is to be filled in. A specimen filled-in OMR Application form was also provided in the Information Brochure to facilitate the candidates to fill in the OMR Application. The details mentioned in the notification/advertisement and instructions found in the form of Information Brochure are mandatory. According to him, the application without signature of the applicant has no effect at all and it lacks authenticity and therefore, the Commission is justified in rejecting the applications of the petitioners. In support of his submission, learned counsel relied on the Division Bench judgment of this Court in Dr. M. Vennila v. Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission (2006(3) CTC 449).  11. In Dr. M. Vennila's case, the Division Bench has held as follows : -  "13. In addition to the same, all the candidates were supplied specimen application form duly filled up. A perusal of the filled in specimen form makes it clear that where and in how many places the applicant has to sign. Apart from this, we also verified all the columns in the application form. We are satisfied that the language used and the columns given in the application form are very clear and there is no ambiguity in the columns of application regarding the places where the applicant has to subscribe his/her signature. 14. As rightly pointed out by the learned Advocate General, the insistence upon signature under each and every page has its own significance. Signature connotes the authenticity of the person who certifies as well as the accuracy and correctness of the particulars provided and furnished by him. In such circumstances, we are of the view that non-signing by the applicants at page 2 of the application form has rendered the particulars furnished by them unauthenticated and the application could not be considered as a valid application. The respondent is fully justified in arriving at a conclusion that the particulars furnished by the petitioners without signature are construed as being not authenticated.  15. As rightly pointed out, the filled in application must be in order and intact in all aspects and before filling up the application form, the applicants are supposed to go through the notification, instructions, etc. to candidates, information brochure and OMR application form properly in order to ensure that the particulars and information which are required to be furnished are duly furnished and to see that the documents are enclosed along with the application form as per requirements." 12. We have gone through the said judgment and we think there is no scope for the petitioners in this batch to convince us to take a different view.  13. In the light of the decision of the Division Bench, it is clear that the Commission was justified in rejecting the applications of the petitioners for not signing the OMR application and/or the declaration column, etc. This batch of writ petitions, numbering 68, is, therefore, liable to be dismissed.  14. In the second batch of writ petitions, numbering 86, the issue is whether the Commission was right in rejecting the applications on the ground of non- production of Veterinary Council Registration Certificate. We are of the view before the earlier Division Bench a similar question never arose for its consideration.  15. In this connection, it will be necessary to refer to Clause 12 of the Notification/Advertisement which enumerated the list of enclosures to be sent along with application. Clause 12 reads as follows :  "12. List of Enclosures to be sent along with Application : The candidates should enclose all the copies of certificates mentioned in para 4 of Information Brochure, under Part III along with a Demand Draft to the value of Rs. 125/- (Rupees One Hundred and twenty five only) unless exemption of fee is claimed. Original Certificates should not be sent. Those applying Online shall also send the copies of certificates as required in the Instructions.  Note : The applications received without the copies of certificates will be rejected."  (emphasis supplied) In Part II of the Information Brochure, a specimen of the filled in application is given at page No. 13, wherein at the bottom of the right hand side of the first page the check-list for production of documents is set out. About 12 types of documents alone are required to be submitted along with the application form which are as follows :  1. Demand Draft 2. Date of birth evidence 3. SSLC/HSC/Diploma/Degree/PG - Evidence of educational qualification 4. Community Certificate 5. Conduct Certificate 6. Fitness Certificate 7. PH Certificate 8. Destitute Widow Certificate 9. No Objection Certificate 10. Identification Certificate 11. Practical Experience Certificate 12. Evidence for the extra-curricular activities. 16. Mr. T.R. Rajagopalan, learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioners in this batch of cases strenuously submitted that the petitioners had in fact disclosed all the required information and had also enclosed all the required documents that are stipulated in the Notification/Advertisement, Information Brochure, Check List. Neither the Notification/Advertisement nor the Check List in part II of the Information Brochure nor the List of Enclosures vide Clause 4 in Part III of the Information Brochure require the candidates to enclose the Veterinary Council Registration Certificate. Learned senior counsel submitted that the applications were invited only from the eligible registered veterinary medical practitioners. There is no specific requirement about the enclosure of the Veterinary Council Registration Certificate. Had the Commission specifically mentioned this in the Notification/Advertisement or in the Information Brochure or in the Check List of the documents enclosed, the petitioners would have enclosed the same. The non-enclosure of Veterinary Council Registration Certificate is neither wilful nor deliberate. Learned senior counsel submitted that all the petitioners are admittedly the registered candidates of the Veterinary Council. The Commission was therefore not right in rejecting their application on the ground of non-production of Veterinary Council Registration Certificate.  17. Mr. Suresh Kumar, learned counsel appearing for the Commission, however, submitted that Clause 11(2) of the Instructions, etc. to the Candidates, supplied along with the application clearly stipulates that candidates applying for the posts for appointment to Veterinary Assistant Surgeon ought to have registered their names with the Tamil Nadu Veterinary Council before the date of the Commission's notification for appointment and the copy of the Registration Certificate should be enclosed along with other documents evidencing their qualification. Learned counsel submitted that Dr. M. Vennila's case (cited supra) covers this batch also. Learned counsel submitted that nearly two-thirds of the applicants have submitted their Registration Certificate issued by the Veterinary Council. Therefore, the non-production of the Registration Certificate by the petitioners cannot be said to be a bona fide mistake and the Commission was therefore justified in rejecting their applications for want of Registration Certificate.  18. We find considerable substance in the submissions of Mr. T.R. Rajagopalan.
