The employer was directed to work out the money value of the same and to pay the arrears within 12 weeks from the date of judgment. There was also a further direction to the employer to forthwith reinstate the petitioner in service with attendant and consequential benefits. Against the said judgment of the Single Bench, the employer filed a writ appeal but the same was dismissed by the Division Bench. thereupon the employer filed the appeal in the Supreme Court by special leave. After considering the earlier judgments of the Supreme Court in Straw Board Manufacturing Co. v. Gobind', `Punjab Beverages Limited Chandigarh v. Suresh Chand and another' and `Tata Iron and Steel Limited v. S.N. Modak', the Supreme Court held as follows :-  "16. From the conspectus of the views taken in the decisions referred to above the position is manifest that while the employer has the discretion to initiate a departmental inquiry and pass an order of dismissal or discharge against the workman the order remains in an inchoate state till the employer obtains orders of approval from the Tribunal. By passing the order of discharge or dismissal de facto relationship of employer and employee may be ended but not the de jure relationship for that could happen only when the Tribunal accords its approval. The relationship of employer and employee is not legally terminated till approval of discharge or dismissal is given by the Tribunal. In a case where the Tribunal refuses to accord approval to the action taken by the employer and rejects the petition filed under Section 33(2)(b) of the Act on merit the employer is bound to treat the employee as continuing in service and give him all the consequential benefits. If the employer refuses to grant the benefits to the employee the latter is entitled to have his right enforced by filing a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. There is no rational basis for holding that even after the order of dismissal or discharge has been rendered invalid on the Tribunal's rejection of the prayer for approval the workman should suffer the consequences of such invalid order of dismissal or discharge till the matter is decided by the Tribunal again in an industrial dispute. Accepting this contention would render the bar contained in Section 33(1) irrelevant. In the present case as noted earlier the Tribunal on consideration of the matter held that the employer had failed to establish a prima facie case for dismissal/discharge of the workman, and therefore, dismissed the application filed by the employer on merit. The inevitable consequence of this would be that the employer was duty bound to treat the employee as continuing in service and pay him his wages for the period, even though he may be subsequently placed under suspension and an enquiry initiated against him. 17. In the facts and circumstances of the case it is our view that the High Court committed no illegality in issuing a direction to the appellant for reinstating the respondent and pay him the back wages. 18. The appeal, being devoid of merit, is dismissed, with costs, which is assessed at Rs. 10,000." 10. From the above mentioned decisions of the Supreme Court it can be seen that in the case of refusal of approval to the action taken by the employer under Section 33(2)(b) of the Act, the Supreme Court has consistently held that the dismissal or discharge of the workman would be of no effect: that the workmen would be deemed never to have been dismissed or discharged; that the workman would continue to be in service as if there never was any dismissal or discharge by the employer; and that the employer would be bound to consider the workman as his employee and pay him full wages for the period. It is significant that even in M/s. Punjab Beverages Pvt. Ltd. case the Supreme Court has held that if permission or approval is refused by the Tribunal, the employer would be precluded from discharging or dismissing the workman and the action of discharge or dismissal already taken would be void. But in the said case the Supreme Court has further held that mere contravention of Section 33(2)(b) of the Act (i.e. the failure to make an application for approval) did not have the effect of rendering the order of dismissal void or inoperative and that it would not entitle the workman to an order of reinstatement. It has to be noted that in Straw Board Manufacturing Vs. Gobind the Supreme Court was not called upon to consider the consequences of the failure of the employer to make an application for approval of his action under Section 33(2)(b) of the act and hence the Supreme Court did not consider that aspect. In Tata Iron & Steel Company Vs. S.N. Modak also the Supreme court was not considering a case of failure of the employer to make an application for approval of his action under Section 33(2)(b) of the Act. But in M/s. Punjab Beverages Pvt. Ltd. a Bench of three learned Judges was considering a case in which the application for approval of the action taken by the employer under Section 33(2)(b) of the Act was dismissed as withdrawn and thereupon the workman filed an application before the Labour Court under Section 33C(2) of the Act for determination and payment of the amount of wages on the ground that in the absence of approval of the Industrial Tribunal the order of dismissal was void and the workman continued to be in service and was entitled to receive his wages. The principal question considered by the Court in that case was : "What is the effect of contravention of Section 33(2)(b) on an order of dismissal passed by an employer in breach of it ?" The Court specifically considered whether contravention of Section 33(2)(b) would render the order of dismissal void and in-operative so that the aggrieved workman could say that he continued to be in service and was entitled to receive wages from the employer. The Court held that the mere contravention of Section 33 by the employer would not entitled the workman to an order of reinstatement. The court also held that withdrawal of the application for approval stood on the same footing as if no application under Section 33(2)(b) had been made at all. The Court further held that contravention of Section 33(2)(b) did not have the effect of rendering the order of dismissal void and in-operative and hence the workman was not entitled to maintain the application for determination and payment of wages under Section 33C(2).  11. The legal position emerging from the above mentioned judgments of the Supreme Court may be summarised as follows :-  (a) During the pendency of any proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, the employer may discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, a workman concerned in such dispute, for any misconduct not connected with the dispute. (b) Such discharge or punishment shall be in accordance with the Statutory Orders applicable to the workman or, where there are no such standing orders, in accordance with the terms of the contract, whether expressed or implied, between him and the workman. (c) No workman shall be so discharged or dismissed unless he has been paid wages for one month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending, for approval of the action taken by the employer. (d) The condition as to payment of one month's wages is fulfilled when the employer tenders the wages to the workman. If the workman chooses not to accept the wages, he cannot later complain that there was no payment of wages to him by the employer. (e) The application to be made by the employer under the proviso to Section 33(2)(b) is for approval of the order of discharge or dismissal passed by him and not for prior permission to discharge or dismiss the workman. (f) The dismissal or discharge, the payment of wages and the making of an application for approval should be simultaneous and part of the same transaction. In other words, when an employer takes action under Section 33(2)(b) by discharging or dismissing a workman, he should immediately pay the workman or offer to pay the workman wages for one month and also make an application to the Tribunal for approval at the same time. (g) An order of discharge or dismissal passed under Section 33(2)(b) is incomplete and inchoate until approval is granted by the Tribunal in terms of Section 33(2)(b). The relationship of employer and employee is not effectively terminated by passing the order of discharge or dismissal until approval thereto is accorded by the Tribunal in terms of Section 33(2)(b). By passing the order of discharge or dismissal, de facto relationship of employer and employee is ended but not de jure. (h) If approval is granted by the Tribunal it takes effect from the date of the order passed by the employer for which approval was sought. (i) If the tribunal does not approve the action taken by the employer, the workman would be deemed never to have been dismissed or discharged and would remain in service of the employer. In other words, if the Tribunal does not approve the action of the employer the dismissal or discharge of the workman would be of no effect and the workman would continue to be in service as if there never was any dismissal or discharge by the employer and the employer will be bound to treat the workman as his employee and pay him full wages for the period. (j) An application under the proviso to Section 33(2)(b) is a separate and independent proceeding. It is not an interlocutory proceeding in the pending industrial dispute. In spite of the final determination of the main industrial dispute, the application for approval under Section 33(2)(b) will survive and the question about the validity of the order of discharge or dismissal will still have to be tried.  (k) If approval is refused by the Tribunal, the action of discharge or dismissal already taken by the employer would be void. (l) Even if approval is granted by the Tribunal that would not validate the action of discharge or dismissal. The approval granted by the Tribunal would merely remove the ban under Section 33(2) against the discharge and dismissal of the workman and the validity of the order of discharge or dismissal would still be liable to be tested in a reference at the instance of the workman under Section 10 which the workman would be entitled to raise. (m) Even if the order of discharge or dismissal has been passed in contravention of Section 33 such contravention will not invalidate the order though it will invite penalty under Section 31(1). (n) Against an order of discharge or dismissal passed in contravention of Section 33, the workman has remedy both under Section 10 and under Section 33A. The order of discharge or dismissal is not rendered void and inoperative by the contravention of Section 33. (o) The mere contravention of Section 33 by the employer would not entitle the workman to an order of reinstatement, because, the enquiry under Section 33A is not confined to the determination of the question of contravention but even when there was contravention, the Tribunal has to go further and deal with the merits of the order of discharge or dismissal. (p) A workman can proceed under Section 33C(2) only after the Tribunal has adjudicated on a complaint under Section 33A or on a reference under Section 10 that the order of discharge or dismissal was not justified and has set aside that order and reinstated the workman. A proceeding under Section 33C(2) is a proceeding in the nature of execution proceeding in which the Labour Court calculates the amount of money due to a workman from its employer, or, if the workman is entitled to any benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money proceeds to compute the benefit in terms of money. It is not competent to the Labour Court exercising jurisdiction under Section 33C(2) to arrogate to itself the functions of the Industrial Tribunal and entertain a claim which is not based on an existing right but which may appropriately be made the subject matter of an industrial dispute in a reference under Section 10 of the Act. (q) The withdrawal of the application under Section 33(2)(b) stands on the same footing as if no application under Section 33(2)(b) has been made at all. (r) If the employer refuses to reinstate the workman and pay his wages even after the rejection of the application for approval by the Tribunal., the workman is entitled to have his right enforced by filing a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. 12. In the present case the application filed by respondent No. 2 under Section 33(2)(b) of the Act for approval of the action taken against the petitioner was considered on merits and was dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal refusing to grant approval. The Tribunal held that the applicant- management failed to prove that the workman was guilty of any mis-conduct. The order of the Tribunal refusing to grant approval was not challenged by respondent No. 2 at any time and consequently the said order became final and binding on respondent No. 2. After the dismissal of the application under Section 33(2)(b) of the Act, the petitioner requested respondent No. 2 to reinstate him in service and to pay the back-wages for the period he was kept out of service. However, respondent No. 2 did not reinstate the petitioner in service or pay his wages. In the above circumstances, applying the legal principles stated earlier, the petitioner is entitled to be reinstated in service with full back-wages. However, having regard to the facts and circumstances of this case, I am not inclined to issue any writ of mandamus to respondent No. 1 directing him to initiate prosecution proceedings against respondent No. 2. Hence the writ petition is allowed with the following directions :  (a) Respondent No. 2 shall reinstate the petitioner in service forthwith and shall pay to the petitioner full back-wages for the period he was kept out of service i.e. from 16th May, 1991. (b) Since the petitioner has been kept out of service for a very long period, respondent No. 2 shall pay to the petitioner 25% of the back- wages within six weeks from today and the balance amount of back-wages shall be paid within a period of six months from today. (c) Consequent on his reinstatement in service, the petitioner shall be given all benefits as if he continued in service without any break. The writ petition stands disposed of in the above terms. There will be no order as to costs.  Let copy of this order be given Dasti to the learned counsel for the parties.  Order accordingly.
summary:
A. Industrial Disputes Act, Sections 33(2)(b), 33-A and 10 - Dismissal and termination from service - If approval of the Tribunal for dismissal or termination is refused, the workman is entitled to full back wages and reinstatement as if he had remained in service and termination order was never passed. Even if approval is granted, a workman can still claim adjudication under Section 10. An application under the proviso to Section 33(2)(b) is a separate and independent proceeding. If approval is refused by the Tribunal, the action of discharge or dismissal already taken by the employer would be void. If approval is granted by the Tribunal that would not validate the action of discharge or dismissal.  [Paras 6 to 11]

B. Industrial Disputes Act, Sections 33(2)(b), 33-A - Prosecution for violation of provisions of Section 33(2)(b) - Only two kinds of punishment are subject to the above conditions and they are discharge and dismissal.  [Para 3]

C. Industrial Disputes Act, Sections 33(2)(b), 33-A - Payment of wages during pendency of proceedings - If a workman refuses to accept wages, the employer is required to tender them to the employee. If the workman chooses not to accept, he cannot later complain that there was no payment of wages to him by the employer. [Para 4]

text: G.S. Singhvi, J. - In this petition (amended), the petitioner has prayed for quashing seniority list of Punjab Agricultural Service Class-I (for short, `PAS-I') Officers circulated vide memo dated 6.3.1985 (Annexure P7), so far as it concerns him and respondent No. 3. He has further prayed for setting aside the order vide which the benefit of military service was given to respondent No. 3 in terms of Rule 5 of the De-mobilised Armed Forces Personnel (Reservation of Vacancies in the Punjab State Non-Technical Service) Rules, 1968 (for short, `the 1968 Rules'). Still further, he has prayed for issuance of a writ in the nature of quo warranto declaring that respondent No. 3 is not eligible to hold any post in Punjab Agricultural Service Class-II (for short, `PAS-II') or PAS-I. The petitioner has also prayed for issuance of a writ of mandamus to the State Government to consider his case for promotion to the posts of Joint Director, Additional Director and Director of Agriculture and promote him on those posts w.e.f. 24.5.1984, 21.2.1992 and 12.6.1997 respectively.  2. The facts :-  On being selected by Punjab Public Service Commission (for short, `the Commission'), the petitioner was appointed to PAS-I on temporary basis vide memo, dated 11.7.1974 (Annexure P1). He was promoted as Joint Director, Agriculture (Extension and Training) vide order dated 18.2.1985 issued by the State Government. 3. Respondent No. 3 - Shri Avtar Singh Randhawa joined service as Agriculture Inspector which is a Class-III post on 5.11.1962, in July, 1963 he joined Indian Army on deputation. He was released from the Army in May, 1968. Thereafter, he served in the parent department till January 6, 1972, when he rejoined the Army. He was finally released from the Army some time in 1973. In the meanwhile, the Department of Agriculture sent requisition dated 13.9.1971 to the Commission for recruitment of 13 Class-II Officers. Of these, four posts were reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and three were reserved for Released Armed Forces Personnel. While he was serving the Indian Army (second stint), respondent No. 3 applied for recruitment to PAS-II in pursuance of the advertisement issued by the Commission and on being recommended by the Commission, he was appointed as Chief Agricultural Office vide order dated 9.1.1973. He joined that post on 16.4.1973. By an order dated 25.1.1977, he was promoted to PAS-I. Later on, the competent authority passed order dated 23.1.1976 giving him the benefit of deemed appointment to PAS-II w.e.f. 1.11.1963 in terms of Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules. By another other dated 20.9.1982, the State Government revised his promotion to PAS-I and he was given the benefit of deemed promotion w.e.f. 3.11.1971. During the pendency of this petition, he was promoted as Joint Director w.e.f. 17.10.1989, as Additional Director w.e.f. 22.2.1992 and as Director w.e.f. 23/24.6.1997.  4. After recruitment of respondent No. 3 to PAS-II, the State Government circulated tentative seniority list of PAS-I officers vide memo dated 26.2.1980 (Annexure P4) showing their position as on 1.1.1979. The petitioner's name figured in that list at S.No. 22, but that of respondent No. 3 did not find mention in it. However, in the revised tentative seniority list prepared in pursuance of the decision of the High Court in Deep Singh Sihota v. State of Punjab, 1983(1) S.L.R. 665 which was circulated vide memo dated 25.5.1984 (Annexure P5), the petitioner's name was shown at No. 23 and that of respondent No. 3 was shown at No. 13. This was done because in the meanwhile, respondent No. 3 had been given the benefit of deemed appointment to PAS-II and PAS-I w.e.f. 1.11.1963 and 3.11.1971 respectively. The petitioner submitted representation dated 25.6.1984 (Annexure P6) to protest against his placement below respondent No. 3 by asserting that the latter could not have been given the benefit of deemed appointment in terms of Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules. However, the State Government did not accept his representation and in the final seniority list circulated vide memo dated 6.3.1985 (Annexure P7), inter-se position of the petitioner and respondent No. 3 was maintained.  5. The petitioner has challenged his placement below respondent No. 3 in the final seniority list of PAS-I mainly on the ground that respondent No. 3 could not have been given the benefit of Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules. He has averred that respondent No. 4 had joined Army service on 20.7.1963 whereas the post, with reference to which he has been given the benefit of deemed appointment in terms of Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules, was advertised by the Commission on 18.5.1963 and the last date fixed for receipt of the applications was 11.6.1963. According to the petitioner, the benefit of deemed appointment can be given only to a Released Armed Forces Personnel with reference to the first opportunity available to him for appointment to the civil services after joining Indian Army and as respondent No. 3 did not get such opportunity after 20.7.1963, he could not have been given the benefit of deemed appointment. He has further averred that as on 1.11.1973, respondent No. 3 was not even eligible to be appointed to PAS-II because he did not have the requisite experience for recruitment as Horticulture Development Officer (Grapes). The further case of the petitioner is that even as on 9.1.1973 or 16.4.1973, respondent No. 3 was not eligible to be appointed to PAS-II because he did not possess the qualification of Post Graduation in Agriculture prescribed under Rule 5 of the Punjab Agricultural Service (Class II) Rules, 1947 (for short, `the 1947 Rules') as amended vide notification dated 25.8.1972. He has referred to the example of Shri Raghbir Singh, who was denied appointment to PAS-II only on the ground that he did not possess the qualifications prescribed under the amended Rule 5 of the 1947 Rules and pleaded that the official respondents cannot adopt different yard-stricks for judging the eligibility of the candidates for recruitment to PAS-II.  6. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 have filed written statement to contest the writ petition. They have averred that respondent No. 3 had applied for recruitment to PAS-II in pursuance of advertisement dated 4.3.1972 issued by the Commission for recruitment of 13 PAS Class-II officers for which requisition dated 13.9.1971 was sent by the Agriculture Department and on the recommendations of the Commission, he was appointed as Chief Agricultural Officer vide order dated 9.1.1973. They have further averred that respondent No. 3 was given the benefit of deemed appointment to PAS-II w.e.f. 1.11.1973 because Shri Ajit Singh Doabia was appointed as Horticulture Development Officer with effect from that date. They have controverted the petitioner's assertion that respondent No. 3 was not eligible to be appointed as Horticulture Development Officer (Grapes) and have averred that he possessed the qualifications prescribed under the 1947 Rules. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 have also controverted the petitioner's plea that they had adopted different yard-sticks for judging the eligibility of the candidates for recruitment to PAS-II or PAS-I. For the sake of convenient reference, the averments contained in paragraph 17(i) and 17(v) of the written statement filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are reproduced below:-  "17(i) Not admitted. According to Rules 5(1) of the Demobilised Armed Forces Personnel (Reservation of Vacancies in the Punjab State Non Technical Service) Rules, 1968, seniority and pay of the candidates who are appointed against the vacancies reserved under Rule 3 and who :- (i) in the case of Emergency Commissioned Officers are released according to a programme; or (ii) In the case of Short Service Commissioned Officers; are released on the expiry of the tenure of their service; or (iii) are invalidated owing to a disability attributable to or aggrated by military service; shall be determined on the assumption that they joined the service or the post, as the case may be, under the State Government at the first opportunity they had after they joined the military service or training prior to the Commission".  Further as provided in Rule 5(3) of the Rules ibid, all candidates appointed against the reserved vacancies under Rule 3 shall rank below the candidates appointed by direct recruitment in the year to which the former candidates are allowed. According to Rule 6 of the Rules ibid, the provisions of these Rules shall have effect, notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other rules.  The copy of the advertisement appended as Annexure/P/8 to the petition is not the strictly relevant document in this case. The actual position i.e. however, that the Punjab Public Service Commission advertised two posts of Horticulture Development Officer (Grapes) on 18.5.1963 with the following qualifications :-  (a) B.Sc. (Agri) with Horticulture or Botany and Applied Botany as a major Subject.  (b) Three years' experience of development work of fruit production; (c) Adequate knowledge of Hindi or Punjabi. In the Punjab Agriculture Service (Class II) Rules, 1947, then in vogue, the following qualifications have been prescribed for direct recruitment to Class II posts:-  "has obtained diploma or a degree of a recognised institution in the particular branch of science or subject in which proficiency is required or a candidate for the particular scientific or technical post for which he is to be recruited."  Thus, the qualifications and experience prescribed for the post of Horticulture Development Officer were not in conformity with the said statutory provisions of the Rules. On the post of Horticulture Development Officer Shri Ajit Singh Doabia was appointed on 31.10.1963 through direct recruitment. Respondent No. 3 joined the military service on 20.7.1963. He is B.Sc. (Agri.) with Horticulture. He was assigned assumed date of seniority as 1.11.1963 below Sh. Ajit Singh Doabia under rule 5.3 of the Demoblilised Armed Forces Personnel (Reservation of Vacancies in Punjab State Non-Technical Services) Rules, 1958.  17(v) The position has been explained in para 8 above. With regard to the non-appointment of Sh. Raghbir Singh Sidhu to PAS, Class I, it is stated that on the recommendations of the Punjab Public Service Commission, appointment orders were issued on 5th October, 1972 to 12 persons for PAS. Class I posts. In the meantime 4 more posts fell vacant on 7.12.1972, respondent No. 1 asked the Commission to recommend the names of next four candidates for these posts from the merit list prepared by the Commission while selecting candidates for PAS-I in September, 1972. But the Commission had advertised 3 posts on February 10, 1973 with the qualification as B.Sc. (Agri.). Respondent No. 2 vide D.O. letter dated 12.2.1973 brought to the notice of the Commission that the Service Rules had since been amended and according to which revised qualifications, for direct recruitment to PAS Class I it was at least 2nd Class degree of M.Sc. (Agri.). Respondent No. 1 vide D.O. Letter dated 1.2.1973 had also brought this amendment to the notice of the Chairman, Punjab Public Service Commission. Besides this, for one post of Deputy Director (Cotton Extension), the Commission had recommended the name of Sh. Raghbir Singh Sidhu from the merit list prepared by them during September, 1972. Being a B.Sc. (Agri.) degree holder, Sh. Raghbir Singh Sidhu was not given appointment as Class I by the Government." 7. In his separate written statement, respondent No. 3 has pleaded that the writ petition is liable to be dismissed on the ground of laches. He has averred that the petitioner has not explained the delay of 12 years between the date of his appointment to PAS-II and the filing of writ petition and, therefore, he should be non-suited on this ground alone. He has justified his placement above the petitioner in the revised seniority list issued in compliance of the direction given by the High Court in Deep Singh Sihota's case (supra) and averred that Letters Patent Appeal and Special Leave Petition filed against the order of the learned Single Judge were dismissed by the Division Bench and the Supreme Court respectively. He has also justified the decision of the government to give him the benefit of the deemed appointment to PAS-II and PAS-I by asserting that he was selected to join Indian Army much before 11.6.1963 i.e. the last date fixed for receipt of applications in pursuance of advertisement dated 18.5.1963. On the issue of his eligibility to be appointed to PAS-II, respondent No. 3 has averred that he fulfilled the prescribed qualifications.  8. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and carefully perused the record.  9. At the out-set, I deem it proper to mention that during the course of hearing, Shri D.V. Sharma had produced the record containing documents in which the case of respondent No. 3 for grant of benefit of deemed appointment to PAS-II and promotion to PAS-I was dealt with and made a statement that his appointment to PAS-II ws ante-dated from 16.4.1973 to 10.11.1963 vide order dated 23.11.1976 and his promotion to PAS-I was ante-dated from 215.1.1977 to 3.11.1971 vide order dated 20.9.1882. Shri Sharma also stated that the petitioner and respondent No. 3 have already retired from service. Shri R.D. Bawa, learned counsel for the petitioner did not controvert either of the two statements made by Shri D.V. Sharma.  10. The first question which needs consideration is whether the selection and appointment of respondent No. 3 to PAS-II is liable to be nullified on the ground that he was not eligible to be considered for appointment in pursuance of advertisement dated 4.3.1972. According to the petitioner, the qualifications prescribed under Rule 5 of the 1947 Rules for recruitment to PAS-II was amended vide notification dated 25.8.1972 (published in Gazette dated 1.9.1972) and Post Graduation in Agriculture was made an essential qualification and respondent No. 3 did not have Post Graduate Degree in Agriculture at the relevant time. The stand taken by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 is that the requisition for 13 posts of PAS-II which were advertised by the Commission on 4.3.1972 had been sent on 13.9.1971 and the same was not withdrawn despite the amendment of Rule 5 of the 1947 Rules and, therefore, the Commission was justified in making selection from among the candidates, who possessed the qualifications prescribed under the unamended rule.  11. In my opinion, the selection and appointment of respondent No. 3 to PAS- II cannot be nullified on the ground that he was not qualified for that post. The question whether or not respondent No. 3 was eligible to be recruited to PAS-II was directly considered by this Court in Kulwant Singh Grewal v. The State of Punjab and others, 1990(5) S.L.R. 518 and answered in the negative in the following words :-  "Admittedly, respondent No. 1 sent the requisition to the Punjab Public Service Commission for filing up of 13 posts in P.A.S. Class II Service on September 13, 1971 and in the requisition it was specified that qualification for these posts was B.Sc. (Agriculture). The Punjab Public Service Commission advertised these posts and the last date for receipt of the applications was April 4, 1972. These posts were advertised much prior to the amendment of Class II Rules. The only condition prescribed was that the applicant should have the basic qualification of B.Sc. (Agriculture). The process of selection begins with the issuance of advertisement and ends with the preparation of select list. Indeed, it consists of various steps like inviting applications, scrutiny of applications, rejection of defective applications or elimination of ineligible candidates, conducting examinations, calling for interview or viva-voce and preparation of list of successful candidates for appointment. When such are the different steps in the process of selection, a candidate on making application for a post pursuant to an advertisement does not acquire any right of selection. But if he is eligible and otherwise qualified in accordance with the relevant rules and the terms contained in the advertisement, he does acquire a vested right for being considered for selection in accordance with the Rules as they existed on the date of advertisement. If amendment is made in the Rules during the pendency of selection, unless the amended rules suggest otherwise. It will operate prospectively. However, if by express language or by necessary implication, it can be inferred that the amended rules apply prospectively (retrospectively-Ed) normally would operate prospectively. On the date of advertisement and on the last date of submitting the application, respondents 3 to 5 were eligible for applying for P.A.S. Class II posts. Subsequent amendment in the Class II Rules will not render them ineligible irrespective of the fact that on the date when the appointment letters were issued, the amended rules had already come into force."" 12. In view of the above noted judgment, I have no hesitation to reject the petitioner's challenge to the eligibility of respondent No. 3 to be appointed to PAS-II.  13. There are two other reasons why the petitioner's challenge to the appointment of respondent No. 3 to PAS-II should be negatived. Firstly, he has approached the Court after a gap of 12 years and no satisfactory explanation has been given for not challenging the appointment of respondent No. 3 during this long interregnum. If the petitioner was to file Civil suit in the year 1985 for quashing the appointment of respondent No. 3 to PAS-II w.e.f. 9.1.1973/16.4.1973, the same was bound to be dismissed as barred by limitation. Therefore, by applying the ratio of the judgments of the Supreme Court in State of M.P. and another v. Bhailal Bhai, AIR 1964 S.C. 1006; M/s Tilok Chand Moti Chand & others v. H.B. Munshi, Commissioner of Sales Tax, Bombay and another, AIR 1970 S.C. 898; Kamini Kumar Das Choudhury v. State of West Bengal and others, AIR 1972 S.C. 2060 and P.S. Sadasivaswamy v. State of Tamil Nadu, 1976(1) S.L.R. 53, I am inclined to uphold the objection of delay and laches raised by respondent No. 3. Secondly, no useful purpose would now be served by entertaining the petitioner's prayer for issuance of a writ of quo warranto because respondent No. 3 has already retired from service.  14. The second question which merits consideration is whether orders dated 23.1.1976 and 20.9.1982 for giving the benefit of deemed appointment to respondent No. 3 to PAS-II w.e.f. 1.11.1963 and promotion to PAS-I w.e.f. 3.11.1997 is ultra vires to Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules. For appreciating the petitioner's plea that respondent No. 3 was not entitled to the benefit of deemed appointment and promotion to PAS-II and PAS-I respectively, it will be useful to notice Rule 5 of the 968 Rules. The same reads as under :-  "5(1) Seniority and pay of the candidates who are appointed against the vacancies reserved under Rule 3 and who - (i) in the case of Emergency Commissioned Officers are released according to a programme; or (ii) in the case of Short Service Commissioned Officers, are released on the expiry of tenure, of their service; or (iii) are invalidated owing to a disability attributable to or aggravated by Military service, shall be determined on the assumption that they joined the service or the post as the case may be under the State Government at the first opportunity they had after they joined the Military service or training prior to the commission."  15. A critical analysis of the rule reproduced above shows that a candidate, who is appointed against the vacancy reserved for Released Armed Forces Personnel, is entitled to have his seniority fixed on the assumption that he had joined service under the State Government at the first opportunity he had after joining Military service or training prior to the commission. According to the petitioner, the advertisement with reference to which Shri Ajit Singh Doabia was appointed as Horticulture Development Officer on 1.11.1963 was issued on 18.5.1963 and the last date fixed for receipt of the applications was 11.6.1963 and as respondent No. 3 had joined the Army 20.7.1963, he could not have been given the benefit of deemed appointment w.e.f. 1.11.1963. In my opinion, there is no merit in the plea of the petitioner. The use of expressions "they joined the service or post" and "under the State Government" in Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules clearly show that the candidate must be eligible and available for taking up the job under the State Government on the first available opportunity. In the present case, that opportunity could come to respondent No. 3 only on 1.11.1963 when Shri Ajit Singh Doabia was appointed as Horticulture Development Officer (Grapes). Therefore, the mere fact that the post on which Shri Ajit Singh Doabia was appointed had been advertised prior to the joining of respondent No. 3 in the Indian Army cannot disentitle him from the benefit of deemed appointment to PAS-II.  16. The petitioner's challenge to the eligibility of respondent No. 3 to be appointed to PAS-II w.e.f. 1.11.1963 on the ground that he did not have three years experience of development work in relation to Food Production also merits rejection. The qualifications prescribed under the 1947 Rules (as they then stood), for recruitment to the post of PAS-II was as under :-  "has obtained diploma or a degree of a recognised institution in the particular branch of science or subject in which proficiency is required of a candidate for the particular scientific or technical post for which he is to be recruited." 17. Therefore, the requirement of experience incorporated in the advertisement cannot be relied upon for denying the benefit of Rule 5 of the 1968 Rules, more-so because Rule 3 of the said Rules does not lay down any particular qualification for recruitment to PAS-II.  18. There is one more reason for my disinclination to entertain the petitioner's challenge to the deemed appointment and promotion of respondent No. 3 to PAS-II and PAS-I respectively. He has neither placed on record copies of orders dated 23.11.1976 and 20.9.1982 vide which respondent No. 3 was given the benefit of deemed appointment and promotion nor he has prayed for quashing of those orders. In the absence of a specific prayer, I do not find any justification to nullify those orders.  No other point has been argued.  For the reasons mentioned above, the writ petition is dismissed.  Petition dismissed.
summary: A. Rules 3 and 5 of the A. De-mobilised Armed Forces Personnel (Reservation of Vacancies in the Punjab State Non-Technical Service) Rules, 1968 - Benefit of deemed appointment - Extension of - Respondent was eligible and available for the job under State Government on first available opportunity - Hence was entitled to benefit of deemed appointment. [Para 15] B. Challenge to appointment or promotion as to delay - Petition filed after 12 years of appointment - No satisfactory explanation given for delay - Petition suffers from delay and laches. [Para 13] C. Rule 5 of the Punjab Agricultural Service (Class II) Rules, 1947 - Appointment - Commission was justified in making selection as per qualification prescribed in unamended rules irrespective of issuance of date of appointment letters. [Paras 11, 12] D. Challenge to promotion or deemed appointment as to non-production of orders - Since orders cannot be nullified in absence of any specific prayer, Petitioner cannot nullify the orders as he has neither placed on record copies of orders nor prayed for their quashing. [Para 18]

text: Vinod K. Sharma, J. - Present revision petition has been filed against the order dated 6.1.2005 passed by the learned Civil Judge (Junior Division), Gurgaon dismissing an application filed by the petitioner under Order 7 Rule 11 read with Section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code) for rejection of the plaint.  2. The plaintiff-respondent filed a suit for permanent injunction to challenge the order passed under Section 14-B of the Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act (for short the Act) imposing damages for non- payment of contribution in time for the period from June, 1993 to January, 2001.  3. Besides contesting the suit on merit an application was moved for rejection of plaint under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code on the plea that the suit as framed was not competent and was liable to be rejected. It was pleaded in the application that the suit was barred under sub-section (D) Order 7-1 as any person aggrieved by a notification issued by the Central Government or an order passed by the Central Government or any authority, under the proviso to sub-section (3), or sub-section (4), of Section 1, or Section 3, or sub- section (i) of Section 7-A, or Section 7-B (except an order rejecting an application for review referred to in sub-section (5) or Section 7-C, or Section 14-B of the Act, may prefer an appeal to a Tribunal against such notification or order. It was also pleaded that when a specific remedy is available to the plaintiff the suit was not maintainable and therefore, the plaint was liable to be rejected. It was also pleaded that the civil Court has no jurisdiction to try the present suit as the plaintiff-respondent had a remedy of appeal before the Tribunal under Section 7(i) of the Act. Provisions of Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act were also invoked.  Said application was contested on the plea that if the authorities acted against the statute or did not follow procedure prescribed by law/statute then the civil Court has every jurisdiction to entertain and try the suit.  4. Learned trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaint can be rejected under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code, if it does not show any cause of action or the plaintiff has not paid the proper court-fee or the jurisdiction of the civil Court has been specifically barred. However, no such provisions were shown which barred the jurisdiction of the civil Court. Resultantly, the application was dismissed.  5. Learned counsel for the petitioner by placing reliance on the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of NDMC v. Satish Chand (deceased) by LRs Ram Chand, 2003(4) RCR(Civil) 373 : 2003(10) Supreme Court Cases 38 contended that the jurisdiction of the civil Court was impliedly barred as remedy of appeal was provided under the statute itself against an order passed under Section 14-B of the Act which was challenged by the plaintiff-respondent. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in NDMC v. Satish Chand (supra) has been pleased to lay down as under :-  "Section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 gives a wide jurisdiction to the civil Courts to try all suits of civil nature "excepting suits of which their statute itself contains a provision that the jurisdiction of a civil court is barred." An implied bar may arise when a statute provides a special remedy to an aggrieved party like a right of appeal as contained in the Punjab Municipal Act. Section 84 of the Act provides a complete remedy to a party aggrieved by the assessment and levy of tax. Section 86 provides that the remedy of appeal is the only remedy available to a party to challenge the assessment and restrains a party from taking recourse to any other mode. A provision like this is the implied bar envisaged in Section 9 CPC against filing a civil suit. Besides, the position in law has been well settled by the Supreme Court in various decisions. Sections 84 and 86 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 bar the jurisdiction of the civil Court, where the grievance relates to the assessment or the principle of assessment by necessary implication." 6. Learned counsel for the petitioner further made a reference to Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act to contend that as equally efficacious relief can be obtained by the plaintiff by filing statutory appeal, therefore, suit for injunction as framed was not competent.  7. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that learned trial Court failed to notice that besides the reasons observed in the order the plaint can also be rejected when from the statement made in the plaint the suit seems to be barred by any law. The contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner, therefore, was that in view of vesting of jurisdiction in the Special Tribunal constituted under the Act filing of suit would be deemed to be impliedly barred.  8. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent placed reliance on the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh and others v. State of Haryana and another, 2006(3) RCR(Civil) 491 : 2007(4) RAJ 607 (SC). The law relating to the jurisdiction has been discussed in the said judgment as under :-  "15. The law relating to jurisdiction has been the subject-matter of various decisions. In State of Tamil Nadu v. Ramalinga Samigal Madam, 1985(4) SCC 10 it was, inter alia, held as follows :- "8. The principles bearing on the question as to when exclusion of the Civil Court's jurisdiction can be inferred have been indicated in several judicial pronouncements but we need refer to only two decisions. In Secretary of State v. Mask and Company, AIR 1940 PC 105, the Privy Council at page 236 of the Report has observed thus : It is settled law that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is not to be readily inferred, but that such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. It is also well settled that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. In Dhulabhai v. State of M.P., 1968(3) SCR 662, Hidayathullah, C.J., speaking for the Court, on an analysis of the various decisions cited before the Court expressing diverse views, culled out as many as 7 propositions; out of them the first two which are material for our purposes are these : (1) Where the statute gives a finality to the orders of the special tribunal the Civil Court's jurisdiction must be held to be excluded if there is adequate remedy to do what the Civil Courts would normally do in a suit. Such provisions, however, do not exclude those cases where the provisions of the particular Act have not been complied with or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. (2) Where there is an express bar of the jurisdiction of the Court, in examination of the Scheme of the Particular Act to find the adequacy or the sufficiency of the remedies provided may be relevant but is not decisive to sustain the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. Where there is no express exclusion the examination of the remedies and the scheme of the particular Act to find out the intendment becomes necessary and the result of the inquiry may be decisive. In the latter case it is necessary to see if the statute creates a special right or a liability and provides for the determination of the right or liability and further lays down that all questions about the said right and liability shall be determined by the tribunals so constituted, and whether remedies normally associated with actions in Civil Courts are prescribed by the said statute or not. xxx xxx xxx 14. Thirdly, having regard to the principles stated by this Court while enunciating the first proposition in Dhulabhai case it is clear that even where the statute has given finality to the orders of the special tribunal the Civil Court's jurisdiction can be regarded as having been excluded if there is adequate remedy to do what the Civil Court would normally do in a suit. In other words, even where finality is accorded to the orders passed by the special tribunal one will have to see whether such special tribunal has powers to grant reliefs which Civil Court would normally grant in a suit and if the answer is in the negative it would be difficult to imply or infer exclusion of Civil Court's jurisdiction. Now take the case of an applicant who has applied for ryotwari patta under Section 11 staking his claim thereto on the basis of his long and uninterrupted possession of the ryoti land but the Settlement Officer on materials before him is not satisfied that the land in question is ryoti land; in that case he will refuse the patta to the applicant. But can he, even after the refusal of the patta, protect the applicant's long and uninterrupted possession against the Government interference ? Obviously, he cannot, for it lies within his power and jurisdiction merely to grant or refuse to grant the patta on the basis of materials placed before him. But such a person even after the refusal of the ryotwari patta would be entitled to protect his possessory title and long enjoyment of the land and seek an injunction preventing Government's interference otherwise than in due course of law and surely before granting such relief the Civil Court may have to adjudicate upon the real nature or character of the land if the same is put in issue. In other words since the Settlement Officer has no power to do what Civil Court would normally do in a suit it is difficult to imply ouster of Civil Court's jurisdiction simply because finality has been accorded to the Settlement Officer's order under Section 64-C of the Act." 16. In Richpal Singh and others v. Dalip, 1987 RRR 598 : 1987(4) SCC 410, it was held as under :- "12. It is well settled that ouster of jurisdiction of civil Courts should not be inferred easily. It must be clearly provided for and established." 17. Strong reliance was placed by learned counsel for the appellant on 1979(2) All ER 1016. Para 15 of the State of Tamil Nadu's case (supra) deals with question relating to jurisdiction. These cases deal with cases where there was no exclusion of any other remedy. 18. The principles culled out from various decisions of this Court are that even when the statute has given finality to the orders of the special tribunal, the Civil Court's jurisdiction can be regarded as having been excluded if there is adequate remedy to do what the Civil Court would normally do in a suit. Section 26(1)(d) on the other hand specifically excludes jurisdiction of the Civil Court so far as matters which are required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Financial Commissioner, the Commissioner, Collector or Prescribed Authority. The entitlement, choice of land and the allotment are matters which are to be dealt with specifically by the authorities under the Act. Additionally, Section 18 provides a forum to ventilate the grievance under the Act in respect of several matters. This is a case of exclusion of the remedy in certain contingencies. It is not a case where the controversy cannot be resolved by the forum provided under the Act. Further in case of any grievance the validity of the order could have been questioned before the forum provided. That has not been done and on the other hand, the suit was filed after about nine years. Above being the position, the appeal is without merit and is dismissed. No costs." This judgment does not support the contention raised by the learned counsel for the respondent. Rather in the said case also jurisdiction of the civil Court was held to be barred because of statutory remedy provided under the statute.  9. Learned counsel for the respondent thereafter placed reliance on the Full Bench judgment of this Court in the case of State of Haryana and others v. Vinod Kumar and others, 1986 PLJ 161 to contend that civil Court jurisdiction to entertain any case against an order passed by Tribunal of special jurisdiction in violation of the provisions of the statute or principles of natural justice, cannot be treated to be barred as the order of the Tribunal would be a nullity.  However, this contention of the learned counsel for the respondent also cannot be accepted as he has not chosen to challenge the order of recovery passed by the authorities under the Act by filing appeal before the special Tribunal constituted under the Act. Once the jurisdiction is given to a special tribunal then the remedy of the civil Court is to be held to be impliedly barred. It is only in case of tribunals not acting in accordance with law or acting in violation of the statute that an order can be challenged as a nullity before the civil Court, as was held in the case of State of Haryana v. Vinod Kumar and others (supra). However, in the present case the plaintiff instead of choosing remedy provided under the statute has chosen to maintain the present suit which would be deemed to be barred in view of the law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of NDMC v. Satish Chand (deceased) by LRs Ram Chand (supra). Even otherwise, in view of the provisions of Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act the suit filed by the plaintiff was barred under law and, therefore, was liable to be rejected.  Consequently, this revision is allowed. The impugned order is set aside and the plaint filed by the plaintiff-respondent is ordered to be rejected.  Petition allowed.
summary: Civil Procedure Code, Section 9 - Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Sections 7(i) and 14-B - Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 41(h) - Bar to civil Court jurisdiction - An implied bar on civil court jurisdiction exists due to the availability of an effective alternate remedy in the special Acts, even in absence of specific bar- EPF Act provides for an appeal against any order passed under it - Unless the order is null and void passed without jurisdiction, the civil Court cannot accept suit against such orders. [Para 9]

text: R. Gururajan, J. - These two writ petitions are directed against the award of the Labour Court passed in KID No. 68/96 dated 22-12-98.  2. Respondent a driver in the Corporation caused an accident on 2-9-94 which resulted in the death of 3 passengers and injuries to 41 passengers. He was subjected to disciplinary proceedings. Charges were held to have been proved in the enquiry. Consequently, he was dismissed from service on 30-3-96. The said dismissal was challenged before the Labour Court in KID No. 68/96. Parties entered appearance and filed their respective statements. Labour Court raised a preliminary issue with regard to the correctness of the enquiry. The said issue was held in favour of the Corporation. Thereafter, Labour Court has chosen to order reinstatement of the workman together with a fine of Rs. 10,000/-. This award is challenged by the management as well as the workman.  3. Heard Smt. Renuka, the learned counsel appearing for the Corporation. She would submit that the matter requires serious consideration by this Court. According to her, the workman has caused 3 deaths in addition to injuries to 41 passengers on account of his rash and negligent driving. She says the Labour Court having held that the enquiry was fair and proper ought to have rejected the reference and ought not to have reinstated the workman. She finds fault with the findings of the Labour Court. Even otherwise, she says that the Labour Court cannot grant a fine of Rs. 10,000/- despite there being 3 deaths in the case on hand. She ultimately wants the award to be set aside.  4. Per contra, Sri Mukkannappa, learned counsel took great pains to say that the material facts did not require any dismissal. Counsel says that the material on record would support that there is no negligence on the part of the workman. Even otherwise, learned counsel strenuously relies on a circular dated 6-9-2004 in the matter of punishment. He further says that the workman has been reinstated pursuant to the interim order and after reinstatement there is no allegation of any accident being caused by him.  5. After hearing, I have carefully perused the material on record. Admitted facts would reveal of a charge of rash and negligent driving resulting in an accident that occurred on 2-9-94. In response to the article of charge, workman submitted an explanation and in the explanation he contended that the vehicle was sick in condition, that the vehicle completed 10 lakh Kms. ran on the road, brake condition of the vehicle was weak, the bus had over capacity, etc. Being dissatisfied enquiry was conducted. Workman participated in the enquiry. Enquiry officer found the workman guilty of the charges levelled against him. Management accepting the same, dismissed him from service. Labour Court has ruled that the enquiry is fair and proper. Thereafter, the Labour Court has chosen to interfere in the case on hand. Labour Court says that there is no eye-witness examined by the enquiry officer, Labour Court notices that the criminal proceedings are pending, Labour Court notices that three lives have been lost in addition to injuries to passengers, Labour Court rules that the workman has to be reinstated on humanitarian grounds subject to the condition of the result of the criminal case and also subject to the workman paying Rs. 10,000/- recoverable in 10 monthly equal instalments.  6. Let me see as to whether the Labour Court is justified in passing the impugned award in the case on hand.  7. Labour Court as I mentioned earlier held that the enquiry is fair and proper. In the light of his finding on the preliminary issue, the only issue that requires to be taken into consideration by the Labour Court is as to whether the findings of the enquiry officer are perverse or not.  8. Labour Court unfortunately has not adverted to this aspect of the matter. But however, I have gone through the findings of the enquiry officer in terms of the material made available to me. Enquiry Officer has chosen to examine the witnesses and on the said basis he has chosen to find him guilty. The findings in the given circumstances cannot be said to be perverse as understood in the eye of law. In fact, the defence of the workman is one of mechanical failure on account of the brake being weak. This defence is not available in the light of the motor vehicle's accident report (M.W. 9 before enquiry officer). The accident report would clearly go to show that the brakes were found to be in good condition. Inspector of the motor vehicles has certified that the accident was not due to any mechanical defect of the vehicle. In the light of the report the defence of the workman i.e. of mechanical defects has no legs to stand and the said defence has been rejected by the enquiry officer. As I mentioned earlier, unfortunately the Labour Court without taking note of these aspects of the matter has chosen to exercise its power under S. 11-A by way of reinstatement subject to the condition of the result of the criminal case and subject to the workman paying Rs. 10,000/- in 10 equal monthly, instalments. Section 11-A is no doubt available to the Labour Court in the matter of punishment but labour Court cannot lightly interfere with the punishment unless the said punishment shocks the conscience of the Court.  9. Material on record would show that 3 lives were lost on account of the accident in addition to injuries to 41 passengers. Labour Court should have been serious in the matter of awarding reinstatement after noticing this ghastly accident wherein 3 deaths and injuries to 41 passengers is caused. In such circumstances, there cannot be any sympathy by the Labour Court and any such sympathy would be a misplaced sympathy as understood in law. It is unfortunate that the Labour Court has not chosen to apply its mind in the matter of interfering under S. 11-A of the Act. Labour Court failed to see that admittedly the Corporation is rendering public service and the public servants have to be careful in the larger interest of the travelling public. Labour Court has failed to see that in service sector apart from employer and employee, there is an invisible third party viz, the public and the interest of third parties is to be taken into consideration while exercising powers u/S. 11-A of the Act. In the case on hand, unfortunately Labour Court has dealt with the case very lightly in granting the relief of reinstatement. I am also surprised to see that the Labour Court has, subject to the pending criminal proceeding and subject to payment of Rs. 10,000/- ordered reinstatement. This finding in my view exceeds the power granted under S. 11-A of the Act. Looking from any angle, the learned Labour Court was absolutely not justified in interfering in a matter like this.  10. Sri Mukkannappa, learned counsel however invites my attention to a circular issued by Law Department in No. KST/CO/LAW/3577 04-05 dated 26/12-9- 2004. Admittedly it is only an internal circular and such circulars cannot override the regulations of the KSRTC. It is also seen that the corporation has chosen to provide dismissal only in the event of two fatal cases. I am unable to understand the logic behind this. If the workman is guilty of rash and negligent driving then it does not matter as to how many accidents he has to his credit. Even otherwise, the circular would not come to the rescue of the workman in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. Therefore, not much assistance can be derived at by the workman by relying on the circular.  11. In somewhat identical circumstances, the Supreme Court in 2005 AIR SCW 84 in the case of Cholan Roadways Ltd. v. G. Thirugnanasambandam has noted as under :  "In the instant case the Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal as also the learned single Judge and the Division Bench of the High Court misdirected themselves in law in so far as they failed to pose unto themselves correct questions. It is now well-settled that a quasi-judicial authority must post unto itself a correct question so as to arrive at a correct finding of fact. A wrong question posed leads to a wrong answer. In this case, furthermore, the mis-direction in law committed by the Industrial Tribunal was apparent in so far as it did not apply the principle of res ipsa loquitur which was relevant for the purpose of this case and, thus, failed to take into consideration a relevant factor and furthermore took into consideration an irrelevant fact not germane for determining the issue, namely, the passengers of the bus were mandatory required to be examined. The Industrial Tribunal further failed to apply the correct standard of proof in relation to a domestic enquiry, which is "preponderance of probability" and applied the standard of proof required for a criminal trial. A case for judicial review as, thus, clearly made out."  The said Judgment is squarely applicable to the facts of this case. I have also recently in W.P. 38587/99 held that such death cases cannot be viewed lightly by Courts. In the given circumstances and in the facts of the case, I am satisfied that a case is made out by the management. It is needless for this Court to say that if any driver whose act of rash and negligent driving result in death of innocent passengers, unless the workman proves to the satisfaction of the authorities that he is innocent of the matter, dismissal is the only answer.  12. Before concluding I must notice that this Court has ordered reinstatement at the time of admission. The workman's counsel argued that he has worked for 5 years and that should be taken into consideration by this Court while providing the relief. I am not inclined to accept this argument in the light of rash and 'negligent driving of the bus resulting in 3 deaths and injuries to 41 passengers. This Court has passed that order on 19-3-1999 at this order cannot be taken as a defence in a case like this.  13. Before concluding I deem it proper to observe that discretionary powers under Art. 226 of the Constitution should be used cautiously. The orders in granting interim relief in such case would not be in the interest of anybody. Moreover, any such reinstatement would not be in the interest of the Corporation or the public in general. I also deem it proper to notice that this Court comes across several instances of deaths on account of rash and negligent driving of the drivers of the Corporation. I want to remind the Corporation of its essential duty to provide efficient services in the light of laudable object of the Motor Vehicles Act. In view of frequent death cases reported, the Corporation should see that remedial action is taken in reducing the rising accident cases in the Interest of the general public.  Petition filed by the workman is rejected. Petition filed by the management is accepted. Dismissal is upheld. Ordered accordingly. No costs.  Order accordingly.
summary: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 11-A - Dismissal from services - The driver of Roadways caused an accident in which three passengers died and 41 others were injured due to rash and negligent driving, leading to the termination of his services after an enquiry. The Labour Court's pending proceedings granted reinstatement with a fine, but under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, the Labour Court should not have interfered. Therefore, the termination of services was upheld. [Paras 8, 9 and 10]

text: S.S. Sudhalkar, J. - The petitioner had joined military service on 9.2.1962 and he was discharged on compassionate ground on 3.7.1969. He joined civil service i.e. service as Physical Training Instructor on 23.7.1969 after being relieved from the military service. The petitioner has, in this petition, claimed benefit of said military service towards pension, seniority and increments in civil service.  2. Notice of motion was issued. Written statement has been filed.  3. The contention of the respondents is that the petitioner is not entitled to the benefit of military service because only those persons who are either recruited or discharged during the emergency are entitled to the said benefits. It may be mentioned that emergency was declared on 26.10.1962 and it was lifted on 12.1.1968.  4. The claim of the petitioner regarding grant of benefit of the military service towards seniority appeared to be belated and the petitioner was given an opportunity to explain so to why he should not be non-suited on the ground of laches alone. Learned counsel for the petitioner after seeking adjournments, conceded that he did not press for the benefit of military service towards seniority and prayed that his claim for the benefit of said service towards increments and pension be considered.  5. We have here learned counsel for the parties.  6. The question that remains to be considered is when the petitioner had joined military service before the declaration of the emergency whether he could be granted the benefit of military service. Learned counsel for the petitioner has relied on the judgment of this Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 10292 of 1989 (Moti Singh v. District and Sessions Division, Bhatinda and another), decided on 13.1.1992. In the said judgment, the learned Single Judge observed that the provision which defines the military service in the Punjab Government National Emergency (Concession) Rules, 1965 (hereinafter referred to as "the Rules") does not differentiate between a person who was enrolled or commissioned in the Indian army prior to the proclamation of emergency or thereafter. Rule 2 of the Rules defines military service as under :  "2. Definition :- For the purpose of these rules, the expression `military service' means the service rendered by a person who had been enrolled or commissioned during the period of operation of the proclamation of emergency made by the President under Article 352 of the Constitution of India on the 26th October, 1962, in any of the three wings of the Indian Armed Forces (including the service as Warrant Officer) during the period of the said emergency or such other service as may hereafter be declared as military service for the purpose of these rules. Any period of military training, followed by military service shall also be reckoned as military service." On reading the above rule, we agree with the observation of learned Single Judge. The petitioner remained commissioned in the Army during the period of emergency and there being no express bar to include those who joined prior to the proclamation of emergency in the military for the benefits of said service, we do not accept arguments of learned counsel for the respondents that the benefit of military service cannot be granted to the petitioner.  7. As a result, the petition is allowed and the respondents are directed to consider the period of military service rendered by the petitioner for the purpose of increments and pension. These directions be carried out within a period of three months from today. However, we direct that the arrears so calculated shall be confined to three years and two months prior to the date of filing of the present writ petition which was filed on 15.7.97.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Article 226 - Punjab Government National Emergency (Concession) Rules, 1965, Rule 2 - Benefit of Military service - A petitioner discharged on compassionate grounds from military service prior to emergency and then joined civil service - No explicit prohibition in Rule 2 for including military personnel who joined before the emergency for benefit of service - Therefore, benefit of military service allowed for increments and pension - However, delay and inaction on pressing for seniority benefit. [Paras 4, 6 and 7]

text: Nirmal Singh, J. - Petitioner-Saroj Bala has invoked jurisdiction of this Court under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution for the issuance of writ in the nature of mandamus directing the respondents to consider her case for regularisation on the basis of instructions issued by Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms (Personnel Policies Branch) dated 22.10.1982, Annexure P-3.  2. The brief facts of the case are as under :-  Petitioner was appointed as Clerk-cum-typist in the grade of Rs. 400-600/- on temporary basis initially for six months by the District Education Officer (Primary) Faridkot vide order dated 22.4.1980. Petitioner joined duty on 25.4.1981 (forenoon). Petitioner continued on the post till 16.2.1981 when she was transferred in Government Girls School, Baghapurana. She was adjusted against the vacant post of a clerk on the same terms and conditions. 3. Petitioner has claimed that on the basis of Instructions of Punjab Government dated 22.10.1982, her services may be regularised as she was fulfilling all the conditions of eligibility as mentioned in the Instructions Annexure P-3. It was, further, averred in the petition that the District Education Officer vide memo No. E-1-2(1)/82-83/61113-317 dated 24.11.1982 informed heads of all the Government Higher Secondary/ High Schools in Faridkot District that the Government has decided to regularise the ad hoc services of employees appointed to the posts under Punjab Government carrying an initial pay of not less than Rs. 325/- per mensem and not more than Rs. 699/- per mensem. The case of the petitioner duly recommended by District Education Officer, Faridkot was sent to the Govt. for consideration, but the office of Director, Public Instructions (Schools) Punjab, Chandigarh on 22.11.1983 wrote a memo to the District Education Officer that petitioner's case was not covered under the instructions. It was also directed that services of the petitioner be dispensed with.  4. The petitioner has prayed that the order passed by the Director, Public Instructions (Schools) Punjab dated 22.11.1983, Annexure P-5 be quashed and her services be regularised.  5. Respondents have filed written statement and admitted that petitioner was appointed purely on temporary basis with a clear indication that her services will be terminated without assigning any reasons. The services of petitioner were no more required, hence her services were terminated. It was also admitted that petitioner was appointed as clerk against the vacant post of Superintendent and not against the vacancy of clerk, for which requisition was sent to the Employment Exchange. Therefore, the case of the petitioner is not covered for regularisation under the Instructions Annexure P-3.  6. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record.  7. It is the admitted case of the parties that petitioner was appointed as clerk-cum-typist for six months in the grade of Rs. 400-600/-. As per terms and conditions of the appointment letter, her services can be dispensed with at any time without assigning any reason. It is also on record that petitioner was appointed against the vacant post of Superintendent on the same terms and conditions in Govt. High School, Baghapurana.  8. Mr. H.S. Gill, learned DAG submitted that the case of the petitioner is not covered by the Instructions dated 22.10.1982, as the petitioner was not appointed as Clerk and she was appointed against the vacancy of Superintendent.  9. I have considered the submission made by learned DAG, but his contention is devoid of merit. It is the case of the respondent that petitioner was appointed against the vacant post of Superintendent. As per the appointment letter, Annexure P-1 the petitioner was appointed as clerk-cum-typist. This appointment was against the post of Superintendent. If the petitioner has been appointed against the vacant post of Superintendent, it cannot be said that petitioner has not worked as clerk-cum-typist. The Punjab Government issued instructions dated 22.10.1982 regularising the services of the employees who have been appointed on ad hoc basis. The relevant portion of the Instructions is as under :-  (1) That the ad hoc employees should have completed a minimum of one year service on the date of issue of this order, while calculating the period of service, any break of notional nature falling (filling) of posts and in the same department may be ignored, in other words, the break in ad hoc service would not be ignored in cases where :- (a) The employees concerned left service on volition whether to join some other department or for some other reasons; (b) the ad hoc appointment was against a post/vacancy for which no regular recruitment was intended/required to be made e.g. leave arrangement or filling of other short term vacancies; (ii) That they fulfil the conditions of eligibility as prescribed (i.e. they have been recruited through the employment exchange or by open advertisement) academic qualifications experience and condition of age in accordance with the department service rules and instructions issued by the Government. (iii) That their record of service is satisfactory. (iv) That they have been found medically fit for entry into Govt. service and that their character and antecedents have also been so verified and found suitable for Govt. service.  (v) That a regular post/vacancy is available for regularisation; (vi) That they have been found fit for regularisation by the departmental selection committees to be constituted in accordance with the Instructions contained in Govt. Circular Letter No. 12/19/80-IGE/3582 dated 28.3.1980. These departmental selection committees shall also consider cases of common categories of employees; (vii) Inter se seniority of ad hoc employees will be determined on the basis of service rendered on ad hoc basis. The older member will be senior to the younger member appointed on the same date. All such ad hoc employees will be placed junior to those working on regular basis. 10. The case of the petitioner is fully covered by the Instructions issued by the Government of Punjab. It is no ground for State to say that the petitioner was appointed against the vacancy of a Superintendent.  11. During the course of arguments, Mr. V.K. Jindal pointed out that petitioner has been regularised by the respondents on the basis of the Instructions issued by the Government. Learned Deputy Advocate General Punjab has not denied this fact.  12. Even if the petitioner has been regularised subsequently, on the basis of the instructions issued by the Government, the petitioner cannot be denied of her right of regularisation on the basis of the instructions dated 22.10.1982 (Annexure P-3) when she was fulfilling all the conditions laid down in the said letter.  13. For the reasons recorded above, the writ petition is accepted and order Annexure P-5 is quashed. Petitioner is entitled to be regularised on the basis of instructions Annexure P-3. She is also held entitled to all the consequential benefits flowing therefrom.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 226/227 - Regularisation - Punjab Government's instructions dated 22.10.1982 to regularise ad hoc services of employees - Petitioner appointed as Clerk-cum-Typist on temporary basis under an order dated 22.4.1980 - Petitioner applied for regularisation under the aforementioned instructions - Request was denied as petitioner not covered under the instructions - Decision was made to discontinue her services - However, during arguments, petitioner's counsel pointed out that petitioner was regularised on the basis of the instructions - Court held that the petitioner was fully covered by the instructions issued by the Government of Punjab - She fulfilled all the conditions laid down in the instructions - Therefore, she is entitled to be regularised on the basis of the instructions dated 22.10.1982 and to all corresponding benefits. [Paras 10, 11, 12, and 13]

text: S.S. Nijjar, J. - We have heard learned counsel for the parties. The petitioner joined the service as a Handloom Export (Expert ?) in Punjab State Handloom Weavers Cooperative Society Limited in the year 1981. In 1990, in addition to his own duties, he was assigned the work of Production Centre, Processing House and Yarn Bank. On 31st August, 1998, he was transferred from Hoshiarpur to Shoddy Spinning Plant which was established at Humbra. The petitioner immediately joined on the transferred post. His place at Hoshiarpur was taken by another employee. On 4.7.2000, the petitioner was served with a charge- sheet for not handing over the complete charge of the Production Centre at Hoshiarpur. On the basis of the inquiry report submitted by the Enquiry Officer, he was removed from the service, by order of the Managing Director dated 9.1.2001. Against the order of removal, the petitioner filed a statutory appeal on 6.7.2001. The order of removal was set aside by the Appellate Authority with liberty to the punishing authority to impose minor penalty. Aggrieved against the aforesaid order, the employer-respondent No. 1 filed revision petition under Section 69 of the Punjab Cooperative Societies Act, 1961 before the Additional Secretary Cooperation (Appeals) Punjab exercising the powers of State Government. The revision petition has been accepted and the order passed by the Appellate Authority has been set aside by order dated 10.10.2002 (Annexure P3).  2. The petitioner has challenged the aforesaid order dated 10.10.2002 by filing the present writ petition under Articles 226/227 of Constitution of India.  3. The learned counsel for the petitioner has vehemently argued that the revision petition is not maintainable under Section 69 of the Act. According to the learned counsel, no revision petition is maintainable against an order passed by the appellate authority under the Service Rules of 1995 of the respondent No. 1 society. The impugned order dated 10.10.2002 (Annexure P-3) passed by the Revisional Authority is wholly without jurisdiction; and void ab initio. In support of his submissions, learned counsel has relied upon the Division Bench judgment of this Court in the case of Govt. Employees Co-op. House Building Society Ltd. v. Dy.
