In over-all facts and circumstances of this case, respondents are directed to pay interest @ 10% per annum on various amounts, referred to above from March 1, 1990, i.e. about three months after husband of the petitioner died, till the time payment on the aforesaid heads was actually made over to the petitioner. Parties are, however, left to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Article 226 - Retiral Benefits - Delay in payment - Interest - Petitioner's husband's post-retiral benefit was delayed without justifiable cause - Petitioner will receive interest at a rate of 10% per annum for the delayed payment - Respondents are instructed to pay the interest. [Para 3]"

text: G.B. Pattanaik, J. - The judgment and order dated 22nd December, 1992 of the Division Bench of Allahabad High Court is the subject matter of challenge in these appeals. By the said judgment the High Court directed the appellant- bank to appoint the respondents against the vacancies of Field Supervisors and prohibited the appellant from filling up the vacancies by making appointments to the post of Field Supervisors from outside the list prepared in May, 1984 in Civil Appeal Nos. 2650-55 of 1993. By the said common judgment the High Court also directed the appellant to appoint the respondent in Civil Appeal No. 2649 of 1993 as Probationary Officer.  2. The respondents filed writ petitions contending inter alia that an advertisement had been issued inviting applications for 35 posts of Probationary Officers (Branch Managers) and 35 posts of Field Supervisors on 18.7.1983. The respondents applied for one of the posts of Field Supervisor/Probationary Officer and appeared at the written test conducted by the appellant for selection. On being declared successful in the written test they were also called for interview and finally were included in the list of selected candidates and as such was eligible to be appointed as Field Supervisor/Probationary Officer. Subsequent to the said advertisement the appellant decided to increase the number of posts of Field Supervisors from 35 to 55 but notwithstanding the respondents' inclusion in the list of successful candidates only 26 Field Supervisors and 36 Probationary Officers were appointed. The life of the panel of successful candidates which was to remain operative for one year was extended for a period of six months by the Board of the bank in its meeting dated 28.3.1985. But yet the respondents could not be appointed and on account of disgruntlement amongst the respondents there was an agitation and ultimately an agreement was reached between the officers of the bank and the members of the union and the bank agreed to further extend the life of the panel until all persons included in the list are absorbed. This agreement was reached on 16.10.1985. But in spite of the aforesaid agreement no appointments having been made, they approached the High Court for necessary direction.  3. The bank in its counter-affidavit denied its liability to appoint all the persons who were in the panel as Field Supervisors or Probationary Officers. The further stand of the bank was that inclusion of a candidate's name in the panel does not confer an indefeasible right to be enforced by way of issuing a writ of mandamus. The bank also took the stand that in accordance with the resolution of the Finance Ministry conveyed to all banks the life of a panel lapses after one year, and therefore, respondents cannot claim any right to be appointed as Field Supervisors or Probationary Officers. Supplementary affidavits were also field on behalf of the bank indicating therein that no posts are available, and therefore, question of appointment of respondents does not arise.  4. The High Court by the impugned judgment came to the conclusion that it cannot be believed that there is no vacancy in the bank to the post of Field Supervisor. The High Court also relying upon a notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms came to the conclusion that list prepared does not got exhausted after expiry of one year and it remains valid till all the candidates mentioned in the list are appointed. According to the High Court the bank has an obligation to appoint candidates against the declared vacancies and that claim cannot be resisted. With these conclusions the High Court directed the bank-appellant to appoint the respondents as Field Supervisor/Field Officer and hence the present appeal.  5. Mr. Mehta, the learned counsel appearing for the appellant contended that an applicant has no indefeasible right to be appointed even if he is selected and included in the merit list and even if a vacancy exists in the post for which the application had been made. But in the case in hand there did not exist any vacancy, and therefore, the High Court committed serious error in issuing the impugned direction to appoint the respondents against the post of Field Supervisor. Mr. Mehta further submitted that the life of the panel which was drawn on 2.5.1984 expired on 2.5.1985. By virtue of the decision of the Board the said life has been extended for six months and again by virtue of the agreement between the parties dated 13.10.1985 it stood further extended by six months and panel expired on 30.4.1986. In this view of the matter no direction could have been given by the High Court to issue appointment letters to the respondents by its judgment dated 22nd December, 1992. Mr. Mehta also urged that the High Court committed serious error in relying upon the notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms on the question of the period for which a panel would remain alive inasmuch as the said circular of the Home Department has no binding effect so far as the appellant bank is concerned and on the other hand it is a circular of the Finance Ministry which is binding and under which the life of a panel remains valid for a period of one year from its preparation. The learned counsel also submitted that the conclusion of the High Court that vacancy exists is erroneous and in arriving at that conclusion the High Court relied upon the decision of the bank to open more branches and consequential creation of vacancies but in fact no such branch has been opened and no vacancy exists. Mr. Mehta lastly submitted that under the constitutional scheme engrafted under Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution a court can at the most direct consideration of the case of an applicant if it finds that he has been denied of such consideration but the court cannot direct appointment of an applicant against any post.  6. Mr. Rakesh Dwivedi, the learned senior counsel appearing for the respondents did not dispute the legal proposition that mere inclusion in the list of successful candidates does not confer an indefeasible right to be appointed. He, however, contended that the employer while filling up of the vacancies for which advertisement had been issued has to act bona fide and not arbitrarily and in the case in hand the High Court has granted the relief after coming to the conclusion that there exist vacancies in the cadre and no justifiable reason had been advanced for not filling up those vacancies and in such a situation the court would be amply justified in issuing mandamus to the employer to consider a case of appointment of the applicant who after undertaking the test got themselves selected and are waiting for appointment. On the basis of assertion made by the appellant in the special leave petition filed in this court to the effect "by 31.12.1985 19 more branches were opened" Mr. Dwivedi submitted that the High Court was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that there exist vacancies and non-filling up of those vacancies has rightly been held to be arbitrary. Mr. Dwivedi, the learned senior counsel further submitted that the bank not having controverted the contention that out of the Field Supervisors who had been appointed, six of them resigned, even though the court specifically directed to give reply, the conclusion that there exist vacancies in the cadre of Field Supervisors is unassailable and as such the right of the respondents to be appointed against those vacancies cannot be arbitrarily taken away. The learned counsel ultimately submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case in hand there is no infirmity in the judgment of the High Court requiring interference by this Court.  7. In view of rival submissions at the Bar the following questions arise for our consideration :  (I) Is the High Court justified in arriving at the conclusion that there exist vacancies in the post of Field Supervisors in the bank ? (II) Does inclusion of name in the list of selected candidates confer any right to be appointed which could be enforced by issuance of a writ of mandamus ? (III) What is the period for which a list of successful candidates remains alive and after expiry of its life can the court direct appointments to be made from the said list ? (IV) Did the agreement dated 13.10.1985 contain any stipulation that the list of successful candidates would remain alive until those in the list are appointed in the bank ? 8. Coming to the first question it transpires that the appellant bank opened only two branches in the rural area in the year 1982. For extending its banks, it had applied to the Reserve Bank of India for 30 new licenses for opening of new branches. Calculating the number of officers which may be necessary to man these new branches, advertisement had been issued on 18.7.1983 inviting applications for 35 posts of Probationary Officers and 35 posts of Field Supervisors. The appellant then applied to the Reserve Bank for licenses to open 27 more branches in the year 1983 and during 1984 and 1985 similar applications had been made for licenses to open 20 branches in 1984 and 17 branches in the year 1985. In anticipation of grant of licenses by the Reserve Bank of India and consequential opening of branches in different rural areas the appellant had taken the decision to increase the number of posts of Probationary Officers as well as Field Supervisors. But as against 94 applications for licenses for opening new branches in fact only 46 branches had been opened and there could not be expansion of business activity by opening new branches because of the revised licensing policy of the Reserve Bank of India issued in October, 1985. The appellant had categorically asserted before the High Court that there exist no vacancy in the cadre of Field Supervisor or Probationary Officer and in view of such assertion it was for the respondents who claim the right of being appointed to establish that in fact vacancies exist. But we do not find any reliable materials produced by the respondents from which a conclusion could be arrived at that there exist vacancies in the bank. The High Court, however, entered into the arena of calculation basing upon the principle that there should be appointment of one Field Officer for 500 accounts as was decided by the Board in its resolution and taking into account the 46 branches which the bank had the number of vacancies in the post of Field Supervisors must be much more than 55 and only 26 Field Supervisors had been appointed pursuant to the advertisement dated 18.7.1983. This process of conclusion in our considered opinion is wholly erroneous and is not permissible for a court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution. As has been stated earlier the process of selection to different posts in the bank being made in anticipation of opening of new branches and the requirement of officers for new branches. But that does not mean that at the material point of time in fact any vacancy exists and at any rate no materials having been produced by the respondents, the court could not have come to the conclusion that vacancies exist. It is in this connection, it would also be appropriate to notice that whether six of the Field Supervisors appointed resigned and thus consequential vacancies were available. We have carefully scrutinised the averments made in the writ petitions filed by the respondents in the High Court as well as the rejoinder affidavit filed in the said court and we do not find any assertion has been made in that regard. From the impugned judgment, however, it appears that in course of argument a contention in that regard had been advanced by the respondents and the bank had been called upon to give its reply but no positive reply had been filed the High Court jumped to the conclusion that in fact six persons resigned and consequential vacancies were there. We, however, are unable to sustain this line of reasoning of the High Court. The writ petitioners not having made any averments alleging resigning of six of the Field Supervisors after being appointed the bank had no obligation to give any reply. In course of hearing if a contention had been raised and supporting material is produced then the bank might have been obliged to file the specific reply but no such materials appears to have been produced by the writ petitioners before the High Court and in such context absence of reply by the bank does not ipso facto establishes the contention raised. It is too well settled that the petitioner who approaches the court invoking the extra-ordinary jurisdiction of the Court under Article 226 must fully aver and establish his rights flowing from the bundle of facts thereby requiring respondent to indicate its stand either by denial or by positive assertions. But in the absence of any averments in the writ petition or even in the rejoinder affidavit it is not permissible for a court to arrive at a conclusion on a factual position merely on the basis of submissions made in course of hearing. The High Court, therefore, in our view committed serious error in coming to the conclusion that there existed vacancies in the post of Field Supervisor on the materials produced before it. In fact the respondents herein who were the petitioners in the High Court had not produced any material in support of their stand that vacancies existed and yet appointments have not been made. We are of the considered opinion that conclusion of the High Court that there existed vacancies is unsustainable in law and is accordingly set aside.  9. Coming to the second question, it requires no detailed scrutiny and it is well established that inclusion of name in the list of successful candidates does not confer an indefeasible right to be appointed. It has been so held in the Constitution Bench decision of this Court of the case of Shankarsan Das v. Union of India, 1991(3) SCC 47 : 1991(2) SCT 555 (SC). In the said case the court has gone to the extent of following:  "It is not correct to say that if a number of vacancies are notified for appointment and adequate number of candidates are found fit, the successful candidates acquire an indefeasible right to be appointed which cannot be legitimately denied. Ordinarily the notification merely amounts to an invitation to qualified candidates to apply for recruitment and on their selection they do not acquire any right to the post. Unless the relevant recruitment rules so indicate, the State is under no legal duty to fill up all or any of the vacancies." 10. Mr. Dwivedi, the learned senior counsel for the respondents also did not join issue on this principle of law. He, however, had raised the issue on the question that there was no justifiable reason for not appointing respondents in the vacancies which still exist and consequentially the action of the appellant must be held to be arbitrary. But this submission is devoid of any force in view of our conclusion on the first question that there did not exist any vacancy in the post of Field Supervisor or Probationary Officer. In this view of the matter, neither any right accrued to the respondents on being included in the list of successful candidates nor their non-appointment can be held to be arbitrary or discriminatory.  11. So far as the third question is concerned, namely, for how long a panel prepared should be kept alive, it appears that the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs (Banking Division) by its letter dated 30th September, 1980 had communicated to the Chairman of all regional rural banks that the panel should normally be kept alive only for a period of one year and if any deviation from the said guidelines becomes necessary in the interest of the bank then it should be undertaken with the prior permission of the Board of Directors and under intimation to the Government in the Banking Division. Notwithstanding the aforesaid guidelines issued as it was observed that several rural banks still took recourse to extending the validity of the panel for long periods stretching over the 2/3 years on obtaining the approval of the Board, the Ministry of Finance by its letter dated 19th September, 1983 again communicated to the Chairmen of all regional rural banks that preparation of panels to cover the requirements of regional rural banks for 2/3 years and then extend the validity of the panel beyond one year cannot be construed as merely a deviation and it is doubtful if it can be considered even as being in the interest of the regional rural banks from long term point of view. Under Section 24 of the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976, a rural bank in the discharge of its functions is required to be guided by such directions as the Central Government may after consultation with the Reserve Bank give in regard to matters of policy involving public interest. In view of the aforesaid provisions of the Act, the directions/guidelines issued by the Central Government indicating the periods for which the life of a panel would kept alive has a binding effect on the bank, and therefore, in our considered opinion so far as the life of the panel prepared by the rural banks are concerned it must be held that same remain alive ordinarily for a period of one year. The High Court committed serious error in relying upon the circular of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms to come to the conclusion that the panel remains alive until all the persons in the panel are appointed. The said conclusion is wholly erroneous and cannot be sustained.  12. Though the panel ordinarily remains alive for one year but in accordance with the guidelines of the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, it would be open to Board to extend the said period under intimation to the Government in the Banking Division. In the case in hand the resolution of the Board dated 28.3.1985 indicates that the life of the panel had been extended by a further period of six months, and therefore, after expiry of the said period it was not open for the court to issue direction to appoint people from the said panel.  13. Coming to the next question the answer to the same depends upon the terms and conditions of the agreement between the parties dated 16.10.1985. The minutes of discussion as recorded no doubt indicates that some members of the Board did express their view that the life of the panel should be extended till the last candidate is absorbed by the bank as it is the moral and legal responsibility of the bank. It further appears that it was decided to have the concerted efforts for obtaining licenses for opening new branches but the very agreement between the parties was to the effect that list of successful candidates for the appointment of Field Supervisors and Probationary Officer declared on 2.5.1984 will be valid for a further period of six months after 31.10.1985 and that the management of the bank will appoint as far as possible the remaining selected candidates in the aforesaid list as soon as possible. This being the terms of agreement the conclusion is inescapable that such agreement did not confer a right on the respondents to be appointed to the posts of Field Supervisors/Probationary Officers and the court would not be justified to make it enforceable by issuing a writ of mandamus. The High Court, therefore, in our considered opinion, committed serious error of law in issuing the impugned directions calling upon the appellant to appoint the respondents to the posts of Field Supervisor/Probationary Officer.  14. In the premises aforesaid, the impugned judgment dated 22.12.1992 of the High Court is set aside and these appeals are allowed, the writ petitions filed by the respondents stand dismissed, however, there will be no order as to costs.  Appeals allowed.
summary: A. The respondent, who was successful in the written test and interview for the post of Field Supervisor in a bank, approached the court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. However, the respondent failed to produce any material evidence that a vacancy existed, which was a requirement to establish his rights, as the court cannot arrive at a conclusion on factual positions based solely on submissions made during the hearing without any supporting evidence. The High Court was erroneous in concluding that there existed vacancies based on the material produced before it. [Para 8] B. Inclusion of a candidate's name in the list of successful candidates does not guarantee an indefinite right to be appointed. [Para 9] C. The life of the panel of successful candidates, such as in the case of the respondent for the post of Field Supervisor in a bank, is usually valid for one year. However, it's within the board's power to extend this period, under intimation to the Government in Bank Division, which it did for the respondent's panel. Still, respondent could not be appointed, as it was not mandatory for all candidates on the panel to be appointed. The High Court was incorrect in issuing a directive to the bank to appoint people from the expired panel. [Paras 11 and 12]

text: S.S. Nijjar, J. (Oral) - This order shall dispose of four writ petitions i.e. C.W.P. Nos. 834 of 2003, 4106 of 2003, 8408 of 2003 and 18455 of 2002. For facility of reference, facts as pleaded in Civil Writ Petition No. 834 of 2003 shall be referred to.  2. Respondent No. 2 Wazir Singh had been employed in the petitioner-Guru Jambheshwar University, Hisar on daily wages as a Chowkidar/Security Guard w.e.f. 21.12.1995 through verbal order on his request. This appointment was, however, subsequently terminated when it came to the notice of petitioner that Haryana Government had banned the appointment on daily wages. Respondent No. 2 was subsequently appointed on contract basis for 60 days from 2.7.1997 to 30.8.1997 through appointment letter No. EN-11197/29130 dated 21.7.1997. Even this appointment of respondent No. 2 was a back door entry as the vacancy was never published in any newspaper nor he was employed through the Employment Exchange. In the meantime, the petitioner advertised the vacancies for all the posts of Security Guard for regular appointment. Respondent No. 2 applied for the post of Security Guard. He was not selected for regular appointment. The regularly selected candidates joined the service. The services of respondent No. 2 were terminated on the basis of the condition that he is appointed for a fixed period of 60 days or till regular selection is made by the petitioner. Consequently, on 29.8.1997, the term of appointment of respondent No. 2 ended by efflux of time. Not satisfied, the respondent No. 2 filed a demand notice on 6.9.1997 on the basis of which the appropriate Government by letter dated 15.6.1999 referred the industrial dispute to the Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal-cumn-Labour Court, Hisar. Respondent No. 1 under Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (for short, "the Act"). The Labour Court framed the following issues :-  1) Whether the termination of services of Wazir Singh is justified and in order ? If not, along with reinstatement, to what amount of back wages, he is entitled to ? 2) Whether the respondent is guilty of unfair labour practice, as alleged ? 3) Whether the petitioner was engaged on contract basis and termination falls u/s 2(oo) (bb) of I.D. Act ? 4) Whether the respondent is not 'industry' ? 5) Whether this Court has no jurisdiction ? 6) Whether the petitioner has no locus-standi, as alleged ? 7) Relief." 3. After the parties led their evidence, the Labour Court has come to the conclusion that since the workman had completed 240 days, his services could not have been terminated without complying with the provisions of Section 25-F of the Act. It has also been held that merely because the respondent No. 2 had accepted the unreasonable conditions contained in the appointment letter would not dis-entitle the workman from claiming the relief under the Act. In coming to the aforesaid conclusion, the Labour Court relied on the Division Bench judgment of this Court in Bhikhu Ram v. The Presiding Officer, Labour Court- cum-Industrial Tribunal, Rohtak, 1998(1) RSJ 703 and held that the petitioner-University had indulged in "unfair labour practice". The Labour Court has also relied on the judgment delivered in the case of The State of Punjab and others v. Yash Pal and another, 2000(2) SCT 882 (P&H) : 2000(3) RSJ 1 to hold that it was for the petitioner to prove that respondent No. 2 could not be granted any relief as the matter was squarely covered under Section 2(oo)(bb).  4. Learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that the petitioner is a newly set-up University. At the initial stage some adhoc/temporary appointments had been made. Respondent No. 2 was one of those employees, who had been appointed on contract basis. His services had, therefore, come to an end by the efflux of time and no relief could have been granted to him under the Act. He further submitted that services of a large number of employees, who were similarly situated as respondent No. 2, had been terminated by the petitioner. In each case, an industrial dispute was raised and the workman had been ordered to be reinstated by the Labour Court. Therefore, the petitioner had filed a large number of writ petitions challenging the individual awards. These were 21 writ petitions. A Division Bench of this Court, by an order dated April 1, 2003 has allowed the writ petitions and the impugned award(s) of the Labour Court have been set-aside. The main judgment has been delivered in Civil Writ Petition No. 180 of 2003, Guru Jambheshwar University, Hissar v. Sat Pal Singh and another, 2003(3) S.C.T. 857.  5. In Sat Pal's case (supra), the Division Bench of this Court was dealing with writ petitions filed in identical cases. In those cases, it has been held as under :-  " We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and perused the record of the writ petition and are of the view that the impugned award cannot be sustained. As is clear from the facts noticed above, the workman had been engaged on daily wages and thereafter on contractual basis pending regular selection to the post of a Clerk. He participated in the regular selection but failed to qualify even in the typing test. He was, therefore, not selected. When the regularly selected persons were appointed the services of the workman were terminated. We are clearly of the view that such a termination was in accordance with the terms contained in the letter of appointment. Such a termination falls within exception contained in Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Act and, therefore, it did not amount to 'retrenchment' within the meaning of the Act. In this view of the matter, the Labour Court grossly erred in law in holding that the termination amounted to retrenchment and that the provisions of Section 25-F of the Act had to be complied with. As already observed, the termination of the services of the workman was in terms of the stipulation contained in the letter of appointment and, therefore, it was outside the ambit of retrenchment. This being so, there was no question of complying with the provisions of Section 25-F of the Act. The findings recorded by the Labour Court are contrary to the plain language of Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Act and cannot, therefore, be sustained." These observations are fully applicable to the facts of the present writ petitions.  6. It is a matter of record that the appointment of respondent No. 2 was without following any known procedure for selection and appointment. He had obviously been given appointment for a fixed period till the regular selections car be made. The appointment order clearly speaks as under  "Sub : Contractual Appointment. The Vice-Chancellor is pleased to engage you as Security Guard on contract basis for a period of 60 days w.e.f. 2.7.97 upto 30.8.97 on the rates approved by the Deputy Commissioner. This engagement shall not entitle you to claim regularisation of service or regular pay scale. Further, it is made categorically clear that in case of vacancy having been filled up by normal procedure before the expiry of period of above contract, you shall cease to be in position forthwith." The aforesaid condition makes it abundantly clear that the appointment was on contract basis. It was also only made till the vacancies are filled up on regular basis. The appointment itself being contractual in nature was liable to come to an end by the efflux of time or on appointment of candidates on regular basis.  In such circumstances, we are unable to accept the submission made on behalf of respondent No. 2/workman that the termination of service was in violation of Section 25F of the Act. In view of the provisions of Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Act, the protection of Section 25-F would not be available to respondent No. 2.  In view of the above, these petitions are allowed. The impugned awards of the Labour Court are set-aside and the orders passed by the petitioner-University terminating the services of the workmen are upheld. There shall be no order as to costs.  Petitions allowed.
summary: According to the provisions of Section 2(oo)(bb) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a workman appointed on a contract basis until regular vacancies are filled is liable to have their contract come to an end when a regular candidate is appointed. In such a case, the protection of Section 25-F would not be available to the workman. Therefore, the labour court's award was set aside and the respondent- university's order terminating the services of the workman was upheld. [Para 6]

text: R.L. Anand, J. - Smt. Krishna Johar, petitioner, has filed the present writ petition under Article 226/227 of the Constitution of India against the respondents and it has been prayed by her that the order Annexure P-3 be quashed and directions be issued to the respondents to treat her as continuing Head Accountant with all consequential benefits.  2. The case set up by the petitioner is that she was duly selected and appointed as Clerk under the respondents and joined her duties on 28.8.1968. On account of her good performance she earned promotion as Junior Auditor w.e.f. 16.2.1976 on seniority-cum-merit basis. Her performance as Clerk as well as Junior Auditor was to the best of the satisfaction of her superiors. Her services are being governed by Haryana Khadi and Village Industries Board (Services) Regulations, 1976. She was selected and promoted as Head Accountant vide order dated 12.4.1993 on the basis of seniority-cum-merit. She took over as Head Accountant on 15.4.1993. Her entire record was unblemished and she was never found wanting in the performance of her duties. She was placed on probation for a period of one year. Nothing adverse was conveyed to her. After the completion of prescribed probation period she could not be subjected to any further period of probation. After the completion of probation period of one year on 14.4.1994 again she was put on probation period vide order dated 10.3.1995. Since there was a tussle going on regarding seniority and promotion etc, she was harassed in various ways. On 17.2.1995 adverse remarks were conveyed to her for the year 1993-94. She made a representation and refuted the observations. On 10.7.1996, she was issued show cause notice vide which it was decided to revert her to the post of Junior Auditor after her having worked in the capacity of Head Accountant for over three years. She duly gave the reply to the show cause notice, but respondent No. 4 passed the order reverting her without going into the facts and circumstances of the case and brushing aside the settled law on the point. The petitioner alleged that she has already completed one year of the probation on 14.4.1994 and her probation period could not be extended. The ACR which was conveyed to her after a long period has no significance and the entire action of the respondents is illegal, unfair, mala fide, unjust and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The order of the reversion of the petitioner was passed by respondent No. 4 in order to accommodate a person of his convenience in place of the petitioner. With these broad allegations, the petitioner has filed the present writ petition.  3. Notice of the writ petition was given to the respondents, who filed a joint written statement and denied the allegations. According to them, the petitioner was promoted as Head Accountant on 12.4.19943. She joined on 15.4.1993. She was put on probation and it was extended from time to time. She was on probation for a total period of three years. Adverse remarks were conveyed to her. She did not improve her work and in accordance with the provisions of the Regulations she was reverted from the post of Head Accountant to the post of Junior Auditor. According to the Regulations, if the probation period is not satisfactory, an official can be reverted to the post from which one was promoted. The probation period of the petitioner was extended for one year i.e. from 15.4.1994 to 14.4.1995 vide order dated 10.3.1995 and it was further extended for six months from 15.4.1995 to 15.10.1995. Further it was extended for six months from 15.10.1995 to 14.4.1996 vide order dated 26.10.1995. In the year 1993-94 the petitioner was given a warning. She committed serious mistakes in income tax deduction at source. She was graded below average for the year 1993-94. Against these remarks, representation was received which was filed being time barred. In the year 1994-95 the petitioner was given a warning and she was adjudged below average. She did not make any representation against these remarks. Again on 28.11.1995, she was conveyed adverse remarks for the first six months of the year 1995-96. The remarks were "below average - not fit for promotion - careless in work - does not try to improve - does not know the job of an Accountant even". No representation was made. She was asked to do the work of Ram Chander, Accountant, who went on leave. The petitioner refused to do the work saying that it is a complicated job. Later on, the work was given to one Mr. Sohan Lal, Clerk, who did the same. In short, the stand taken up by the respondents is that the work and conduct of the petitioner was not satisfactory. She was given various warnings etc. As the work of the petitioner was not found satisfactory against the post of Head Accountant, therefore, she was reverted to the post of Junior Auditor.  4. I have heard Mr. Rameshwar Sharma, Advocate on behalf of the petitioner, Mr. K.L. Arora, Advocate on behalf of the respondents and with their assistance have gone through the record of the case.  5. It is the common case of the parties that the services of the petitioner were governed by Haryana Khadi and Village Industries Board (Services) Regulations, 1976. Regulation 9 reads as under :-  "9. Condition of service :- (1) Probation of Members of Service :- Persons appointed to any post shall remain on probation for a period of two years, if recruited by direct appointment and one year, if recruited, otherwise, provided that :- (a) any period, after such appointment, spent on deputation on a corresponding or a higher post shall count towards the period of probation. (b) In the case of an appointment by transfer, any period of work in equivalent or higher rank, prior to appointment to the service may, in the discretion of the appointing authority, be allowed to count towards the period of probation; and (c) any probation of officiating appointment to a service shall be reckoned as period spent on probation, but no person who has so officiated, shall on the completion of prescribed period of probation, be entitled to be confirmed, unless he be appointed against a permanent vacancy. (2) If in the opinion of the appointing authority, the work or conduct of a person during the period of probation is not satisfactory, it may :- (a) if such person is recruited by direct appointment, dispense with his services; and (b) if such person is recruited otherwise :- (i) revert him to his former post; or (ii) deal with him in such other manner as the terms and conditions of the previous appointment permit; (3) On the completion of the period of probation of a person, the appointing authority may :- (a) if his work or conduct, in his opinion, has been satisfactory - (i) declare that he has completed his probation satisfactorily; (ii) if his work or conduct has not been in its opinion satisfactory :- (i) dispense with his service, if recruited by direct appointment or if recruited otherwise revert him to his former post, or deal with him in such other manner, as the terms and conditions of his previous appointment permit; or (ii) extend his period of probation, and thereafter, pass such orders as it could have passed on the expiry of the first period of probation :- Provided that the total period of probation including extension, if any, shall not exceed three years." 6. A reading of the above would show that a person appointed to any post shall remain on probation for a period of two years, if recruited by direct appointment and one year, if recruited, otherwise. Clause (2) of regulation 9 (supra) lays down that if in the opinion of the appointing authority, the work and conduct of a person during the period of probation is not satisfactory and if such person is recruited by direct appointment, his services can be dispensed with and if the employee is promoted he can be reverted to his former post. The proviso to clause (3) of Regulation 9 further lays down that the total period of probation including extension, if any, shall not exceed three years. It is also the case of the parties that the petitioner was promoted to the post of Head Accountant on 12.4.1993. Further, the case of the respondents is that since the work and conduct of the petitioner was not found satisfactory, therefore, her probation period was extended from time to time and last extension which could be granted to the petitioner ought to be 12.4.1996. So far as the position of law is concerned, it is very clear. The authorities are supposed to take the decision either before the date of expiry of the last date of the probation period or within a reasonable time as to whether the employee who has been promoted should be allowed to continue with the post or he/she should be reverted to the former post. If the decision is not taken within three years from the date of the promotion, the intention of the law is further that in the event of non-passing of any order by the authorities, such employee shall be deemed to have cleared the probation making a way for his confirmation. In the present case the action was taken by the respondent authorities against the petitioner on 10.7.1996 when it issued a show cause notice. There is nothing on the record to suggest that the petitioner was informed that her period of probation is not going to be extended beyond 12.4.1996. The show cause notice which was issued on 10.7.1996 has also not been issued within a reasonable time after 12.4.1996.  7. Faced with this difficulty, the learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the respondents are an insignificant office and the establishment's people are not familiar with the intricacies of law. The file was processed somewhere in the month of May 1996 and some delay could always occur in the issuance of show cause notice. Therefore, if the respondent authorities had issued the notice on 10.7.1996, it should not be considered fatal. I am not convinced with the submissions raised by the learned counsel for the respondents. We are dealing a case of statutory provisions. According to the Regulations, the period of probation could not be extended beyond three years. Meaning thereby, it was obligatory on the part of the Board to take a decision immediately before the expiry of the last date of probation or just after the expiry of the probation period. In the present case the notice was issued somewhere in the month of July, 1996. In such a situation some guidance has also been given to the law courts by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and another v. S. Manjunath, 2000(2) SCT 810, where it was observed that if there is an implicit term in the scheme of Regulation governing the service that on the expiry of the period of probation beyond the maximum term provided therein, an employee will be deemed to have been confirmed, inasmuch as the Corporation cannot terminate his service on the expiry of such period. In this regard it will be useful for me to reproduce para 5 of the judgment as under :-  "5. All the three writ petitions were initially heard by a learned Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court and by a common order dated 3.11.95 those writ petitions were allowed on the view that there was an implicit term in the scheme of Regulation governing their services that on the expiry of the period of probation beyond the maximum term provided therein, an employee will be deemed to have been confirmed inasmuch as the Corporation cannot terminate their services on the expiry of such period. In coming to such a conclusion, the learned Single Judge followed an earlier decision of Division Bench dated 5.2.82 in writ Appeal No. 100/91 (M. Balachandra Rao v. KSRTC and another). The Corporation, aggrieved by such orders, pursued the matter in Appeal before a Division Bench in Writ Appeal No. 36-38/96. The Division Bench adverted to the decisions of this Court reported in State of Punjab v. Dharam Singh, AIR 1968 SC 1210; Paramjit Singh v. Ram Rakha, 1979(3) SCC 478 and M.K. Agarwal v. Gurgaon Gramin Bank, AIR 1988 SC 286 and observed that the position in the appeals is no different from the one dealt with in those decisions of this Court and consequently confirmed the order of the learned Single Judge. Hence, the above appeals." 8. Further, this High Court in N.K. Dutta v. Punjab State Coop. Supply and Marketing Federation Ltd., 1994(4) SCT 625 (P&H) : 1995(1) RSJ 777 held in the contest of the Staff Regulations that once the period of probation came to an end, the petitioner will have to be treated as confirmed by operation of rules. It was observed by his Lordship that "Moreover in view of the judgments of the Supreme Court, once the period of probation came to an end, the petitioner will have to be treated as confirmed by operation of rules." No law to the contrary has been cited by the learned counsel for the respondents.  In this view of the matter, the writ petition is allowed, the order Annexure P-3 is hereby quashed and a writ of mandamus is issued to the respondents to treat the petitioner as continuing Head Accountant with all the consequential benefits. There shall be no order as to costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16, 226, 227 - Haryana Khadi and Village Industries Board (Services) Regulation 1976, Regulations 9(2) and 9(3) - Reversion - Probation - Deemed Completion - Petitioner returned to post of Junior Auditor from Head Accountant - Petitioner argues that reversion order is invalid as probation period is completed - Respondents argue that reversion is allowed per Regulation 9 if probation was not satisfactory - Maximum probation period is three years per Regulation 9 Clause (3) - Decision had to be made before probation period ended - Therefore, employee is deemed confirmed - Petition allowed. [Paras 7 and 8]

text: R.S. Mongia, J. - Shri S.K. Maini, Respondent No. 2, was an employee of M/s Carona Sahu Co. Ltd. (Petitioner) (in short C.S.C.) and was working as a Shop Manager of the shop known as Carona Shop Store, Near Nehru Gardens, Jalandhar City, since the year 1970. According to the petitioner, the said respondent had committed serious misconduct in the year 1980. On the basis of the said misconduct, he was charge-sheeted on 11th November, 1980. Prior to the issuance of the charge-sheet, Respondent No. 2 had been placed under suspension. After considering the reply of Respondent No. 2, a regular departmental enquiry was ordered against him and one Shri lqbal Singh, Advocate, was appointed as an Enquiry Officer. After allowing both the sides to lead evidence, and giving them opportunity of being heard, the Enquiry Officer gave the report against Respondent No. 2. On the basis of the said enquiry report, the services of Respondent No. 2 were terminated, which was challenged by him by raising an industrial dispute before the Labour Court at Jalandhar. The primary ground for challenging the termination order was that the enquiry held by the C.S.C was not fair and proper and it was just a farce, and the name was violative of the principles of natural justice. The plea of the C.S.C. before the Labour Court was that the enquiry was fair and proper and no fault could be found in the termination order. By way of preliminary objections, it was stated that the reference was bad in law as the petitioner-Management was registered under the Punjab Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 1958, and the said Act has over-riding effect over the Industrial Disputes Act. Secondly, it was pleaded that Respondent No. 2 was working on the post of Manager, and, therefore, not covered under the definition of `workman' as given (in Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as the Act).  2. The learned Labour Court, Jalandhar, vide its award dated 21st April, 1986, held that Respondent No. 2 was a workman as defined in the Act and that the domestic enquiry held against Respondent No. 2 was neither fair nor proper. Consequently, the order of termination was set aside and it was ordered that Respondent No. 2 would be reinstated into service with full back wages. The C.S.C. challenged the said award by way of the present writ petition. The Motion Bench had stayed the reinstatement of Respondent No. 2 subject to the provisions of Section 17-B of the Act.  3. The learned counsel for the petitioner raised the following points to assail the award of the Labour Court :-  (1) That Respondent No. 2 is not a workman as defined under Section 2(s) of the Act.  (2) The enquiry conducted by the Management was fair and proper and the same could not be held to be vitiated on the ground that the Enquiry Officer was a person, who was the standing Counsel of the Management, or that Respondent No. 2 was not allowed to engage a lawyer.  (3) The Labour Court went wrong in not affording opportunity to the petitioner to lead evidence and prove the charge against Respondent No. 2 after the Labour Court had come to the conclusion that enquiry was not fair and proper.  4. Point No. 1.  To find out whether Respondent No. 2, who was working as a Shop Manager, can be said to be a workman or not, it would be appropriate to notice the definition of `workman' as given in Section 2(s) of the Act, as it existed at the relevant time :-  "Workman' means any person (including an apprentice.), employed in any industry to do any skilled or unskilled, manual, supervisory, technical or clerical work for hire or reward, whether the terms of employment be express nor implied, and for purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, or retrenched in connection with or as a consequence, of the dispute, or whose dismissal, discharges or retrenchment has led to that dispute, but does not include any such person :  (i) who subject to the Army Act, 1950 (XLVI of 1950) or the Air Force Act, 1950 (XLV of 1950, or the Navy (Discipline) Act, 1934 (XXXIV of 1934) or;  (ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prisoner; or;  (iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or;  (iv) who is being employed in a supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding five hundred rupees per mensem or exercises, either by the nature, of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature."  5. There is a catena of authorities that mere nomenclature or designation of the post would not determine as to whether particular individual is a workman or not under the Act. It will depend on the dominant nature of duties performed by the individual and not the ancillary duties as to whether the individual is a workman under the Act or not. There is no dispute between the parties on this proposition of law, and, therefore, no authority need be referred to. It is further not disputed that at the time of termination of services of Respondent No. 2, he was drawing wages exceeding Rs. 500/- per mensem. The argument of the learned counsel for the petitioner proceeded that Respondent No. 2 was employed mainly in a managerial and administrative capacity and was also discharging duties and functions mainly of administrative, managerial and supervisory nature, and, therefore, under exceptions (iii) and (iv) to Section 2(s) Respondent No. 2 could not be said to be a workman. However, the case of Respondent No. 2 was that he was employed mainly to do clerical work and a fraction of his duties may be managerial or supervisory but those were incidental or ancillary to the main clerical duties.  6. It would be necessary to know as to what were the duties which were to be performed by the Manager of the shop. While dealing with this point, the Labour Court has referred to the evidence produced before it. Shri Ramesh Chander Sethi, a Shop Manager of C.S.C. had appeared as a witness of the Management and had also produced his affidavit (Ex. M/1 before the Labour Court). The contents of the affidavit were testified by him while appearing as MW-1 It has been stated in the affidavit that Shri S. K. Maini's main duties were of managerial nature. He was managing the entire affairs of the store and the store-cum-shop was under his independent managerial charge. He was empowered to employ Helpers and Salesmen for the store-cum-shop temporarily and on his recommendation, the Head Office used to confirm all such temporary employees. He could also recommend leave of the employees working under him and the same was sanctioned by the Head Office. It was further stated that the recommendations of Respondent No. 2 in all such cases, in office routine and general management and control in the shop were approved by the Head Office and his recommendations were almost final.  7. Some of the duties of the Manager are deducible from the duties of the salesman. A salesman is to prepare cash memos for shoes, sundries etc. sold, to receive cash from customers and then hand over the same to the Manager; to deposit sale proceeds in the Bank, if so instructed by the Shop Manager/Incharge; to assist the Manager/Incharge in placing orders to Head Office and to receive the consignment intended for the shop; to assist the Manager in daily routine and also to assist him in taking ground inventory every fortnight at the time closing the statement; to attend to customer's complaints and settle or forward the complaint form to the Head Office according to the instructions of the Manager; to strictly follow Shop opening and closing time and avail lunch interval in timings fixed by the Manager from time to time; and to carry out all instructions issued by the shop Manager in the interest of the Company.  8. Another document, which was produced before the Labour Court, to show the duties of the Shop Manager, is dated 1st May, 1979. According to this document, incidental expenses of the shop such as cartage to and from station, packing material etc. are to be borne by the Shop Manager out of the amount recovered by sale of wooden cases. He is also to see that the shop is kept clean and the various requisite and stock is maintained well. The manager is required to send a bonus commission statement to the Head Office after the expiry of each quarter and he is not authorised to accept any process of law in the name of or on behalf of the company or represent the company without written permission of the company in any legal matter or in any other matter not connected with the routine work of the shop. He is to inform the company immediately without losing any time about any process of court served upon him. Subject to the terms and conditions mentioned and to any directions or orders which may from time to time be given to him by the Company the Manager has general control over the shop, but he is not authorised to pledge in any way the credit of the company. He is to keep proper accounts in form or forms as are approved by the Company of moneys, cheques, drafts, etc received at the shop by way of sale proceeds or otherwise are to be forwarded to the Head Office or to be deposited in the Bank account of the Company. He is to personally open and close the shop at a fixed time. He can depute a Helper to act as a Salesman in the event of Salesman being absent from duty for 5 days or more at a time and may appoint temporary Helpers for the said period at the prescribed rate of salary. If the Helper is absent from duty for 4 days or less, he can entrust the work to a sweeper, and can also appoint part-time sweeper. If a permanent appointment is to be made, the application and other documents duly completed, are to be sent to the Head Office. Shri Sethi in his statement had stated that he (Shri Sethi) was authorised to impose fine and to charge-sheet salesman/helper and that he was empowered by the Head Office to do so. In his cross-examination, he stated that other Managers had similar powers.  9. It was further brought on the record of the Labour Court that under the Punjab Shops and Commercial Establishment Act, 1958, Respondent No. 2 used to fill forms C and D prescribed under that Act, as an employer.  10. The case of Shri S.K Maini, Respondent No. 2, before the Labour Court, was that though he was designated as a Shop Manager, but he had no administrative or managerial authority. He was not allowed to grant leave to his co-workers nor he could get explanation or charge-sheet them. He used to collect cash from all sort of customers. He used to write and maintain cash books. He stated in the cross-examination that there was no officer in the shop, but supervision was done by the Assistant Manager with Headquarters at Ambala, who used to visit shop 5/6 times a year. He further stated that he did not recruit any temporary employee and did not recommend any such employee for confirmation as no temporary employee was employed by him.  11. After considering all the duties, as referred to above the learned Labour Court came to the conclusion that Respondent No. 2 was a workman under the Act.  12. The learned counsel for the petitioner argued that from the duties of the Shop Manager, which have been referred to above, it will be evident that primary and the dominant duties of respondent No. 2 were managerial or administrative and to some extent supervisory as well and the clerical duties were incidental or ancillary. There is no dispute on the point that Respondent No. 2 did not use to perform any duties of a Salesman for selling the articles. According to him, Managerial duties as opposed to clerical duties, would be that if the person has the power or authorisation to take immediate decision for the time being regarding the establishment under him. In the instant case, Respondent No. 2 was authorised to take decision as to if a particular salesman is not there for a few days, whether to have a Helper or not. He could assign duties of a Helper to a Sweeper. He could also decide when to open or close shop. He could employ temporarily a Helper. The salesman was also required to get instructions from the Manager which the salesman was to carry out. These duties cannot be. performed by a person who is assigned the clerical work and the duties as indicated above, cannot be termed as clerical duties. The evidence has also come that the Manager could recommend leave and also recommend persons for permanent appointment. These duties cannot be said to be clerical. It was further argued that so far as the evidence regarding the supervisory nature of duties was concerned, that was shut out on the ground that no such pleas was taken in the written statement. In' the written statement, the plea was that the respondent is not a workman under Section 2(s). Consequently, evidence on all the exceptions under Section 2(s) could be led to show that Respondent No. 2 was performing administrative or managerial duties as also supervisory. The learned counsel also submitted that the only test is that a person working in a supervisory capacity or in a managerial capacity must have the power to employ a person or to grant him leave or to take disciplinary action against him, then it will only be an employer who can be said to be not a workman and all others who do not have such a power, though performing administrative, managerial or supervisory duties, would be brought under the definition of "workman".  13. The learned counsel for the petitioner cited Vimal Kumar Jain v. Labour Court, Kanpur, 1987 (Supp.) SCC 40, that a Maintenance Engineer who supervises the work of maintenance, has the power to make temporary appointments, grant leave and initiate departmental proceedings, would not be a workman. He also cited Shri T.P. Srivastava v. M/s. National Tobacco Co. of India Limited, JT 1991(4) SC 121, to the effect that Section Salesman who looked after sales promotion and the duties required imaginative and creative mind, could not be termed as a person doing skilled, unskilled or clerical work.  14. On the other hand, learned counsel for Respondent No. 2 argued that the primary and the dominant duties of Respondent No. 2 were clerical in nature and some duties here or there, which may be managerial, administrative or supervisory in nature were just incidental or ancillary to the main duties and such duties would not No. 2 from the purview of take out Respondent No. 2 from the purview of the definition of "workman". The learned counsel cited a Supreme Court judgment reported as National Engineering Industries Ltd. v. Shri Krishan Bhagoria and others, A.I.R. 1988 S.C. 329 where an employee working as Internal Auditor in a company who was performing the main duties of reporting and checking up on behalf of the Management but had no independent right or authority to take decision and his decision did not bind the Company, was held to be not performing any supervisory duties, and, therefore, was held to be a workman under the Act. He also referred to a judgment of the Supreme Court reported as Shri S.K. Verma v. Sri Mahesh Chandra and another, 1983(2) S.L.J. 570. This was a case concerning a Development Officer of Life Insurance Corporation, who was not a whole-time employee of the Corporation. His operations were restricted to a defined area and was liable to be transferred; he had no authority whatsoever to bind the Corporation in any way; the principal duties were to organise and to develop the business of the Corporation in the area allotted to him and for that purpose he could recruit active and reliable agents and was to train them to canvass new business and to render post-sale services to policy-holders; to assist and inspire the agents but had no authority to appoint agents or to take disciplinary action against them and was not required to supervise the work of agents and such agents were not his subordinates. There was no subordinate staff working under him. It was under these circumstances that it was held by the Supreme Court that the Development Officer was not engaged in any administrative or managerial work and, therefore, was a workman under the Act. The learned counsel also relied upon another judgment of the Supreme Court reported as Ananda Bazar Patrika (Private) Ltd. v. Its Workmen, 1969(II) LLJ 670. In this case, the employee was the Incharge of the Provident Fund Section of the Ananda Bazar Patrika (Private) Ltd. and was designated as Manager. In the written statement filed on behalf of the Management, it had been pleaded that the employee used to supervise the work of the Clerks working under him, allot work to them, give them directions regarding work, grant them permission to leave office during working hours and recommend their leave. However, when the employee came in the witness box he was not asked in the cross-examination any question as to whether he was supervising the work of the Clerks working under him or used to allot work to them or gave them directions regarding their work. On the other hand, the employee had stated that the main duties which he was required to carry out, were those of writing out the cash book and of filing up the various returns required to be prepared in the section of which he was the Incharge. On this evidence he was held to be a workman.  15. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties and examining the nature of duties performed by Respondent No. 2 and after applying the principles laid down in various judgments cited at the bar, I am of the view that the Labour Court went wrong in holding that Respondent No. 2 was a workman. It is no doubt true that mere designation of the post held by an employee is not at all the determining factor as to whether he is workman under the Act or not. The main and dominant nature of duties performed by the employee would be the determining factor. The managerial or the administrative duties are different than the supervisory nature of duties and some of them may even overlap. The Legislature itself had made a distinction between the managerial and administrative type of duties and the supervisory nature of duties. Clauses (iii) and (iv) of Section 2(s) of the Act may be referred to in this connection. According to me, a person would be said to be performing the managerial or administrative type of duties if he is managing the show of the Management at a particular place where he is employed and is really the Incharge or the master of that show for the time being. If he can take decisions, even though temporarily for the time being, to run the show, he will be discharging the managerial or the administrative duties of the Management. Seen in this background it will be evident that the predominant duties of Respondent No. 2 were administrative or managerial and to some extent even supervisory. The power to employ or dismiss or even to initiate disciplinary action may not be the sole basis. This test may became very relevant in case it is to be found out whether the duties are supervisory in nature. The details of duties have already been referred to above which Respondent No. 2 was performing. Out of all the duties couple of duties like maintaining accounts filling in certain proforma may be clerical. However, his major job was administrative or managerial. The authorities cited by the respondents's counsel were decided on the facts of those cases and were mainly in the context of finding out whether the employee was discharging duties of supervisory nature. In Ananda Bazar Patrika's case (supra), cited by the counsel for the respondent, if it had been proved by the Management that the employee used to supervise the work of the Clerks, allot them work and give them directions regarding work or grant them permission to leave and recommend their leave, then the employee may not have come under the definition of `workman' but these things were not even put to the employee when he was in the witness box.  16. The Labour Court was also not right in shutting out the evidence of the Management when it tried to show that some of the duties of Respondent No. 2 were supervisory in nature. The management had pleaded that Respondent No. 2 was not a workman under Section 2(s) of the Act and it could legitimately lead evidence to take out the respondent from the purview of the definition of `workman' to bring the case under exception (iii) or (iv) of Section 2(s) of the Act.  From the above discussion, I hold that Respondent No. 2 was not a workman under Section 2(s) of the Act.  17. Point No. 2.  The Labour Court had held that the domestic enquiry against Respondent No.2 was vitiated primarily on two grounds. viz (i) that the Enquiry Officer was an employee of the Management being their standing counsel, and (ii) that Respondent No. 2 was not granted permission to have the assistance of a lawyer. I am afraid these were not good grounds to hold that the domestic enquiry was vitiated. The duties and the interest of an employee of the Management while holding an enquiry against a person do not clash. If it were so, then no employee of the Management can become an Enquiry Officer and in all cases another employee of some other Management or a third person would have to be engaged for the purpose of enquiry. It is well known in service jurisprudence that one of the employee in the department holds an enquiry against a delinquent official, be it a Corporation or an employee in Government service. There is no such bar to the employee of the Management being appointed as an Enquiry Officer unless it is held that the enquiry officer is biased or that in the particular enquiry the Enquiry Officer had an interest against the delinquent official. Apart from above, it may be observed that Respondent No. 2 never raised any objection against the appointment of the Enquiry Officer, who was an Advocate. This being the position, he could have been allowed to raise this point that the Enquiry Officer should not have held the enquiry.  18. As far as the permission to have the assistance of a lawyer is concerned, it may be observed that it is not necessary that in all cases, the workman should be allowed to be represented by a lawyer. Simply because the Enquiry Officer is a Law Graduate, would not entitle the workman to have the assistance of a Lawyer. Under the Standing Orders of the Management, the workman is only entitled to the assistance of another employee and not a lawyer. No fault could be found with the enquiry on this ground.  19. Point No. 3.  Under Section 11-A of the Act, even if the Labour Court had found that the enquiry was vitiated, as it was not properly held, then permission should have been granted to the Management to lead evidence to prove the charges before the Labour Court. In other words, the Labour Court should have turned itself into an Enquiry Officer. In the Workman of M/s. Firestone Tyre and Rubber Co. of India (Pvt) Ltd. v. The Management and others, (1973)1 S.C.C. 813, various principles as emerged after the introduction of section 11-A of the Act were enunciated. The relevant principles in this case are as follows :-  "(4) Even if no enquiry has been held by an employer or if the enquiry held by him is found to be defective, the Tribunal in order to satisfy itself about the legality and validity of the order, had to give an opportunity to the employer and employee to adduce evidence before it, it is open to the employer to adduce evidence for the first time justifying his action, and it is open to the employee to adduce evidence contra.  (5) The effect of an employer not holding an enquiry is that the Tribunal would not leave to consider only whether there was a prima facie case. On the other hand, the issue about the merits of the impugned order of dismissal or discharge is at large before the Tribunal and the latter, on the evidence adduced before it, has to decide for itself whether the misconduct alleged is proved. In such cases, the point about the exercise of managerial functions does not arise at all. A case of defective enquiry stands on the same footing as no enquiry.  (8) An employer, who wants to avail himself of the opportunity of adducing evidence for the first time before the Tribunal to justify his action, should ask for it at the appropriate stage. If such an opportunity is asked for the Tribunal has no power to refuse. The giving of an opportunity to an employer to adduce evidence for the first time before the Tribunal is in the interest of both the management and the employee and to enable the Tribunal itself to be satisfied about the alleged misconduct."  The Labour Court was not right in denying the opportunity to the Management to lead evidence on the ground that it wanted to fill in the lacuna in the evidence which had been left by it before the Enquiry Officer. Under the principles enunciated above, the Management had a right to adduce evidence before the Labour Court, in case it was held that the enquiry was vitiated on any ground.  For the foregoing reasons, this writ petition is allowed and the award of the Labour Court, dated 21st April, 1986 is set aside. There will be no order as to costs.
summary:
A. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 2(s)(iii) and (iv) - Workman - The designation of an employee's post is not the sole factor when determining whether or not someone is a workman - The primary nature of their duties is what needs to be considered - Management or administrative duties differ from supervisory duties - If someone supervises the work and has the power to make temporary appointments, grant leave, or initiate departmental proceedings, they cannot be considered a workman according to the Industrial Disputes Act. [Paras 5, 13 & 15]

B. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Sections 11(a) and 2(s)(iii) and (iv) - Workman/ Pleadings - When the management argues that an employee is not a workman, they can provide evidence to exclude the employee's workman status as part of their defense. [Para 16]

C. Constitution of India, Article 14 - Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 10 - Punjab Civil Services (Punishment & Appeal) Rules, 1970, Rule 876 - Natural justice - The Enquiry Officer being a law graduate is not grounds for a workman to have the right to a lawyer's assistance - A workman can only have another employee assist them - Denying a workman a lawyer's assistance does not invalidate the inquiry. [Para 18]

D. Constitution of India, Article 14 - Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 10 - Enquiry Officer - An Enquiry Officer being an employee of the same Department does not automatically make the departmental inquiry flawed. [Para 17]

E. Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 11(a) - Enquiry - If the Labour Court finds that the inquiry was flawed, the management can request permission to present the prima facie case against the employee before the Labour Court at a suitable time. [Para 19]

text: M.K. Mukherjee, J. - I.A. No. 2 of 1994 in S.L.P. (C) No. 14944 of 1994.  The application is allowed. The applicant-respondent No. 5 be transposed as petitioner No. 6. Office will amend the case title of the petition accordingly.  S.L.P. (C) Nos. 8911-12 of 1994 with S.L. P. (C) No. 14944 of 1994.  Special leave granted.  2. These appeals are directed against the common judgment and order dated March 30, 1994 rendered by the Calcutta High Court disposing of a number of Letters Patent Appeals and Writ Petitions. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeals are as under.  3. In 1983 two writ petitions were filed in the High Court by the appellants herein on behalf of and at the instance of a large number of applicants seeking appointments as Assistant Teachers in different primary schools of West Bengal, began, run and managed by District Primary School Boards/Councils within their respective territories. They contended that though they had the requisite educational qualifications and basic training for such appointments the Boards/Councils were preparing panels and giving appointments to untrained applicants and persons of their own choice in utter disregard of the Rules framed and circulars issued in that behalf. A learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the writ petitions by a judgment dated September 28, 1989 with a finding that the appointment of untrained candidates as Assistant Teachers in the primary schools was unauthorised and illegal and a direction that the respondents should appoint only trained candidates in the recognised primary schools in the different districts of the State against existing vacancies.  4. Assailing the above judgment of the learned Single Judge the respondents preferred a Letters Patent Appeal before a Division Bench of the High Court which was disposed of on May 10, 1991 with the following directions :  "Accordingly, taking all the facts and circumstances into consideration, I direct the different District School Boards and the concerned authorities to take immediate steps for preparation of fresh panels in accordance with law and in terms of the Rules referred to above. I further direct that all appointments against the additional posts sanctioned by the State Government from time to time due to enhancement in the roll strength in the existing schools in different districts be filled up by the trained candidates only. So far as the normal vacancies existing in the schools are concerned, at least 50% must be filled up by trained candidates only. In respect of remaining 50% of such vacancies, untrained candidates should be considered along with trained candidates on some rational and reasonable principle." 5. Against the above judgment and order the appellants moved this Court by filing Special Leave Petitions which were disposed of on September 30, 1991 with the following observations and directions :  "There are certain rules which relate to selection of teachers. The Division Bench of the High Court has dealt with the manner and procedure of the selection. Taking note of the fact that there are a good number of vacancies existing and rules have been made prescribing the process to be followed, the Court has laid down that the 50% of the normal vacancies should be filled up by the trained teachers and all additional vacancies should go to them and the remainder of the 50% of the normal vacancies could be filled by trained and untrained teachers. In a part of its decision the Division Bench has indicated what actually is meant by the term 'rational and reasonable number'. We gather that in terms of the directions of the Division Bench, panels have now been drawn up. We are of the view that, if and when the panels are under challenge it should be open to the aggrieved parties to take their definite stand one way or the other depending upon the facts of the case, but the general guidelines given by the High Court do not require to be disturbed." 6. On a clarification sought of the above order this Court made the following order on April 27, 1992 :  "if there are any panels drawn which are inconsistent with the directions dated May 10, 1991 of the Division Bench of the High Court and if any appointments are made from such inconsistent penals, it will be open for the petitioners to challenge the same before the High Court." 7. Thereafter some of the appellants herein again moved a writ petition before a learned Judge of the High Court alleging that the respondents were preparing and giving appointments in utter disregard of the earlier order of the Division Bench of the High Court dated May 10, 1991 as affirmed by the Supreme Court and contrary to the Rules framed and circulars issued in that behalf and prayed for cancellation of the panels so prepared and illegal appointments given. On that petition an interim order was made on September 24, 1992 to the effect that the district authorities should prepare panels in accordance with the order of the Division Bench dated May 10, 1991 after giving an opportunity to all the members of the writ petitions to appear before the Interview Board. An interim injunction restraining the respondents from issuing any appointment letter was also passed. Similar interim orders were issued on other writ petitions filed on behalf of the applicants. Against the interim orders passed on some of those petitions, the respondents filed Letters Patent Appeals before a Division Bench of the High Court and obtained their stay. In course of hearing of one of those matters the Division Bench felt that the appeals as also all the connected writ petitions should be heard together and ordered accordingly.  8. In course of the hearing of the matters it having been brought to the notice of the Division Bench that the panels were being prepared in utter breach of the directions given by the earlier Division Bench of the High Court in its order dated May 10, 1991 and the extant Rules and Circulars and that the legitimate claims and aspirations of the trained teachers were being ignored, the Bench appointed two special officers to submit an illustrative inspection report about the preparation to panels of two of the Districts, namely, Midnapur and Howrah. On perusal of the reports submitted by the two officers the Division Bench found that there were gross irregularities in regard to the preparation of panel so far as Midnapur District was concerned (some of the instances of such irregularity have been detailed in the impugned judgment). On such finding the Bench gave the following directions :-  "As regards District Midnapore, it has been submitted that the Director, School Education (Primary) has already granted his approval in the matter and as such question of reopening the same does not and cannot rise. We are, however, not inclined to accept this contention as advanced by Mr. Bhuiya appearing for the Midnapore School Council. This Court cannot lend a deaf ear and a blind eye to the irregularities as noted in the report of the Special Officers. The approval, if any, cannot thus be sustained and the same, therefore, is set aside and cancelled. The Director of School Education (Primary) is directed to consider the matter afresh and it is hereby ordered accordingly. This reconsideration of the matter by the Director shall be effected having due regard to the report of the Special Officers and in the event the Director is of the view that the reports of the Special Officers and the instances mentioned therein require further consideration, he would do so and recast the panel accordingly. This order is passed upon consideration of the fact that this Court ought not to usurp the power of the Director in the matter of grant of approval. The Director is to act strictly in accordance with law having due regard to the provisions of law and the judgment of this Court in the earlier matter as noted above." (emphasis supplied) 9. In respect of the panel prepared for the District of Howrah the Bench observed that it could not be said to be that irregular though certain instances had been brought to its light, but the irregularities did not constitute a major problem for the purpose of giving effect to the panel.
