A person dies while taking the wife to a hospital and the cry of the lady for bare subsistence would go unheeded on a certain technicality. The breadearner is no longer available and prayer for compassionate appointment would be denied as "it is likely to open a Pandora's box" - this is the resultant effect of our entry into the new millennium. Can the law courts be mute spectators in the matter of denial of such a relief to the horrendous suffering of an employee's family by reason of the death of the breadearner ?" We are of the view that over and above what the Apex Court has reminded us, we cannot forget the constitutional philosophy enshrined in Articles 15 and 16 of the Constitution of India. When a request made by a widow for compassionate appointment is granted the constitutional objective of strengthening and improving the status of women could be achieved. By granting compassionate appointment to a widow in this case we can strengthen and improve the status of the woman and could also achieve gender equality especially in a case where the widow has satisfied all the requirements of the compassionate appointment scheme. The Apex Court while dealing with clause (3) of Article 15 in Government of A.P. v. P.B. Vijayakumar, AIR 1995 S.C. 1648 : 1995(4) SCT 169 (SC) held as follows :  "The insertion of clause (3) of Article 15 in relation to woman is a recognition of the fact that for centuries, women of this country have been socially and economically handicapped. It is in order to eliminate this socio-economic backwardness of women and to empower them in a manner that would bring about effective equality between men and women that Article 15(3) is placed in Article 15. Its object is to strengthen and improve the status of women. An important limb of the concept of gender equality is creating job opportunities for women. To say that under Article 15(3), job opportunities for women cannot be created would be to cut at the very root of the underlying inspiration behind this Article. Making special provisions for women in respect of employment or posts under the State is an integral part of Article 15(3). This power conferred under Article 15(3), is not whittled down in any manner by Article 16." We can therefore look at the claim of a widow for compassionate appointment in the light of the constitutional principles as well.  7. We are of the view that the Canara Bank authorities have committed a grave error in not entertaining the application preferred by the widow and lost sight of the horrendous suffering of the widow who is to look after the minor children, widowed mother of the deceased, widowed sister and a mentally and physically handicapped brother of the deceased by birth. All of them were under the care and support of the deceased.  8. We may in this connection also refer to some of the provisions in the scheme which would indicate that the granting of terminal benefits to the dependent of a deceased employee is of not much consequence in considering the application for compassionate appointment. Clause 3.2 of the scheme says that in case the dependent of deceased employee to be offered appointment is a minor, the Bank may keep the offer of appointment open till the minor attains the age of majority. This would indicate that granting of terminal benefits is of no consequence because even if the terminal benefit is given, if the applicant is a minor, the Bank would keep the appointment open till the minor attains the age of majority. So also in the case of member of the family sponsored for appointment desires to wait till he/she attains certain educational qualifications, his/her candidature would be considered provided the date so stipulated is within four years from the date of death of the employee. This would also indicate that the granting of terminal benefits is of no consequence. Further we may also notice clause 10 which deals with special provisions. It is stated that if the applicant is employed elsewhere, and if the job in the Bank is going to help him/her financially, such requests may also be entertained as per norms. Further, if any member of the family is already employed with the Bank, the Bank may consider giving employment to another member of the family depending on the merits of individual. Conjoint reading of all those clauses would show that granting of terminal benefits is of no consequence in the matter of considering the claim for compassionate appointment. In view of the above mentioned circumstance we have no hesitation to hold that the petitioner is legally entitled to have his application considered for compassionate appointment in the service of the Canara Bank.  We, therefore, find no reason to disturb the finding of the learned Single Judge and dismiss the appeal for the reasons indicated hereinbefore. The Canara Bank should forthwith consider the application of the widow and pass orders within a period of three weeks from today. We express our deep anguish and concern at the insensitive and abdurate manner in which the Canara Bank authorities had dealt with the request of a widow placed in an infelicitous circumstance with two minor children of aged 7 and 3, aged mother of 74 years, a brother of 48 years (both mentally and physically handicapped by birth) and a widowed sister of aged 46 years of the deceased.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: The request of a widow for a compassionate appointment was rejected by stating that terminal benefits were already provided after the death of the deceased. This reasoning is not fair as the benefits were legitimate and not a matter of compassion. The bank in question has been directed to review the widow's application and make a decision within three weeks. [Paras 5, 7 and 8]

text: N.K. Agrawal, J. - In this writ petition filed under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India, the petitioners have prayed for issuance of a writ of mandamus directing respondent No. 1 to grant pension to the petitioners under the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 1980.  2. On notice of motion having been issued, respondents have put in appearance and filed written statements.  3. Sh. H.S. Giani, learned counsel appearing for Union of India, contends that the persons who are certifiers of the petitioners and have claimed imprisonment along with the petitioners in the Central Jail, Lahore, have issued such certificates (co-prisoner certificates) to numerous people and such certificates have been found issued indiscriminately and have created false claims for grant of Samman Pension under the scheme.  4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the paper book.  5. From the perusal of written statement filed on behalf of State of Punjab, it is observed that after verifying the claim of the petitioners, the State of Punjab has recommended the case of the petitioners for grant of pension under the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme.  6. In this view of the matter, we direct the Union of India to re-consider the case of the petitioners for grant of pension under the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 1980 in the light of recommendations of the Punjab Government.  Writ Petition disposed of accordingly.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 1980 - Pension - The petitioner received a certificate from his co-prisoners in Central Jail, Lahore, which was verified by the Punjab Govt. to recommend his case for grant of Swatantrata Sainik Pension under the scheme. Other individuals were also granted pension on the basis of the same certificates. As a result, the government was instructed to grant the petitioner a pension under the 1980 scheme. [Paras 5 and 6]

text: Jayasimha Babu, J. - The petitioner, who was an employee of the second respondent Pallavan Transport Corporation, has filed the writ petition in December, 1991, challenging the order of the second respondent dated 17.10.1986, by which he was informed that he was retired from service on 30.6.1987, as also a letter from the second respondent dated 28.8.1990 by which his request for reinstating him in service on the ground that his age has been wrongly noted in the Service Register was rejected by the second respondent.  2. The principal contention of the petitioner is that the service record contains an entry in the column 'date of birth' as 5.6.1937, which has been scored off and below which the date 1.7.1929 is entered and, therefore, this amounts to alteration of the date of birth by the employer to the prejudice of the employee, and that such alteration has been effected without notice to the employee, thereby rendering the alteration illegal.  3. It is not in dispute that the petitioner had joined the service under the Deputy Director of Transport on 22.8.1956 and on the formation of the second respondent Corporation, he became an employee of the second respondent with effect from 1.5.1975. It is also not in dispute that the petitioner had been promoted as Foreman in the year 1983. He was holding that post at the time he was retired from service with effect from 30.6.1987. The petitioner also does not dispute the fact that the pay slip, which has been issued to him, contained his date of birth as 1.7.1929. It is also not in dispute that the date of birth of the petitioner as entered in the seniority list is 1.7.1929. The petitioner was served with this memo on 17.10.1986 and immediately after its receipt, he addressed a letter to the employer on 24.10.1986 in which he requested that his service book may be furnished to him to enable him to verify the date of birth entered in the service Register, and in the letter no mention was made to the alleged error in the date of birth as recorded by the employer. He did not, in that letter, dispute the date which was notified to him as the date of his retirement.  4. The petitioner started making representations regarding the alleged error in the date of birth noted in the register only on his letter dated 8.12.1986 and for the first time, it is claimed therein that his date of birth is 5.6.1937. He made further representations all of which were rejected by the employer. The petitioner waited till December, 1991 to file this petition. The explanation given is that he had made numerous representations, the last of which was rejected by the employer on 28.8.1990.  5. Learned counsel for the petitioner made a submission which on the face of it is plausible, but which, after considering the factual background and after looking into the original records placed before the Court by the employer, cannot be accepted. Learned counsel is right in his submission that the date of birth of the employee once entered in the service register should not be altered to the prejudice of the employee, without notice to the affected employee. Learned counsel relied on decisions of the Supreme Court in State of Orissa v. Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei, AIR 1967 SC 1269, and in Sarjoo Prasad v. General Manager, AIR 1981 SC 1481, in support of his submission. Learned counsel also referred to a decision of a Division Bench of this Court in support of the same proposition, in The General Manager (Personal Branch) Southern Railway, Madras v. S.M. Muhammed Yukub, AIR 1959 Madras 88, as also a decision of the Division Bench of the Orissa High Court in K. Venkataramana v. Union of India, etc., 1974 All India Service Law Journal 299.  6. Learned counsel rightly did not dispute the proposition that an employee at the fag end of the service cannot seek alteration of the date of birth unless the rules governing the service permit such application being made, what was forcefully pleaded before the Court was that correction in the service register should be effected only after an enquiry is held after due notice to the affected employee, if the correction in the service register relates to the date of birth and the corrected date is one which is anterior to the date originally entered. While the submission so made may be accepted as a general proposition, nevertheless, the same has been applied with reference to the facts and circumstances of a given case and cannot be applied in vacuum.  7. The decisions relied on by the learned counsel in support of the submissions were all cases where there was no dispute that the correction had been made several years after the original entry was made and it was also not in dispute in those cases that before a new entry was substituted in the place of the original entry, the affected employee had not been served due notice.  8. The present case however is not one of that nature. The respondents have placed before the Court the original service book which was maintained by the Government Transport Department, which shows that the petitioner had entered the services in the year 1956. In that service book, the date of birth of the petitioner at page 1 is entered as 1.7.1929. Above that entry, the figures 5.6.1937 had been written and has been scored off and initialled. On the next page in Column No. 6 which is captioned as 'date of birth' by Christian Era, the entry is 1.7.1929 and that date is also written in words in brackets below the figures and has been initialled. In column 13 of the next page, the petitioner had signed his name in full in English. In the service Registers maintained by the second respondent Corporation after the year 1975 which have been marked by it as Volumes 2 and 3, the same date of birth 1.7.29 has been entered throughout. In the seniority list maintained by the Corporation which was also placed before the Court, the same date of birth is entered in respect of the petitioner. The petitioner has, in his affidavit, himself admitted the fact that in the seniority list as also in the pay slips issued to him, the date of birth was entered. A specimen of the pay slip was also placed before the Court which shows that the date of birth of the employee as also the date of joining the service are entered in the pay slip.  9. The materials so placed before the Court below indicate that the petitioner was aware of the entry in the service book regarding his date of birth as 1.7.1929 and that entry was made at the time of this recruitment. The figures 5.6.1937 once written on page 1 had been scored out and the date 1.7.1929 was written at or about the time of the petitioner joining the service of the State Transport Authority. At page 2 of book, it contains only the date 1.7.1929 and there is no mention of any other date, as date of birth of the petitioner.  10. The fact that the petitioner had knowledge of the date of birth having been entered in the employer's record is evident from the fact that this entry which was periodically made known to the employee in the pay slip and he was also aware of it on account of the entry of that date having been entered in the seniority list as well.  11. It is therefore difficult to accept the submission made by the learned counsel for the petitioner that the petitioner was illiterate, was not academically qualified and, therefore, could not apprehend what was set out in the pay slip or other documents and had no occasion to see the corrections of the alleged erroneous entry.  12. It was suggested by the learned counsel that an enquiry is essential to find out whether the correction at page 1 of the service book was made contemporaneously or at a subsequent point of time. This submission would have had some force if there was any independent material which would prima facie establish that the petitioner's date of birth is in fact that date that was scored out into record. No such material is placed before court. The assertion of the petitioner that the date birth of his elder brother is later in point of time cannot by itself constitute a basis to doubt the correctness in the entry in the service Register. So also the fact that the petitioner obtained passport in the year 1978 in which a different date is same as his date of birth, long after the joining the service of the respondents and was fully aware of the date of birth entered in the record as 1.7.1929 also cannot constitute any basis for doubting the correctness of the entry in the service Register.  13. Learned counsel for the respondents rightly referred to the Standing Orders of the Second respondent. Standing Order 32 which requires the employees of the second respondent who are already in service, to apply within a period of six months from the date of coming into force of the Standing Order viz., 27th June, 1978 to see correction in the date of birth if there was any error in that entry. The petitioner admittedly did not make any such application within the time so provided and in fact he did not apply till after the date on which he was to retire was notified. Even after such intimation, his immediate response was not that he was not due for retirement but only that the retirement benefits have to be settled earlier. In fact, the petitioner has received all his retirement benefits on 30.6.1987 as is evident from the second respondent's letter dated 3.12.1987, a copy which has been produced by the petitioner.  14. The importance of applying in time for having any erroneous entry regarding the date of birth in the employer's records rectified has been stressed by the Supreme Court in more than one decision. Learned counsel for the respondent referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Harnam Singh, (1993) 82 FJR 301 : 1993(3) S.C.T. 120, wherein the Supreme Court ruled out that any application by employee for correction of date of birth must be made without unreasonable delay even if no period of limitation is prescribed. The Supreme Court further pointed out that application made just before superannuation did not merit consideration. The same principle was reiterated by the Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. T.V. Venugoplan, 1994(4) SCT 375 (SC) : 1994(6) SCC 302. Also to the same effect, is the decision in State of Orissa v. Brahamarbar Senapathi, 1994(2) MLJ 735 : 1996(2) S.C.T. 651.  15. The petitioner was clearly aware that his date of birth as entered in the employer's record was 1.7.1929 and the fact that he had such knowledge is evident from the entry in the service book and it is also admitted fact that the date of birth was shown in the pay slips and the seniority list. No protest was made by the petitioner till after the intimation of the date of retirement and even then, not immediately, but much later. If the petitioner really was right in his claim, he had an opportunity to establish such a claim when the standing orders were notified in the year 1978 and all workmen were permitted to seek correction of their date of birth as entered in the employer's record provided, such an application was made within a period of six months. Admittedly, no such application was made. As laid down by the Supreme Court, applications for corrections of the date of birth or protest regarding the date entered in the employer's record at the fag end of the service do not carry much credibility and ought not to be entertained. The petitioner appears to have based his case in the present petition solely on the fact that in page 1 of the service book, the date that had been entered has been scored out and below which the date 1.7.1929 is entered. But that should be read along with what is entered in the very following page and the periodical information given to the petitioner regarding the date. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that at page 2 the instructions are that the entries in the page should be periodically attested and such attestation has not been done. In view of that instruction, he states that the entry made in Column 6 which has not been attested at the interval of five years cannot be relied upon. The purpose for which such instructions have been set out, is not at all clear as none of the entries therein by themselves require periodical reviewing. The entry made is regarding the name, place of birth, parents name, date of birth and identification marks. None of these are things which will change, only the residence may change from time to time. The mere fact that this entry was not attested at five years intervals does not affect the genuineness of the entries already made.  16. Learned counsel for the respondents further submitted that the petition is liable to be dismissed on the ground of laches as the petition was filed four years after the employee's retirement and five years after intimation about the date with effect from which he would retire. There is substance in the submission. Learned counsel for the petitioner in this context relied on a judgment of this Court in Shawallace & Co. Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu rep. by the Commissioner and Secretary, Labour Department and others, 1987(1) LLJ 177 wherein this court held in para 38 of that judgment that repeated representations made to the authority for reconsidering the matter would not constitute sufficient reason for delay in approaching this Court. This petition clearly suffers from laches. This petition is therefore liable to be dismissed on the ground of laches as well as on merits.  17. The petitioner is, therefore, not entitled to any relief in the petition and the writ petition is dismissed. No costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: The correction of the date of birth in the service register for an industrial dispute is addressed in Item 2 and Item 6 of Schedule 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act (14 of 1947). The petitioner must file an application within six months of the standing orders' coming into force. However, the petitioner failed to do so, as evidenced by the fact that he was aware of the erroneous entry, which was periodically disclosed to him in pay slips and seniority lists. The petitioner's request for correction was four years after his retirement and five years after he was informed of the date on which he would retire, demonstrating a delay that is likely to and therefore cause his plea to be dismissed. [Paras 13, 15 and 16]

text: M. Katju, J. - This writ petition has been filed against the impugned order of dismissal dated 10.9.1998 Annexure 15 to the writ petition.  2. We have heard Sri Ravi Kant, learned counsel for the petitioner and Sri V.K. Singh for the respondent.  3. The petitioner was appointed as Logging Officer in the U.P. Forest Corporation in 1986. He was placed under suspension by the order of the Managing Director of the U.P. Forest Corporation dated 11.3.1997 vide Annexure I-A to the writ petition. In that suspension order it was mentioned that various irregularities were detected in the storage of tendu leaves in 1994 season. Complaints had also been received regarding under-weighing and other irregularities in Karwi Logging Division in 1994. The petitioner challenged the aforesaid order of suspension in writ petition No. 10118 of 1997 but the same was dismissed with the direction that the enquiry be completed within six months of production of certified copy of the order. Thereafter on 22.7.1997 the petitioner was served with a charge-sheet true copy of which is Annexure 3 to the writ petition. The petitioner made a request that certain relevant documents be made available to him vide letter dated 1.8.1997 Annexure 4 to the writ petition. In paragraph 29 of the writ petition it is stated that when no reply was received in response to the said letter he made another request through letter dated 1.9.1997 Annexure 5 to the writ petition which was sent under postal certificate. Thereafter the petitioner gave another reminder dated 11.9.1997 vide Annexure 6 to the writ petition and then he wrote another letter dated 24.9.1997 vide Annexure 7 to the writ petition.  4. In paragraph 32 of the writ petition it is stated that on 29.8.1997 the petitioner was informed that he may inspect the relevant records any day in the office of the Divisional Logging Officer, Karwi Division Bench, vide Annexure 8 to the writ petition. In paragraph 33 to the writ petition it is alleged that it was only through latter dated 15.9.1977 that the entire records which were required to be inspected by the petitioner were transmitted from Lucknow to Karwi vide Annexure 9 to the writ petition. In paragraph 34 of the writ petition it is alleged that while on the one hand the respondent corporation had fixed 15.9.1997 for inspection of record at Karwi, on the other hand the enquiry officer submitted his enquiry on 13.9.1997. This enquiry report was supplied to the petitioner through a show cause notice dated 26.2.1998. True copy of the show cause notice and the enquiry report are Annexures 10 and 11 to the writ petition. In paragraph 36 of the writ petition it is stated that the petitioner was granted time till 21.8.1998 for sending reply with a condition that no further extension was possible beyond that. The petitioner did not either gave his reply to the show cause notice nor did he indicate the papers which he wanted to inspect. The second show cause notice states that by letter dated 15.12.1997 the petitioner was asked to indicate the papers which were not made available to him by 20.12.1997. In paragraph 38 of the writ petition it is alleged that this was a false allegation since the enquiry officer had submitted his ex parte report on 13.9.1997 and thus the letter dated 15.12.1997 was absolutely vague and meaningless.  5. In paragraph 39 of the writ petition it is alleged that it was false to state that the petitioner did not indicate the documents whose copies he wanted. In paragraph 40 it is stated that the inspection of the record was carried out by the petitioner on 16.9.1997. It is alleged that even on that date the petitioner was not shown the entire record.  6. The petitioner gave a reply to the charge-sheet on 9.10.1997 vide Annexure 12 to the writ petition. In paragraph 42 of the writ petition it is alleged that the petitioner did not commit any breach of instructions and in fact has been scrupulous and meticulous. In paragraph 43 it is stated that the Regional Manager did not raise any objection to the constitution of the Committee. In paragraphs 44 to 59 of the writ petition the petitioner has made various averments on the merits of the matter which were enquired into. The petitioner gave a reply to the second show cause notice through letter dated 30.3.1998 vide Annexure 13 to the writ petition.  7. In paragraph 61 of the writ petition it is stated that while furnishing copy of the enquiry report the corporation had not furnished copy of the supplementary enquiry report. However, the petitioner gave a reply dated 11.3.1998 vide Annexure 14 to the writ petition. Thereafter the impugned dismissal order dated 10.9.1998 was passed.  8. In paragraphs 64 to 69 of the writ petition again various averments on the merits of the matter which were enquired into have been made.  9. In paragraphs 70, 71 and 72 of the writ petition it is alleged that the rules of natural justice were violated as the petitioner was not afforded opportunity of putting his defence in writing not leading his evidence and witnesses. The opportunity to inspect the papers only on 16.9.1997 was meaningless as enquiry report was submitted on 13.9.1997.  10. A counter-affidavit has been filed by the Divisional Logging Manager, Karwi. In paragraph 4 of the same it has been stated that the petitioner had been charge-sheeted for causing loss to the tune of Rs. 2,20,894.40 by doing under-weighment in respect of tendu leaves for 1994 season and causing a total loss of Rs. 5,83,092.00 by disobeying the orders of the higher authority in collusion with his subordinates. In paragraph 6 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the enquiry officer afforded full opportunity to the petitioner in respect of inspection of documents and cross-examination of witnesses. In paragraph 8 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the Managing Director being the appointing and disciplinary authority of the petitioner served a copy of the enquiry report along with the letter dated 26.2.1998 upon the petitioner calling him to show cause. The petitioner sent a reply but it was not found satisfactory and hence the impugned order was passed. In paragraph 9 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the enquiry was conducted in a most impartial and judicious manner in which the petitioner was given full opportunity to place his defence. It was denied that the petitioner was not given opportunity to inspect the record. The petitioner made a complaint dated 25.12.1997 to the enquiry officer that he has not been shown certain papers but the enquiry officer found that the papers pertained to the previous year and a different logging division and those papers were not relevant for the purpose of the present enquiry and hence those irrelevant papers were not supplied to the petitioner. It is further stated in paragraph 9 of the counter-affidavit that the charge of misappropriation to the tune of Rs. 8,03,986.51 was proved against the petitioner. In paragraph 12 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that an adverse entry had been awarded to the petitioner earlier and he was given a warning. In paragraph 20 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the petitioner being incharge of the tendu patta was responsible for storage and weighment and he was found guilty in the enquiry. In paragraph 25 of the counter-affidaivt it is stated that all the necessary papers relevant to the enquiry were supplied to the petitioner. However, those records which had no relevance were not supplied to him. In paragraph 35 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the committee as directed in the Nideshika and by the higher authority was not constituted and persons who were not authorised to be the member of the committee were made members of the committee. In paragraph 43 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the petitioner was found guilty of misappropriating the corporation money and embezzlement. In paragraph 46 of the counter-affidavit it is stated that the shortage up to 2% was deliberately shown by the petitioner for unlawful gain.  11. We have also perused the rejoinder affidavit.  12. The findings recorded by the enquiry officer in the enquiry report are findings of fact and we cannot interfere with the same in writ jurisdiction. It appears that the procedure which was fixed by the forest corporation was that if the shortfall in the weight of bag is less than 2% then the weight should be verified by the logging officer of the division, and in case the shortfall is more than 2% then it should be verified by a committee consisting of the Divisional Logging Manager, logging officer and Godown Officer vide Annexure S.C.A. 4. The petitioner did not follow this procedure and hence he committed misconduct. Neither the competent persons were deputed to verify the weight nor the competent committee as directed by the order dated 18.8.1992 was constituted by the petitioner.  13. It appears that the petitioner did not appear before the enquiry officer. The charge-sheet was tried to be served upon him but he managed to avoid service. Ultimately the Regional Manager of the Corporation constituted a committee of three persons to serve the charge-sheet but the committee also could not find the petitioner in order to serve him. They ultimately pasted the charge-sheet on the petitioner's residence on 15.7.1997 and a press release was given in the newspapers Dainik Jagaran and Rastriya Sahara on 17.7.1997 about the charge-sheet. Thereafter the petitioner received the charge-sheet on 22.7.1997 wherein he was allowed 15 days' time to submit his reply. On 1.8.1997 the petitioner moved an application before the enquiry officer for extending time to file his reply to 21.8.1997 but the petitioner did not file his reply even on 21.8.1997. Hence the enquiry officer had no option but to proceed with the enquiry which he completed on 13.9.1997. The petitioner did not appear before the enquiry officer but on the other hand approached the Managing Director for showing the record and in pursuance to the direction of the Managing Director the petitioner was shown the entire record on 16.9.1997. Thereafter the petitioner filed his reply on 9.10.1997. The Managing Director in order to be fair sent the reply of the petitioner to the enquiry officer to supplement his report and the enquiry officer after going though the reply submitted a supplementary report dated 20.2.1998. The Managing Director sent the enquiry report dated 13.9.1997 and supplementary report dated 20.2.1998 to the petitioner calling upon him to give his reply and the petitioner sent his reply by letter dated 30.3.1998. Thereafter the impugned order was passed.  14. In our opinion, there is no illegality in the procedure adopted by the respondent and there was no violation of natural justice. The petitioner was given full opportunity of placing his defence. The petitioner was avoiding completion of the enquiry and for this purpose he was procrastinating in the matter. It appears that for this reason he insisted that the record pertaining to Obra and Renukoot divisions be shown to him, which were irrelevant.  15. The enquiry officer has gone into the matter in great detail and found the charge against the petitioner proved. It was found that the petitioner gave misleading information about shortfall in the weight of the bad of tendu leaves and the shortfall in the weight was shown for the purpose of misappropriation of money of the corporation in collusion with the subordinate staff. Neither the competent persons nor the competent committee as mentioned in the order dated 18.8.1992 was constituted by the petitioner.  16. In the facts and circumstances of the case we see no reason to interfere with the impugned order. At any event this is not a fit case for interference under Article 226 of the Constitution. The petition is dismissed. No order as to costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 226 and 311 - Dismissal - Misconduct - The petitioner, who was working as a logging officer, was found to have provided false information about the weight of tendu leaves in order to embezzle money - Despite being given ample opportunity to defend himself, he failed to appear before the enquiry officer and avoided service of the charge-sheet - The charge-sheet was eventually posted at his residence and released to the press - The enquiry officer thoroughly investigated the matter and found the charges against the petitioner to be true - The respondent did not violate any procedures or natural justice - There is no reason to interfere with the order of dismissal. [Paras 13, 14, 15 and 16]

text: S. Rajendra Babu, J. - Leave granted.  2. In these cases the appellants were selected by the Bihar Public Service Commission (hereinafter referred to as `Commission') for appointment as Motor Vehicle Inspectors pursuant to an advertisement issued by the Commission on 12.5.1989. The advertisement indicated that candidates possessing the following qualification and experience are eligible for appointment to the said post :  "Qualification :- (Required minimum technical qualification- educational qualification). (Ka) Matriculation (Kha) Diploma in Automobile Engineering or Mechanical Engineering after completing three years course would be necessary from a recognized institution/Board/University. (G) The diploma holder or post diploma holder in Automobile Engineering would be preferred. Note : Such candidates, who have mechanic level qualification related to Motor trade, would not be competent. Experience : (Ka) For the candidates, who after completing three years course of Automobile Engineering have obtained diploma, must possess three years practical experience in an Automobile Engineering Workshop registered under the Factories Act. (Kha) Such candidates, who have obtained diploma in Mechanical Engineering after completing three years course compulsorily, must posses five years practical experience in an Automobile Engineering Institution registered under the Factories Act. (Ga) Candidates having post diploma in Automobile Engineering compulsorily possess two years practical work experience in a workshop of Automobile Engineering institution registered under the Factories Act." 3. When the process of selection was pending, a new rule was introduced in Recruitment Rules requiring the person to be selected as a Motor Vehicle Inspector to possess a driving licence. Pursuant to the selection made by the Commission, the appellants were appointed as Motor Vehicle Inspectors in the year 1991 and they have continued to hold the said posts till date.  4. On the ground that the selected candidates do not possess the qualification or experience in appointment in an appropriate automobile institution registered under the Factories Act, 1948 or they did not possess driving licence, their appointments were challenged by some of the candidates who were not selected in several writ petitions. The learned Single Judge of the High Court who dealt with these writ petition did not examine the contentions raised on behalf of the writ petitioners in the necessary detail with reference to each selected candidate but directed the Transport Commissioner to do that exercise. On appeal, the Division Bench of the High Court set aside the report sent by the Transport Commissioner pursuant to the order made by the learned Single Judge which was received during the pendency of the appeal and directed fresh consideration of the matter by the Transport Commissioner.  5. We fail to understand as to how the matter of selection and appointment to a post could have been entrusted to the Transport Commissioner when the Commission had been specifically entrusted with such a job and such Commission, which is an autonomous authority having a constitutional status, has selected the candidates whose appointments were in challenge. If the selection of these candidates were improper the same should have been set aside with appropriate directions to redo the process of selection or at best, the High Court could have directed the Government, which is the appointing authority, to take appropriate steps in the matter. However, in the facts and circumstances of this case, we need not dilate on this aspect nor do we need to examine various elaborate contentions addressed by either side. Suffice to say that all the selected candidates, who are in employment, except one, possess necessary qualification and in regard to that one excepted candidate, it cannot be disputed that he possessed equivalent qualification. Thus the dispute narrows down to one aspect, that is, the selected candidates may not possess necessary experience which is now required to be examined by the Transport Commissioner.  6. The selected candidates, who have been appointed, are now in employment as Motor Vehicle Inspectors for over a decade. Now that they have worked in such posts for a long time, necessarily they would have acquired the requisite experience. Lack of experience, if any, at the time of recruitment is made good now. Therefore, the new exercise ordered by the High Court will only lead to anomalous results. Since we are disposing of these matters on equitable consideration, the learned counsel for the contesting respondents submitted that their cases for appointment should also be considered. It is not clear whether there is any vacancy for the post of Motor Vehicle Inspectors. If that is so, unless any one or more of the selected candidates are displaced, the cases of the contesting respondents cannot be considered. We think that such adjustment is not feasible for practical reasons. We have extended equitable considerations to such selected candidates who have worked in the post for a long period, but the contesting respondents do not come in that class. The effect of our conclusion is that appointments made long back pursuant to a selection need not be disturbed. Such a view can be derived from several decisions of this Court including the decisions in Ram Sarup v. State of Haryana & Ors., 1979(1) SCC 168; District Collector & Chairman, Vizianagaram Social Welfare Residential School Society, Vizianagaram & Anr. v. M. Tripura Sundari Devi, 1990(3) SCC 655; and H.C. Puttaswamy & Ors. v. The Hon'ble Chief Justice of Karnataka High Court, Bangalore & Ors., 1991 Supp. (2) SCC 421 : 1991(1) SCT 116 (SC). Therefore, we must let the matters lie where they are.  7. In the special features of this case, we set aside the order of the High Court and dismiss the writ petitions. The appeals are, therefore, allowed. No costs.  Appeal allowed.
summary: A. Constitution of India, Articles 226, 319 and 323 - Selection Commission - In case of any defect found in the conduct of selection, the Court can only set it aside and direct the commission or the appointing authority to redo the process of selection - Issuing directions to any other authority will be unconstitutional, as the Commission is the exclusive constitutional authority for selections. [Para 5]  B. Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16 and 226 - Selection and Recruitment - Lack of experience at the time of recruitment can be compensated by working on a post - Terminating the services of a candidate after years of experience on the grounds of lacking experience at the time of recruitment will have unpredictable consequences.  [Para 6]

text: M.R. Agnihotri, J. - This order shall dispose of C.W.P. Nos. 4573 of 1979 (Madan Lal v. Registrar) and 31 of 1980 (B.K. Sethi v. Registrar). Though the cases have come before us on a reference dated 21st November, 1988, by the learned Single Judge of this Court, yet in view of the latest decision of their Lordships of the Supreme Court in Union of India and others v. Mohd. Ramzan Khan, 1991(1) SCT 111 : 1991(1) S.L.R. 159, the matter need not be gone into and both the writ petitions can be disposed of on the short ground as they are covered by the same.  2. After hearing the learned counsel, we find that the principal point involved in the writ petitions has already been decided in Mohd. Ramzan Khan's case (supra), as copy of the inquiry report was not supplied to the petitioners before the final order imposing major punishment of dismissal from service was passed against them.  3. The learned counsel for the respondents tried to distinguish the aforesaid Judgment of their Lordships of the Supreme Court on the ground that the case before the Hon'ble Supreme Court was of a Government servant whereas in the present cases, the petitioners are employees of the Punjab State Cooperative Supply and Marketing Federation Limited, Chandigarh, who are governed by the Punjab State Supply and Marketing Cooperatives Services (Common Cadre) Rules, 1967, and that the judgment of the Supreme Court is only prospective in nature and should not be applied retrospectively to the cases in hand where the impugned orders of dismissal from service were issued before the pronouncement of the judgment in Mohd. Ramzan Khan's case (supra).  4. With respect to the learned counsel, we do not find any merit in either of the pleas raised by him. So far as the applicability of the principles of natural justice is concerned, the relationship of master and servant will not permit any such consideration to be countenanced, the result whereof may place an employee of cooperative society governed by the statutory service rules at allowed level or at a disadvantageous position than an employee of the State Government. Secondly, their Lordships of the Supreme Court while deciding Mohd. Ramzan Khan's case held that the observations, "shall have prospective application and no punishment imposed shall be open to challenge on this ground." This certainly does not mean that the law laid down by their Lordships will not be applicable even to the cases which are sub judice and are still pending adjudication in the High Courts in the country.  5. In view of the aforesaid situation, we allow these petitions and quash the impugned-orders of dismissal dated 23rd May, 1975 (Annexure P.3) as well as the order of the appellate authority dated 5/6 September, 1979 (Annexure P.5) in CWP. No. 4573 of 1979 (Madan Lal's case), and the order of dismissal dated 18th October, 1979/5th November, 1979 (Annexure P.5) in CWP No. 31 of 1980 (B.K. Sethi's case). Resultantly, the petitioners shall be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary and other allowances to which they would have been entitled had the impugned orders of dismissal from service not been against them.  There shall be no order as to costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: According to Articles 141 and 311 of the Constitution of India, authorities must provide delinquent officers a copy of inquiry report before passing the final order of dismissal as a major punishment. The law established by the Supreme Court in Ramzan Khan's case is also applicable to cases pending in High Courts. [Paras 2 and 4]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. - The petitioners, who were recruited as Draftsmen in the Punjab P.W.D. Irrigation Branch are aggrieved by the order, dated June 19, 1991, by which the Government directed that their services be regularised with effect from February 1, 1985 and that their seniority had been finalised by the competent authority vide order dated September 21, 1988 (Annexure P.9) and that the action of the Government in passing the order dated June 19, 1991 (Annexure P.10) is inter alia violative of the principles of natural justice. They claim that the representations submitted by various persons, including respondent Nos. 2 to 59 had been accepted without any notice to them. A few facts may be noticed.  2. The petitioners possess the qualification of Diploma in Engineering. They were selected by a Departmental Selection Committee for appointment to the posts of Draftsmen. Believing that selection for regular appointment could be made only by the Subordinate Service Selection Board, the department appointed the petitioners on ad hoc basis. It is averred that vide letter dated April 7/10, 1981 the categories of posts which required an Engineering Degree or Diploma or a technical degree or diploma were specifically excluded from the purview of the Subordinate Services Selection Board. As such, the recruitment to the Post of Draftsman was not required to be made on the recommendations of the Board. In view of this the office of the Chief Engineer vide letter dated February 1, 1984 recommended that "necessary concurrence of Government to treat the selection of J.Es. and Draftsmen by the Chief Engineer's Committee as regular, may kindly be conveyed at an early date." In pursuance to this recommendation the Government of Punjab in the department of Irrigation and Power issued a letter dated February 1, 1985 approving the selection of Draftsmen made by the Chief Engineer's Selection Committee. As a consequence the Chief Engineer issued an order dated March 7, 1986 (Annexure P.8) observing that the "services of draftsmen selected by the Chief Engineer's Selection Committee, have been regularised from the date, they submitted their joining reports, after having been sponsored for appointment as such, by this office." Thereafter, the seniority list of the Drawing establishment was issued in which the various petitioners were assigned their due position on the basis of their date of joining service.  3. It appears that certain persons, who had been promoted from the posts of Tracers to the post of Draftsmen submitted representations challenging the dates from which the services of the persons, like the petitioners, had been regularised. After examining these representations, the Chief Engineer recommended to the Government that the decision conveyed vide Memo dated February 1, 1985 (Annexure P.7) be reviewed "so that seniority list of Draftsmen may be prepared accordingly to avoid unnecessary litigation and to give due justice to all the Draftsmen working in the department". As a result the Government issued an order dated February 5, 1990 advising that the servicers "of the ad hoc employees selected by the Chief Engineer's Committee.....be regularised from the date on which the Government have approved the selection i.e. 1.2.1985." A copy of this order has been produced on record as Annexure R/2/5. In pursuance to this letter certain further correspondence appears to have ensued. Finally, vide letter dated June 19, 1991, it was directed that the seniority of the Draftsmen who had been appointed on ad hoc basis by the Chief Engineer's Selection Committee should be regularised with effect from February 1, 1986 and their seniority be also fixed from that date i.e. February 1, 1985. Aggrieved by this order the petitioners have approached this Court through the present writ petition. This order has been challenged inter alia on various grounds including that the action was violative grounds including that the action was violative of the principles of natural justice, contrary to the rules governing the service and that vested rights could not be taken away. It was also alleged that the action of the Government was without any legislative sanction and was wholly lacking in jurisdiction.  4. Certain persons, who were likely to be affected by the decision of the writ petition, moved C.M. Petition No. 5661 of 1991 praying that they be impleaded as respondent Nos. 2 to 59. Notice of the application was given to the learned counsel for the petitioners. Finally, vide my order dated November 1, 1991 this prayer was allowed and the applicants were impleaded as respondent Nos. 2 to 59.  5. Separate written statements have been filed on behalf of No. 1 and respondent Nos. 2 to 59.  6. In the written statement filed on behalf of respondent No. 1, it has been inter alia stated that the conditions of service of the petitioners are governed by the provisions of Public Works Department (Irrigation Branch) Draftsmen and Tracers State Service Class-III Rules, 1960. The issuance of the various letters and orders, including those at Annexures P.6, P.7, P.8, P.9 and P.10 has also been admitted. It has been further stated that the orders impugned in this petition are absolutely legal and valid. The averment made on behalf of the petitioners that the order dated February 1, 1985 (Annexure P.7) had been reviewed by the impugned order without affording any opportunity to the petitioners has not been specifically denied. Various other contentions have been controverted. It has, however, been specifically admitted that the post of Draftsman had been taken out of the purview of the Subordinate Services Selection Board and the appointments had been made by the Departmental Selection Committee constituted by the Chief Engineer. It has been further stated that the petitioners do not have an absolute right to seniority. The Government enjoys the"unfettered right to amend the seniority list of the petitioners in accordance with the rules and the regulations and the policy of the Government as per Annexure P/10. To the same effect is the written statement filed on behalf of respondents Nos. 2 to 59. A replication was filed on behalf of the petitioners, with which two documents were produced.  7. I have heard Mr. Sarjit Singh, learned counsel for the petitioners and M/s J.S. Khehar and S.S. Dhaliwal for the respondents. The primary contention raised on behalf of the petitioners is that the action of the Government in reviewing the order dated February 1, 1985 by which the proposal of the Chief Engineer for the regularisation of the services of the petitioners had been approved without giving any notice to the petitioners was violative of the principles of natural justice. It was contended that in pursuance to the order dated February 1, 1985 (Annexure P.7), the Chief Engineer had issued an order dated March 7, 1986 regularising the services of the petitioners with effect from the date they submitted their joining reports. Still further, the seniority of the Drawing establishment which included the petitioners was finally determined. An extract from that list has been appended as Annexure P.9. Subsequently, the Government had issued the impugned order by which the date of regularisation was changed from the date of joining to February 1, 1985. It was further directed that the seniority of the petitioners would be determined on that basis. As a result the impugned order affected the seniority and other chances of promotion of the petitioners. It was also pointed out that this order deprived the petitioners of a vested right inasmuch as their seniority which had already been finalised was sought to be changed to their prejudice. Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents conceded that no hearing was given to the petitioners and others who were likely to be affected by the issue of the impugned order.  8. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and having perused the record of the case, I find that vide orders dated April 7/10, 1981 the posts requiring a technical degree or diploma had been taken out of the purview of the Board. As such the selection and recruitment was not required to be made through the agency of the Board. It was on account of this fact that the Chief Engineer had made a recommendation to the Government for the grant of approval to the selections. This approval had been accorded by the Government by its letter dated February 1, 1985. In pursuance to this approval by the Government the services of the petitioners had been regularised from the date they had submitted their joining reports. Even their seniority had been determined on that basis. Once this had happened, certain persons, like respondent Nos. 2 to 59, who had been promoted from the posts of Tracers submitted representations. Those representations were considered by the Chief Engineer and a recommendation was made to the Government for reviewing the order. The Government reviewed the order on February 5, 1990 and conveyed the final directions vide its letter of June 19, 1991. During all this process neither the Chief Engineer nor the Government afforded any opportunity whatsoever to the petitioners. If an opportunity had been afforded the petitioners could have brought the full facts to the notice of the competent authority and shown that the post had been taken out of the purview of the board, the Selection Committee had been properly constituted; the constitution of the Selection Committee and the actual selections made by the Committee had been duly approved by the Government, the appointments of the petitioners had been duly regularised by the competent authority with effect from the date of the submission of the joining reports; the appointments had been wrongly made on ad hoc basis and in fact they had to be made on regular basis from the inception and that there was no reason or rule justifying the review of the action by the Government. Failure to grant a hearing to the petitioners deprived them of an opportunity to bring the relevant facts to the notice of the authority. As a result by the issue of the impugned order, the seniority etc. of the petitioners were bound to be adversely affected. The course of action adopted by the Government was violative of the principles of natural justice. It resulted in a material miscarriage of justice. It vitiates the action of the Government in reviewing the order dated February 1, 1985.  9. In view of may above finding, I do not consider it necessary to go into the other contentions raised on behalf of the petitioners.  10. Accordingly, the writ petition is allowed. The order dated June 19, 1991 (Annexure P.10) is quashed. Since an interim direction had been given on July 16, 1991 for maintenance of status quo and the respondents have not changed the seniority list etc., no further directions by way of grant of consequential relief are required to be issued. C.M. Application No. 4673 of 1991 has, thus, become infructuous and is disposed of as such. In the circumstances of the case, I make no order as to costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Seniority/Regularisation of services/Hearing/Natural justice - Duly appointed petitioners through departmental committee must have their services regularised from their joining dates, and their seniority assigned accordingly. However, their seniority was disturbed without giving them an opportunity to defend themselves against the representations of promotees. The government must provide an opportunity for petitioners to bring all relevant facts in their favour before taking any action. The government's decision to disturb seniority without giving the affected persons a hearing violates the principles of natural justice and denies them justice. Therefore, the order must be quashed due to the violation of principles of natural justice - Punjab PWD (Irrigation Branch) Draftsmen and Tracers State service Class-III Rules, 1960. [Para 8]

text: Viney Mittal, J. - The present Regular Second Appeal has been filed by the plaintiff Anil Mehta, whose suit for declaration had been originally decreed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rohtak but on appeal filed by the State of Haryana (defendants), the said suit was dismissed after accepting the aforesaid appeal.  2. A suit for declaration was filed by the plaintiff stating that he was a member of the Civil Services of the State of Haryana serving in the Medical Hospital, Rohtak, employed as Senior Photographer since January, 1978. The plaintiff claimed himself to be a regular Government employee. Vide order dated April 10, 1980 passed by the Director Principal Medical College, Rohtak, he was ordered to be removed from service. The aforesaid order was challenged by the plaintiff on the ground that the same was punitive in nature and although framed innocuously, was in fact meant to inflict punishment on him for no fault of his whatsoever. It was further stated by the plaintiff in the plaint that earlier also on August 12, 1978, a termination order had been passed against the plaintiff. The plaintiff had filed a civil suit challenging the aforesaid earlier order dated August 12, 1978. The State Government had filed a written statement in the aforesaid case and the stand taken was that the matter against the plaintiff would be enquired into and necessary orders as per the Rules would be passed in case he was found responsible for any charge. The plaintiff maintained that on the aforesaid stand taken by the defendant in the written statement, he withdrew his suit. Thereafter the plaintiff was allowed to continue in service. According to the plaintiff, the present order dated April 10, 1980 is founded on charges of serious misconduct, which have never been enquired into nor any charge sheet had ever been served upon him and therefore, although he was infact sought to be removed on the charges of misconduct but the order of removal has been couched in a simplicitor language of termination. The validity of the aforesaid order has been challenged on various grounds.  3. The defendant, upon a notice of the suit, appeared. It contested the suit. A written statement was filed, wherein the stand taken by the defendant was that the appointment of the plaintiff was made as a Senior Photographer. It was stated that the plaintiff could not apply in pursuance to the advertisement No. 13/77 published in different newspaper but be merely submitted an application on a plain paper. The plaintiff was also required to give the proof of his experience for 7 years as photographer in some recognized Government/public or private organisation/Agency. The defendants maintained that the certificates provided by the plaintiff were examined in the Rohtak University and it was found that the plaintiff was not eligible for the post and as he was merely self-employed and his experience certificates were not authentic, the Selection Committee of the University considered his name as a special case subject to his furnishing the eligibility certificate with regard to experience. Thereafter the plaintiff arranged to obtain a certificate dated October 27, 1977 to the effect that the plaintiff was running a Photography Establishment at Rohtak since June 26, 1968. Even this certificate did not fulfil the eligibility conditions laid down by the Selection Committee. However, the plaintiff was appointed on purely temporary basis against a temporary post with further condition that he was not to be treated as a member of the civil Services of the State of Haryana. A categorical stand was taken by the defendants that the termination order did not imply to inflict any punishment on the plaintiff but since the plaintiff did not fulfil the prescribed qualifications/eligibility, therefore, the order of termination had been passed. The defendants have further maintained that the services of the plaintiff were terminated as per the terms and conditions of his appointment letter dated April 10, 1980, wherein it was specifically provided that his services were terminable without any notice on either side till he becomes a regular employee. Thus asserting that the order of termination of the plaintiff was a simplicitor order of termination, casting no stigma upon him, and was therefore, fully was legal and valid and was in accordance with the terms and conditions of the appointment letter issued to the plaintiff.  4. The learned trial Court decreed the suit filed by the plaintiff. The matter was taken up in appeal by the State of Haryana. The learned District Judge, vide his judgment and decree dated July 16, 1982 accepted the aforesaid appeal filed by the defendant and consequently dismissed the suit filed by the plaintiff. The plaintiff has now filed the present regular second appeal challenging the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge.  5. I have heard Shri D.S. Bali, learned Senior counsel appearing for the appellant and Shri G.P.S. Nagra, learned Assistant Advocate General, Haryana, appearing for the respondents and with their assistance have also gone through the record of the case.  6. Shri D.S. Bali, learned senior counsel appearing for the plaintiff has reiterated the various pleas raised by the plaintiff in his plaint, to challenge the order dated April 10, 1980, whereby the services of the appellant have been terminated. Shri Bali has submitted that in fact prior to the passing of the order under challenge, an earlier order had been passed against the plaintiff on August 12, 1978. The aforesaid order had been challenged by the plaintiff by filing an earlier suit. In the written statement filed by the State of Haryana, in the aforesaid civil suit, it was conceded by the State that the case of the plaintiff would be "enquired into and necessary order will then be passed as per Rules, if found responsible for any charge........." On the basis of the aforesaid stand taken by the defendant in the earlier written statement, Shri Bali submits that the present order dated April 10, 1980 was not different from the earlier order and once the defendant had undertaken to proceed into the matter by holding an enquiry, it was not open to the authorities now to pass the order of termination without taking resort to the disciplinary proceedings.  7. On the other hand, Shri G.P.S. Nagra, learned Assistant Advocate General, Haryana has submitted that the stand taken by the defendants in the earlier written statement could not be used as a defence by the plaintiff in the present case in as much as in the earlier written statement also the defendants had merely stated that the case of the plaintiff would be examined and if he was found responsible for any charges, then enquiry into the matter would he held. However, according to Shri Nagra, the present order has been passed by the defendant not on the basis of any charges but in terms of the appointment order itself and was an order simplicitor for dispensing with the services of the plaintiff. On that basis Shri Nagra has further submitted that since the plaintiff was a temporary employee and was not fulfilling the requisite eligibility conditions with regard to his experience, therefore, his services were liable to be dispensed with/terminated without any notice in terms of the appointment letter itself.  8. I have given my thoughtful consideration to the entire matter. In my considered opinion, the order dated April 10, 1980 by means of which the services of the petitioner have been terminated could not be termed to be an order casting any stigma upon the plaintiff giving him any cause for making a grievance. The said order was not shown to be founded on any misconduct. Nothing has been pointed out by Shri Bali from the record of the case to show that the defendant authorities had ever found the involvement of plaintiff in any case of misconduct or that any charges were sought to be levelled against him or that any disciplinary proceedings were contemplated against him. The order dated April 10, 1980 passed by the Director Principal of the Medical College is exhibit P-4 on record. It reads as under :-  "As your services are no longer required, the Governing Body of Medical College, Rohtak has terminated your services with immediate effect under the terms and conditions contained in your appointment letter No. 1/ME- II/78/287 dated 7.1.1978." Faced with this difficulty, the learned counsel for the appellant has relied upon a judgment of the Gujrat High Court in 1981(2) SLR 622, Bhavansinh Ravsinhji Rathod v. State of Transport Corporation Ahmedabad and another, wherein it has been held that even in a case where there is an innocuous order of termination of services, the Court is competent to screen and X-ray innocent looking order. It may be that order in the garb of discharge is in fact a penal order. The learned counsel has further place reliance on a judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Gujarat Steel Tubes Limited v. Gujarat Steel Tubes Mazdoor Sabha and others, AIR 1980 S.C. 1896, to canvass the proposition that the form of the order of termination or the language in which it is couched is not conclusive and the Court is well within its powers to lift the veil to see the true nature of the order.  9. I have gone through the aforesaid judgments relied upon by the learned counsel for the appellant, but in my considered view both these judgments are not applicable to the facts of the present case. There is nothing on record to show that the plaintiff was involved in any misconduct or that at any stage any action for any such misconduct was envisaged against him. In fact the plaintiff was appointed vide appointment letter dated January 7, 1978. A copy of the aforesaid appointment letter is proved on the record as exhibit R-1. It might be pertinent to notice Clause 6 of the aforesaid appointment letter at this stage :-  "This appointment is terminable without any notice on either side till it becomes regular after the verification of your antecedents." 10. It has not been shown by the plaintiff that at any stage his services were ever regularised. No order in this regard has been produced on record by him. Thus the plaintiff, till his termination, was apparently a temporary employee. In such a situation, Clause 6 of the appointment letter empowered the authorities to dispense with the services without the issuance of any notice.  11. Shri G.P.S. Nagra, learned Assistant Advocate General, Haryana has also relied upon the law laid down by the Apex Court in Birla VXL Ltd. v. State of Punjab and others, 1999(1) SCT 263 (SC) : 1998(4) RSJ 311 and Chandra Prakash Shahi v. State of U.P. and others, 2000(2) RSJ 741, to contend that in the case of a temporary employee, the services can be terminated on the ground of unsuitability and in such a situation the order of termination was a simplicitor order and did not attract the provisions of Article 16 nor the protection of Article 311(2) of the Constitution of India. It was also held that such an order did not cast any stigma unless and until it was shown that the order had been passed on some other considerations. On the basis of the aforesaid law it is maintained by the learned counsel appearing for the respondent that the order dated April 10, 1980 was not stigmatic and was perfectly within the power and domain of the competent authority.  12. I agree with the submissions made by the learned counsel appearing for the respondent and find that the order dated April 10, 1980 passed by the Director Principal of the Medical College did not cast any stigma upon the plaintiff nor was the same punitive in nature.  13. Thus finding no merit in the present appeal, the same is hereby dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: When the order of termination is a simplicitor order and does not cast any stigma upon the employee, the services of a temporary employee can be terminated on the grounds of unsuitability as per the Constitution of India, Articles 16 & 31. The employee's services were not proven to be regularised, and no allegation of any kind was levelled against him, so the termination order was not illegal. [Paras 8, 10 & 11]

text: Nirmal Singh, J. - Through the medium of the present petition, the petitioner seeks direction in the nature of certiorari quashing Order No. Estt/Resign/126 BN/2001/285-91 dated 19th January 2001, whereby the resignation of the petitioner has been accepted without pensionary benefits. Further direction is also sought in the nature of mandamus commanding the respondents to allow the petitioner to resume duty against the post on which he was working as also to pay him salary by treating the petitioner in service.  2. Brief facts of the case are that the petitioner came to be appointed as constable in Border Security Force on 20th July 1986. After undergoing the basic training, the petitioner was posted in 78th Bn BSF and served various parts of the country. The petitioner was promoted as Lance Naik and posted as such in 126th Bn BSF. While the petitioner was posted in aforesaid Battalion, a case under sections 19-A, 22-E and 26 of BSF Act came to be registered against him on the grounds that the petitioner absented himself without prior permission from Bn. Headquarters on 8th October 2000, brought liquor in the Unit on 9th October 2000 as also found in drunken state on 5th December 2000. Charge-sheet was framed against the petitioner vide No. Estt/ROE/SL/126BN/2000/11741-45 dated 6th December 2000 but no proceedings were initiated against him even after framing the charge-sheet. According to the petitioner, the respondents through coercive method got his signatures on the papers and vide impugned Order No. Estt/Resign/126 BN/2001/285-91 dated 10th January 2001, accepted the resignation of the petitioner without pensionary benefits. Further the respondents vide another Order No. Estt/126BN/Resign/2001/58 dated 15th January 2001 struck the petitioner from the roll of BSF and turned him out from the unit where he was posted. The petitioner approached the respondents for allowing him to continue in service, requested them not to give effect to his resignation as also order dated 10th January 2001. Further case of the petitioner is that order dated 10th January 2001 was required to be withdrawn as the petitioner signed the documents without any knowledge what was stated therein. The petitioner preferred representation under Rules 167 and 168 of the BSF Rules for allowing him to resume duty and also treat him on duty but till date they have not considered the representation.  3. On being put to notice, counter has been filed on behalf of the respondents stating therein that the petitioner was enrolled in Border Security Force on 21.7.1986 as constable. After completion of basic training, the petitioner was posted to 126 Bn. The petitioner was found absent without proper permission from the aforementioned Unit without proper permission on 8.10.2000 and reported on 9.10.2000. The petitioner was medically examined and found in the state of intoxication. The petitioner was advised by the respondent- authorities to improve himself otherwise he will be dealt under BSF Act and Rules. It is further stated that on 3.12.2000, when the troops were fallen at Bn. HQ for Arms cleaning, the petitioner was again found absent from the unit line. On searching, he was found in a civilian house in an intoxicated condition in the nearby village. The petitioner was medically examined from PHC 82 Mile Dist Dhalai. The Second Command of 126 Bn. BSF was directed to record the evidence against the petitioner for offence under BSF Act. The petitioner also earned 4 bad entries during his service and he was habitually absentee. While the recording of Evidence was in progress, the petitioner approached respondent No. 5 as also Staff Officer of Unit and requested for early acceptance of his resignation as the petitioner was unable to serve in BSF due to domestic problems. The petitioner was advised by the respondent- authorities to continue in service but he insisted upon the respondents to accept his resignation. Keeping in view his previous record of the petitioner as also to maintain discipline in the force, the resignation of the petitioner was accepted by Unit Commander on 10th January 2001. After acceptance of the resignation of the petitioner, the recording of evidence was withdrawn.  4. Grievance of the petitioner is that order dated 10th January 2001 impugned in the present petition is against law and rules because the respondents could not struck the petitioner from the roll of BSF as there was disciplinary proceedings pending against him. According to BSF Regulations, once a disciplinary proceedings are set against a BSF personnel it must be brought to its finality. The respondents through coercive steps got his signatures on papers and thereafter issued order dated 19th January 2001 whereby resignation of the petitioner without pensionary benefits has been accepted. Further grievance of the petitioner is that without initiating the proper proceedings, the respondents could not be struck the petitioner from the roll of BSF.  5. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and perusing the record, I am of the considered view that this petition has no merit and deserves to be dismissed.  6. Admittedly, the petitioner was booked under Sections 19(a), 22E and 26 of BSF Act for the offence committed by him. According to Section 19(2) of BSF Act if a member of the force absents without leave, he on conviction by a Security Force Court, shall be liable to suffer imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or such less punishment as is mentioned in said section. In terms of Section 22(e) of the said Act, if a member of the force neglects to obey any general, local or other order, on conviction by a Security Force Act he shall be liable to suffer imprisonment for a term which may extend, in the case of the offences specified in clauses (d) and (e) to two years and in the case of the offences specified in the other, clauses to ten years or in either case such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. In terms of Section 26 of the said Act, any person of the force who is found in a state of intoxication, whether on duty or not, on conviction by a Security Force Court, shall be liable to suffer imprisonment for a term which may extended to six months or such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. Earlier the petitioner was advised by the respondents to improve himself and the petitioner also earned four bad entries during service.  7. Perusal of the record reveals that when the petitioner was being tried under the aforementioned sections and the recording of evidence was in progress, the petitioner was apprehending that he will be convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment, he at once tendered his resignation on the ground of domestic problem before the respondents. Thereafter, the petitioner also appeared in person before the Commandant as well as Staff of the Unit where he was posted and made a verbal request for acceptance of his resignation as he was unable to serve the Border Security Force due to domestic problem. On the request of the petitioner, the Commandant of the Unit accepted the resignation tendered by the petitioner vide order impugned dated 10th January 2001 and accordingly, he was struck from the strength of the Border Security Force with effect from 15.01.2001 in accordance with BSF Rule 1969. After acceptance of the resignation of the petitioner, the respondents in their wisdom thought it fit to withdraw the proceedings pending before the Summary Security Force Court against the petitioner. Accordingly, proceedings were withdrawn. The competent authority had no motive to get the signatures of the petitioner on the blank paper for converting into the same as resignation of the petitioner. It is the petitioner, who on his own tendered his resignation before the respondents due to domestic problems. Learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that when the signatures of the petitioner have been obtained under coercion, same cannot be used against him. In the present case there is no iota of evidence that the respondents got signatures of the petitioner on the blank paper through coercive method. Perusal of the record shows that the petitioner had tendered resignation due to fear of the conviction under BSF Act. The plea of the learned counsel for the petitioner that through coercive steps the respondents got the signatures of the petitioner on the blank paper with an motive to use the same against him, cannot be accepted.  8. In order to strengthen the case of the petitioner, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner has placed reliance on various judgments of the Apex Court reported as Punjab National Bank v. P.K. Mittal, (AIR 1989 SC 1083), Nand Keshwar Prasad v. Indian Farmers Fertilizers, 1999(1) SCT 276 : (1998)5 SCC 461), Shambhu Murari Sinha v. Project and Development India Ltd. & another, 2002(2) SCT 400 : (AIR 2002 SC 1341), Raj Kumar & Ors v. Union of India & Anr., 2006(1) SCT 456 : (2006(1) Supreme 159). Plain reading of the aforementioned judgments of the Apex Court does not help the case of the petitioner because issues involved in all these aforementioned cases are different in nature and does not relate to the issue involved in the present petition of the petitioner.  9. Before accepting the resignation of the petitioner, the petitioner was time and again briefed and advised by the respondents to continue in service but the petitioner insisted them for acceptance of his resignation due to domestic problem. Keeping in view the previous record of the petitioner as also repeated requests made by him, the resignation tendered by the petitioner was accepted by the Unit Commandant vide impugned order and accordingly the petitioner was discharged from the roll of the BSF. Therefore, the impugned order passed by the respondents is legal and justifiable in the eye of law.  In view of the above, there is no merit in this petition and as such same is dismissed.  Petition dismissed.
