Present respondents filed a writ appeal before the High Court questioning correctness of the judgment. The High Court noticed that the view expressed by the Division Bench in P. Nageswara Rao's case (supra) was dis-approved by this Court in A.P.S.R.T.C. v. S. Narsagoud, 2003(4) SCT 785 : (2003(2) SCC 212) and, therefore, allowed the writ appeal directing dismissal of the writ petition.  4. In support of the appeal, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that when an order of re-instatement is passed for all practical purposes there will be continuity in service and, when the re-instatement is done the pay has to be fixed after taking into consideration the notional increments which would have otherwise accrued.  5. Learned counsel for the respondents on the other hand supported the order passed by the High Court.  6. The principles of law on the point are no more res integra. This Court in S. Narsagoud's case (supra) succinctly crystallized principle of law in para 9 of the judgment :  "We find merit in the submission so made. There is a difference between an order of reinstatement accompanied by a simple direction for continuity of service and a direction where reinstatement is accompanied by a specific direction that the employee shall be entitled to all the consequential benefits, which necessarily flow from reinstatement or accompanied by a specific direction that the employee shall be entitled to the benefit of the increments earned during the period of absence. In our opinion, the employee after having been held guilty of unauthorized absence from duty cannot claim the benefit of increments notionally earned during the period of unauthorized absence in the absence of a specific direction in that regard and merely because he has been directed to be reinstated with the benefit of continuity in service." 7. The position was re-iterated in A.P. State Road Transport Corporation and Ors. v. Abdul Kareem, 2007(1) R.A.J. 493 : (2005(6) SCC 36). In view of what has been stated by this Court in S. Narsagoud and Abdul Kareem cases (supra), there is no merit in this appeal which is accordingly dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: According to Section 17 of the Industrial Disputes Act, a Labour Court's order for reinstatement of a worker does not necessarily entitle the worker to fixation of pay after accounting for notional increments earned during their absence. This is because there is a difference between an order for reinstatement with a simple direction for continuity of service and an order where reinstatement is accompanied by a specific direction for entitlement to all consequential benefits, including increments earned during the period of absence. The case 2003(4) SCT 785 (SC) is referred to for support. [Para 6]

text: H.S. Bedi, A.C.J. (Oral) - The appellant-writ petitioner was enrolled in the Indian Army on 22.3.1955 and was invalidated out of service on the recommendation of the medical board in the year 1963 and was placed in medical category `EEE' with his disability assessed at 100%. He was accordingly granted disability pension consisting of both elements i.e. disability and service. The appellant continued to draw his disability pension upto the year 1973, when his disability was re-assessed by the Re-survey Medical Board and it was reduced to below 20%. As a consequence thereof, the respondents declined the disability pension to the appellant. The appeal filed by the appellant was rejected on 20.10.1989. Aggrieved by the said order, the appellant filed Civil Writ Petition No. 837 of 1999, which too was dismissed by a learned Single Judge vide impugned judgment dated October 7, 2002, on the plea that as the Re-Survey Medical Board had assessed the disability at less than 20%, the appellant was not entitled to the disability pension and that if at all, he was entitled to special gratuity only on that account. Hence, the present appeal.  2. Mr. Rajesh Sehgal, the learned counsel for the appellant, has argued that though the appellant may not be entitled to the grant of disability pension but he was nevertheless entitled to service pension as provided by rule 183 read with 186 of the Pension Regulations for the Army from the time when he was invalidated from the service. He has, in this connection, relied upon a Division Bench judgment of this Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 12311 of 1996 (Ex. Sigmn Amarjit Singh v. Union of India and others, decided on 27.2.1997, copy appended as Annexure P-10 to the paper book. In this judgment, it has been categorically held that in case the disability was assessed at below 20%, the claimant would not have any right to get disability element of the pension but he would nevertheless be entitled to the service element of the pension for life. Mr. Sehgal informs us that a Special Leave Petition filed against the abovesaid judgment had been dismissed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.  We accordingly, while following the aforesaid judgment, allow the appeal and direct that the appellant would have his arrears for a period of three years prior to the date of filing of the writ petition.  Appeal allowed.
summary: Pension Regulations for the Army, Rule 183 - Constitution of India, Article 16 - A member serving in the Army who has a disability below 20% is not eligible for disability pension, but may receive service pension. This was established in the case of Sigmn Amarjit Singh v. Union of India, Civil Writ Petition No. 12311 of 1996, decided on 27.2.1997. [Para 2]

text: Amarjeet Chaudhary, J. - This writ petition is filed by Constable Zile Singh of Haryana Police, seeking direction to the respondents to depute him to Lower School Course. The petitioner has claimed his admission to the said course on the basis of his excellent performance in the written test and has challenged the admission of respondents 5 to 8 to the course which had commenced on July 1, 1991,  2. The case of the petitioner is that he alongwith 55 other Constables had appeared in the written test but only 55 were declared successful. Respondent No. 5 Bhup Singh had failed in the written test. Despite that, he had been selected for admission to the Lower School Course. The other plea is that Kanshi Ram respondent No. 6 had never appeared in the test. But he too has been deputed for training to the said course. The counsel contended that the candidates who were close to the High dignitaries have been deputed for training to the Lower School Course in violation of the provisions of the Punjab Police Rules. The counsel further contended that the names of the selected candidates are entered in the list in order of merit determined by the Departmental Promotion Committee, on the basis of the tests and parade, written test, interview and examination of service record. The candidate has to obtain at least 50% marks in each of the tests. Kanshi Ram respondent No. 6 had obtained only 5 marks in the examination of service record and as such he should not have been deputed to the Lower School Course. It has also been argued that the respondents had awarded more than the prescribed marks on the assessment of service record which is contrary to the Punjab Police Rules. According to the learned counsel the petitioner was higher in merit in view of his performance in the tests. Despite that, he has not been deputed to the said course in an arbitrary manner.  3. In the reply filed by the Superintendent of Police, Sirsa, respondent No. 4, on behalf of respondents 1 to 4, it has been stated that 419 Constables including two lady Constables were eligible to appear in B-I test held on 15.1.1991 at Sirsa. 339 Constables including two lady Constables appeared in B-I test on 15.1.1991. 56 Constables including Bhup Singh respondent No. 5 had passed the written test and had secured 26 marks out of 50. The respondents have denied that any list was displayed. The result was announced verbally on 16.1.1991 at Police Lines, Sirsa. 32 seats were allocated to Sirsa district. 56 Constables had qualified the written test out of whom 54 had qualified all the tests. Therefore, merit list was prepared in accordance with the provisions of Rule 13.7 of the Punjab Police Rules (hereinafter referred to as the Rules) as applicable in the State of Haryana and the selection was made accordingly. The name of the petitioner figured at serial No. 50 of the list and had secured only 60 marks. As per the seats allocated i.e. 32, the Constable at Serial No. 32 had secured 68-1/2 marks. The respondents have denied that Kanshi Ram respondent No. 6 had not appeared in the test. It has been stated that Kanshi Ram had appeared in the examination and selected for training on the basis of performance in the written test. In Para 5 of the written statement it has been categorically denied that only 15 marks are allotted for Character Roll.  4. The learned Deputy Advocate General had contended that there are no fixed marks for the assessment of service record which is done on the basis of education, courses passed and commendation certificate during service. It was argued with vehemence by the Deputy Advocate General that candidates were selected on the basis of their performance in parade, written test, interview and examination of service record.  5. On the direction of the Court, the respondents have also produced the case file pertaining to the selection of candidates to the Lower School Course.  6. I have considered the respective submissions of the counsel for the parties and perused the paper book.  7. In order to appreciate the arguments of the learned counsel or the parties, it will be worthwhile to advert to the Provisions of Punjab Police Rules. Relevant extract of Rule 13.7 of the Rules is as under :  "..... Names shall be entered in the order of merit, determined by the Departmental Promotion Committee on the basis of tests in  (i) Parade, (ii) Written test in general law, (iii) Interview and (iv) Examination of Service record;" The interview and examination of service record do not constitute test in view of the abovesaid provision of the rules.  Sub-Rule (3) of the Rules reads as :  ".......  The candidates will have to obtain at least 50% of the marks in each test. The maximum marks for each test shall be 100. The syllabus for the parade and written test shall be prescribed by the Inspector-General through a Standing order, which may be reviewed after every three years."  (4) "The assessment of service record will be done on the basis of education, courses passed and commendation certificates earned during the service. The marks assigned to these shall be as follows :  i) Education : B.A. and above ... 5 marks Matric and above ... 3 marks Middle and above ... 2 marks ii) Course passed : Courses upto 1 month duration ... 1 mark Courses upto 3 months duration ... 2 marks Courses upto 6 months duration ... 3 marks Courses upto 9 months duration ... 4 marks Courses exceeding 9 months duration ... 5 marks iii) Commendation certificates : Class I 3 marks Class II 2* subject Class III 1* to a maximum of 15 marks for both 8. A perusal of the extract of sub-rule (1) of Rule 13.7 of the Rules reveals that only two tests have been prescribed, i.e. parade and written test. The interview and examination of service record by no stretch of imagination can be held to be tests. Marks in the interview are given on the performance in interview and the marks for the examination of service record are given on the basis of education, courses passed and commendation certificates earned during service. The examination of record too is not a test. The rule is that a candidate has to obtain 50 per cent of the marks in each test i.e. written and parade tests.  A candidate is to secure 50% marks in these two tests and is not required to obtain 50% marks in interview and examination of service record.  The contention of the petitioner's counsel that more than 15 marks cannot be assigned for examination of service record does not find favour with the Court. The break-up of the marks assigned for assessment of service record has been given in sub-rule (4) of Rule 13.7 of the Rules. A candidate under group (i) cannot be given more than 5 marks for education. A candidate who has passed all the courses under group (ii) will be entitled to 15 marks. Under group (iii) if a candidate is in possession of commendation certificate of Class I he shall be entitled to three marks, for Class II, 2 marks and for Class III, 1 mark subject to a maximum of 15 for both. A Graduate candidate who had passed all the courses and is in possession of Class-I, Class-II and Class-III certificates, he will be entitled to 28 marks. In view of this it cannot be said that marks are to be assigned from only 15 marks as no limit is prescribed under sub-rule (4).  9. The relevant merit of the petitioner vis-a-vis other respondents 5 to 8 is as under :-  Candidate Law Paper Parade Interview Record Total Devi Singh 28-1/2 24 4 19 75-1/2 Ranbir Singh 25-1/2 24 4 18 71-1/2 Bhup Singh 26 22 4 18 70 Kanshi Ram 36-1/2 24 4 5 69-1/2 Zile Singh, (Petitioner) 25 16 3 16 60 10. The petitioner had secured 50th position and no candidate, who was lower in merit to the petitioner, has been deputed for training to the Lower School Course. The respondents had prepared a merit list of 54 candidates out of which only 30 candidates have been deputed, the last being Kanshi Ram, respondent No. 6. I find no illegality in the impugned selection of Constables for admission to Lower School Course.  11. For the foregoing reasons, the writ petition is dismissed being devoid of any merit. Parties are, however, left to bear their own costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 16 and 226 - Punjab Police Rules, 1934, Rule 13.7(1) Extract of - Selection of constables for admission to Lower School Course - Two prescribed tests: parade and written test - Interview and examination of service record not considered tests - Passing score of 50% required for parade and written test, not for interview and examination - Petitioner ranked 50th and no lower-ranked candidate sent for training - Merit list of 54 candidates created, only 30 deputed for training - Impugned selection of Constables for admission of Lower School Course deemed legal. [Paras 8 and 10]

text: D.S. Sinha, J. - Order-sheet indicates that instant petition was filed on 15.1.1998 and was directed to come up on 19.1.1998. However, the petition came up on 20.1.1998 on which date a supplementary-affidavit was filed. The case was directed to be listed after three weeks. Next date fixed in the case was 25.11.1998. The order-sheet of that date indicates that the learned counsel for the petitioners was directed to file an amended petition within two days. Thereafter, the matter was before the Court on 8.1.1999, and the Court passed the following order :-  "Hon'ble M. Katju, J. Hon'ble R.K. Singh, J. As prayed list on 27.1.1999 along with the record of Second Appeal No. 2110 of 1987 showing the name of counsel for the parties in that appeal also. It is made clear that both these cases will be heard and disposed of on that date. This order has been passed in presence of Sri U.S. Awasthi, counsel for the respondents. Sd./-  M. Katju  Sd./-  R.K. Singh" 2. The order-sheet dated 27.1.1999 indicates that again, on prayer being made in that regard, the Court directed the case to be listed along with Second Appeal No. 2110 of 1987 on 23.2.1999. While passing the order the Court also passed an order making it clear that the case would be heard and decided finally on the date fixed. But, on 23.2.1999 the case was left out. It came up before the Court on 11.3.1999. On 11.3.1999 Shri Santosh Kumar Tripathi, one of the two learned counsel, appearing for the petitioners, requested that the case be passed over and listed in the next cause list. The prayer was accepted. The case was up before the Court on 20.7.1999 and it was directed to come up the next day i.e. 21.7.1999. On 21.7.1999 the case was directed to be listed in the next week on the request of the counsel.  3. After lapse of about one year, on 3.7.2000, the case was listed again. On this day Shri Santosh Kumar Tripathi, one of the two counsel appearing for the petitioners, stated that the other counsel Shri U.K. Shandilya had instructions to argue the case but he was out of station. On this statement Shri Tripathi prayed that the case might be adjourned for the day. The prayer of Shri Tripathi was accepted. The petition was listed again on 11.7.2000. But, it was passed over as Shri Santosh Kumar Tripathi had sent an illness slip praying for adjournment of the case and the case was adjourned. On 19.7.2000 when the case was listed next Shri Santosh Kumar Tripathi again sent an illness slip praying for adjournment of the case. The illness slip of Shri Tripathi was honoured and the case was adjourned.  4. Now the case is up for consideration today. Shri Santosh Kumar Tripathi, one of the two counsels appearing for the petitioners, is present and prays for adjournment of the case on the ground that Shri U.K. Shandilya is not available. Shri Tripathi insists that the case must be adjourned and refuses to argued the case despite being invited repeatedly.  5. It is not the stand of Shri Tripathi that he has ceased to be counsel for the petitioners. It is also not the case of Shri Tripathi that he has no instructions to argue the case.  6. Indeed, from the demeanour of Shri Tripathi, it appears that he wants to compel the Court to accept his request for adjournment of the case. At this stage, it will be relevant to notice that the prayer for adjournment is oral. There is no application in writing stating full facts and circumstances constituting sufficient cause warranting adjournment of the case as required by Rule 12 of Chapter VI of the Rules of Court, 1952 which provides procedure for motion for adjournment of any case.  7. In view of the fact that the case has been pending for admission for more than two and a half years; that the case has been adjourned at the behest of the learned counsel for the petitioner on a number of occasions, specially on the last three consecutive occasions, to be precise, on 3.7.2000, 11.7.2000 and 19.7.2000; and that there is no application giving sufficient cause for adjournment, the Court declines to entertain the oral prayer for adjournment and once again invites Shri Santosh Kumar Tripathi to argue the case. Shri Tripathi again insists for adjournment and refuses to argue and assist the Court in deciding the case.  8. It is to be remembered that for so long as his engagement is not terminated by the litigant after obtaining leave of the Court or he is permitted by the Court to withdraw from the case an Advocate appearing in a case is legally obliged to conduct the case, and refusal to do so amounts to professional misconduct. Apart from his professional obligation towards his client an Advocate being an officer of the Court owes the duty to assist the Court in the administration of justice. Refusal to assist the Court by the duly engaged Advocate, besides being breach of trust reposed in him by the litigant, amounts to obstruction in administration of justice which may invite proceeding for contempt of the Court.  9. Sri U.S. Awasthi, the learned counsel appearing for the respondent No. 1, and Shri Vinay Malaviya, the learned Standing counsel for State of U.P., appearing for respondents, are present and willing to assist the Court in adjudication of the case.  10. In the backdrop of what has been said above, availing the valuable assistance of the aforementioned two counsel, the Court proceeds to consider the petition on merits.  11. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority, the respondent No. 1, (hereinafter called `NOIDA') issued an advertisement in the newspaper "Hindustan Times" on 28.6.1997 inviting offers through tender, inter alia, for a commercial plot bearing No. K-89 in Sector 18 of NOIDA falling in Khasra No. 401. According to notice, the tenders were to be opened on 10.7.1997 at 3.00 p.m.  12. The invitation to offer in pursuance of the advertisement was subject to specified general terms and conditions. These terms and conditions are on record before the Court as Annexure No. `1' to the Supplementary-Affidavit of Col. Virender Kumar Oberoi, the petitioner No. 2.  13. Clauses I and III of General Condition No. 3 and the Condition No. 7, which are relevant in the context, read thus :-  Condition No. 3 "(I) The Chief Executive Officer, NOIDA or any other officer authorised by the Chief Executive Officer, NOIDA reserves the right to reject any tender including the highest tender without assigning any reason." "(III) After the acceptance of the tender by the Chief Executive Officer, NOIDA or any officer authorised by Chief Executive Officer, NOIDA, tenderer will be informed of such acceptance in writing through allotment letter and the tenderer shall within 30 days thereof pay 25% of the tendered amount in cash or in Bank Draft, drawn in favour of NOIDA payable at NOIDA/Delhi/New Delhi. If this 25% amount is not paid, the deposit of Earnest Money will be forfeited. No extention of time shall be granted for deposit of the amount under any circumstances." Condition No. 7 "7. In case due to unavoidable circumstances the possession of plot is not handed over to allottee then full amount so deposited would be refunded back in due course to allottee. However, no interest would be paid to allottee." 14. Responding to the advertisement of NOIDA, inviting offers in regard to plot No. K-89 falling in Khasra No. 401, on the terms and conditions extracted above, the petitioners submitted tender giving his bid which, according to the petitioner, was found to be highest. The petitioners assert that despite several approaches by them through various communications between 10.7.1997 and 13.12.1997 no letter of allotment was issued to them.  15. Feeling aggrieved the petitioners have filed instant writ petition urging this Court to direct the respondents to issue letter of allotment in respect of Plot No. K-89, Sector-18, NOIDA. Further prayer of the petitioners is that appropriate writ, order or direction directing the C.B.I. to conduct enquiry into the conduct of the respondents and their prosecution according to law be issued. The prayer for quashing Condition No. 3(1) of General Conditions has also been made.  16. On record of the petition, there is a letter dated 1.1.1998 addressed to the Chairman of the petitioning-company M/s. Parasvnath Developers Ltd. which runs as under :-  "To The Chairman, M/s. Parasvnath Developers Ltd. G-2, Arunanchal, 19, Barakhamba Road, New Delhi-110119. Dear Sir, Against Scheme No. 9/-98 XXX(02) your tender for plot No. K-89 Sector-18 was received and opened on 10.7.1997. Plot No. K-89 falls in KR No. 401 village Chalera Bangar Mazra Atta. In second appeal No. 2110/87 Amar Singh v. NOIDA, the Hon'ble Court has passed ad-interim order dated 19.8.1997 staying the dispossession of the plaintiff-appellant from the disputed land. Under clause 7 of terms and condition of brochure, bid is not accepted and the plot No. K-89 Sector 18 is withdrawn from the scheme. The full amount deposited by you is hereby refunded to you as per details given below:- 1. Cost form No. 1000/- Cheque No. 188220 dt. 24.12.97 drawn on State Bank of Patiala, Noida. 2. Processing fee Rs. 10,000/- as per Draft No, 358225 dt. 10.7.97 submitted by you. 3. Earnest money Rs. 15,00,000/- as per Draft No. 900157 and 358226 dt. 9.10.97 submitted by you. Yours faithfully,  (K.K. Gupta)  Desk Officer (Comm.)" 17. From the letter dated 1.1.998, it transpires that plot No. K-89 falls in Khasra No. 401 of village Chalera Bangar, Mazra Atta in respect to which a dispute between one Shri Amar Singh and NOIDA is pending before this Court in Second Appeal No. 2110 of 1987 where an interim order dated 19.8.1997 was passed by the Court staying dispossession of Shri Amar Singh, the appellant in the appeal. The record of Second Appeal is before the Court and reveals that in fact there is an interim order in favour of Shri Amar Singh restraining NOIDA from dispossessing him from the disputed land till further orders. The record also shows that the interim order is still continuing. The letter dated 1.1.1998 discloses that the reason for not accepting the bid of the petitioners and not making consequential allotment of the plot in question is the interim order dated 19.8.1987 passed by this Court in Second Appeal No. 2110 of 1987, Amar Singh v. NOIDA.  18. In not accepting the bid of the petitioners and withholding the allotment of the plot in question in favour of the petitioners, NOIDA has acted in conformity with the interim order dated 19.8.1987 passed by this Court in Second Appeal No. 2110 of 1987, mentioned above. Indeed, the NOIDA is under legal obligation to obey the interim order of this Court so long it is operative. Therefore, in the opinion of the Court, NOIDA committed no illegality in not accepting the bid of the petitioners and not making allotment of the plot in question in their favour. The action of the NOIDA cannot be, by any stretch of imagination, held to be contrary to law. Under the General Terms and Conditions extracted earlier NOIDA had every right to reject the tender of the petitioners notwithstanding their bid being highest.  19. The controversy almost identical to the one raised in this petition, was also raised before a Division Bench of this Court in Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 976 of 1996, Shri Virat Bhushan v. New Okhla Industrial Development Authority through its Chairman and another, decided on 21st August, 1997. Relying on the decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court rendered in cases Surendra Pal Singh v. Zila Parishad, Muzaffarnagar, reported in 1991(2) UPLBEC 925, Asia Foundation and Construction Ltd. v. Trafalgar House Construction (1) Ltd., reported in 1997(1) SCC 738, State of U.P. v. Vijay Bahadur Singh, reported in AIR 1982 SC 1234, and Agra Cantt. Vendors Co-operative Society Ltd., Agra v. The Union of India, reported in 1984 UPLBEC 181, the Division Bench rejected the claim of the petitioner for acceptance of his bid despite his bid being highest, and dismissed the petition. Neither it is appropriate nor is there any justification for taking a view contrary to the view taken by the said Division Bench.  20. Shri U.S. Awasthi, the learned counsel for the respondent NOIDA, draws the attention of the Court to the averments made in paragraph 3 of the counter-affidavit of Shri K.K. Gupta, filed on the behalf of the respondent No. 3, wherein it is stated that the money deposited by the petitioners in pursuance of their bid has been refunded to the petitioners and it has been accepted by him. There is nothing no the record to show that the averments made in paragraph 3 of the counter-affidavit have been rebutted by the petitioners. Shri U.S. Awasthi contends that in view of the fact that the amount tendered by the petitioners was returned to them and the same had been accepted by them, they are estopped from claiming the reliefs prayed for. The contention of Shri Awasthi is well-founded.  21. All told, in the opinion of the Court, the petition is devoid of substance and deserves to be dismissed. It is dismissed accordingly. The interim order/orders shall stand vacated. However, there is no order as to costs.  22. The Second Appeal No. 2110 of 1987, Amar Singh v. NOIDA, shall no longer be treated to be linked with instant writ petition, and may be listed before the appropriate Bench for disposal.  Petition dismissed.
summary:
A. Constitution of India, Article 226 - Allotment of Plot - The highest bidder in a tender invitation by Development Authority does not have a right to allotment if there are pending interim orders restraining dispossession of occupants of a disputed plot. Petitioners in such a situation cannot claim relief, as their bid is not accepted and the tender amount is returned to them. [Paras 18 and 20]

B. Advocates Act, 1961, Section 35 - Allahabad High Court Rules, 1952, Chapter VI, Rule 12 - Contempt of Courts, Act, 1971 - Professional Misconduct - Denying assistance and argument to a court is a professional misconduct and contempt of courts, as decided by a court when rejecting an advocate's request for adjournment in a case. [Paras 7 and 8]

text: T.H.B. Chalapathi, J. (Oral) - By this judgment, three writ petitions - CWP No. 9317 of 1995, CWP 5319 of 1994 and CWP No. 13115 of 1995 - are proposed to be disposed of together as the facts are similar in all the cases.  2. For the sake of facts, CWP 9317 of 1995 (Smt. Raj Kaur Yadav) may be adverted to.  3. The petitioners, in these cases, were selected and appointed as lecturers in the year 1992 in the subjects of Commerce, History, Geography, Pol. Science and Home Sciences by the Public Girls College, Rewari (Haryana). On their appointment, the petitioners joined as lecturers in the college some time in November/December 1992. Though they are working as lecturers and though the management is taking their services as lecturers in the various subjects mentioned above they have not been paid the salary right from the inception till today. That necessitated the petitioners to approach this court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India for a direction to the respondents to pay their salary. It is the further case of the petitioners that the college is an aided college and 90% of the salary payable to the lecturers ought to be granted as grant-in-aid by the Government to the management. The management has not been paying salary to the petitioners on the ground that they have not received the grant-in-aid. It is also averred that the Director, Higher Education Haryana is the authority to sanction the posts and he has taken a decision to accord the sanction to these posts but he submitted his proposal to the Govt. for according the sanction which, according to the petitioners, is not necessary.  4. It is the case of the Government that the courses in the subjects of Commerce, History, Geography, Pol. Science and Home Sciences have been introduced by the college and the posts have not been sanctioned and, therefore, the Govt. need not give the grant-in-aid to the management as against the unsanctioned posts and since the posts on which the petitioners are working remained unsanctioned, the management is not entitled to the grant-in-aid. While it is the contention of the management that the college which is an aided college cannot charge any tuition fee from the girl students studying in Govt. and affiliated colleges up to the Graduation level, the college can only be run by the grant-in-aid. It is further averred that the college can run only on the grant-in-aid and it will not be possible for the management to pay the salary to the staff without grant-in-aid.  5. Admittedly, the management recruited the petitioners as lecturers in various subjects mentioned above in the year 1992 and the petitioners joined the services of the college in November/December, 1992. The petitioners were selected by a selection committee which consisted of the representatives of the Vice Chancellor, Maharishi Dayanand University (hereinafter referred to as M.D. University) and the representative of the Director Higher Education and the subject expert apart from the President of the management and the Principal of the College concerned. Thus, it is clear that the selection has been made on the basis of interview and in accordance with the procedure. Therefore, no fault can be found with the selection of the petitioners as lecturers in the college. The management after selecting and appointing the petitioners as lecturers in the college approached the Govt. in the year 1993 for sanctioning the posts against which they were recruited vide Annexure P9 dated 9.10.1993. It is clearly mentioned in the reply filed by the Director, Higher Education, that on the letter of management dated 9.10.1993 (Annexure P9) for sanctioning the posts mentioned therein, a proposal was sent to the Govt. for the sanction of posts for this college. But according to the scheme of the grant-in-aid it appears that it is the Director, Higher Education alone who is entitled to sanction the posts in the affiliated colleges. It is clear from Memo No. 22/2/85-Edu.1(2) dated 1.4.1986 from the Commissioner & Secretary to the Govt. Haryana, Education Department, addressed to the Director Higher Education that the grant will be payable against the posts which have been sanctioned by the Director, Higher Education. In that letter which is filed along with the reply of the writ petition as Annexure R-1, it is stated that no grant will be payable against the posts which have not been sanctioned by the Director. It means that the sanction has to be accorded only by the Director, Higher Education in which case there is no necessity for the Director, Higher Education to refer the matter to the Government for its sanction. The recommendation itself can be taken as an approval or sanction of the posts which have been created by the management. The Director, Higher Education, also deputed his nominee to participate in the interview for the selection of the lecturers in which the petitioners have been selected. Thus, it is clear that the Director, Higher Education, is very well aware of the fact that the management was recruiting the lecturers in the subjects of commerce, history, geography, pol. science and home sciences. Thus, it can be deemed that the sanction has been duly accorded to the creation of posts. Further, from the averments in the reply, it is clear that the Director, Higher Education, has concluded that necessary sanction of these posts of lecturers has to be accorded. In these circumstances, it is not open to the Government to deny the release of grant-in-aid to the management. The petitioners have been working in the college since 1992 and have not been paid anything towards their salary for the last six years. It is quite unjust on the part of the management as well as the govt. to deny the salary to the lecturers who have been duly selected and appointed in accordance with the rules. It is not the case of the Government that the petitioners have been selected by any back door entry. There is also no denial of the fact that the posts have been created in accordance with the norms fixed by the MDU to which this college in question has been affiliated. No objection has been taken either by the University or the Government when the new courses in the subjects referred to above have been introduced in the college. Neither the Director, Higher Education, nor the University can say that the new courses have been introduced without their knowledge since the selection has been made in the presence of the nominees of the Director, Higher Education, and also the University in the selection committee. In these circumstances, I am of the opinion that the petitioners are entitled to the salary with all allowances admissible in accordance with the rules. Accordingly I direct the management to pay the salary to the petitioners with all admissible allowances within a period of four months from today.  The Government is directed to release the grant-in-aid to this college in respect of the salary payable to the petitioners within four months.  Petition allowed.
summary: As per the Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 30, in Aided Colleges, the Director of Higher Education is responsible for granting sanction for creation of new posts, not the State Government. If the University allows the college to introduce new courses and the Director's nominee participates in the selection of lecturers, resulting in the Director's recommendation for approval and sanction to the Government, it is deemed and implied sanction. No sanction from the Government is required. The Director is instructed to release the grant-in-aid for the posts with arrears. [Para 5]

text: S.R. Nayak, J. - The Manager, Vijaya Bank, Padubidri Branch, Padubidri, D.K. District, who is the petitioner in W.P. No. 18335/96, feeling aggrieved by the order of the learned Single Judge of this Court dated 1st day of February 1999 (reported in 1999 Lab IC 2224) has preferred this writ appeal.  2. The learned Single Judge, by the order under appeal has dismissed the writ petition filed by the Appellant.  3. The events leading to the filing of the writ petition be noted briefly in the first instance and they are as follows : The Appellant at the request of the 3rd respondent had sanctioned an Open Loan Cash Credit of Rs. 3,00,000/- and Key Loan Cash Credit of Rs. 6,00,000/- to meet the working capital requirements. The 3rd respondent had secured four loans by hypothecation of goods/stocks etc., and also by the personal guarantee given by the husband of the Managing Partner of the 3rd respondent. The hypothecated goods/stocks had been insured for a sum of Rs. 12,00,000/- with United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Udupi by the Appellant Bank, through the 3rd Respondent. It is stated that the premia were paid by the Appellant Bank and debited to the Cash Credit Account of the 3rd Respondent. It appears the hypothecated goods/stock stored in the factory premises of the 3rd respondent were destroyed by fire on 9th September, 1990. The Appellant Bank lodged an Insurance claim with United India Insurance Company through the 3rd Respondent. Since the parties did not agree for any acceptable terms, the dispute was carried on by the third respondent to the Karnataka State Commission for Consumer Redressal under the Consumer Protection Act. The Commission by its Order dated 23-01-1995 held that the 3rd respondent is entitled to a sum of Rs. 9,49,168.60 towards Principal and Interest till the date of payment to it. Having declared so and taking into account the hypothecation agreement between the Appellant and the 3rd respondent the Commission disposed of the Complaint 23 of 1993 in the following terms :  "IN THE RESULT, therefore, this complaint is allowed. The opp. Party No. 1, United India Insurance Company is directed to pay a sum of Rs. 9,49,168.60 to Opp. Party No. 2, Vijaya Bank, Padubidri Branch, Padubidri, to the account of the complainant in the said Bank with interest at 15% p.a. from 19-03-1992 till the date of its payment". 4. In pursuance of the above order of the Commission, the United India Insurance Company transmitted a sum of Rs. 13,77,624.25 by way of two cheques bearing Nos. 013909 dated 13-3-95 for Rs. 10,00,000/- and 013919 dated 13-3-95 for Rs. 3,77,624/- vide its forwarding letter dated 15-03-1995. The said letter reads as follows :  "Ref : 71200/FCL 120/90 Date : 15-03-1995 The Manager,  Vijaya Bank, Padubidri,  Udupi Taluk. Dear Sir, Re : Complaint No. 23/93 before State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Bangalore, A/c. M/s. Akshaya Cashew Industries, Padubidri Claim No. 120/90. ..... We are satisfying the Award passed by the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. Our Cheques bearing No. 013909 dated 13-3-1995 for Rs. 10,00,000/- and 013919 dated 13-3-1995 for Rs. 3,77,624/- drawn in your favour A/c. Akshaya Cashew Industries are enclosed herein. Please get the enclosed voucher for Rs. 13,77,624/- duly discharged by the complainant and counter signed by you before passing on the credit to their account. Computation of the aggregate amount is as under : Award - Rs. 9,49,168.00 Interest @15% from 19.3.92 to 15.3.95 - Rs. 4,25,955.65 Costs - Rs. 2,500.00 Rs. 13,77,624.25 Rounded off to Rs. 13,77,624/-" As could be seen, the interest was calculated by the United Insurance Company at 15% for the period from 19-3-1992 to 15-3-1995. Of course, the total sum of Rs. 13,77,624.25 includes cost of Rs. 2,500/- also.  5. When the matter stood thus, the 1st respondent herein, in the purported exercise of the power conferred under Sub-section (3) of Section 8-F of the Employees', Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (for short the "Act") directed the Appellant to pay forthwith a sum of Rs. 30,217.75 by way of Demand Draft drawn in favour of Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Mangalore, from out of money being held by the Appellant on account of and on behalf of the 3rd respondent. The direction of the st Respondent reads as follows :  "NOW, THEREFORE, in exercise of the powers conferred on me under sub-section (3) of Section 8F of the Act, you are hereby directed to pay forthwith Rs. 30,217.75 (Rupees Thirty thousand two hundred seventeen and palse seventy five only) by way of Demand Draft drawn in favour of Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Mangalore, from out of money being held by you on account of and on behalf of the above said defaulting Establishment/Employer". 6. On receipt of the above notice, the Appellant by his letter dated 13-02- 1995 addressed to the 1st respondent informed the 1st respondent that there is no credit balance outstanding in the account of the 3rd respondent. While informing so, the Appellant also informed the 1st respondent that the 3rd respondent had to pay a sum of Rs. 15,00,000 to the Appellant Bank towards its liability. This was followed by an affidavit duly sworn to by the Manager of the Appellant Bank dated 18-06-1996 as required under Section 8F(3)(vi) of the Act which reads as follows :  "AFFIDAVIT I, Sri Krishna M. Shetty, S/O. Mynda Shetty, aged about 47 years, resident of Padubidri, do hereby solemnly affirm and state on oath as follows : That I am the Branch Manger of Vijaya Bank, Padubidri Branch, Padubidri, D.K. That M/s. Akshaya Cashew Industries, Padubidri, is a Constituent and an esteemed customer of Vijaya Bank, Padubidri Branch, to whom various credit facilities were granted by the Bank by way of OLCC for Rs. 3,00,000/- (Rupees Three Lacs only) and KLCC for Rs. 6,00,000/- (Rupees Six lacs only) for its day-to-day operation which it has been making use of. That the said credit facilities are allowed to the aforesaid Cashew Industry against the Hypothecation/pledge of its Raw-materials, Semi-finished and finished goods strictly in terms of the conditions laid down while granting the said credit facilities. That, by an order contained in reference No, KN/MN/ENB/12807/95/559 dated 30- 10-1995 of the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Mangalore, followed by yet another order in reference No. KN/MNG/Recovery Cell/227/10-96-97 dated 05-06-1996 of the Recovery Officer, Employees Provident Funds, Sub-Regional Provident Fund Office, P.B. No. 572, Balmatta, Mangalore, purported to have been issued under Sec. 8F of the Employees Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provision Act 1952, a demand is raised by the authorities on the Bank to remit a sum of Rs. 30,217.75 to them by debiting the Bank A/c. of M/s. Akshaya Cashew Industry maintained in the Bank. This amount is said to be the arrears of PF contribution and other charges statutorily due and payable by the aforesaid Akshaya Cashew Industry under the provisions of the Employees Provident Funds and the Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. That, by letter No. ROU : AKR/20755/95 dated 29-12-1995 issued by our Regional Office, Udupi, addressed to Mr. S. Raghuram, Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Sub-Regional Office, Mangalore, that the Bank has informed the authorities that on a request from the said Cashew Industry for certain financial assistance, the bank has sanctioned Rs. 9,00,000/- (Rupees Nine lacs only) by way of OLCC/KLCC towards it working capital against hypothecation/pledge of goods and as such the said cashew industry is indebted to the Bank, under all these loan accounts. That, on the date of receipt of order dated 30-10-95 of the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Mangalore, and thereafter, the aforesaid cashew industry remained a Debtor to the Bank and that at no time, the bank is or has due any amount to the cashew industry, nor does it hold any money for or on behalf of the said Akshaya Cashew Industry. Nor does the bank hold any assets of the aforesaid Cashew Industry as to attract the provisions of the Section 11(2) of the said Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. On the other hand, the said cashew industry is due and has been due to the Bank to an extent of Rs. 5,94,000/- (Rupees Five lacs ninety four thousand only) with interest from 01-04-1995 in all its loan accounts. That this affidavit is made and executed in accordance with the provision contained in Clause (vi) of the Sub-section (3) of Section 8F of the Employees' Provident Funds Miscellaneous Provision Act, 1952. Sworn at Padubidri, D.K. on this 18th day of June 1996.  (KRISHNA SHETTY)"  7. The demand raised by the 1st respondent was not complied with by the Appellant. Since the 1st respondent has passed the prohibitory order under Section 8F (3) of the Act the Appellant Bank being aggrieved by the said action of the 1st respondent, approached this Court by way of Writ Petition No. 18335/1996.  8. The learned Single Judge having opined that a sum of Rs. 4,25,965.65 awarded by the Commission towards interest and a sum of Rs. 2,500/- awarded by the Commissioner towards cost could not form part of the hypothecated property and, therefore, the 1st respondent was justified in raising the demand as envisaged Under Sub-section (3) of Section 8-F of the Act, dismissed the writ petition.  9. We have heard Sri S.R. Goutham, learned Counsel for the Appellant Bank and Sri Harikrishna Holla, Learned Standing Counsel for the Provident Fund Commissioner. Having heard the learned Counsel for the parties, the only question that arises for decision is, whether sums of Rs. 4,25,965.65 and Rs. 2,500/- awarded by the Commissioner towards interest and cost respectively could form part of hypothecated property or not. If answer to this question is in the positive, it cannot be said that the 1st respondent could not have raised a demand for sum of Rs. 30,217.75 under Section 8-F(3)(i) read with Sec. 11(2) of the Act. Before proceeding further, it will be beneficial to notice the relevant provisions of the Act which will have bearing in the decision-making. Sub-section (2) of Section 11 of the Act reads as follows :  "(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), if any amount is due from an employer, whether in respect of the employee's contribution (deducted from the wages of the employee) or the employer's contribution, the amount so due shall be deemed to be the first charge on the assets of the establishment, and shall, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, be paid in priority to all other debts". 10. Clause (1) of Sub-section (3) of Section 8-F undoubtedly makes it very clear that the Commissioner could take steps under the said Clause to recover the arrears of the Provident Fund Contribution due from the employer only in the event of the finding that the money in the hand of the person to whom the notice is sent is the money due to the employer or it may, in course of time, become due to the employer. In other words, the money in respect of which the demand is raised under Clause (1) of Sub-section (3) of Section 8-F should be the money due to the employer or it may become due to the employer later. Therefore, in order to apply the provisions of Clause (1) Sub-section (1) of Section 8-F and to sustain the impugned action of the Commissioner, it has to be established that on the date the Appellant Bank received the impugned notice issued by the Commissioner, it held the money to an extent of Rs. 30,217.75 due to the employer.  11. The facts are not in dispute. It is seen from the records that a sum of Rs. 15,00,000/- or more was due from the employer to the Appellant Bank on the day the Appellant-Bank received the impugned notice from the Commissioner. This position is very much reflected in the reply of the Appellant Bank dated 13-02-1995 and also from the sworn affidavit filed under Clause (vi) of the Sub-section (3) of Section 8-F of Act. However, it is the contention of the learned Counsel for the 1st respondent that the interest and the cost awarded by the Commission could not be regarded as a part of the hypothecated property and therefore, the Appellant Bank is entitled to lay its claim over the interest and costs awarded by the Commission in terms of the hypothecation agreement. This submission is not acceptable to us. The relevant question is, by the time the Appellant Bank received sum of Rs. 13,77,624.25 from the insurance company, what was the liability of the employer. The liability of the employer in terms of the hypothecation agreement was more than Rs. 15,00,000/-. If this fact is not in dispute, it is trite, when the Appellant- Bank received sum of Rs. 13,77,624.55, it could legitimately and in terms of the right reserved to it under the contract, adjust sum of Rs. 13,77,624.25 towards the liability of the employer. Therefore, we are at a loss to understand how it could be said that sum of Rs. 13,77,624.25 received from the insurance company could be regarded as the money due to the employer or may become due to the employer later. In our considered opinion, the stand taken by the Appellant-Bank by its letter dated 13-02-1995 and the Affidavit dated 18-06-1996 is well justified and is in accordance with law. This follows that the impugned action taken by the Commissioner in the purported exercise of power conferred under Section 8-F of the Act is without authority of law and cannot be sustained.  12. Perhaps, realising the difficulty to sustain the contention that the interest and costs could not form part of the hypothecated property, the learned counsel drew our attention to the provisions of Sub-section (2) of Section 11 of the Act and would maintain that in the light of the provisions of sub-section (2), the claim of the first respondent-Department has priority over any claim of the Appellant-Bank. This submission is not acceptable to us. The provisions of sub-section 3(i) of Section 8-F and provisions of Sub- section (2) of Section 11 should be read harmoniously and reasonably. The contribution which the employer is obligated to make under the provisions of the Act could not be fastened on anyone else except as directed by the Act itself. In other words, in enforcing the liability of the employer to pay provident fund contributions, against third parties, it becomes imperative for the Court to interpret the statute strictly. If it is so interpreted, it will not leave any doubt in anybody's mind that the Commissioner could raise the demand under Sub-section 3(i) against a third party only when he finds the money of the employer in the hands of such third party to whom the notice is sent or in course of time, required money will become due to the employer. It is an established fact that on the date the Appellant Bank received the money from the Insurance Company or the date on which it received the notice issued by the Commissioner under Section 8-F(3)(i) of the Act there was no money in the hands of the Bank which was due to the employer. Therefore, in issuing the impugned notice dated 2-3-1995, the Commissioner acted ultra vires of the Act.  13. The Commissioner being a statutory authority, the power to be exercised by him should be traceable to one or the other provisions of the Act, and if the Court finds that the particular power exercised by him is ultra vires the Act, the Court would be justified in stepping in and nullifying such action. We do not think, we should burden this judgment with case law in that regard.  14. In conclusion, with great respect, we cannot fall in line with the opinion of the learned Single Judge. In the result and for the foregoing reasons, the writ appeal is allowed. The order of the learned Single Judge dated 1-2-1999 passed in W.P. No. 18335 of 1996 (reported in 1999 Lab IC 2224) is set aside and the proceedings of the Commissioner impugned in the writ petition are quashed, with no order as to costs.  Appeal allowed.
summary: According to Sections 8F(3)(i) and 11(2) of the Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, an employer is liable to make contributions. However, enforcement against third parties can only be made when the Commission finds that the employer's money is or will be in the hands of such party. If not, any demand notice made to a third party would be without authority of law and ultra vires of the Act as stated in Paras 11 and 12.

text: R.L. Anand, J. - By this judgment we dispose of L.P.A Nos. 1408 of 1989 (P.G.I. Chandigarh v. The Presiding Officer, Labour Court, U.T. Chandigarh) and 1475 of 1989 (Kewal Krishan v. P.G.I. Chandigarh and others) as both the Letters Patent Appeals have arisen from one judgment dated 2nd June, 1989 passed in C.W.P. No. 3255 filed by the P.G.I. Chandigarh against the award dated 24.6.93 passed by the Labour Court, Chandigarh Administration, Chandigarh. It may be mentioned at the first instance that the Labour Court while allowing the reference made at the instance of Shri Kewal Krishan modified the punishment awarded by the punishing authority and stopped four annual grade increments of Shri Kewal Krishan workman without cumulative effect and ordered for the reinstatement of the woman into service with full back wages. The learned Single Judge further awarded punishment to the workman (Shri Kewal Krishan) by observing that he would not be entitled to the back wages upto the date of the enforcement of the award. However, he would be entitled to the backwages from the date of filing of the writ petition. Both the parties, i.e., the P.G.I. as well as Shri Kewal Krishan were not satisfied with the judgment of the learned Single Judge and have come in the present two appeals.  2. The brief facts of the case are that Shri Kewal Krishan was appointed as a Clerk in the Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh (for short 'the P.G.I.') on 1.12.1960. On 1.4.1977 a sum of Rs. 7509/- was allegedly received by him. Out of this amount a sum of Rs. 2400/- was entrusted to him by Dr. A.N. Gupta, Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaeocology, which was received by way of donation from someone. This amount of Rs. 2400/- was not deposited. However, the rest of the amount collected on that day was deposited. In a letter dated July 8, 1977 Shri Kewal Krishan workman allegedly admitted his fault and deposited the amount of Rs. 2400/-. During the course of reconciliation of the amount credited in the State Bank of India, Medical Education Branch, Chandigarh, the shortage of Rs. 2400/- was detected. Consequently, upon the discovery of the shortage, an inquiry under Rule 14 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, was initiated against him. His explanation was called. The reply submitted by the workman was not considered satisfactory, and he was charge-sheeted for the embezzlement. The workman participated in the inquiry proceedings but the Inquiry Officer found him guilty of the charges levelled against him. As a consequence, his services were ordered to be terminated. The workman issued a demand notice and the matter was referred to the Labour Court for adjudication.  3. The stand of the workman was that he never embezzled the amount. Rather he was forced to deposit the alleged embezzled amount. The defence taken by the workman was found weak by the Inquiry Officer, who held him guilty of the allegations. The Labour Court while affirming the findings of the Inquiry Officer against the workman held that in view of the circumstances that the workman had put in a service of about 23 years and that he had also deposited the embezzled amount, the punishment of his termination from service was not proportionate to the charges levelled against him. The Labour Court also held that the punishment awarded to the workman was highly excessive and harsh and by invoking the provisions of Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, it was ordered that four annual grade increments of Shri Kewal Krishan be stopped without cumulative effect with effect from the year 1977, which in the view of the Labour Court would meet the ends of justice.  4. Aggrieved by the award of the Labour Court, the P.G.I. filed C.W.P. No. 3255 of 1983. The learned Single Judge, however, held as follows:-  "..... The litigation is going on since 1977, so it would be appropriate to exercise jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India and to modify the Award of the Labour Court in the quantum of punishment. In addition to the punishment awarded by respondent No. 1 to the workman, he would also not be entitled to the backwages upto the date of enforcement of the Award by respondent No. 1. The workman-respondent would, however, be entitled to the backwages from the date of filing the present writ petition in this Court." 5. We have heard Shri Arun Nehra, Advocate, on behalf of the P.G.I., and Shri R.S. Mittal, Senior Advocate, with Ms. Aarti Gupta, Advocate, on behalf of Shri Kewal Krishan-workman, and with their assistance have gone through the record of the case.  6. First of all we would like to dispose of L.P.A. No. 1408 of 1989 filed by the P.G.I. and the main thrust of the argument of the learned counsel appearing for the P.G.I. was that the Labour Court was not justified in invoking the provisions of Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and could not substitute its own punishment over the punishment which was awarded by the punishing authority and that the award given by the Labour Court suffers from irreparable vices. It was also submitted that the case in hand was a case of embezzlement amounting to Rs. 2400/- on the part of the workman and his action in no manner could be justified and no lenient view could be taken in his case. In short it was submitted that the punishment which was awarded by the punishing authority was not only adequate but could be the only punishment which could be awarded specially for Kewal Krishan- workman, who committed misappropriation and embezzlement while working in a public institution like the P.G.I.  7. On the contrary it was argued by the counsel appearing on behalf of Shri Kewal Krishan-workman that the Labour Court had rightly and properly exercised the jurisdiction under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and that the discretion which has been exercised on sound judicial principles should not be lightly interfered until and unless the High Court feels in the writ jurisdiction that the findings of the Labour Court were perverse. In the present case the findings were not perverse. Rather it was duly appreciated by the Labour Court that the workman had put in 23 years unblemished service in the P.G.I. and the punishment awarded by the punishing authority was irrational, excessive and did not commensurate with the allegations and, therefore, it could not be lightly interfered. The learned counsel further submitted that the learned Single Judge was not justified in further imposing the punishment on the workman by ordering that Shri Kewal Krishan-workman would also not be entitled to the backwages upto the date of the enforcement of the award, but would be entitled to the backwages from the date of the filing of the present writ petition. In the opinion of the counsel the learned Single Judge while exercising the powers under Article 226 of the Constitution of India could not interfere or modify the findings of the Labour Court in the matter of punishment.  8. After considering the rival contentions of the parties we are of the considered view that both the L.P.As. are devoid of any merit. Under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act the Labour Court has the power to set aside the order of discharge, dismissal or termination and could direct reinstatement of the workman on such terms and conditions, if any, as it thinks fit and can give such other relief to the workman, including the award of any lesser punishment in lieu of discharge or dismissal as the circumstances of the case may require. A perusal of Section 11-A of Industrial Disputes Act would show that if the Labour Court is satisfied that the order of discharge or dismissal was not justified, it has the power to modify the punishment by relying on the materials on record. The learned Labour Court studied the implications of these allegations. It also took into consideration the extent of embezzled amount and also the factum that the embezzlement was of temporary nature because the workman has deposited the alleged embezzled amount. The Labour Court also took into conderation the total period of service put in by the workman and his past record. Once there is a proper appreciation of the evidence on the part of the Labour Court when it stopped four annual grade increments of the workman without cumulative effect, it was a reasonable punishment in lieu of the order of termination. Also we are not interested to interfere in the findings of the learned Single Judge because Article 226 gives ample powers to the High Court to rescind or modify the punishment which had been awarded by the Labour Court. The learned Single Judge had given cogent reasons in his judgment when he thought it proper not to remand the case to the Tribunal with a view to re-examine the question of quantum of punishment being an old matter as the litigation was going on since 1977. We do not find any error of jurisdiction on the part of the learned Single Judge when he exercised his powers under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India and modified the award of the Labour Court in the quantum of punishment.  9. In support of the appeal of his client and while attacking the judgment of the learned Single Judge Shri R.S. Mittal, learned counsel appearing for Shri Kewal Krishan-workman, relied upon two authorities of the Hon'ble Supreme Court reported as Management of Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., Bangalore v. Mohd. Usman and another, AIR 1984 S.C. 321, and Jitendra Singh Rathore v. Shri Baidyanath Ayurved Bhawan Ltd. and another, AIR 1984 S.C. 976, and submitted that once the Labour Court after evaluating gravity of misconduct holding that punishment of termination is disproportionately heavy and reducing it to stoppage of increments by modifying the punishment awarded by the punishing authority, no interference could be plausible on the part of the High Court. We have the occasion to go through both the authorities and find that both the authorities are distinguishable on facts. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has not laid down that in no circumstance the High Court while exercising the powers under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India could interfere into the findings of the Labour Court when it has modified the punishment awarded by the punishing authority. Rather the principle of interference has been recognised but only with a stipulation that there could be some important legal principle, as laid down in Management of Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., Bangalore v. Mohd. Usman and another, AIR 1984 S.C. 321. The other authority, i.e., Jitendra Singh Rathore v. Shri Baidyanath Ayurved Bhawan Ltd., AIR 1984 S.C. 976, is again distinguishable, because in the cited case the High Court did not record a finding that there was a loss of confidence of the employer and there was no indication in the judgment of the High Court as to how many years of service the employee had put in and how many years of service was still left under the Standing Order. However, in the present case the learned Single Judge took that into consideration while modifying the award of the Labour Court and held that litigation between the parties was going on since 1977 and the workman had already put in 23 years of service and there was no propriety to remand the case to the Labour Court. However, Hon'ble the Supreme Court did recognise that under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act a wide discretion has been vested in the Labour Court in the matter of awarding relief according to the circumstances of the case. In the present case learned Single Judge did not substitute the punishment than the one awarded by the Labour Court.  10. Our attention has also been invited by the Shri R.S.Mittal to Management of Craigmore Estate, Kullakamby Post, Nilgiris Dist. v. Labour Court, Coimbatore and another, 1981(2) Labour Law Journal 23; Shri Ganeshar Aluminium Factory C/o. Jeewanlal (1929) Limited v. Industrial Tribunal, Madras and another, 1982(1) Labour Law Journal 159; and Management of Binny Limited v. Additional Labour Court, Madras and another, 1979(2) Labour Law Journal 280, and the consensus of all these authorities is that under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act the Labour Court while holding misconduct having been proved against the workman, when came to the conclusion that the punishment was disproportionate to the proved charges, had powers to reduce the punishment, as has rightly been done in the present case by the Labour Court when it stopped four annual grade increments of the workman without cumulative effect. These authorities are helpful to us in adjudicating the controversy in the present two letters patent appeals.  11. Shri Arun Nehra, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the P.G.I., cited band of authorities of this Court as well as the Hon'ble Supreme Court reported as Jitendra Singh Rathore v. Shri Baidyanath Ayurved Bhawan Ltd. and another, AIR 1984 S.C. 976; The State of Haryana and others v. Amar Nath Bansal, 1993(4) SCT 734 (P&H) : 1993(4) Recent Services Judgments 427; Workmen of Bharat Fritz Warner (P) Ltd. v. Bharat Frilz Warner (P) Ltd. and another, 1990(2) S.L.R. 20; The Depot Manager, APSRTC Bus Depot, Warangal v. D.S. Rao and another,1995(7) S.L.R. 432; and M/s Hindustan Steels Ltd., Rourkela v. A.K. Roy and others, AIR 1970 S.C. 1401; and a judgment dated 19.9.1988 in C.W.P. No. 3788 of 1986 (Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh v. The Presiding Officer, Labour Court, Union Territory, Chandigarh, and another), and vehemently submitted that the present is a case of loss of confidence on the part of the Management in the workman, who committed embzzlement to the tune of Rs. 2,400/- and in these circumstances the Labour Court was not justified in modifying the punishment by stopping four annual grade increments of the workman without cumulative effect. He submitted that under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India the High Court has the power to interfere in the finding of the Labour Court passed under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and that the learned Single Judge though exercised that power, had not interfered in the award of the Labour Court by restoring the punishment which was awarded to the workman by the Labour Court.  12. We have the occasion to go through the citations relied upon by Shri Arun Nehra, learned counsel for the P.G.I., and we are of the opinion that there is no dispute with the proposition of law that the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India can modify the punishment than the one awarded by the Labour Court. However, we cannot lose sight of the fact that every case has its own facts. With the introduction of Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act the concept of penology has gone a sea change. The learned Single Judge in his judgment had taken care of all the factors such as the length of service of the workman, the gravity of the allegations, especially the fact that the parties were litigating since 1977 and thereafter ordered that the workman would not be entitled to the backwages upto the date of the enforcement of the award, but would be entitled to the backwages from the date of the writ petition itself. Once the discretion has been used in a proper manner by the learned Single Judge, it cannot be said to be perverse. We are not inclined to interfere with the well reasoned judgment dated 2nd June, 1989.  13. Resultantly, we do not find any merit in these appeals. Thus we affirm the findings and observations of the learned Single Judge. Both the appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Letters Patent Appeal, Clause 10 - Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Sections 10 and 11-A - Punishment - Back wages - The Labour Court, while allowing the reference, modified the punishment imposed by the punishing authority and stopped four annual grade increments of the worker without cumulative effect. The court ordered reinstatement of the worker with full back pay. The Single Judge upheld the punishment but ruled that the worker would not be entitled to back wages up until the date of enforcement of the award. The worker would, however, be entitled to back wages from the date of filing the writ petition. The Single Judge considered all factors such as the length of service, the gravity of allegations, and the length of litigation since 1977. As the discretion exercised by the Single Judge was appropriate, it cannot be deemed unreasonable. The well-reasoned judgment should not be interfered with. [Paras 8, 11 and 12]

text: Vijinder Jain, C.J. - The present appeal under Clause X of the Letters Patent is directed against judgment dated 21.2.2007 vide which the learned single Judge, while disposing of CWP No. 13284 of 2001 filed by respondent No. 1- H.P.S. Chawla, directed the appellant along with respondent No. 2 to release the requisite benefits to him without delay and within a period of two months and in the event of their failure to do so, he was held entitled to get back those benefits with interest at the rate of 6% per annum with effect from 19.2.2000, i.e. from the date of the order passed by the Appellate Authority.  2. Respondent No. 1 was alleged to have committed certain irregularities, as a result of which, after the disciplinary proceedings had confirmed the allegations against him, he was directed to be removed from the appellant's service by the competent authority. However, while removing him from service, it was observed by the disciplinary authority that his removal shall not be disqualification for his future employment and that he will be eligible to receive terminal benefits as are admissible to him. Since the benefits flowing from the order of the disciplinary authority were not being awarded to him, respondent No. 1 filed the aforesaid writ petition which has been disposed of in the manner indicated hereinabove.  3. The appellant, which was the principal employer of respondent No. 1, has filed the present appeal for setting aside the impugned judgment.  4. Shri R.S. Mittal, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the appellant has contended that as per Regulation 22(1) of the UCO Bank (Employees) Pension Regulations, 1995 (for short, `the Regulations'), resignation or dismissal or removal or termination of service of an employee of the bank shall entail forfeiture of his entire past service and consequently, he shall not qualify for pensionary benefits. He further contended that similarly, Rule 10 of the Employees Gratuity Fund Rules (hereinafter referred to as `the Rules') framed by the appellant in exercise of the powers conferred by the provisions of Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 provides for forfeiture of whole of the gratuity payable to an employee if his services have been terminated on account of any misconduct resulting in financial loss or damage to the Bank or for any act involving moral turpitude.  5. On the strength of the aforesaid provisions, learned counsel urged that the judgment of the learned Single Judge is liable to be set aside as the services of respondent No. 1 were terminated on account of grave misconduct.  6. We have thoughtfully considered the contentions raised by the learned counsel for the appellant and have perused the whole record, but are unable to agree with him. Regulation 22(1) of the Regulations and Rule 10(b) of the Rules, which are relevant for the purpose of this appeal are reproduced below :-  "Regulation 22(1) of the Regulations  22. Forfeiture of Service. - (1) Resignation or dismissal or removal or termination of an employee from the service of the Bank shall entail forfeiture of his entire past service and consequently shall not qualify for pensionary benefits. Rule 10 of the Rules  10(b) The gratuity payable to an employee shall be wholly forfeited if the services of such employee have been terminated for any act which constituted an offence involving moral turpitude provided that, such offence is committed by him in the course of his employment." 7. The disciplinary authority of the appellant-Bank had passed the order of removal of respondent No. 1 from service, but had taken a benign view of the situation by observing that "he should be given the retiral benefits along with the penalty of removal from the service. This will give respite to him for putting his life in the dreary world. I feel it certain that he deserves the penalty of termination from service....." Thereafter, it went on to impose the penalty by ordering his removal, but also by observing that it shall not be a disqualification for his future employment and that he shall be entitled to the terminal benefits.  8. The appellant as a principal employer did not agitate against the aforesaid observations of the disciplinary authority and accepted the verdict. Once respondent No. 1 came to the Court for getting the order implemented, then it did not lie in the mouth of the appellant to take up the plea that the Regulations debarred the grant of retiral benefits to an employee who is removed or terminated from service. The disciplinary authority consciously took a benign decision and turned a blind eye to the Regulations, which was accepted by the appellant and consequently, it cannot now rake up the plea as aforesaid to deny the benefits to respondent No. 1. Moreover, the perusal of the impugned judgment shows that these contentions have been noticed and adequately met and we do not find any infirmity therein.  Consequently, we find no merit in the appeal which is dismissed in limine.  Petition dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 226 - UCO Bank (Employees) Pension Regulations, 1995, Regulation 22(1) - Estoppel - Employees Gratuity Fund Rules, Rule 10 - Removal from service on account of misconduct - The punishing authority has discretion regarding forfeiture of retiral benefits - If the punishing authority decides that the delinquent should receive his retiral benefits while being removed from service and the employer does not contest this decision, the employer cannot oppose implementation of the order in the employee's claim petition. [Paras 6 to 8]

text: D.P. Kundu, J. - The petitioner is an employee of Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Ltd., a Govt. of India Undertaking (hereinafter referred to as respondent No. 1). While the petitioner was working as Senior Assistant Security Officer by a chargesheet dated 28th June, 1993 issued by Manager Administration (hereinafter referred to as the respondent No. 3) certain charges were levelled against the petitioner. Initially, the petitioner only challenging the said charge-sheet and the departmental proceeding initiated against him in view of the aforesaid chargesheet instituted the present writ proceeding being C.O. No. 17377(W) of 1993. On 14.9.1993 Susanta Chatterji, J., (as his Lordship then was), inter alia, passed the following order :  "Having heard the learned Advocates appearing for the respective parties and considering the materials on record, I pass the following order : Respondents shall carry on disciplinary proceedings, but shall not give effect to any order that may be passed in the disciplinary proceedings without the leave of the Court. The disciplinary proceedings should be carried on in conformity with the rules of natural justice and the petitioner shall get assistance of a defence assistant. The petitioner is personally present in Court to-day and the same be treated as leave by the authority and no action shall be taken against him for the same leave." Pursuant to the aforesaid order dated 14.9.1993 passed by the Court the respondents proceeded with the departmental proceeding which was initiated against the petitioner. After completion of the enquiry the respondent No. 1 preferred an application praying for leave of the Court to give effect to the order of dismissal. While the aforesaid application of the respondent No. 1 praying for leave of the Court was pending the petitioner preferred an application for amendment of the writ application. On 9.3.1998 after hearing the ld. Advocates for the parties the Court passed the following order :  "Heard the learned Advocates for both the parties. Amendment application preferred by the writ petitioner is allowed. The writ petitioner is directed to file a copy of the writ application incorporating the amendments allowed to-day by 12th March, 1998. A copy of such application incorporating the amendments including the annexures should be served upon the learned Advocate for the respondents by 12th March, 1998 positively. I make it clear that in case the writ applicant fails to serve a copy on the respondents by 12th March, 1998 as directed above, the interim order shall stand vacated. The respondents are directed to file affidavit-in-opposition within 23rd March, 1998 and reply thereto, if any, be filed within 26th March, 1998. Let this matter come up on 30th March, 1998 as Item No. 1 irrespective of any other matters. With the above observations, the amendment application filed by the writ petitioner and the application filed by the respondent No. 1 on 20.12.1996 are disposed. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the both the parties to take down the gist of this order for communication." In compliance with the aforesaid order dated 9.3.1998 the writ petitioner filed a copy of the writ application incorporating the amendments allowed by the Court on 9.3.1998.  2. In the writ application as amended the petitioner has challenged the charge-sheet, the enquiry proceeding, the finding of the Enquiry Officer and the order of dismissal. In view of the Court's order dated 14.9.1993 the respondents could not give effect to the order of dismissal. Therefore, the writ petitioner is still in service of respondent No. 1.  3. The ld. Advocate appearing for the writ petitioner argued the following points :  1. The charge-sheet had not been issued by the competent authority as envisaged in Rule 26 of the Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Ltd. (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules. 2. Charge-sheet had been issued with a closed mind, therefore, the charge- sheet had been issued with initial bias. 3. Complainant was senior in rank to the Enquiry Officer and for that reason the enquiry is vitiated. 4. During the enquiry a principal witness for the company viz. PW5 read out from a written statement which was seriously objected to at the time of enquiry but the Enquiry Officer permitted the said witness to give his evidence reading from the written statement and for this reason the enquiry is vitiated.  5. There was a preliminary enquiry in respect of the subject matter of the charge-sheet where the witnesses made statements but these statements were never disclosed to the writ petitioner, for this reason the enquiry is vitiated.  6. Standing orders and rules governing the service condition and conduct, discipline and appeal do not contemplate the misdemeanors alleged to have been committed by the writ petitioner as misconduct.  7. The punishment of dismissal sought to be imposed on the writ petitioner is shockingly disproportionate to the gravity of the charges levelled against the petitioner.  8.
