In the enquiry report the Enquiry Officer recorded "defence could not disprove the charge" this shows that the approach of the Enquiry Officer was wrong and not good in law vitiating the entire enquiry.  9. Enquiry report was submitted by the Enquiry Officer after his retirement with a back date and this action of the Enquiry Officer has vitiated the enquiry proceeding.  4. In course of hearing large number of decisions were cited by the learned advocates for both the parties. It is not necessary to refer to all those decisions because this case can be disposed of on Point Nos. 2 and 6 which go to the very root of the matter and Point No. 9.  5. By my judgment and order dated 9.3.1998 in C.O. No. 15653(W) of 1996 (Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Officers' Association and another v. Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited and others) I held that the respondent No. 1 is a `State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India. At the time of hearing of this case I wanted to know from the ld. Advocate appearing for the respondents whether he disputes that respondent No. 1 is a `State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India. The ld. Advocate for the respondents stated that he is not disputing that the respondent No. 1 is a `State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India. Since the respondent No. 1 is a `State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India Part-III and Part-IV of the Constitution apply in every action of the respondent No. 1. (Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi, AIR 1981 SC 487, All India Sainik Schools Employees' Association v. The Defence Minister-cum-Chairman, Board of Governors, Sainik School Society, AIR 1989 SC 88). In the matter of a disciplinary proceeding against an employee of a `State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India, touching the livelihood of the employee all actions of the `State' should pass the test of both Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution of India.  6. By catena of decisions of Supreme Court scope of judicial review has now become well settled. Suffice it to refer to M/s. Shri Sitaram Sugar Co. Ltd. v. Union of India reported in AIR 1990 SC 1277. Paragraph 49 of the reported decision of M/s Shri Sitaram Sugar Co. Ltd.'s case (supra) is quoted hereinbelow :-  "Where a question of law is at issue, the Court may determine the rightness of the impugned decision on its own independent judgment. If the decision of the authority does not agree with that which the Court considers to be the right one, the finding of law by the authority is liable to be upset. Where it is a finding of fact, the Court examines only the reasonableness of the finding. When that finding is found to be rational and reasonably based on evidence, in the sense that all relevant material has been taken into account and no irrelevant material has influenced the decision, and the decision is one which any reasonably minded person, acting on such evidence, would have come to, then judicial review is exhausted even though the finding may not necessarily be what the Court would have come to as a trier of fact. Whether an order is characterised as legislative or administrative or quasi judicial, or, whether it is a determination of law or fact, the judgment of the expert body, entrusted with power, is generally treated as final and the judicial function is exhausted when it is found to have "warrant in the record" and a rational basis of law : Rochester Tel. Corp. v. United States, 1938(307) US 125 : 83 Law Ed. 1147. See also Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation, 1948(1) KB 223."  7. I by my judgment and order dated 15.6.1998 in C.O. No. 13764(W) of 1989 (Prasanta Das & others v. M/s Webel Video Devices Ltd. & another) held :  "It is now well settled that the proper legal effect of a proved fact is essentially a question of law. Whenever an inference is drawn from certain conclusion of facts, that inference is a question of law in its essential nature. (Nafar Chandra v. Shukur, reported in 45 Indian Appeal 183 at page 187). The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Ram Gopal v. Shamskhaton reported in 19 Indian Appeal 228(C) at page 232 observed : "the facts found need not be questioned. It is the soundness of the conclusions from them that is in question and this is a matter of law." This view had been approved by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Lakshmi Dhar Misra v. Ranglal reported in 76 Indian Appeal 271 at page 276.  In my opinion, while exercising power of judicial review, High Court can and should examine the soundness of the conclusions from the facts found in the departmental proceeding because that is a matter of law, which is very much within the power of judicial review of the Court."  Re. Point Nos. 2 and 6.  8. By a charge-sheet dated 28th June, 1993 issued by Manager (Administration) certain charges were levelled against the petitioner. For proper understanding of the charges levelled against the petitioner, the relevant portion of the charge-sheet is quoted hereinbelow:-  "SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SINGHA,  SR. ASSTT. SECURITY OFFICER,  Man No. 007969,  SECURITY DEPARTMENT (MAIN WORKS),  G.R.S.E. Limited  It has been reported against you as under :-  1. that 7th June, 1993 was a day of Bangla Bandh and you were detailed for duties at G.R.S.E. Main Workshop that day and as such you were asked to report in the night of 6th June, 1993. Accordingly, you came to Main Works at about 2130 hours on 6th June, by a Scooter driven by you and parked the said Scooter in the Parking space adjacent to gate No. 1.  2. that as the local situation appeared to be more or less normal in the evening of 7th June, 1993, Sri M.K. Bhattacharyya, Sr. Security Officer, advised you to be off from your duty and to go back home, if possible, and to report for duty on the next day i.e. 8th June, 1993 in your routine `B' shift positively as there was shortage of security officers to be available on duty in the Department on that day. You as such left the Main Works at about 1715 hours on 7th June, 1993 on a Scooter driven by you through Gate No. 1 giving a lift of Sri T.P. Makal, Asstt. Security Officer, who was also off from his duty on completion of General shift at that time and who happens to be residing nearby your locality.  3. that you had submitted two (2) Taxi Bills both dated 8th June, 1993 to Sri M.K. Bhattacharyya, Sr. Security Officer, claiming for reimbursement of Taxi fare for Rs. 35/- and Rs. 40/- for undertaking journeys by Taxi for coming in the Main Works on 6th June, 1993 and for return journey to home on 7th June, 1993 respectively.  4. that though you had undertaken the above journeys by a Scooter driven by you yet have claimed Taxi fares for reimbursement of the expenses for the said journeys falsely.  5. the above acts alleges to have been committed by you amount to misconduct under the following Rules of Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules of the Company applicable to you :-  (i) Sub-rule 1 of Rule 5  "Theft, fraud or dishonesty in connection with the property of the Company within the premises of the Company." (ii) Sub-rule 5 of Rule 5  "Acting in a manner prejudicial to the interest of the Company." (iii) Sub-rule 20 of Rule 5  "Commission of any act subversive of discipline or of good behaviour." 6. You are, hereby directed to submit you explanation in writing in respect of charges levelled against you, within 10 days from the date of receipt of this letter as to why disciplinary action should not be taken against you.  7. Should you fail to submit your explanation as advised, it will be presumed that you have no explanation to offer and further action will be taken as per the Rules of the Company in this regard."  9. The petitioner by his letter dated 16th July, 1993 submitted his explanation in respect of the charges levelled against him. In his said explanation, the petitioner had, inter alia, stated as follows :  "I am stating all above because I feel and when an officer is not only questioned on his submitted Taxi-fare claim but a charge-sheet is issued for its explanation particularly when as per TA/DA rules for officers of the company "Taxi" covers car, scooters, rickshaws, cycle rickshaws, tangas etc. Hence the taxi claim preferred for journey by scooter on hire and rickshaw on hire by the said amount over and above the taxi on hire is well within the Rules of Reimbursement of the taxi hire charges by the company and thus no false claim was preferred by me. However, in any event as the taxi bills are not yet reimbursed to me, nor I have received the same till date, by no stretch of imagination it can be alleged that I have committed any act of theft, fraud or dishonesty and in the facts of this case none are attracted. ............. Having made the claim for reimbursement for taxi fare strictly in terms of TA/DA Rules for Officers (effective 1st August 1988) of the company I have neither committed any theft or fraud or dishonesty in connection with the property of the company, within the premises of the company nor I have acted in a manner prejudicial in the interest of the company nor it tantamounts to commission of any act subversive of Discipline or good behaviour." (Emphasis added) Therefore, it is clear from the aforesaid explanation of the petitioner that he claimed for reimbursement for taxi fare and in terms of TA/DA Rules for Officers (effective 1st Aug. 1988) of the Company. May be, the provisions of the aforesaid TA/DA Rules have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case but at best that would only make the claims of the petitioner liable for rejection. At no stretch of imagination can such claims be treated as theft, fraud or dishonesty in connection with the property of the company nor can it be said to be an act in any manner prejudicial to the interest of the company nor it tantamounts to commission of any act subversive of discipline or good behaviour. It is not disputed that claims have not yet been reimbursed to the petitioner. It is important to note that Rule 2(9) of the TA/DA Rules of 1988 clearly lays down that the term `Taxi' shall cover cars, scooters, rickshaws, cycle rickshaws, tangas etc. The petitioner in his explanation dated 16th July, 1993 (reply to the charge-sheet) clearly stated that he made the claims for reimbursement for taxi fare strictly in terms of TA/DA Rules for Officers effective from 1st August, 1988. There remains no doubt that while making claims under and strictly in terms of the TA/DA Rules, 1988 the peritioner did not commit any wrong by mentioning `Taxi' instead of `scooter' in view of Rule 2(9) of the aforesaid TA/DA Rules, 1988. If the subject matter of the claims made by the petitioner is not covered by the aforesaid TA/DA Rules, 1988 then the petitioner would not get the reimbursement but such claims for reimbursement under TA/DA Rules, 1988 cannot be viewed as misconduct of any nature. If it is viewed as misconduct then that would be too unreasonable, unfair, irrational and arbitrary necessitating judicial intervention by judicial review. From the enquiry report it does not appear that there is any other set of rules dealing with TA/DA of Officers. No mention had been made in the enquiry report about any such other TA/DA Rules. The learned advocate appearing for the respondents in course of his argument also did not refer to any other TA/DA Rules for officers. Therefore, an officer covered by the said TA/DA Rules 1988 can claim for reimbursement only under the provisions of TA/DA Rules 1988. A claim for reimbursement under the said TA/DA Rules 1988 if not maintainable is liable to be rejected but no disciplinary proceeding can be legally initiated against the claimant on the allegations of misconduct of any nature for making such claims and if any such disciplinary proceeding is initiated that would amount to (a) absolute arbitrary exercise of power and (b) gross abuse or misuse of power and authority, rendering such initiation of disciplinary proceeding null and void. Ordinarily, "arbitrary" is synonymous with bad faith or failure to exercise honest judgment and an arbitrary act would be one performed without adequate determination of principle and one not founded in the nature of things. (Huey v. Davis, Tex. Civ. App. 556 S.W. 2d 860, 865).  10. In the report submitted by the enquiry officer it was, inter alia, recorded as follows :-  "Shri M.K. Bhattacharyya asserted further that T.K.S. made futile attempt to get the applicability of TA/DA Rules extended for journey from and to his residence after distorting the said rule which is well within the jurisdiction of Calcutta Corporation. And also by taking the extended meaning of `taxi' to scooter and rickshaws. Sri Bhattacharyya asserted further that those meant for a place of out station duty at least eight Km. away from the Head Quarters. Hence applicability of TA/DA Rules in respect of false Taxi reimbursement claims are totally unjustified." It appears from the enquiry report that Sri M.K. Bhattacharyya, Sr. Security Officer of the Security Department besides appearing as a prosecution witness also acted as presenting officer. From the above quoted recording of the enquiry officer it is evident that the disciplinary authority was very much aware that the petitioner made his claims under and in terms of TA/DA Rules of 1988.  11. It is not in dispute that the claims in question made by petitioner were connected with his official duty. Right from the explanation to the charges the petitioner maintained his stand that he submitted those claims under and in terms of TA/DA Rules of 1988. Rule 2(9) of the TA/DA Rules 1988 laid down that the term `Taxi' in TA/DA Rules 1988 includes "Scooter", "Rickshaw" etc. Therefore, the petitioner while submitting his claims under and in terms of TA/DA Rules 1988 did not commit any misconduct by claiming Taxi charge. If TA/DA Rules 1988 are not applicable for journey from and to his residence, the claim might have been rejected and the matter would have ended there.  12. That apart mere submission of claims in question itself did not make the petitioner entitled to get the reimbursement. Before payment could be made claims were to be sanctioned or recommended by the Chief Security Officer. The enquiry officer in his report recorded the case of the disciplinary authority, inter alia, as follows :-  "T.K.S. submitted in the afternoon two taxi reimbursement claims for recommendation of C.H.S.O. and forwarding subsequently to the Transport Officer for proceeding (processing ?) for cash reimbursement." 13. What are the provisions for reimbursement of claims of officers in force in Respondent No. 1 ? As stated earlier in this judgment, except TA/DA Rules of 1988 no other provision has either been referred to in the enquiry report or produced before the Court during hearing of the case. Therefore, it is apparent that except TA/DA Rules of 1988 there is no other provision which enables an officer to claim reimbursement for travelling. Whenever an officer wants to make a claim for reimbursement he has to submit his claim under and in terms of TA/DA Rules of 1988 and that is what the petitioner did. There was nothing in it not to speak of misconduct.  14. In view of the discussions made hereinabove I am of the opinion that initiation of the disciplinary proceeding under challenge was arbitrary, whimsical, fanciful, unreasonable, unfair and irrational. I am also of the opinion that the said disciplinary proceeding was initiated in gross abuse or misuse of power and authority. I am of the opinion that entire disciplinary proceeding under challenge is null and void.  15. The ld. Advocate for the respondents referred to Probodh Kumar Bhowmick v. University of Calcutta reported in 1993(2) CLJ 456 wherein it was held by S.B. Sinha, J. that in absence of any provision of statute an employer has inherent right to initiate a disciplinary proceeding as against its employees. It was held that it is beyond anybody's comprehension that although an employee might have committed a serious misconduct like defalcation, theft, misbehaviour with a lady or similar other matter he cannot be punished. It was held that misconduct, inter alia, envisages breach of discipline although it would not be possible to lay down exhaustively as what would constitute misconduct and indiscipline. It is wide enough to include wrongful omission or commission whether done or omitted to be done intentionally or unintentionally. I have already held hereinabove that the claims made by the petitioner for reimbursement under TA/DA Rules of 1988 may not be maintainable making them liable to rejection but under no stretch of imagination can those be construed as misconduct committed by the petitioner. Therefore, I am of the view that Probodh Kumar Bhowmick's case (supra) does not help the respondents.  16. No doubt a disciplinary authority has power and authority to initiate a disciplinary proceeding against an employee by issuing charge-sheet. But such power or authority should not be exercised arbitrarily, irrationally, unreasonably and unfairly. The disciplinary authority when acts as a servant of a `State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India is bound to act justly, fairly, rationally, reasonably and not arbitrarily. If he fails to act accordingly, the action of the disciplinary authority shall violate the provisions of Article 14 of the Constitution. Application of mind is not only a requisite condition but a condition precedent. Before initiating any disciplinary proceeding, the disciplinary authority should with an open mind consider the relevant materials ignoring the irrelevant one and should honestly form an opinion that a disciplinary proceeding should be initiated by issuing charge-sheet. The disciplinary authority cannot arbitrarily initiate a disciplinary proceeding injuring the dignity of an employee. Dignity of the individual has been assured in the preamble of our Constitution. Disciplinary authority only because of its status and authority cannot arbitrarily, whimsically, fancifully initiate a disciplinary proceeding against an employee. I am of the view that arbitrary, fanciful and whimsical initiation of disciplinary proceeding is not only violative of Article 14 of the Constitution but also injures the dignity of the employee. In our social system when disciplinary action is initiated arbitrarily, fancifully or whimsically against an employee on the allegation of misconduct like theft, fraud etc. then not only the employee concerned but also members of his family suffer from indignity. Power is there with the disciplinary authority but that power should not be abused or misused. Such power should be exercised honestly keeping the mind open and without any bias. Such power should not be exercised arbitrarily, fancifully or whimsically. In view of the discussions made hereinabove I am of the opinion that the initiation of the disciplinary proceeding against the petitioner, which is subject matter of the present litigation, was arbitrary, fanciful and whimsical and violated Article 14 of the Constitution and injured the dignity of the petitioner. No prejudice need be proved for enforcing the fundamental rights. Violation of a fundamental right itself renders the impugned action void (A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak, AIR 1988 SC 1531). The ld. Advocate for the respondents referred to Arun Kr. Mitra v. Central Vigilance Commission reported in 1986(1) CHN 390 wherein S.R. Roy, J. (as he then was) held that no fixed principle can be laid down for determining whether a charge-sheet was issued with a bias and/or closed mind or not. It was held that every case has to be distinguished on its own peculiar facts and circumstances. It has been pointed out by me hereinabove that the disciplinary authority without applying his mind initiated disciplinary proceeding arbitrarily, whimsically, fancifully, irrationally and unfairly against the petitioner and that was possible because the disciplinary authority had closed mind at the time of initiating the departmental proceeding. The disciplinary authority was biased against the petitioner and as consequence of such bias the disciplinary authority without applying his mind initiated disciplinary proceeding arbitrarily, whimsically, fancifully, irrationally, and unfairly. The enquiry officer in his enquiry report recorded (at page 90 of the writ petition) as follows :-  "On 21.6.1993 the matter was reported to C & MD through the then Manager (Admn.). On the basis of such report and relevant documents, Manager (Admn.) issued charge-sheet No. `illegible' dated 28.6.1993 to T.K.S." But that is not the correct recording of the state of affairs. The Chief Security Officer in his letter dated 21st June, 1993 addressed to the Chairman and Managing Director stated :  "G.M. (CM & IE) and Manager (Admn.) have agreed to issue show cause to Shri Singha." This letter of the Chief Security Officer dated 21st June, 1993 clearly indicates that even before the said letter was written by the Chief Security Officer the Manager (Admn.) agreed to issue show cause to Shri Singha. Therefore it is incorrect to say that on the basis of the report dated 21st June, 1993 issued by the Chief Security Officer and relevant documents, Manager (Admn.) issued charge-sheet dated 28.6.1993 to the petitioner. It is apparent from the letter dated 21st June, 1993 issued by the Chief Security Officer that Manager (Admn.) had already committed to issue charge-sheet against the petitioner without having any record before him and without applying his mind to the records. Thus it is clear that even before the relevant materials were placed before the Manager (Admn.) for the purpose of deciding whether a disciplinary proceeding should be initiated or not, the Manager (Admn.) agreed to issue charge-sheet and therefore at the time of taking decision he was biased and not keeping an open mind. Therefore, Arun Kr. Mitra's case (supra) does not help the respondents.  17. The ld. Advocate for the respondents also referred to Ram Ch. Ram v. Union of India & others reported in 94 CWN 574. The questions involved in Ram Ch. Ram's case (supra) are different from the questions involved in the present case and therefore, Ram Ch. Ram's case (supra) does not help the respondents.  18. Under these circumstances I am of the opinion that the initiation of the disciplinary proceeding against the petitioner is null and void.  Re. Point No. 9  19. Conduct, discipline and appeal of the petitioner are governed by Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Ltd. (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1977 (hereinafter referred to as DAR). Rule 23 of DAR lays down the penalties which may be imposed on an employee for misconduct committed by him or for any other good and sufficient reasons. Penalties have been divided into two categories (1) minor penalties and (2) major penalties. Dismissal and removal from service have been classified as major penalties. Rule 26 of the DAR laid down the procedure for imposing major penalties. The ld. Advocate for the respondents argued that DAR have no statutory force of law. Assuming arguendo that DAR have no statutory force of law even then respondent No. 1 and his officers are bound to comply with the provisions of DAR. By virtue of DAR the respondent No. 1 laid down the standards by which it professes its action to be judged. It is well settled rule of administrative law that an executive authority must be rigorously held to the standards by which it professes its action to be judged and it must scrupulously observe those standards on pain of invalidation of an act in violation of them.  20. In Votarelli v. Seaton, 359 US 535, 3 L ed 2d 1012, 79 S ct 968. Justice Frankfuter in his separate opinion (at page 1012) laid down the following principle :-  "An executive agency must be rigorously held to the standards by which it professes its action to be judged. See Securities & Exch. Com. v. Cheneray Corp., 318 US 80, 87, 88, 87 L ed 626, 632, 633, 63 S ct 454. Accordingly, if dismissal from employment is based on a defined procedure, even though generous beyond the requirements that bind such agency, that procedure must be scrupulously observed. See Service v. Dulles, 354 US 363, 1 L ed 2d 1403 77 S Ct 1152. This judicially evolved rule of administrative law is now firmly established and, if I may add, rightly so. He that takes the procedural sword shall perish with the sword. Therefore, I unreservedly join in the Court's main conclusion, that the attempted dismissal of Vitarelli in September 1954 was abortive and of no validity because the procedure under Department of the Interior Order No. 2738 was invoked but not observed." (Emphasis added) 21. The above quoted principle laid down by Mr. Justice Frankfuter has been accepted as applicable in India by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in A.S. Ahluwalia v. Punjab State, AIR 1975 SC 984, Sukhdev v. Bhagatram, AIR 1975 SC 1331, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, AIR 1979 SC 1628, B.S. Minhas v. Indian Statistical Institute, AIR 1984 SC 363.  Rule 26(16) of DAR reads as follows :  "After the completion of the production of the evidence, the employee and the Presenting Officer may file written briefs of their respective cases within 15 days of the date of completion of the production of evidence." 22. In course of argument the ld. Advocate for the petitioner vehemently argued that the enquiry officer submitted his enquiry report after his retirement from service on and from 1st July, 1996. On behalf of the respondents two supplementary affidavits have been filed. One supplementary affidavit was affirmed by Shri Beni Madhab Saha, the Director (Personnel) of the respondent No. 1 on 18th April, 1998. In the said supplementary affidavit affirmed on 18th April, 1998 the Director (Personnel) of respondent No. 1 in paragraph 4 and 5 stated as follows :-  "I confirm and assert that I had no knowledge about the submission of Report by the Enquiry Officer on the material date of affirmation of Affidavit-in- opposition on 7th June, 1996. But subsequently it transpired that the Enquiry Officer had already submitted his report in a sealed cover with the endorsement `Confidential' addressed to Chairman and Managing Director. Since this was in a closed sealed cover I had no way to know the contents thereof when I made the earlier affidavit on 7.6.1995. I further say as head of the Personnel Department that there cannot arise any question of submission of Report by the Enquiry Officer after his retirement or by ante-dating the same. This type of practice is not allowed by our organisation." 23. Another supplementary affidavit was affirmed by Pralay Kanti Sarkar, Enquiry Officer, on 18th April, 1998. In paragraphs 2 and 3 of the supplementary affidavit said Shri Pralay Kanti Sarkar stated as follows :-  "I was appointed as Enquiry Officer to enquire into the charges levelled against Shri Tapan Kumar Singha by charge-sheet dated 28th June, 1993. I conducted the enquiry from 27th August, 1993 to 17th May, 1996 and I submitted my Report on 28th May, 1996 before my retirement. I have been shown paragraph 19 of an Affidavit affirmed by Shri Tapan Kumar Singha on 26th March, 1998 and I have gone through the same. I confirm that I submitted my Report in a closed confidential cover to Shri Birendra Nath Mukherjee, P.A. to General Manager (Pers.) for onward transmission to the Chairman and Managing Directorate's Secretariat on 28th May, 1996 itself and the allegation of submission of Report after retirement by ante-dating the same is totally baseless." From the Enquiry Report submitted by the Enquiry Officer it also appears that the enquiry was concluded on 17.5.1996. I accept the statement of the Enquiry Officer that he conducted the enquiry from 27th August, 1993 to 17th May, 1996 and submitted his enquiry report on 28th May, 1996. From the enquiry proceeding also it appears that witnesses were examined before the enquiry officer on 17th May, 1996. Therefore, the petitioner, in view of above quoted Rule 26(16) of DAR, had right to file written briefs of his case within 15 days from the date of completion of production of evidence. True that Rule 26(16) does not make it obligatory to file written briefs within 15 days of the date of completion of the production of evidence but the petitioner was entitled to file written briefs within 15 days of the date of completion of the production of evidence. This procedure is consistent with the principle of fairness in action. Since the Enquiry Officer submitted his enquiry report on 28th May, 1996 i.e. well before the 15 days from the date of completion of production of evidence, the petitioner had been deprived of the opportunity to file written briefs. Following the above quoted principle laid down by Mr. Justice Frankfuter I am of the view that the proposed dismissal of the petitioner from the service of respondent No. 1 is abortive and of no validity because the procedure under DAR was invoked but Rule 26(16) of DAR was not observed.  24. In view of the discussions made hereinabove, I set aside and quash the entire disciplinary proceeding including the charge-sheet and the proposed order of dismissal. Since I find that the grounds stated hereinabove are sufficient to set aside the entire disciplinary proceeding initiated against the petitioner including the charge-sheet and the proposed order of dismissal, I am not dealing with the other points argued by the ld. Advocate for the petitioner. The writ application is then disposed of. However, there shall not be any order as to costs.  Order accordingly.
summary: A. Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16 and 311 - TA/DA Rules, 1988, Rule 2(9) - Departmental Enquiry - Chargesheet - Misconduct - Petitioner claimed taxi charges for reimbursement of TA/DA - Term taxi in TA/DA Rules 1988 includes "Scooter", "Rickshaw", etc. - Disciplinary proceedings against petitioner violated Article 14 of the Constitution - Entire disciplinary proceedings quashed. [Paras 11 and 16]  B. Constitution of India, Articles 311 - Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Ltd. (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976, Rule 26(16) - Departmental Enquiry - Natural Justice - Petitioner was entitled to file written briefs within 15 days of completion of production of evidence under Rule 26(16) - Petitioner deprived of opportunity to file written briefs - Proposed dismissal of petitioner is abortive and of no validity - Proposed order of dismissal set aside. [Paras 23 and 24]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. - The petitioner who was appointed as a Clerk in the Kharga Army Canteen impugns the provision in the Standing Order by which it has been provided that the "maximum permissible service for an employee is 15 years" and that "the services of an employee will be automatically relinquished based on completion of age limit or maximum permissible service, whichever occurs first". The maximum age upto which an employee can serve is 60 years. The petitioner alleges that the provision is arbitrary and thus violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.  2. The respondents contest the petitioner's claim. It has been inter alia pleaded that the Canteen is not an instrumentality of the State as contemplated under Article 12 of the Constitution. It has been further pleaded that the Government of India has got nothing to do with the running of the Canteen. The employees who can be civilians or ex-servicemen are paid their salaries "from the profits of the Canteen and not from the State ex- chequer". The finances for running the canteen "are arranged by the units themselves..." The appointment of the petitioner is contractual and the service conditions are governed by the Standing Orders of the Canteen. Prior to June 1988, no age of retirement or the tenure of appointment had been fixed. Consequently, an amendment was made in the Standing Orders on June 5, 1988. If the petitioner has any grievance, he has the remedy of filing a civil suit for damages. According to the respondents, the writ petition is wholly lacking in merit and deserves to be dismissed.  3. The petitioner has filed a replication and produced certain documents.  4. Counsel for the parties have been heard.  5. Mr. Rameshwar Malik, learned counsel for the petitioner has contended that the impugned provision is vitiated as no opportunity had been granted to the petitioner before the amendment of the Standing Order. He has further submitted that the impugned provision cannot apply to the persons who are already in service. According to the learned counsel, the provision cannot be applicable to civilian employees but can be implemented only against ex- servicemen who are employed in the canteens. It has been further submitted that in all other Canteens, an employee is entitled to continue upto the age of 60 years. The action of the respondent-Canteen in fixing a tenure of 15 years is, thus, arbitrary and unfair. The claim made on behalf of the petitioner has been controverted by Mr. R.P. Singh Ahluwalia who has appeared on behalf of the respondent-Canteen.  6. The two questions that arise for consideration are :  (i) Is the Respondent-Canteen a State within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution ? (ii) Is the impugned provision illegal and ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution ? Reg :(i)  7. Mr. Malik submits that the Respondent-Canteen is under the direct and complete control of the Ministry of Defence. It functions under the instructions issued by the Army Headquarters. The items for sale in the canteens are provided by the Canteen Stores Department. Reference has also been made to the fact that a committee had been appointed by the Rajya Sabha. It had submitted its report on September 13, 1991. This report dealt with the service conditions of the civilian employees of the Defence Unit-run Canteens. On the basis of this report, it is contended that the Canteen is an instrumentality of the State. These facts as averred in the replication have been controverted in the affidavit filed on behalf of the Respondent-Canteen. It has been inter alia pointed out that the 'canteen' is not the creation of any Statute, Act or legislation. The conditions of service of the employees are governed by the Standing Orders issued by the Canteen from time to time. The Ministry of Defence or the Quarter Master General Branch have got nothing to do with the Canteen or its employees. It has also been emphasised that the Canteen is regularly paying rent as well as water and electricity charges for the use of the premises provided to it. The accounts are audited by the Private Chartered Accountants namely M/s. Batra & Co. of Ambala. The Canteen Stores Department supplies the goods at the fixed rates. The registration number is issued for the running of the canteen.  8. The canteen is not created by or under a Statute. There is no law or statutory provision governing its affairs. There is nothing on record to show that any funds are provided by the Government. Still further, there is no evidence of any control much less than of a pervasive control of the Government in the running of the Canteen. It is true that the Canteen Stores Department has issued a registration number to the respondent. It is also true that the Department supplies various articles as required by the Canteen. This is, however, no evidence of control by the Government. The registration number is allotted only for the purpose of regulating the supply of goods which in the very nature of things, is a purely commercial transaction. Furthermore, even the accounts of the Canteen are not audited by any agency of the Government. There is no control or regulation regarding the appointment of personnel. Taking the totality of circumstances into consideration, it cannot be said that the tests enunciated by their Lordships of the Supreme Court in Ajay Hassia's case are fulfilled.  9. Accordingly, it is held that the Respondent-Canteen is not an instrumentality of the State. The first question is, thus, answered in the negative.  10. A copy of the Standing Order has been produced as Annexure R-31 with the written statement. A perusal thereof shows that the affairs of the Canteen are managed by a managing committee. The terms and conditions of the Staff are laid down in Appendix 'B'. In para 3(b), it was categorically provided that "the Canteen Managing Committee shall have the option to terminate the services of any of the canteen staff after giving him 30 days' notice..." In case of misconduct, the services could be terminated without any notice. Under Para 4, the scales of pay and allowances of the staff were to be decided by the managing committee with the approval of the Patron-in-Chief. It is, thus, clear that prior to the impugned amendment, there was no security of tenure. The services of an employee could be terminated at any time by giving him a 30 days' notice. No age of retirement had been prescribed. It was by the impugned amendment that the age upto which a person could serve in the Canteen was fixed. It was also provided that an employee could serve for a maximum period of 15 years. In the circumstances of the case, the action cannot be said to be arbitrary or unfair. Normally, ex-servicemen are appointed in the Canteens. Sometimes, even civilians are selected. A tenure of 15 years or permission to serve upon the age of 60 years whichever is earlier, is in the circumstances of the case, just and fair.  11. Mr. Malik submits that the provision is violative of the principles of natural justice as no opportunity had been afforded to the petitioner before the amendment of the Standing Order.  12. The contention is wholly untenable. The employer has the right to stipulate the conditions of service. Prior to the impugned amendment, the petitioner did not have a right to continue in service till any particular age. Even in the order of appointment, a copy of which has been produced as Annexure P-1 with the writ petition, it has nowhere been stipulated that the petitioner shall have a right to continue in service till she attains a particular age. The impugned provision in the Standing Order does not violate any term of appointment. There is nothing to show that the petitioner had a right to continue in service till she attained the age of 60 years. In this situation, it cannot be said that her conditions of service were varied to her disadvantage or that the impugned provision is not applicable to her. Accordingly, the contention raised by Mr. Malik that the action is violative of the principles of natural justice or that the impugned provision cannot apply to the person who had joined service prior to June 1988, cannot be sustained.  13. Equally lacking in merit is the contention that the impugned provision can be applicable only in case of ex-servicemen and not in case of civilians. There is no basis for such a contention.  14. It was then submitted that in other canteens, the employees have a right to continue till the age of 60 years. Nothing has been produced to show that it is actually so. Even if it is assumed that certain canteens have permitted the employees to continue in service upto the age of 60 years without prescribing the maximum period of service, it cannot be said that the action is illegal. If each canteen is an independent unit, it has a right to take its own policy decision. The provision made by one managing committee does not bind another.  15. No data has been placed on record to show that the provision is in any way arbitrary or unfair. Even if it is assumed that the Respondent-Canteen is an instrumentality of the State, there appears to be no reason to support the contention that the action of the respondent is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.  16. Accordingly, I find no merit in this writ petition. It is dismissed. However, in the circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: A. Constitution of India, Article 12 - Army Canteen - Is not a State instrumentality. [Para 9] B. Constitution of India, Article 14 - Standing Order - Tenure of Service - Canteen employees can be terminated with a 30-day notice - No retirement age was specified - The impugned amendment fixes the period of service up to 15 years. [Para 10]

text: Swatanter Kumar, J. - This regular second appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned first appellate court dated 25.5.1998, wherein the learned Additional District Judge, Kurukshetra, dismissed the first appeal preferred by the State of Haryana against the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court dated 17.2.1998.  2. The plaintiff, who was working as a Superintendent of Police in the State of Haryana had instituted a suit for declaration that adverse remarks recorded in his Annual Confidential Report by the defendant for the year 1993-94 were illegal, null and void and not binding on him. He further prayed for a direction that the same be expunged from his service record and be not considered for any purpose. The suit was contested by the State on merits and the preliminary objections with regard to the maintainability of the suit and the territorial jurisdiction of the Court to entertain and decide the suit were raised. The learned trial Court framed four issues and all the material issues were answered in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant and decreed the suit of the plaintiff by a well considered judgment and placing reliance upon the various judgments of this Court as well as Hon'ble Supreme Court of India.  3. As already noticed, the learned first appellate Court, while affirming the finding of facts arrived at by the learned trial Court, has held as under :-  "Further a perusal of other annual confidential report of the plaintiff ranging from 1982 and 1993 shows that he had been earning good or very good. All of a sudden how he became such like person as reflected in his annual confidential report. No material/dates were relied upon by the reporting officer, which goes to show that recording of adverse remarks against the plaintiff in his annual confidential report for the year 1993-94 were based on no material and were without subjectivity or objectivity in contravention of instructions as laid down with regard to writing of confidential reports." 4. Having perused the record, I am of the considered view that the remarks recorded in the confidential report for the year 1993-94 had far reaching consequences. It in fact, adversely reported on the entire service record of the plaintiff. He was described as a burden on the department and deserved to be weeded out. The officer concerned nowhere recorded that his integrity was doubtful. That being so and the entire previous record right from 1982 to 1993 being `good' or `very good' would create a contradiction in the observations of the authorities concerned. Such serious remarks normally should be supported by some material or should be recorded with reference to some definite incident or conduct of the concerned official to the knowledge of the reporting officer. As no evidence of any kind or other official record maintained in the normal course of its business was placed before the learned Courts below, I am unable to see any error in the concurrent view taken by the learned courts below.  5. Consequently, I find no merit in this regular second appeal. The same is dismissed in limine.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India Article 14, 16 and 226 - Adverse remarks - In the plaintiff-respondent's annual ACR for the year 1993-94, adverse remarks were recorded without any basis and were subjective and biased against him, violating instructions - The plaintiff's entire service record was affected by this and he was labeled a burden to the department who needed to be weeded out - The contradiction in the observations between the plaintiff's previous "good" or "very good" records from 1982-93 and the adverse remarks is problematic - Such severe remarks should have some supporting evidence or be based on a specific event - The state's appeal was dismissed. [Para 4]

text: Arun Kumar Mitra, J. - The writ petition relates to challenge of charge- sheet, inquiry proceeding and a command order directing the petitioner to join the inquiry. Facts in brief are inter alia as follows :-  2. The petitioner is a Constable in the Railway Protection Force of C & TE/Undal under Asansol Division, Eastern Railway. The petitioner was charge sheeted and the charges are;  3. Gross misconduct and negligence of duty and it was clarified as :  "When he was working at RPF/TM-Post/chh/CRJ he was spared to avail one day rest, two days CR, one day CPL and four days CL w.e.f. 19.08.1995 to 26.08.1995 and was supposed to resume his duty on 27.08.1995 but instead of joining his duty he overstayed w.e.f. 27.08.1995 to 11.03.1997 without any authority and proper intimation."  "Further when working at C & TE/OP/Udl he was spared for 30 days LAP on 24.04.1998 and was supposed to join his duty on 24.05.1998 but he overstayed till 31.07.1998."  4. Accordingly, the petitioner is a habitual absentee or habitual offender regarding overstay. On these charges the inquiry was started; inquiry continued; the petitioner submitted his representation.  5. According to the petitioner, charge-sheet is vague and in the statement of allegations it is admitted by the authority that the administration received the intimation from his son that his father was getting treatment at Ranchi and misconduct and negligence does not arise at that juncture.  6. The petitioner challenged this proceeding; inquiry finding as well as the charge-sheet and the command certificate directing the petitioner to join there on the ground that the charge-sheet is biased.  7. In the charge-sheet without preliminary inquiry name of the Inquiry Officer has been mentioned, venue of the inquiry and date and time has also been mentioned. The petitioner also challenged this inquiry finding on the ground that no reason has been assigned in the findings. The Inquiry Officer acted in a partisan manner and failed to record any reason why the petitioner was found guilty of the charges levelled against him.  8. The petitioner also took a ground that the decision making process is bad in law and arbitrary in nature because the proceedings are judicial or quasi judicial in nature and therefore findings must be based on reason.  9. The respondent authorities filed affidavit-in-opposition denying all the allegations made in the writ petition. The respondent authorities in the opposition took the plea that on 11/03/1997 the petitioner submitted the unsigned fit certificate and it was not acceptable in terms of the rules.  10. The respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition in paragraph 10 further stated that although a letter was received from his son on 11. 12.1995 i.e. after lapse of 107 days of his absence about his so called sickness but the intimation was not supported with any documentary proof or medical certificate.  11. It has been stated in the opposition that as per Rule 152(2) of RPF Rules 1987 the Assistant Security Commissioner is the competent authority to issue charge under Rule 153 of RPF Rules.  12. The respondents categorically dealt with all the paragraphs of the writ petition and stated that the Assistant Security Commissioner, Asansol, Eastern Railway under whose disciplinary control the petitioner was posted was empowered under Rule 151 sub Rule (1) in Schedule (iii) of RPF Rules, 1987 to issue charge-sheet against the petitioner. So the charge-sheet issued by him in strictly in terms of the rules.  13. The respondents in their opposition stated that it is the duty and responsibility of the petitioner to report to nearest Railway Doctor for his treatment if he was so sick but he did not do that and his intimation was received after a lapse of 107 days.  14. In the opposition it has been stated that Inquiry Officer gave an opportunity to the petitioner and there is no illegality in the proceeding. In the inquiry report the Inquiry Officer assigned due reasons and as such the inquiry is not vitiated for violation of principles of natural justice.  15. On this statement and counter statement this Court will have to come to a finding as to whether charge-sheet is biased or mala fide-inquiry proceeding and/or finding is bad in law or not and the command certificates directing the petitioner to join the inquiry is also bad in law or not.  DECISION  16. In a disciplinary proceeding the disciplinary authority and the Inquiry Officer are to act in accordance with law. Writ Court has little scope under judicial review to interfere. The Writ Court can neither act as an appellate Court nor can it reappreciate the evidence adduced before the Inquiry Officer. Let me discuss as to what should be the actual procedure in case of inquiry and charge-sheet.  17. Before issuing a charge-sheet the authorities are to conduct a preliminary inquiry and to come to a finding as to whether charge-sheet will be issued on the delinquent employee or not. Without deciding that if the authorities issue charge-sheet it indicates closure in the mind or biasness. In a judgment reported in AIR 2001 SC 343 ( V.K. Khanna v. State of Punjab) the Hon'ble Apex Court has observed that if in the charge-sheet the name of the Inquiry Officer is mentioned and the venue of the inquiry or the date of the inquiry has been fixed then it appears that the authority has already decided in mind to hold the inquiry and that indicates bias. In the instant case on the charge-sheet the name of the Inquiry Officer is there, the date and the place of inquiry has also been mentioned; though here the charges are clear inasmuch as it is of unauthorised absence and that is on record. Therefore, here, the question of preliminary inquiry would not arise but still then when the petitioner has submitted or produced medical certificate and/or when those certificates were not under challenge and admittedly, the son of the petitioner informed the Office (though after a lapse of about 107 days) in that event the absence would not be treated as gross misconduct.  18. That apart the Inquiry Officer in his inquiry report gave a finding but did not disclose reasons. It is settled position of law that when a quasi- judicial authority passes an order it must be backed by reasons. In this case the inquiry finding is not based on reasons and as such the inquiry finding does not get any leg to stand.  19. In the above view of the matter I set aside the inquiry proceeding as well as the charge-sheet but I maintain the charges. This inquiry finding and the charge-sheet is set aside but the authority is given liberty to proceed against the petitioner on the same charges. On the same charges also means the respondents will not have to issue any fresh charge-sheet.  20. The respondent authorities will however, when continuing the proceeding follow that principles of natural justice and the RPF Rules strictly. Fair opportunity is to be given to the petitioner and the proceeding so started will have to be concluded within six months from the date of communication of this order.  21. The writ petition is therefore, disposed of with the above directions.  22. There will be however, no order as to costs.  Urgent xerox certified copy, if applied for, will be given to the parties as expeditiously as possible upon usual undertaking.  Order accordingly.
summary: The Constitution of India, particularly Articles 226 and 311, together with the Railway Protection Force Rules of 1987, including Rules 151(1), 152(2), and 153, outline the disciplinary actions that can be taken against employees for gross misconduct, negligence of duty, and unauthorized absence from duty. As per these rules, charge sheets must be issued, and quasi-judicial authorities must record reasons for their orders. According to the present case, the inquiry officer's findings were without proper reasoning and hence cannot be upheld. Therefore, the charge sheet and the inquiry proceedings were set aside. [Paras 18 and 19]

text: S.M. Rizvi, J. - By medium of this petition, the order of respondent No. 3, the Deputy Sales Tax Commissioner Jammu, dated 8th August, 1990, terminating the services of the petitioner, under Article 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations, w.e.f. 6th February, 1990, has been challenged, inter alia, on the following grounds :-  "(a) That the impugned order dated 8.8.1990 terminating the services of the petitioner under Article 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations being essentially an order of removal from services, can be legally and validly passed only in accordance with the rules and procedure as established by law, requiring, inter alia, that no member of a Civil service of the State shall be dismissed or removed from service except after an enquiry in which he has been informed in writing of the charges against him and the grounds on which it is proposed to take disciplinary action and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and after such enquiry if it is proposed to impose any major penalty, no such penalty be imposed until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of making a representation on the penalty proposed. As such the impugned order dated 8.8.1990 suffers, on the face of it, from the vice of illegality and unconstitutionality and is accordingly liable to be quashed; (b) That Article 12 of the J&K Civil Service Regulations only specifies particular misconduct entailing major penalty of loss of appointment with certain exceptions but there is nothing in Article 128 C.S.R., authorising removal from service without observing the procedure as established by law and prescribed by the Constitution. Consequently, even in the case of loss of appointment in terms of Article 128 C.S.R. the procedure as established by law and envisaged by the Constitution has to be observed on the pain of invalidation of the action taken in break of the procedural safeguards. The impugned order dated 8.8.1990 is, therefore, arbitrary and wholly unauthorised, and as such is liable to be quashed; (c) That the impugned order dated 8.8.1990 is also discountenanced by the law and the Constitution inasmuch as terminates and thus removes the petitioner from service retrospectively. The impugned order dt. 8.8.1990 on this count as well is liable to be quashed; (d) That the treatment meted out to the petitioner by respondents 2 and 3 in the matter of services under the State is clearly arbitrary malicious and hostile inasmuch as the respondent No. 2 even on being urged by the respondent No. 1 to set right the wrong and remove the injustice, has failed without any cause on reason and obviously for oblige considerations to do the needful in vindication of Rule of Law. The impugned order dt. 8.8.1990 in this view of the matter clearly offends the mandate of Article 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution as applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and as such liable to be quashed; (e) That the impugned order dated 8.8.1990 has the effect of nullifying the constitutional guarantees with which the services under the State are hinged and as a sequel thereto has resulted in grave miscarriage of justice and is, therefore, liable to be quashed; (f) That the impugned order has resulted into manifest failure of justice and in order to prevent the failure justice so occasioned from being perpetuated, the impugned order dt. 8.8.1990 merits to be quashed, in the interest of justice." 2. The petitioner was serving as an orderly in the Sales Tax Department, Jammu, on substantive basis, when he applied for leave on medical grounds for a period of thirty days w.e.f. 6th February, 1990, which was recommended to be sanctioned in his favour by his immediate Officer, the Excise and Taxation Officer concerned. Allegedly, he was relieved by the said E.T.O., from the date of application. It is submitted that during !he course of his sickness, an extraordinary exigency cropped up in his family due to the sad and sudden demise of his uncle at Bagh, a place in the Pak Occupied Kashmir, and accordingly, the petitioner was required to accompany his parents to that place, in order to attend the mourning and to share the grief of the bereaved family. Allegedly, he was caught in an extraordinary situation, and under the dictates of situation and circumstances beyond his control, was left with no time to complete the formalities in the department for proceeding to Pak Occupied Kashmir. He, however, kept on seeking extensions of his leave period by submitting applications through his brother from Jammu.  3. On his return from Pak Occupied Kashmir, the petitioner reported for duty in the office of respondent No. 3 where he came to know about the order impugned in this petition. He preferred representation to the concerned Advisor to the Governor, in the form of appeal, against the said order, which however, was rejected.  4. In the reply filed by respondent No. 3 which is not supported by an affidavit it is admitted that the petitioner had applied for leave for a period of thirty days w.e.f. 6.2.1990. It is also admitted that the Excise and Taxation Officer concerned forwarded the petitioner's application to respondent No. 3. It is, however, stated that the leave was not sanctioned as it was not supported by a medical certificate. It is also admitted that at the expiry of 30 days, the petitioner submitted another application for extension of leave for thirty days more. At the expiry of that period, admittedly, he submitted another application for extension of leave for one month more. It is also admitted that the last application for extension of leave was received on 7.5.1990.  5. It is further stated in the reply that the E.T.O. concerned had asked the petitioner to submit a medical certificate in support of his application, but the said letter, sent under registered cover, was received back unserved as the petitioner was not available at his home address. The respondent No. 3 again sent a letter to the petitioner at his home address to resume his duty within 10 days, which too could not served on him. Lastly, a notice was published in the newspaper "Daily Excelsior" on 11.6.1990 asking the petitioner to explain his position and to show cause as to why his services be not terminated under Article 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations. Consequently, the order impugned was passed terminating the services of the petitioner.  6. I have gone through and considered the written arguments submitted by the learned counsel for the parties. The file has also been examined thoroughly.  7. It may be stated at the very outset that the original file of this writ petition was misplaced in the Registry, and it was reported by the Additional Registrar that despite the best efforts of all concerned, it could not be traced out. With the consent of the learned counsel for the parties the record of the file was ordered to be re-constructed, vide Court orders dated 10.5.1993 and 20.5.1993.  8. The petitioner filed the relevant copies for the re-construction of record which were taken on record. However, the copy of the counter having been filed by respondent No. 3 was without any affidavit. The learned counsel for the respondents took some opportunities to get the affidavit of respondent No. 3 filed in support of the counter. On 1.10.1993 he was given one more opportunity in this behalf. Despite of all this, the affidavit has not been filed by respondent No. 3 in support of the counter. No doubt, the reply of respondent No. 3 is there but without any affidavit by him. This reply is legally un-tenable as it is not supported by the affidavit of the deponent. There are some factual averments made in the reply and in order to testify their authenticity, the affidavit was required to be filed by the concerned respondent. In absence of the affidavit, the respondents should have at least produced the documentary proof for such factual averments to be made believable and trustworthy. Nothing of the sort has been done by them.  9. The question is that after the file got misplaced, its record was ordered to be re-constructed. The petitioner filed a copy of the writ petition alongwith copies of annexures supported by an affidavit. He even filed a copy of the counter which was earlier filed by respondent No. 3. The respondent No. 3 took several opportunities to sign the said counter. Last of all, he appears to have signed it but without supporting it by his affidavit. So, the position is that the averments made in the writ petition on an affidavit have remained un-rebutted. The reply of respondent No. 3 without any affidavit, particularly to the factual averments is not sufficient to controvert the averments made in the writ petition on an affidavit.  10. As regards the merits of the case, I think a short controversy is involved, as to whether under Articles 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations; the petitioner's services could be terminated without any inquiry.  11. Admittedly, the petitioner is a Government servant and working substantively against a post of orderly in the Sales Tax Department, Jammu. Admittedly, he applied for leave for thirty days w.e.f. 6.2.1990, which was recommended in his favour by his immediate officer, the concerned Excise and Taxation Officer. Allegedly, the E.T.O. relieved the petitioner after recommending his leave case. While he was on leave, his uncle is reported to have died in Pak Occupied Kashmir and he was required to accompany his parents immediately. The death was allegedly, sudden and the parents of the petitioner too had to leave instantaneously for the Pak Occupied Kashmir, the petitioner, therefore, could not complete the formalities for getting his leave sanctioned properly. He, admittedly, applied for extension of his leave through his brother from time to time. He was away for a total period of about six months only and had even applied lied for extension of leave from time to time. Admittedly, he was not at his home when the respondent No. 3 sent letters to him for resumption of his duty. The notice published in the newspaper "Daily Excelsior" also could not be communicated to him as he was not in Jammu, but had gone to the Pak Occupied Kashmir, Presumably, the "Daily Excelsior" has no circulation in the Pak Occupied Kashmir and, therefore, the petitioner had no knowledge of the notices given to him for resumption of his duty, either by registered post at his Jammu address or in the `Daily Excelsior' newspaper, published in Jammu. Even if it is presumed as correct that a notice was given to the petitioner through a registered post at his Jammu address while he was in the Pak Occupied Kashmir and the same was also published in the Daily Excelsior Jammu, when he was not in Jammu, the question is as to whether the mere giving of notice to an allegedly absentee Government servant for resumption of his duty, which too was not admittedly served upon him, is sufficient to terminate his services without following the procedure is established by law. Whether Article 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations contemplates the dismissal of a Government servant without an inquiry as to the alleged un-authorised absence.  12. I have already decided a case of a similar nature entitled : Dr. Zaffar Mahdi v. State which has been upheld by a Division Bench of this Court also, wherein the law has been thoroughly discussed on the involved points referred to above. It has been held that mere notice to a Government servant allegedly un-authorisedly absent is not sufficient to terminate his services, and Article 128 (supra) does not contemplate an order of dismissal without an inquiry into the alleged absence. A Government servant enjoys protection of his service as enshrined in Article 311 of the Constitution of India and Section 126 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir. Not only that, the procedure is given in the Jam Jammu and Kashmir Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1956 which is to be followed as a mandate of law before any punishment is imposed on any Government servant for any mis-conduct conduct. No doubt, Article 128 (supra) envisages loss of appointment of a Government servant un-authorisedly absent, but the procedure as laid down in Appeal Rules referred to above is to be followed before passing an order. In the Ranbir Penal Code, punishments for commission of offences are provided, but that does not mean that the same can be imposed without following the procedure as laid down in the Criminal Procedure Code.  13. In this regard, the Government appears to have sought a legal opinion from its Law Department, about the correctness or otherwise of the order of the respondent No. 3 terminating the service of the petitioner without an inquiry, and the same is contained in Annexure "P/H" to the writ petition, which, for the sake of facility is reproduced below :  "GOVERNMENT OF JAMMU & KASHMIR FINANCE DEPARTMENT NO : DT-STS/488-91 DATED : 10.6.1992 To The Commissioner Sales Tax Jammu and Kashmir Government, Srinagar. Sub : Recruitment to all sanctioned posts falling outside the purview of State Subordinate Service Recruitment Board. Sir, Shri Qamar Ali had submitted a petition to re-join his duties which was forwarded to you under letter No. even dated 19.8.1991 with the directions to examine treating the same as an appeal against the order of Deputy Commissioner Sales Tax (Administration) Jammu. Vide your letter No. : P-STC/2052/Adm. dated 5.3.92 you have informed Shri Qamar Ali that the petition cannot be treated as an appeal and that their is no reason to interfere with the orders of Dy. Commissioner Sales Tax (Administration) Jammu. The ex-employee submitted another petition before the Advisor (H) who desired to examine with reference to Rides. The case has accordingly been examined in terms of J & K CS (OCA) Rules, 1956 and Law Department also consulted. Termination of service for un authorised absence from duty is a major punishment and can be inflicted upon a member of the service only after following the procedure. A formal charge-sheet has to be issued and after the reply or no reply, an inquiry officer is to be appointed. In the absence of enquiry the order of termination is bad in law and cannot be sustained. The stage for appointment of an I.O. is already over. As such the appeal authority has to pass a appropriate order on the appeal which can includes quashing of impugned order merely for non-compliance of procedure. I am accordingly directed to advise you to again examine the case accordingly and furnish a report about action taken to this department. Yours faithfully, Sd/- SPECIAL SECY. TO GOVERNMENT FINANCE DEPTT." 14. The Law Department had given a correct opinion to the department that the termination of service for un-authorised absence from duty is a major punishment, and could not be inflicted upon a member of service without following the procedure as established by law. A formal charge-sheet was required to be issued to the delinquent and after its service, or otherwise or after his reply or otherwise, the inquiry was to be conducted into the matter after appointing an Inquiry Officer for the purpose, in ex parte or otherwise.  15. The respondent No. 3 has passed the order impugned without following the procedure as established by law. He has only issued a notice to the petitioner, that too, was not admittedly served upon him. He has mis- construed the important and extent of Article 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations. The said article does not contemplate the dismissal/termination from services of a Government servant without inquiry. No doubt, for un-authorised absence, a Government servant can be removed or dismissed from service, but only after he is given sufficient opportunity of being heard as envisaged in Article 311 of the Constitution of India and Section 126 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir read with Section 33 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1956, Article 128 (supra) only specifies the punishment which can be imposed upon a Government servant for his unauthorised absence. However, before imposing such punishment the Inquiry into the correctness or otherwise of his unauthorised absence is mandatory, as otherwise, such action would be arbitrary, unreasonable, unjust and without any guidelines, which is not sustainable at the touch-stone of the principles of natural justice. The termination of services of a Government servant under Article 128 (supra) is essentially an order of removal from service, and such punishment can be imposed only in accordance with the rules and procedure as established by law, requiring, inter alia, that no member of a Civil Service of the State shall be dismissed or removed from service except after an injury in which he has been informed in writing of the charges against him and the grounds on which it is proposed to take disciplinary action, and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, in respect of those charges and after such inquiry if it is proposed to impose any major penalty, no such penalty be imposed until he has been given a reasonable opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed.  16. Viewed thus, it is manifest that the order impugned has been passed without an inquiry into the alleged misconduct of the petitioner for his alleged unauthorised absence and a major punishment of removal from service imposed upon him in flagrant violation of law and the rules on the subject. The import and extent of Article 128 of Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations has been offended by the respondent No. 3 while passing the said order after issuing a mere notice to the petitioner for resumption of his duty which too was not served upon him. Undoubtedly, the treatment meted out to the petitioner by respondents 2 and 3 is clearly arbitrary, malicious and hostile, inasmuch as, the respondent No. 2 even on being urged by the respondent No. 1 to set right the wrong and remove the injustice, has failed without any reasonable cause or reason, and obviously for oblique considerations to do the needful in vindication of Rule of law. The impugned order, therefore, clearly offends and is violative of the mandate of Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of India, as applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. Not only that, it has the effect of nullifying the constitutional guarantees with which the services under the State are hinged, and as a sequal thereto, has resulted in grave to miscarriage of justice to petitioner.  17. In these circumstances of the case, I have no hesitation to issue a writ of certiorari quashing the impugned order dated 8.8.1990. The said order is declared as un-constitutional, illegal and bad in law, and is hereby accordingly quashed. Consequently, I also issue a writ of mandamus commanding the respondents to treat the petitioner in continuous service with all consequential benefits including promotions. He shall be paid all the emoluments as were due to him for the period for which he has remained out of service, pursuant to the erroneous order impugned. He is also held entitled to costs assessed at Rs. 5,000/- to be paid by the respondents 2 and 3.  18. The file shall be consigned to record after its due completion.  Petition allowed.
summary: Article 128 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Service Regulations does not permit termination of services without an inquiry into alleged unauthorised absence. A simple notice alleging unauthorised absence cannot justify termination of a government servant's job. The Constitution of India and Section 126 of J&K Constitution protect a Govt. servant's service, and proper procedures must be followed before imposing any punishment for misconduct. The order impugning the petitioner's alleged unauthorised absence is in violation of various laws and rules. The major punishment of removal from service cannot be imposed without an inquiry into the alleged misconduct. The order of dismissal has been quashed. J&K Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1956, Section 33, Constitution of J&K, Section 126, Constitution of India, Articles 311, 14, 16 and 21 are relevant. [Paras 12, 15 and 17]

text: G.C. Bharuka, J. - Both the workmen and the management have preferred these two writ appeals against the common order passed by the learned Single Judge in two writ petitions filed independently by them against the award of the Industrial Tribunal, Bangalore, in I.D. No. 27/90 (Annexure-A).  Facts  2. In the year 1971, M/s. Systems Manufacturing Limited had established a factory in Peenya Industrial Area, Bangalore, for manufacture of material handling equipment. For various reasons, reasonableness or legality whereof need not be gone into for the present, the workmen of the said factory went on strike from 23.1.1984. According to the Management, the workmen also indulged in various acts of indiscipline during the strike like obstruction of entry into and exit out of the factory premises, prevention of despatches of factory goods, etc.  3. According to the management, all possible efforts were made to persuade the workmen to resume work but it was all in vain. Ultimately, the management closed down the factory with effect from 2.5.1984 and consequently terminated the services of all the workmen after giving notice in terms of Section 25- FFA of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (in short `the Act') and offering closure compensation to them.  4. Subsequent to the above legal steps taken by the management, the contesting parties sat across the table in order to work out a mutual agreement in order to avoid any future litigation with regard to their relationship, rights and obligations. Ultimately, they arrived at a Settlement, which was recorded in writing on 8.9.1984 and signed by all the 52 workmen working on the date of closure of the factory and representative of the management. Copy of the Memorandum of Settlement has been filed as Annexure `A'.  5. The Memorandum of Settlement, after setting out the brief narration of the facts, which had led to the closure of the factory, the circumstances and the purpose of arriving at the Settlement, has spelt out the terms thereof. The material terms of the present purposes are reproduced hereunder. These are :-  Terms of Settlement (i) It is agreed that the 52 workmen whose names are shown in Annexure to this Settlement by virtue of their not resigning voluntarily will be paid their legal compensation like 15 days' pay for every completed year of service along with the all other dues like leave wages, earned wages, overtime wages, notice pay, bonus, gratuity etc. if eligible as per law in this regard. (ii) It is further agreed that in addition to the above-mentioned legal compensation, an amount equivalent to one month's wages for every year of completed service will be paid as ex gratia payment in full and final settlement of all the claims of the Union and workmen, including the claim of re-employment, if and, when the unit is re-opended in any manner. (iii) The Union and workmen have agreed to receive the amounts mentioned in clauses 1 and 2 above, in full and final settlement of all their claims including reinstatement, closure compensations, earned wages, leave wages, bonus, gratuity, overtime payment, service compensation, notice pay, etc. and they will have no other claim whatsoever against the management. (ix) It is further understood that by receiving the compensation as well as the exgratia amounts mentioned in clauses 1 and 2 above, the employer-employee relations will cease and workmen will have no claim for re-employment or for any compensation against this company. (x) Consequent to this Settlement, the management will be free to shift any machinery from the present place to any other premises or to start any manufacturing activities temporarily till the present premises is handed to the buyer who has already finalised the deal. 6. It is not in dispute that the workmen, who are before us, were party to the settlement and had received their statutory compensation as well as the ex-gratia payments as per the Settlement at Annexure `A'. Therefore, from the date of entering into the settlement and as per term (ix) thereof, the relationship of employer and employee become severed and both became entitled to choose their future courses independent of any right or obligation, contractual or statutory, operating over or against each other. It is nobody's case that the settlement at Annexure `A' was entered into because of any coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation. The parties do not dispute that they had agreed to the terms of the Memorandum of Settlement out of their free will in order to defuse the hardships felt by both the parties and considering the considerations contained therein to be the best in their interest. It is also not their case that entering of such a contract was opposed to any law.  7. Therefore, Memorandum of Settlement at Annexure `A' answers to the definition to statutory settlement as defined under Section 2(p) of the Act, which has a binding effect in terms of Section 18 of the Act which declares that :-  18. Person on whom settlements and awards are binding. (1) A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and workman otherwise than in the course of conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement. 8. Notwithstanding the above facts and the statutory provisions, at the instance of the workmen, the State Government by its order No. SWL 176 LDD 90, dated 25.6.1990, referred a dispute to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication of the following questions :-  (a) Are the workmen of M/s. Systems Manufacturing Limited, No. IA Peenya Industrial Estate Area, II Phase, Bangalore, justified in claiming that the closure declared by the said management with effect from 24.4.984 was not bona fide since establishment has stated functioning again. (b) If so, are they justified in claiming reinstatement of the following workmen with back wages, continuity of service and all consequential benefits. 9. The parties appeared before the Tribunal, filed their statement and adduced evidence both oral and documentary. Subsequently, on hearing them, the Tribunal passed its impugned award dated 19.2.1998 (Annexure `L') by holding that :-  "The reference is partly allowed, holding that the closure declared by the II party management with effect from 24.4.1984 (deemed to be dated 2.5.1984) is not bona fide since the establishment has started functioning again and the 1st party workmen are entitled for wages and all other consequential benefits with effect from 2.5.1984 to 31.3.1991. In the circumstances of the case, I pass no order as to costs." 10. As noticed above, being dissatisfied with the said award, both the workmen and the management preferred independent writ petitions. But the learned Single Judge dismissed both the writ petitions by the impugned order concurring with the award of the Industrial Tribunal.  11. We have heard Shri R.N. Narasimha Murthy and Mr. K. Subba Rao, learned Senior Advocates, appearing for the management and the workmen respectively.  12. According to Sri R.N.
